# 03_technical_wedge_hunt: every agent's output

16 physics/engineering/AI-hardware lenses over arXiv, IEEE, OpenAlex and the corpus academic tier; physics skeptic + independent $/share quantifier per finding; synthesis found NO wedge (91 agents, 212 papers read, Opus 5). 91 agent results.


## [Research] research:demand_flexibility

- **lens**: Flexibility of AI load and its effect on the need for firm generation — specifically whether curtailable/shiftable data-center load reduces FIRED HOURS on turbines that do get built, which is the variable GEV's service-agreement billing is contractually indexed to.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The $500M/GW services annuity is a FIRED-HOURS annuity, and new-vintage US combined-cycle utilization has already rolled over 6.8 points — flexible load extends the trend
    - **physical_fact**: Measured from EIA-860M (vintage 2026-07, Operating, status OP, energy_source NG) joined to EIA-923 net generation for 2025: US natural-gas combined-cycle units with first operating year 2015-2019 ran at 64.1% capacity factor (43.2 GW), while units with first operating year 2020 or later ran at 57.3% (23.1 GW) — a 6.8 percentage-point, 10.6% relative decline in the NEWEST cohort. Simple-cycle (GT) 2020+ cohort ran at 10.9%. Separately, Norris et al. (Duke Nicholas Institute, 2025) measure 76 GW of curtailment-enabled headroom on the EXISTING US system at a 0.25% annual curtailment rate (1,643 of 657,000 GWh), 98 GW at 0.5%, 126 GW at 1.0%, 215 GW at 5.0%, across the 22 largest balancing authorities (95% of US load), with average event duration 1.7 hours and 85 curtailment hours/year at the 0.25% rate. The authors state flexibility means 'the immediate pressure to expand generation capacity ... can potentially be alleviated, mitigating or deferring costly expenditures.'
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — Gas Power SERVICES revenue (and the services half of the $88.5B services RPO). GEV's FY2025 10-K states billing terms 'are generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Services revenue is therefore approximately linear in fired hours, not in installed GW. Management's $500M per GW over 20 years (= $25M/GW-yr, Morgan Stanley Laguna, Sep 16 2026) is only self-consistent at baseload: $25M/GW-yr divided by 5,720 fired hr/yr (the 63-65% CF the installed HA fleet actually runs, from 130 HA units and ~3.6M cumulative operating hours) = $4.37/MWh, squarely inside the industry $4-7/MWh LTSA range. The same $/MWh rate at the 2020+ CC cohort's measured 57.3% CF yields $22.0M/GW-yr, and at a flexible-load-suppressed 50% CF yields $19.2M/GW-yr. Direction: negative to Power services revenue and to the terminal value of the annuity the 35x forward multiple is paying for.
    - **direction**: short
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: EIA-860M vintage 2026-07 + EIA-923 2025, gev.db tables `generators` and `generation`
        - **number_or_quote**: CC capacity factor 2025 by first-operating-year cohort: pre2005 49.9% (190.2 GW), 2005-14 52.3% (67.8 GW), 2015-19 64.1% (43.2 GW), 2020+ 57.3% (23.1 GW). Simple-cycle GT 2020+ 10.9%.
        - **reproduction**: CREATE TEMP TABLE cap AS SELECT plant_id,prime_mover,SUM(mw) mw,MIN(op_year) fy FROM generators WHERE vintage='2026-07' AND sheet='Operating' AND status LIKE '(OP)%' AND energy_source='NG' AND prime_mover IN ('CT','CA','CS','GT') AND op_year IS NOT NULL GROUP BY plant_id,prime_mover; then SELECT cohort, CASE WHEN c.prime_mover='GT' THEN 'GT_simple' ELSE 'CC' END, ROUND(100.0*SUM(g.net_generation_mwh)/(SUM(c.mw)*8760),1) FROM cap c JOIN generation g ON g.plant_id=c.plant_id AND g.prime_mover=c.prime_mover AND g.fuel_type='NG' AND g.year=2025 GROUP BY 1,2
      - - **source**: Norris, T.H., Profeta, T.H., Patino-Echeverri, D., Cowie-Haskell, A., 'Rethinking Load Growth: Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems,' Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, Duke University, 2025 (read full 43-page PDF, ICC Docket 25-0677/25-0679 Ex. 2.08)
        - **number_or_quote**: '76 GW of new load ... could be integrated with an average annual load curtailment rate of 0.25%'; 98 GW at 0.5%, 126 GW at 1.0%, 215 GW at 5.0%; average curtailment duration 1.7 hours at 0.25%; 85 curtailment hours/year at 0.25%.
        - **reproduction**: WebFetch https://www.icc.illinois.gov/docket/P2025-0679/documents/371138/files/650737.pdf then pypdf text extraction; search strings '76 GW', '0.25', '85 hours'
      - - **source**: GE Vernova FY2025 10-K, revenue recognition note (gev.db chunks, filing_date 2026-01-29)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'Our billing terms for these arrangements are generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event within the contract, such as an outage.'
        - **reproduction**: SELECT c.text FROM chunks_fts f JOIN chunks c ON c.id=f.rowid WHERE chunks_fts MATCH '"predetermined usage intervals"' AND c.filing_date>'2026-01-01' ORDER BY bm25(chunks_fts) LIMIT 1
      - - **source**: arXiv:2606.25098v1, 'Power-Flexible AI Data Centers: A New Paradigm for Grid-Responsive Compute,' 2026-06-23 (full text read via gev.db accession src:3534)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'The cluster reduced its power consumption by approximately 30% within 40 seconds'; '100% compliance across 200+ distinct National Grid power events on a 130 kW AI cluster of NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs'; power-constrained cluster saw 'approximately 30 ms' increase in average TTFT.
        - **reproduction**: SELECT text FROM chunks WHERE accession='src:3534' ORDER BY id — then regex for sentences containing numeric+unit tokens
      - - **source**: Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 16 2026 (management figure, per task brief) cross-checked against GE Vernova statements that 130 HA machines operate today generating ~$1B of annual HA services revenue
        - **number_or_quote**: ~$500M services revenue per GW of HA over first 20 years (=$25M/GW-yr); realized today ~$1B / ~58.5 GW installed HA = ~$17M/GW-yr.
        - **reproduction**: WebSearch 'GE Vernova "$500 million per GW" services 20 years HA' — 130 HA operating, 195 under contract, ~$1B HA services revenue
    - **materiality_dollars_per_share**: Base case: Power services revenue by 2030 ~$12B (GEV growth algorithm from ~$8B today); hours-billed share assumed 60% (GEV bills on hours AND events) = $7.2B. Apply the MEASURED cohort deterioration of 10.6% relative (64.1% -> 57.3% CF) to that stream: $7.2B x 0.106 = $763M revenue shortfall/yr. Services incremental EBITDA margin assumed 30% (services is the high-margin half of Power; segment guide 17-19% blended with lower-margin equipment): $763M x 0.30 = $229M EBITDA/yr. $229M x 25 = $5.72B / 266,333,581 shares = $21.5/share = 2.29% of $940.33. Bear extension: if curtailment-enabled headroom (76-126 GW) plus solar+storage pushes go-forward CC CF to ~50% (-22% relative vs the 2015-19 cohort), $7.2B x 0.22 = $1.58B revenue, x 0.30 = $475M EBITDA, x 25 = $11.9B / 266,333,581 = $44.6/share = 4.74%. Range $21-45/share (2.3-4.7%).
    - **novelty_check**: Searched: 'GE Vernova services revenue fired hours capacity factor peaker risk analyst'; 'GE Vernova "$500 million per GW" services 20 years HA capacity factor assumption analyst skeptical'; 'GE Vernova services revenue "fired hours" utilization risk short thesis capacity factor decline combined cycle 2026'. Results surfaced the $500M/GW claim itself and the full spread of analyst opinion ($470 GLJ Sell to $1,450 bull), but GLJ's Sell rests on cyclicality and 2027-vintage backlog margin (~3pp vs 10-11pp on 2025 vintage) — NOT on capacity factor or fired hours. Bernstein's defense is about utilities vs data centers, not utilization. I could not find any published note connecting the fired-hours billing term to a measured decline in new-vintage CC capacity factor, or testing the $500M/GW figure for its implied capacity factor. The $4.37/MWh implied-rate cross-check appears to be unpublished. I cannot know nobody has thought of it; I can say I did not find it published.
    - **testable_prediction**: At Q3'26 earnings (CONFIRMED Oct 28 2026) and in the FY26 10-K (late Jan / early Feb 2027): (a) GEV's disclosed HA fleet cumulative operating hours divided by unit count will show average annual hours per unit BELOW the ~5,700 hr/yr (65% CF) implied by 130 units / 3.6M hours — i.e. the newest units are diluting fleet hours-per-unit downward; and (b) realized HA services revenue per installed GW will remain at or below ~$17-18M/GW-yr rather than closing toward $25M/GW-yr. Independently, EIA-923 2026 data (published 2027) will show the 2020+ CC cohort capacity factor at or below 57.3%.
    - **kill_condition**: Killed if (a) the 2020+ CC cohort capacity factor in 2026 EIA-923 data comes in ABOVE the 2015-19 cohort's 64.1%, showing the cohort decline was a ramp-in artifact of units commissioned mid-year rather than a dispatch shift; or (b) GEV discloses HA services revenue per installed GW rising toward $25M/GW-yr while fleet hours-per-unit are flat or falling, which would prove the annuity is driven by per-event parts pricing rather than fired hours and would break the linearity assumption this finding rests on; or (c) GEV discloses that HA service agreements carry fixed-fee or minimum-hours floors rather than pure per-hour billing.
    - **has_dated_test**: True
    - **novelty**: 4
    - **confidence**: 3
    - **materiality**: 3
    - **caveats**: Three material weaknesses the team must carry. (1) The cohort CF decline is measured on only 23.1 GW of 2020+ CC capacity and may be contaminated by partial first-year operation — I could not separate commissioning-year ramp from true dispatch shift with annual EIA-923 data. (2) The AGGREGATE US gas fleet shows NO capacity-factor decline (CT 54.7% -> 56.1% and GT 10.6% -> 11.4%, 2022-2025), so any claim that 'gas capacity factors are collapsing' is false; only the newest-vintage cut supports this. (3) The 60% hours-billed split and the 30% services EBITDA margin are my assumptions, not disclosed figures — the $/share result scales linearly in both. Also note GEV's installed HA fleet runs near-baseload today at 63-65% CF, so this is a forward-looking claim about the NEXT cohort, not an observation about the current one.
  - - **title**: Starts-limited maintenance inverts the services economics: under GER-3620 the cost clock runs on STARTS while GEV's billing clock runs on HOURS — a candidate physical explanation for the 5x jump in unfavorable contract-profitability revisions
    - **physical_fact**: GE's GER-3620 sets heavy-duty gas turbine maintenance intervals as the MINIMUM of factored fired hours OR factored starts — 25,000 factored fired hours or 900 factored starts for combustion/hot-gas-path, 50,000 hours or 1,800 starts for major inspection. Intertek APTECH (Lefton et al.) find that under cycling duty 'turbine inspection and repair intervals are transitioned to being principally based on numbers of starts rather than operating hours,' and that cycling-induced 'parts fallout' — replacement parts found damaged during overhauls — 'is often a factor of two or more over the plant life.' Industry figure: a baseload turbine's ~$2-3M maintenance cost falls due once every ~24,000 hours (~3 years), but the same cost can fall in a single year for a unit started and stopped daily. Arithmetic consequence: a baseload unit at 5,720 hr/yr and ~20 starts/yr is HOURS-limited (combustion inspection every 4.4 years); a curtailment-following unit at ~955 fired hr/yr in 1.7-2.5 hour blocks accumulates 160-480 starts/yr and is STARTS-limited (combustion inspection every ~2-3 years) while producing roughly one-sixth the MWh.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — long-term service agreement CONTRACT PROFITABILITY and the 'net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability' line (10-Q Note 9), plus Power segment EBITDA. GEV's FY2025 10-K states revenue on these agreements is recognized based on COSTS INCURRED while customers are billed on HOURS OF USAGE and maintenance events: 'The differences between the timing of our revenue recognized (based on costs incurred) and customer billings (based on contractual terms) result in changes to our contract asset or contract liability positions.' If contracts were priced on an hours-limited (baseload) assumption but units are dispatched into starts-limited cycling duty, estimated lifetime cost rises relative to estimated lifetime billings, forcing a cumulative catch-up charge. GEV discloses the exact sensitivity: 'Revisions ... that increase or decrease total estimated contract profitability by one percentage point would increase or decrease the long-term service agreements contract assets balance by $0.2 billion.' Observed: net unfavorable revisions were -$218M in H1'26 vs -$42M in H1'25 (5.2x) while management cited 'solid pricing' in services the same quarter — and Q2'26 services revenue rose 10% on 'higher parts volume and favorable pricing.' Revenue and parts volume UP while contract profitability revisions go sharply negative is precisely the signature of a starts-driven cost clock outrunning an hours-driven billing clock.
    - **direction**: short
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: GE GER-3620 (Heavy-Duty Gas Turbine Operating and Maintenance Considerations), as summarized by EthosEnergy and Combined Cycle Journal — I did NOT read the primary GE PDF
        - **number_or_quote**: 'Maintenance intervals are prescribed based on factored fired hours or factored fired starts according to GE's GER 3620 bulletin'; GER-3620 'provides formulas to calculate factored hours and factored starts based on operating conditions—such as peak operation, type of fuel, fast starts, and turning-gear hours'; trips severity factor is one of the starts-based factors.
        - **reproduction**: WebSearch 'GER-3620 "factored starts" gas turbine maintenance interval trip from load equivalent starts severity factor 900 starts'
      - - **source**: Intertek APTECH / Lefton et al. cycling-cost research, accessed via search summaries only (primary NREL/SR-5500-55433 PDF was unreachable — see dead ends)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'turbine inspection and repair intervals are transitioned to being principally based on numbers of starts rather than operating hours'; cycling 'parts fallout ... is often a factor of two or more over the plant life'; 'the average starts on these gas turbines/combined cycle are increasing and the ... run times are generally decreasing, and while capacity factors decrease, the production costs will also rise significantly due to cycling operations.'
        - **reproduction**: WebSearch '"cost of cycling" gas turbine "$/MW/start" combined cycle combustion turbine Lefton Intertek maintenance capital cost per start'
      - - **source**: GE Vernova FY2024 10-K, long-term service agreements disclosure
        - **number_or_quote**: 'Revisions to estimates of future billings or costs that increase or decrease total estimated contract profitability by one percentage point would increase or decrease the long-term service agreements contract assets balance by $0.2 billion'; net LTSA balance $3.5B '= approximately 5% of total estimated life of contract billings'; contracts 'approximately 29% complete based on costs incurred to date and estimate of future costs.'
        - **reproduction**: WebSearch '"contract assets" OR "profitability revisions" gas turbine service agreement GE Vernova margin 2026'; SEC EDGAR CIK 1996810 FY2024 10-K
      - - **source**: GE Vernova FY2025 10-K revenue recognition note (gev.db chunks, filing_date 2026-01-29)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'The differences between the timing of our revenue recognized (based on costs incurred) and customer billings (based on contractual terms) result in changes to our contract asset or contract liability positions.'
        - **reproduction**: SELECT c.text FROM chunks_fts f JOIN chunks c ON c.id=f.rowid WHERE chunks_fts MATCH '"predetermined usage intervals"' AND c.filing_date>'2026-01-01' LIMIT 1
      - - **source**: gev.db xbrl_facts, ticker GEV, tag ContractWithCustomerAssetNetCurrent — NEGATIVE evidence
        - **number_or_quote**: Contract assets: $9,294M (2025-12-31) -> $9,609M (2026-03-31) -> $9,522M (2026-06-30), i.e. +2.5% across H1'26 against mid-teens revenue growth. The predicted 'costs incurred ahead of hour-based billings' balance-sheet build is NOT visible.
        - **reproduction**: SELECT tag,end_date,fy,fp,form,val FROM xbrl_facts WHERE ticker='GEV' AND tag='ContractWithCustomerAssetNetCurrent' ORDER BY end_date
    - **materiality_dollars_per_share**: Observed incremental drag: H1'26 net unfavorable revisions -$218M vs H1'25 -$42M; incremental = $176M per half = $352M/yr annualized. Using GEV's own disclosed sensitivity, -$218M is roughly 1.1 percentage points of total estimated contract profitability burned in six months. If the cycling/starts regime is structural rather than a one-off, capitalize the incremental drag: $352M x 25 = $8.80B / 266,333,581 shares = $33.0/share = 3.51% of $940.33. FLOOR case, ignoring any multiple and counting only lifetime contract profit: total estimated life-of-contract billings implied by the disclosure is ~$70B ($3.5B = ~5%), so one percentage point of contract profitability = ~$700M of lifetime profit; four further percentage points over the next three years = $2.8B / 266,333,581 = $10.5/share = 1.12%. Range $10.5-33.0/share (1.1-3.5%). All of this assumes the revision deterioration is cycling-driven; see caveats.
    - **novelty_check**: Searched: 'gas turbine cycling duty "starts-limited" maintenance cost per MWh increase load following data center services margin OEM'; '"contract assets" OR "profitability revisions" gas turbine service agreement cycling starts-based intervals GE Vernova margin analyst 2026'. The starts-vs-hours interval physics is well documented in the turbine-maintenance trade literature (EthosEnergy, Combined Cycle Journal, Intertek APTECH) and GEV's billing and revenue-recognition asymmetry is plainly disclosed in the 10-K — but I found NO published note, sell-side or otherwise, joining the two to explain the -$218M revision. The task brief flags 'service-contract profitability revisions' as already worked by the team; what is new here is a specific, falsifiable PHYSICAL cause (starts-limited intervals under cycling duty) for an anomaly the team has so far treated as unexplained, plus the disclosed $0.2B-per-percentage-point lever to size it. I could not find this mechanism published.
    - **testable_prediction**: At Q3'26 earnings (CONFIRMED Oct 28 2026): net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability for the nine months of 2026 will exceed $300M (i.e. Q3 alone adds more than ~$80M, continuing or exceeding the H1 run-rate) rather than reverting toward the 2025 pace. Stronger form: GEV will attribute at least part of the revision to outage scope, parts fallout, or higher-than-expected maintenance frequency rather than purely to inflation, tariffs or supply chain. In the FY26 10-K (late Jan / early Feb 2027), the full-year revision figure exceeds $450M and the disclosed one-percentage-point sensitivity rises above $0.2B as the contract base grows.
    - **kill_condition**: Killed if Q3'26 (Oct 28) shows unfavorable revisions decelerating toward the H1'25 run-rate (nine-month total under ~$250M), OR if management attributes the H1'26 -$218M explicitly and entirely to a non-cycling cause — tariffs, a single large contract, Prolec purchase accounting, or input-cost inflation — with no outage-frequency or parts-scope component. Also killed if GEV discloses that its CSAs are predominantly priced on a per-START or per-equivalent-operating-hour basis that already factors starts, which would mean the billing clock and the cost clock are aligned and the asymmetry does not exist.
    - **has_dated_test**: True
    - **novelty**: 4
    - **confidence**: 2
    - **materiality**: 3
    - **caveats**: This is the weakest-evidenced of the three and I am scoring confidence 2 deliberately. The decisive problem: the balance-sheet signature my own mechanism predicts is ABSENT. Contract assets grew only 2.5% in H1'26 ($9,294M -> $9,522M) against mid-teens revenue growth, whereas 'costs incurred running ahead of hours-based billings' should build contract assets faster than revenue. I also found NO cycling trend in the EIA data: simple-cycle heat rate was 11,873 Btu/kWh in 2022 and 11,796 in 2025, and CC heat rate 10,598 -> 10,649 — flat, so aggregate US gas is not measurably cycling harder yet. The mechanism is therefore PROSPECTIVE and the -$218M attribution is a HYPOTHESIS I could not confirm: GEV does not disclose the cause, and tariffs, inflation and Prolec integration are all live alternative explanations that would fully account for it. I could not read the primary GER-3620 PDF or the primary NREL/Intertek cycling-cost report, so the 900-starts and 2x-parts-fallout figures rest on secondary trade sources. Do not pitch this as established; pitch it as the specific thing to listen for on Oct 28.
  - - **title**: KILL: the flexible-load literature cannot touch GEV equipment orders inside the pitch horizon — GEV's own book is HA/combined-cycle, not peakers, and 53 GW is already firm
    - **physical_fact**: Two measurements that jointly kill the obvious bear trade. (1) GEV's own project book is heavy-duty combined-cycle, not peakers: of 130 GE-linked customer projects in the corpus, 74.0 GW is '7HA and 9HA ultra-high-efficiency turbines' plus 3.5 GW of 7HA.02 and 2.6 GW of 9HA.02, against only 0.1 GW of '50-MW simple-cycle turbines' and a single LM6000. So the widely-cited fact that ~60% of US planned gas is simple-cycle peakers (my own measurement: 2027 planned US gas is 6.99 GW GT vs 4.15 GW CC = 63% simple-cycle by MW) describes the market, NOT GEV's book. (2) Duke's curtailment-enabled headroom is concentrated in the top ~1% of hours: 85 curtailment hours/year at the 0.25% rate, average event duration 1.7 hours, and 'Nearly 90% of hours during which load curtailment is required retain at least half of the new load.' Flexibility therefore substitutes for the ENERGY and the PEAK-hour call on generation, not for the capacity accreditation that drives firm equipment procurement.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment EQUIPMENT revenue and gas equipment ORDERS/backlog — direction: NO material impact inside 3-12 months, which is the finding. 53 GW is firm equipment backlog and 63 GW is slot reservations (116 GW 'under contract'); GEV is effectively sold out through 2030 and its FY26 revenue guide of $45.5-46.5B converts backlog already signed. A flexible-load thesis operating on demand destruction must express itself through NEW orders, which is a 2028+ observable, not an Oct 28 2026 or Jan 2027 observable. This finding redirects the team: the flexible-load literature is a SERVICES-line argument (Findings 1 and 2), not an equipment-line argument, and any memo that shorts GEV on 'AI load is flexible so turbine demand falls' is both untestable before the memo horizon and contradicted by GEV's contracted position.
    - **direction**: kills-an-existing-angle
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: gev.db `projects` table, 130 GE-linked customer power projects
        - **number_or_quote**: By model: '7HA and 9HA ultra-high-efficiency turbines' 74.0 GW; 7HA.02 3.5 GW; 9HA.02 2.6 GW; 'HA gas turbine' 1.0 GW; GT26 0.9 GW; Frame 6B 0.2 GW; '50-MW simple-cycle turbines' 0.1 GW; LM6000 ~0.0 GW.
        - **reproduction**: SELECT model, COUNT(*) n, ROUND(SUM(capacity_mw)/1000.0,1) gw FROM projects WHERE oem LIKE '%GE%' AND model IS NOT NULL GROUP BY model ORDER BY gw DESC
      - - **source**: EIA-860M vintage 2026-07, Planned sheet, gev.db `generators`
        - **number_or_quote**: Planned US natural-gas capacity by first-operating year: 2026 GT 2.28 GW vs CC 1.92 GW (54% simple-cycle); 2027 GT 6.99 GW vs CC 4.15 GW (63%); 2028 GT 6.98 GW vs CC 9.12 GW (43%); 2029 GT 4.76 GW vs CC 8.64 GW (36%); 2030 GT 0.49 GW vs CC 17.64 GW (3%).
        - **reproduction**: SELECT planned_year, prime_mover, ROUND(SUM(mw)/1000.0,2) gw, COUNT(*) n FROM generators WHERE vintage='2026-07' AND sheet='Planned' AND energy_source='NG' AND prime_mover IN ('CT','CA','CS','GT') AND planned_year BETWEEN 2026 AND 2030 GROUP BY planned_year, prime_mover
      - - **source**: Norris et al., 'Rethinking Load Growth,' Nicholas Institute, Duke University, 2025 (full PDF read)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'Across all 22 BAs, the average required load curtailment times are 85 hours under the 0.25% curtailment rate (~1% of the hours in a year), 177 hours under the 0.5% ... 366 hours under the 1.0%'; 'Nearly 90% of hours during which load curtailment is required retain at least half of the new load.'
        - **reproduction**: pypdf extraction of https://www.icc.illinois.gov/docket/P2025-0679/documents/371138/files/650737.pdf; search '85 hours', '0.25'
      - - **source**: arXiv:2606.25098v1 'Power-Flexible AI Data Centers' (full text via gev.db src:3534), cross-read with 'Grid Integration of AI Data Centers: A Critical Review of Energy Storage Solutions' (gev.db academic tier)

The review paper independently restates Norris: '76 GW of new load can be integrated without significant upgrades by curtailing 0.25% of new flexible load per year. This amounts to a curtailment of 22 hours/year.'
        - **reproduction**: SELECT text FROM chunks WHERE accession='src:3534'; and SELECT c.text FROM chunks_fts f JOIN chunks c ON c.id=f.rowid WHERE chunks_fts MATCH '"76 GW" OR "100 GW"' AND c.tier='academic'
    - **materiality_dollars_per_share**: This finding's value is the size of the ERROR it prevents, computed on the trade it kills. A flexible-load-driven equipment bear case would need to impair GEV's contracted equipment position: 53 GW firm backlog at ~$1,200/kW HA equipment pricing = ~$63.6B of contracted equipment revenue. A 10% order/backlog impairment = $6.36B revenue x ~15% equipment EBITDA margin = $954M/yr of EBITDA, x 25 = $23.8B / 266,333,581 shares = $89.5/share = 9.52% of $940.33. That $89.5/share of apparent downside is the claim this finding says is NOT supportable and NOT testable before the memo horizon — so the materiality is the avoidance of a headline bear case that collapses under a single question about the 116 GW contracted position. Net testable damage from the flexible-load lens is confined to Findings 1 and 2, i.e. roughly $21-45/share on services revenue and $10-33/share on contract margin, not $89/share on orders.
    - **novelty_check**: Searched: 'data center load flexibility accelerates interconnection more gas turbine orders EPRI DCFlex Emerald AI 2026 curtailment defers generation capacity'; 'Norris Duke Nicholas Institute Rethinking Load Growth 76 GW curtailment headroom'. The Duke headroom result is HEAVILY published (Utility Dive, Latitude Media, Smart Energy International, Daily Energy Insider) and EPRI's DCFlex Flex MOSAIC framework is explicitly marketed as shortening interconnection timelines — so the flexibility story itself has zero novelty. What I did NOT find published anywhere is the disaggregation: nobody appears to have checked GEV's actual model mix against the US peaker-heavy planned mix and concluded that the two facts are about different populations. The team's brief lists 'EIA planned-capacity trends' as worked to death; this finding shows the standard reading of that data does not transfer to GEV's book, which is a correction to existing team work rather than a new claim.
    - **testable_prediction**: At Q3'26 earnings (CONFIRMED Oct 28 2026): GEV gas equipment orders and the gas backlog/slot-reservation total will be FLAT OR UP versus the 53 GW firm / 63 GW reserved position, with no cancellation or deferral attributed to customer load flexibility, demand response commitments, or curtailment-enabled interconnection. Management will continue to describe gas capacity as sold out through 2030 and will reiterate or raise the 20 GW/yr output ramp. In other words, the prediction is a NON-event on the equipment line, which is what makes the equipment-side bear case unpitchable on this horizon.
    - **kill_condition**: This finding is itself killed — and the equipment bear case revived — if on Oct 28 2026 GEV reports ANY of: a net reduction in the 116 GW under-contract figure; slot reservations expiring or converting at below the historical rate with flexibility or interconnection cited; a named hyperscaler deferring or cancelling a gas order in favour of a curtailment/demand-response interconnection agreement; or management guiding the 20 GW/yr output ramp DOWN. Any one of those would mean flexibility is reaching the equipment line faster than the contracted position implies.
    - **has_dated_test**: True

    - **confidence**: 4
    - **materiality**: 4
    - **caveats**: Novelty is deliberately scored low — the underlying Duke and EPRI material is thoroughly published and the team has already worked EIA planned-capacity trends. The value here is corrective, not original. Two limits on the kill itself. First, the `projects` table covers 130 GE-linked projects, not GEV's full 116 GW book, and 84 rows totalling 27.5 GW have a blank model field, so the HA-dominance conclusion rests on the 74 GW row being correctly attributed — the team should verify that single row before relying on it. Second, this finding says nothing about orders BEYOND the horizon: Duke's authors explicitly argue flexibility can be 'mitigating or deferring costly expenditures' on generation capacity, so the equipment bear case may well be right in 2028-2030 — it is simply not testable by Oct 2 2026 or by the Oct 28 print, and a pitch with a 3-12 month horizon cannot rest on it.

It does not: simple-cycle GT heat rate was 11,873 Btu/kWh (2022), 11,918 (2023), 11,844 (2024), 11,796 (2025); CC gas turbines 10,598 / 10,617 / 10,607 / 10,649. Flat to slightly improving. There is no measurable increase in cycling intensity in the US gas fleet through 2025. Any claim that turbines are already cycling harder is unsupported by EIA data.
  - 'US GAS CAPACITY FACTORS ARE COLLAPSING' — FALSE, KILLED. Aggregate 2022-2025 capacity factors are flat to UP: simple-cycle GT 10.6% -> 10.7% -> 11.6% -> 11.4%; CC gas turbine (CT) 54.7% -> 56.8% -> 57.7% -> 56.1%; CC steam (CA) 44.9% -> 48.6% -> 49.1% -> 47.2%. The only support for a utilization-decline story is the VINTAGE-COHORT cut (2015-19 CC at 64.1% vs 2020+ CC at 57.3%), which is a much narrower claim on only 23.1 GW and may be a commissioning-ramp artifact. Do not let anyone pitch the aggregate version.
  - '60% OF US PLANNED GAS IS PEAKERS, THEREFORE GEV'S SERVICES ANNUITY IS DEAD' — KILLED as stated. I confirmed the market fact from EIA-860M (2027 planned: 6.99 GW GT vs 4.15 GW CC = 63% simple-cycle) but GEV's own book does not look like the market: of 130 GE-linked projects, 74.0 GW is 7HA/9HA heavy-duty plus 7.1 GW of other HA/GT26/6B, versus 0.1 GW of simple-cycle 50-MW units and one LM6000. The peaker mix is largely other vendors' aeroderivatives. The surviving version of the argument is about how GEV's HA units are DISPATCHED, not about what GEV sells — which is why Finding 1 is framed on combined-cycle capacity factor, not on peaker share.
  - THE NAIVE 'PEAKERS GENERATE NO SERVICES REVENUE' BEAR CASE — KILLED BY THE PHYSICS, and the team should not use it. Because GER-3620 intervals are the MINIMUM of factored hours OR factored starts (25,000 hr / 900 starts for combustion), a low-hours high-starts peaker hits its combustion inspection on the STARTS path roughly every 2-3 years versus 4.4 years for a baseload unit. Peakers therefore generate MORE maintenance events per GW, not fewer — they just generate far fewer billable fired hours. The damage is to the hours-billed stream and to contract MARGIN, not to event count. Anyone pitching 'peakers mean no outages' will be corrected in Q&A.
  - BULLISH COUNTER-DIRECTION, TESTED AND INCONCLUSIVE ON THIS HORIZON: flexibility as an accelerant of buildout. EPRI's DCFlex/Flex MOSAIC framework is explicitly designed to shorten interconnection timelines and 'accelerate time to power,' which would be bullish for total GW ordered. I could find no quantified estimate anywhere of GW of gas turbine orders ACCELERATED by flexibility commitments, so I could not size this against the bearish channel. Duke's authors point the other way, writing that flexibility means pressure to expand generation capacity 'can potentially be alleviated, mitigating or deferring costly expenditures.' Net: the equipment-line direction is genuinely ambiguous and unquantifiable today, which is a further reason Finding 3 confines the testable thesis to the services lines.
  - MEASURED AI FLEXIBILITY IS SHALLOWER THAN THE NARRATIVE SUGGESTS — worth knowing before anyone over-claims in either direction. The only real production measurement I found (arXiv:2606.25098) is 30% power reduction in 40 seconds on a 130 kW cluster — a small testbed, a shallow depth of cut, and a short duration, with a real but modest 30 ms TTFT penalty. Duke's headroom similarly needs curtailment in only 85 hours/year with ~90% of those hours retaining at least half the load. Flexibility is a thin, infrequent product, not a wholesale substitute for firm generation. Do not pitch it as one.

## [Research] research:load_oscillation_stability

- **lens**: Synchronized AI training load oscillations and grid stability — measured magnitudes/frequencies, what equipment they force onto the grid or behind the meter, and whether GEV captures that spend or bears the cost.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: AI-training torsional fatigue is a wear mode that accrues per oscillation cycle, not per fired hour — it sits entirely outside GER-3620's factored-fired-hours cost model that GEV uses to price its $85B long-term service agreement book
    - **physical_fact**: ERCOT's contractor Electranix simulated a 100 MW synchronous machine with a 12 Hz torsional mode against a measured AI-training load proxy. A realistic AI training profile WITHOUT a 12 Hz component produces 0.042 pu alternating shaft torque (4%). The SAME profile WITH a 12 Hz component produces 0.993 pu (Tau12) / 0.974 pu (Tau23) — a 23x amplification to ~1x rated torque. A fixed-frequency square wave at the 12 Hz torsional mode produces 5.124 pu / 5.028 pu (>5x rated torque). Electranix's stated conclusion: 'Loads with load cycling and co-located load/generator facilities are at high risk' and 'If we assume worst case load behaviours, then we see >>100% torque (low impedance to generator, torsional component present), >30% active power at terminals!!' ERCOT's own separate methodology puts the Maximum Continuous Terminal Variation (MCTV) at 0.01 pu — i.e. a 100 MW generator can tolerate only 1 MW of continuous oscillatory power at its terminals (Endurance Limit 0.1 pu / Load Shape Ratio 10). These are not simulations only: ERCOT documents three field events — the ERCOT 23 Hz event (Jul–Oct 2024), the Dominion Energy 14.7–14.8 Hz data-center event, and a Dominion 1–11 Hz event — all inside the 7–100 Hz turbine-generator shaft torsional band.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — 'net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability' on long-term service agreements (10-Q contract-balance note; -$218M in H1'26 vs -$42M H1'25), and Power Services EBITDA margin. Direction: NEGATIVE. GEV's contractual service agreements bill 'based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Torsional fatigue damage accumulates per stress cycle — at 12 Hz that is ~3.8x10^8 cycles/year — a rate completely uncorrelated with fired hours or starts. GE's own GER-3620 Rev P factored-hours framework penalizes fast starts, trips, peak firing and cycling; it contains no factor for continuous subsynchronous torsional loading. So on an LTSA the cost side rises while the billing side (per fired hour) does not move: margin compresses, and under ASC 606 the revision is recognized as a cumulative catch-up. GEV's own SSTI consulting page confirms the damage mechanism and the parts affected: torsional vibrations 'result in reduced component life of parts such as shafts, buckets (blades), retaining rings, and rotors' and 'adverse interactions have led to growing oscillations and shaft damage, including twisted couplings and broken shafts.' Meanwhile the words 'torsional' and 'subsynchronous' appear ZERO times across GEV SEC filings in the corpus.

Step 2 — exposure: data centers are ~20% of the 116 GW gas backlog and are the fastest-growing cohort, and co-located/behind-the-meter (the Electranix worst case, Zm→0) is the dominant configuration; assume 20% of the $85B LTSA book becomes torsionally coupled to a large AI load = $17.0B of exposed life-of-contract billings. Step 3 — cost: torsional fatigue reduces life of shafts, buckets, retaining rings and rotors (GEV's own list); assume it raises lifetime maintenance cost on exposed contracts by 10% of their billings = $1.70B of lifetime margin destruction. Step 4 — express as LTSA profitability: $1.70B / $85B = 2.0 percentage points. Step 5 — immediate ASC 606 cumulative catch-up using GEV's disclosed sensitivity ($0.2B per 1 point): 2.0 x $0.2B = $400M one-time → $400M / 266,333,581 = $1.50/share. Step 6 — ongoing annual EBITDA drag: contracts are 29% complete, average LTSA ~15 years → ~10.7 years remaining; $1.70B x 0.71 / 10.7 = $113M/yr of EBITDA. Step 7 — capitalize: $113M x 25 = $2,825M / 266,333,581 = $10.60/share. TOTAL BASE = $1.50 + $10.60 = $12.09/share = 1.29% of $940.33. BEAR CASE (30% exposure, 20% cost increase): $5.10B lifetime = 6.0 pts → $1.2B catch-up ($4.51/sh) + $338M/yr x 25 / 266.3M ($31.77/sh) = $36.27/share = 3.86%. CONSERVATIVE CASE (10% exposure, 10% cost): $6.05/share = 0.64%. Cross-check on plausibility: the base-case $113M/yr ongoing drag is ~0.9% of 2025 Power Services revenue ($12B) and is SMALLER than the -$218M of unfavorable revisions GEV already booked in H1'26 alone — so the base case does not require anything worse than the current run-rate to persist.

Every one of these is a seconds-timescale, power-dense requirement with essentially zero energy content (10 MW for 5 s = 0.014 MWh). GEV's FACTSFLEX GFMe is a grid-forming double-star MMC STATCOM with integrated SUPERCAPACITOR storage rated ±300 MVAr that 'can immediately deliver or absorb 150 MW for several seconds' — a near-exact physical match. A 4-hour lithium BESS is over-specified on energy by roughly four orders of magnitude for this duty. GEV also sells synchronous condensers (modular air-cooled, 300 MVAr+ per machine) and, in Gas Power SERVICES, generator-to-synchronous-condenser conversion of existing turbine generators.

I initially concluded the turbine-shaft torsional angle was weak, because the Microsoft paper's own Figure 3 puts AI training FFT energy at 0.2–3 Hz while shaft torsional criticals sit at 7–100 Hz, so the bands do not overlap and the paper's torsional warning looked like rhetoric. That reasoning is wrong in the field: ERCOT documents three real events — ERCOT 23 Hz (Jul–Oct 2024), Dominion Energy 14.7–14.8 Hz, Dominion 1–11 Hz — all inside the torsional band, and Electranix shows that adding a 12 Hz component to a realistic AI profile raises shaft torque from 0.042 pu to 0.993 pu (23x). The risk is driven by a specific spectral component, not by the dominant ~1 Hz peak. Any analysis that reasons only from the 0.2–3 Hz headline band will wrongly dismiss this.

## [Research] research:cooling_pue_shift

- **lens**: PUE / cooling-architecture transition and total facility power per IT megawatt. Net conclusion: the lens's premise is half-wrong and half-underrated. The PUE *level* effect on contracted GW is quantitatively dead (Uptime 2026: fleet PUE 1.52, flat seven years; rack density going 135 -> 230 -> 600 kW swamps any PUE gain). But the cooling transition's real consequence is not magnitude, it is FLEXIBILITY: a direct-to-chip AI hall has <10 s thermal ride-through and only 6.35% of measured facility power immediately curtailable, so the load cannot flex and the gas turbine must. GE Vernova's own GER-3620-P converts that duty into starts-based, not hours-based, life consumption - and GEV bills services per fired hour. That asymmetry is the wedge.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The starts/hours crossover: GEV's services annuity is billed per fired hour but consumed per start, and the incoming order book runs 5x below GE's own crossover point
    - **physical_fact**: GE Vernova's GER-3620-P Figure 36 sets the 7HA.02/9HA.02 combustion and hot-gas-path interval at 25,000 factored fired hours OR 720 factored starts (the .01 variants: 25,000/900; major 50,000/1,440 vs 50,000/1,800). Whichever comes first governs. The implied crossover is 25,000/720 = 34.7 fired hours per start for the .02 machines and 27.8 h/start for the .01. Above that ratio hours govern; below it starts govern. GEV's realized services yield was earned on a fleet far above the crossover: the HA fleet has 3,000,000+ fired hours and 20,400+ fired starts worldwide = 147 h/start, and one early 7HA.02 site reported 48,000 hours against 162 starts = 296 h/start. The incoming duty cycle is on the other side: the US simple-cycle gas turbine fleet ran 987 equivalent full-load hours in 2025 (938 in 2023, 1,014 in 2024; capacity factor 10.7-11.6%), which at a typical 150 starts/yr is 6.6 h/start - 5.3x BELOW the crossover. GER-3620-P adds trip severity factors on top: a trip from 80-100% load counts as 8 starts, from peak load 10, from full-speed-no-load 2 (combustion form: At = 0.5 + exp(0.0125 x %Load)).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment services revenue and Power services margin (and, mechanically, the 'net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability' line in 10-Q Note 9). GEV's 10-K says service billing is 'generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Revenue therefore scales with FIRED HOURS; cost is incurred per MAINTENANCE EVENT. A starts-governed peaker/cycling duty cycle minimizes the revenue driver while accelerating the cost driver. Direction: negative for Power services revenue per GW and negative for Power services margin. This is a structural, recurring drag, not a one-off - which is the part that changes the conclusion the team already reached on the revisions line.

At roughly $800/kW of gas equipment content that is 28.2 GW x $800/kW = $22.6B of equipment revenue. At the 17-19% Power margin guide (use 18%), that is $4.06B of EBITDA; spread over a ~5-year delivery window = $813M/yr. $813M x 25 = $20.3B / 266,333,581 = $76.3/share = 8.1% of $940.33. That is the magnitude of the short the team would have been carrying had they run this angle. The finding's value is that the number is zero, not $76: fleet PUE has not moved in seven years, and the 4.4x rack-density ramp runs the opposite direction on a compounding basis while the PUE term is at most a one-time <=25% level shift on a converting minority of sites.

What I could not find published anywhere is the specific netting exercise applied to GEV's contracted GW: nobody appears to have taken the PUE-deflation argument seriously enough in a GEV context to kill it with numbers. The novelty here is low and I am scoring it as such; the value is defensive, not original.

Any one of those would mean the PUE term has started to bite at portfolio scale and this finding should be withdrawn.

- **dead_ends**:
  - THE LENS'S OWN PRIMARY HYPOTHESIS - 'contracted generation GW was oversized on an air-cooled PUE assumption' - IS DEAD. Uptime 2026 measures fleet PUE at 1.52 with no movement in seven years, DLC penetration ~19%, and rack density is going 135 -> 230 -> 600 kW inside 24 months. The PUE term is a one-time <=25% level shift on a converting minority; the IT term is a compounding multiple. Reported as Finding 2 because killing it is worth more than the angle was.
  - PUE SEASONALITY / LOAD-FACTOR ANGLE - killed on materiality, not on physics. The physics is real and measured: institutional data center PUE of 1.05 in January vs 1.49 in July; partial PUE moving 1.05 to 1.30 as ambient goes -3.9C to 35C; Google states seasonal quarter-over-quarter PUE increases. Because DLC with warm-water/dry-cooler heat rejection is far less ambient-sensitive, a liquid-cooled campus delivers roughly 7-14% more annual MWh per MW of contracted interconnection than an air-cooled one - which is MORE fired hours for dedicated gas, a LONG on Power services. But it applies only to the dedicated/behind-the-meter gas slice and nets out below $10/share. Real, quantified, sub-threshold. Do not pitch it; it is a supporting bullet at most.
  - 'COOLING LOAD WAS THE SHOCK ABSORBER' - the idea that at PUE 1.52 the 34% non-IT fraction electrically damps IT-side swings, so a move to PUE 1.15 raises grid-facing volatility per facility MW by 1.52/1.15 = +32%. Arithmetically clean and I believe it is directionally right, but I could not find a single measurement of the non-IT fraction's damping time constant at the relevant (sub-second to seconds) timescale, and at those timescales chiller electrical draw is probably not slow enough for the argument to hold as stated. Unverifiable with available sources - closed rather than reported.
  - CURTAILABILITY COLLAPSE AS A STANDALONE WEDGE - measured at 6.35% of facility power (arXiv 2609.05406) with <10 s DLC thermal ride-through versus minutes for air-cooled halls, and GER-3620-P's Off-Frequency Operation section explicitly warns that 'off-frequency operation, including rapid Rate of Change of Frequency... When frequency deviation withstand requirements are combined with active power response requirement (also known as governor response), a start-based penalty may be incurred.' The physics is excellent and it is the CAUSAL DRIVER behind Finding 1. But sized on its own it comes to roughly $1.80/share (20 extra factored starts per year against a 720-start budget, on the disclosed ~23 GW of data-center-tied capacity), far below the threshold. Folded into Finding 1 as evidence rather than reported separately.
  - 7HA.02 / 9HA.02 STARTS-INTERVAL REGRESSION AS A STANDALONE WEDGE - GER-3620-P Fig 36 shows the .02 variants carry a 20% TIGHTER starts budget than the .01 (720 vs 900 starts for CI/HGP; 1,440 vs 1,800 for major), moving the crossover from 27.8 to 34.7 h/start, and the corpus project pipeline names 7HA.02 and 9HA.02 as the units being installed. Compounding this, a documented bi-layer thermal-barrier-coating delamination and erosion issue has been reported across the 7HA.02 fleet at user conferences. Sized alone this is ~$6.7/share - below threshold - so it is folded into Finding 1. Worth flagging to the team as an independently checkable fact that strengthens Finding 1 and is also the most likely ALTERNATIVE explanation for the -$218M (see Finding 1's kill condition 2).
  - ELECTRIFICATION AS A SEPARATE LONG off the same load-volatility physics (data-center orders >$5B YTD 2026, more than double the FY25 total, driven by STATCOM/synchronous-condenser/switchgear content sized for transients rather than averages). Materially large but this is the consensus bull leg and I found nothing in the physics that the market has not already priced. Killed on novelty, not on magnitude.

I could not find any quantification of medium-voltage content per MW under 800 VDC versus conventional 415/480 VAC architectures. Speculative; closed for lack of a number.

## [Research] research:grid_alternatives

- **lens**: Grid-enhancing technologies (DLR, advanced power flow control, topology optimization) and advanced-conductor reconductoring as substitutes for new generation — quantified capacity uplift, cost per MW unlocked, deployment timelines, and whether GEV is disintermediated or pulled through. The lens forced me onto the question "what actually determines how hard the existing fleet is run," which is where the real wedge turned out to be: GEV's services annuity is billed per fired hour and per maintenance event, so the *duty cycle* of the installed HA fleet — not installed GW — is the hidden driver of the Power services line. I measured that duty cycle directly from GEV's own milestone disclosures.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The HA fleet's fired-hour clock is measurable from GEV's own press releases: ~6,750 operating hours per unit per year (77% utilization), 47% faster than the US combined-cycle fleet average — which dates the major-inspection wave and validates the $25M/GW-yr services target arithmetically
    - **physical_fact**: GE Vernova's HA fleet accumulated exactly 1,000,000 commercial operating hours between two dated milestone press releases, twice. Interval 1: 2,000,000 h at 2023-09-07 (88 units, ~80 in commercial operation, 47 GW) -> 3,000,000 h at 2025-03-06 (116 units, 67 GW) = 546 days, average ~98 operating units = 6,826 operating hours/unit/yr (77.9% running-hour utilization). Interval 2: 3,000,000 h at 2025-03-06 (116 units) -> 4,000,000 h at 2026-05-26 (128 units, 21 countries, ~74 GW) = 446 days, average 122 units = 6,713 h/unit/yr (76.6%). Two independent, non-overlapping intervals two years apart agree within 1.7%. Compare the US gas fleet measured from EIA-923 in the corpus: 328.2 GW of NG combined-cycle block capacity (CT+CA+CS, EIA-860M vintage 2026-07 Operating sheet) produced 1,503.5 TWh in 2025 = 52.3% block capacity factor = 4,580 equivalent full-load hours/yr (2024: 54.0%, 4,731 h; 2023: 53.0%; 2022: 49.4%). Simple-cycle GT: 161.1 GW, 157.4 TWh in 2025 = 11.2% CF = 977 h/yr. Ratio of HA duty to US CC fleet duty = 6,750/4,580 = 1.474x.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment services revenue (and therefore Power segment EBITDA and the quality of the $88.5B services RPO), UP. GEV's 10-K states service-agreement billing is 'generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Both billing triggers are linear in fired hours. GER-3620 Rev P sets 25,000 factored fired hours for combustion/hot-gas-path and 50,000 FFH for major inspection. At 6,750 h/yr a unit books 5.40 CI/HGP events and 2.70 major inspections per 20 years; at the US CC fleet-average 4,580 h/yr it books only 3.66 and 1.83. Management's own $500M/GW-over-20-years (= $25M/GW-yr, Morgan Stanley Laguna 2026-09-16) is only achievable at the higher duty. The measured duty says the $25M/GW-yr target is arithmetically supported and that today's realized ~$15M/GW-yr is a fleet-immaturity timing artifact, not a structural shortfall: fleet-average accumulated hours are 4,000,000/128 = 31,250 h/unit, so the average unit has passed its first 25,000-FFH combustion/HGP and crosses the 50,000-FFH major-inspection trigger in (50,000-31,250)/6,750 = 2.78 years, i.e. around Q1-Q2 2029, with the 2016-2019 vintage crossing now through 2028.
    - **direction**: long

(1) Management's $500M/GW over 20 years = $25.0M/GW-yr is assumed to correspond to the measured HA duty of 6,750 fired hours/yr, because GER-3620 intervals are hour-denominated and both 10-K billing triggers are hour-linear. (2) If instead new and existing GEV gas ran at the US CC fleet-average 4,580 h/yr, the event count and hourly billing scale down by 4,580/6,750 = 0.679, giving $16.96M/GW-yr. Delta = $8.04M/GW-yr of Power services revenue. (3) Incremental EBITDA margin on services assumed 30% (services is the high-margin half of RPO; Power segment blended margin guided 17-19%, so 30% incremental on services is defensible but is an assumption, not a disclosure). (4) Applied to the 74 GW HA installed base today: 74 x $8.04M = $595M revenue/yr x 30% = $178M EBITDA x 25 / 266,333,581 shares = $16.75/share = 1.78% of $940.33. (5) Applied to 74 GW installed + 53 GW firm equipment backlog = 127 GW at maturity: 127 x $8.04M = $1,021M x 30% = $306M x 25 / 266,333,581 = $28.74/share = 3.06% of $940.33. Range: $16.8 to $28.7/share, i.e. 1.8%-3.1%. Note this values the *duty-cycle assumption*, not the services wave itself; if the market already assumes baseload duty, the finding is confirmatory rather than incremental.
    - **novelty_check**: I searched for (a) 'GE Vernova HA fleet major inspection wave 2027 2028 50000 fired hours services billing step-up sell-side note', (b) 'GE Vernova services revenue per GW capacity factor assumption fired hours HA turbine "500 million" 20 years analyst', (c) 'HA gas turbine fleet utilization hours per year GE Vernova 7HA capacity factor'. The QUALITATIVE claim is published and I must say so plainly: StockStory's GEV research page states 'With 325 HA turbines under contract but only 130 running, a services wave will compound equipment growth once those units reach their first major outage cycle mid-decade.' So 'a services wave is coming' is NOT novel. 'I could not find it published' is the honest answer; I cannot claim nobody has done it internally.

(A) HIGH CONFIDENCE, ~Q3 2027: if the run-rate holds at 6,600-6,900 h/unit/yr and the operating fleet averages ~132 units over the next year, GEV crosses 5,000,000 HA commercial operating hours 12.3-14.0 months after 2026-05-26, i.e. between roughly June 2027 and August 2027, and historically announces it within weeks. (B) NEAR-TERM, 2026-10-28 (GEV Q3'26 earnings, confirmed): Gas Power services revenue growth should exceed the growth in HA installed GW year over year, and HA-turbines-in-installed-base plus the operating-hours figure disclosed in the FY26 10-K (late Jan / early Feb 2027) should imply 6,400-7,000 h/unit/yr when differenced against the 4M/128-unit May-2026 datapoint.

Factored hours penalize fast starts, trips and peak firing, so factored hours are generally >= running hours; using running hours as a proxy is conservative for the event-count argument but is not exact. (2) The milestone figures are round-number crossings announced with press-release lag, so each interval carries a few weeks of date uncertainty; the two intervals agreeing within 1.7% argues the lag is roughly constant. (5) One secondary source (keentelengineering.com) states HGP at 'the equivalent of 32,000 base-load operating hours' rather than 25,000 FFH; at 32,000/64,000 intervals the event counts fall to 4.19 CI/HGP + 2.10 MI per 20 yr at measured duty, and the ratio to fleet-average duty is unchanged at 1.474x, so the *relative* claim is interval-insensitive while the absolute event counts are not.   - - **title**: Grid-enhancing technologies and reconductoring cannot displace GEV gas inside a 3-12 month horizon: the marginal gain of full DLR over the already-mandated ambient-adjusted rating is only 6-14%, and FERC specifically refused to put DLR on the Order 2023 alternative-technologies list
    - **physical_fact**: Three quantified facts bound the substitution. (a) Wind convective cooling — the entire physical basis of DLR uplift — is worth 10%-40% of line thermal capacity, and Oncor's ERCOT comparison found DLR raised wind utilization by 30-70% versus a STATIC rating but only 6%-14% versus an ambient-adjusted rating (AAR), which FERC Order 881 already mandates. The incremental physics available to GETs after Order 881 compliance is therefore single-digit to low-double-digit percent, not the headline 40%. (b) Advanced-conductor reconductoring roughly doubles a circuit's capacity at under half the cost of a new line, but the Goldman School/GridLab 2035 Report's own pathway delivers ~64 TW-miles by 2035 — a decade-scale utility capex program requiring line outages, not a 3-12 month lever. (c) The Brattle/WATT 'Unlocking the Queue' study's headline — DLR + advanced power flow control + topology optimization enabling 5,200 MW in Kansas and Oklahoma — measures additional WIND AND SOLAR INJECTION headroom in the interconnection queue, not firm 24/7 delivery to a load pocket, which is what a data center buys. Regulatory blocker: in Order No. 2023-A, 'The Commission also affirmed its prior decision not to include dynamic line ratings or storage-as-a-transmission-asset on the list of alternative transmission technologies' that transmission providers must evaluate in interconnection studies.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment equipment orders and gas RPO ($87.8B equipment / 53 GW firm backlog + 63 GW slot reservations), NEUTRAL — the bear mechanism does not operate in the window. Secondarily, Power services revenue, mildly UP: to the extent transmission relief does raise dispatch of the existing installed gas fleet rather than deferring new units, it increases fired hours on GEV's installed base, which is exactly the billing trigger in Finding 1. The GETs bear case, if it works at all, transfers value from GEV's equipment line to GEV's higher-margin services line rather than destroying it.
    - **direction**: kills-an-existing-angle

    - **physical_fact**: Computed from IEEE Std C57.91-2011 clause 7 equations (top-oil rise dTO = dTO_rated x ((K^2 R + 1)/(R+1))^n; hot-spot rise over oil dH = dH_rated x K^2m; aging acceleration F_AA = exp(15000/383 - 15000/(theta_H+273)); normal insulation life 180,000 h at 110 C hot-spot) for a typical 65 C-rise OA/FA power transformer (dTO_rated 50 C, dH_rated 30 C, R 4.87, n 0.9, m 0.8, tau_TO 3.5 h, tau_W 0.12 h) under a summer ambient sinusoid (mean 25 C, amplitude 8 C, peak hour 15). Two 24-hour load shapes with the SAME 1.00 pu peak: conventional LF 0.67 and flat data-center-dominated LF 0.92. Steady-state clause-7 model: equivalent aging 5.06 vs 9.89 h/day at K_peak = 1.00, ratio 1.95x (life 97.4 yr vs 49.9 yr); at K_peak = 1.10, ratio 2.00x (29.6 yr vs 14.8 yr). Transient model with the 3.5 h top-oil time constant, which properly credits the conventional profile's overnight oil cooldown: ratio 3.47x at K_peak = 1.00 (198 yr vs 57 yr) and 3.66x at 1.05. Expressed as an equivalent peak: a flat LF 0.92 profile at 1.00 pu ages the unit exactly like a conventional LF 0.67 profile at 1.114 pu, i.e. +11.4% peak. The load factors are not hypothetical: Dominion Virginia reported an 82% load factor for large data centers in 2024, Duke Energy plans new large loads at 80%, and Dominion's own 10-Q defines its 'High load' revenue class as customers 'with actual or anticipated forecast demand of 25 MW or higher and annual load factor of 75% or higher' — a class whose revenue ran $1,450M in H1'26 versus $805M in H1'25.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Electrification segment equipment orders and equipment backlog (transformers, i.e. Prolec GE plus GE Vernova power transformers), UP. The lens connection: DLR, advanced power flow control and reconductoring all raise the thermal rating of the LINE without touching the substation transformer, so every GET or reconductoring project moves the binding constraint from the conductor to the transformer and simultaneously increases the fraction of the year the transformer spends at high loading. GETs are therefore a pull-through into GEV Electrification rather than a disintermediation. Separately, if utilities size data-center-serving transformers on peak MW using the cyclic-loading allowances of IEEE C57.91 clause 7 — allowances that exist precisely because of the overnight thermal recovery a data center removes — they under-specify by roughly 11-15% of MVA for the same peak MW, which shows up as larger unit sizes and more units per substation in Electrification orders.

- **dead_ends**:
  - KILLED — 'DLR uplift is anti-correlated with the summer coincident peak, so GETs cannot relieve peak capacity needs.' This is the most commonly repeated defensive argument against GETs and I could not support it. Great River Energy's deployment (the largest US DLR deployment, reported in T&D World) found DLR unlocked up to 63% additional capacity on hot summer evenings when demand was highest, and peak uplift approached 80% in winter. The physics intuition (static ratings already assume hot, still conditions, so there is little headroom left on a hot still afternoon) does not survive contact with field data. Do not use this argument in the memo.
  - KILLED — 'Flat data-center load shape erodes the N-1 emergency loading capability of existing transformers, forcing utilities to buy transformers with no growth in peak MW.' I built the IEEE C57.91-2011 transient model and solved for the maximum 4-hour long-time emergency loading under a 140 C hot-spot cap, starting from each load shape. Result: the flat 0.92-LF shape loses only 2.0% of emergency capability at a 0.85 pu base peak and 2.5% at 0.95 pu. Immaterial. The reason is structural: a contingency occurs at or near the system peak, where both load shapes are at nearly the same instantaneous loading, so the thermal pre-load is nearly identical and the short winding time constant dominates. This sub-thesis is dead regardless of parameter choices.
  - CLOSED — 'GEV captures the GETs market directly.' It does not to any material degree. The leading DLR, power-flow-control and topology-optimization vendors are independents (LineVision, Ampacimon, Smart Wires, NewGrid); the conductor manufacturers are CTC Global, 3M and Southwire. GEV's participation is confined to GridOS / e-terra EMS-ADMS (into which DLR ratings must feed) and FACTS/STATCOM hardware. Against a $45-46B revenue base and a $250B market cap these lines are too small to move a pitch, and I could find no disclosure sizing them.
  - OPEN BUT UNQUANTIFIED — reconductoring as a pull-through for GEV substation terminal equipment (HV circuit breakers, instrument transformers, disconnect switches, protection relays). Doubling a circuit's ampacity with ACCC/ACCR requires the terminal equipment to be re-rated for the higher current, which is GEV Grid Solutions content. I searched the 2035 Report, its companion 'Supporting Advanced Conductor Deployment: Barriers and Policy Solutions', and DOE's Reconductoring Economic & Financial Analysis (REFA) tool materials and could not find a published cost breakdown giving the substation/terminal-equipment share of a reconductoring project. Without that share I cannot size it. This is a genuine gap worth one more hour of someone's time — the DOE REFA tool may expose the line item directly.
  - NEGATIVE RESULT WORTH KNOWING — the generation-headroom version of the bear case survives on physics but not on timing. From EIA-923 and EIA-860M in the corpus: the US NG combined-cycle fleet is 328.2 GW and ran at only 52.3% block capacity factor in 2025, down from 54.0% in 2024, i.e. roughly 4,580 equivalent full-load hours against a physical ceiling near 7,500-7,900. That is on the order of 500 TWh/yr of unused energy — more than twice current US data-center consumption — sitting in already-built machines. If transmission delivery were the only binding constraint, GETs plus reconductoring really could serve enormous load growth with zero new turbines. I found no mechanism that converts that headroom inside 3-12 months (FERC excluded DLR from Order 2023's alternative-technologies list; reconductoring is a 2035-horizon capex program; the incremental physics of DLR over already-mandated AAR is only 6-14%), but the team should know this is the strongest form of the bear case and it is not dead on a 3-5 year view.

## [Research] research:storage_vs_peakers

- **lens**: Does 4-8h battery storage structurally eat the peaker use case that is ~60% of the near-term US gas wave? Answer: no, it does not eat the GW — but the duty cycle it leaves behind eats the services annuity. The lens inverted: the storage threat to GEV is not an orders threat, it is a fired-hours threat landing on the half of RPO the premium multiple is paid for.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: Peaker/cycling duty preserves GEV's maintenance-event COST cadence while collapsing its fired-hour BILLING by 81-92% — the services annuity per GW is duty-cycle-dependent, and the incoming vintage has the wrong duty cycle
    - **physical_fact**: GE Vernova's own GER-3620 Rev P (released 2021-03-15) Figure 36 sets 7HA.01/7HA.02 combustion and hot-gas-path inspection intervals at 25,000 factored fired hours OR 900 factored starts, whichever comes first (9HA: 25,000/720; major 50,000/1,800 and 50,000/1,440). Figure 22 gives GE's own reference operational profiles for 7F/7FA: Continuous = 8,200 fired h/yr, 21 starts/yr, 400 h/start; Cyclic = 4,800 h/yr, 300 starts/yr, 16 h/start, starts-based maintenance factor 1.0; Peaking = 600 fired h/yr, 150 starts/yr, 4 h/start, starts-based maintenance factor 1.7. Crossing the two: a continuous-duty unit reaches its HGP outage in 3.05 years having accumulated 25,000 billable fired hours (hours criterion binds); a peaking-duty unit reaches the SAME outage in 3.53 years having accumulated only 2,118 billable fired hours (starts criterion binds, 150 x 1.7 = 255 factored starts/yr vs a 900-start limit). Same outage cadence, 8.5% of the billable utilization. Measured US fleet data gives the same result independently and more conservatively: simple-cycle GT fleet ran 926 fired h/yr in 2025 (CF 10.6%, 177.0 GW) vs 4,884 h/yr for the combined-cycle gas-turbine part (CF 55.8%, 190.8 GW) — 19.0%. Separately, GER-3620 Figure 42's hot-gas-path factored-starts criterion charges an adder aL = exp(0.0137 x %load step) for EVERY load step >=20%: a single +/-50% load swing consumes 0.984 factored starts, i.e. as much hot-gas-path low-cycle-fatigue life as one entire base-load start/stop cycle. Trip severity factors are 8:1 from base load, 10:1 from peak, 6.5:1 from 50% load, 2:1 from FSNL.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — (a) Power services revenue (the usage-billed component of long-term service agreements), DOWN; (b) Power segment EBITDA via 'net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability' under ASC 606 cost-to-cost, MORE NEGATIVE. GEV's FY25 10-K (filed 2026-01-29) states service-agreement billing terms 'are generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Revenue is therefore hour-driven; cost is event-driven. Peaker/cycling duty decouples the two: the hot-gas-path outage (parts + labour, the cost) still arrives every ~3-3.5 years because factored STARTS bind, but only ~8.5-19% of the assumed fired hours have been billed against it. Because GEV recognises CSA revenue on a cost-to-cost basis, any upward revision to estimated total contract cost relative to estimated total contract revenue flows immediately to Power EBITDA as a cumulative catch-up. Storage is the accelerant, not the cause: PJM accredits 4-hour storage at 50% vs 60% for a simple-cycle CT, so storage does not remove the gas units (see Finding 2) — it converts their flat runs into deep daily load steps, and every >=20% step is a factored-start adder.
    - **direction**: short
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: GE Vernova, GER-3620 Rev P, 'Heavy-Duty Gas Turbine Operating and Maintenance Considerations', released 2021-03-15, 60 pp, Figure 36 (p.33) and Figure 22 (p.17). https://www.gevernova.com/content/dam/gepower-new/global/en_US/downloads/gas-new-site/resources/reference/GER-3620-P.pdf
        - **number_or_quote**: Fig 36: '7HA.02 ... Combustion (DLN) Factored 25000/900 ... Hot Gas Path Factored 25000/900 ... Major Factored 50000/1800'. Fig 22 (7F/7FA reference profiles): Peaking Hours/Year 600, Starts/Year 150, 'Typical Maintenance Factor (Starts-Based) 1.7'; Continuous Hours/Year 8200, Starts/Year 21.
        - **reproduction**: Downloaded the PDF and extracted text with pypdf (60 pages). Then: Continuous -> min(25000/8200, 900/21) = 3.05 yr, billable hours = 8200*3.05 = 25,000. Peaking -> min(25000/600, 900/(150*1.7)) = min(41.67, 3.53) = 3.53 yr, billable hours = 600*3.53 = 2,118. Ratio 2118/25000 = 8.5%.
      - - **source**: GE Vernova, GER-3620 Rev P, Figure 42 (p.38) hot-gas-path factored-starts criterion and Appendix A.3 Example 3 (p.44)
        - **number_or_quote**: Fig 42: 'L = Annual Number of Load Steps >= 20%; aL = Exp(0.0137 x % Load Step)'; FS = 0.5*NA + NB + 1.3*NP + Ps*F + SUM(aTi-1)*Ti + SUM(aLi-1)*Li. Example 3: '30 load steps beyond +/-20% load ... resulting in total Load Step Factored Starts of 25.4.'
        - **reproduction**: Recomputed GE's own Example 3 table from the formula: sum over the 13 listed step sizes of n*(exp(0.0137*pct)-1) = 25.40, matching GE's stated 25.4 exactly, and each line matches GE's per-row values to 0.05. A single +/-50% step = exp(0.685)-1 = 0.984 factored starts.

  - - **title**: Storage does NOT contest the peaker GW — PJM accredits a 4-hour battery BELOW a simple-cycle peaker, and US peaker utilisation rose while the battery fleet grew 6x. The 'batteries kill the gas wave' bear case is empirically dead.
    - **physical_fact**: PJM's ELCC Class Ratings for the 2026/2027 Base Residual Auction (primary regulatory document, pjm.com): 4-hr Storage 50%, 6-hr Storage 58%, 8-hr Storage 62%, 10-hr Storage 72% — versus Gas Combustion Turbine 60%, Gas Combustion Turbine Dual Fuel 78%, Gas Combined Cycle 74%, Nuclear 95%. A 4-hour battery is therefore credited at 0.83x a simple-cycle peaker and 0.64x a dual-fuel peaker PER NAMEPLATE MW for capacity adequacy. Replacing 1 GW of dual-fuel CT accreditation requires 1.56 GW of 4-hour storage; even 8-hour storage requires 1.26 GW. The mechanism is energy-limitation: a duration-limited resource cannot cover a widening net-peak window, and its marginal contribution falls as more of it is added — arXiv 2303.09560 finds the capacity credit of energy storage declines from 20-50% to 15-40% as storage penetration rises (IEEE RTS-79 plus real-world data). The US field data confirms no displacement has occurred: operating utility-scale battery capacity grew from 8.9 GW (EIA-860M Jan-2023 vintage) to 53.3 GW (Jul-2026 vintage), +499%, while the national simple-cycle peaker fleet's fired hours went UP from 869 h/yr in 2022 to 926 h/yr in 2025 (CF 9.9% -> 10.6%).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment equipment revenue and Power equipment EBITDA margin — protected, not impaired. Also protects the Power services RPO base, since the units get built and enter the services base. This is a defensive finding: it removes the most obvious objection to a long-GEV thesis and, more usefully for a short or a nuanced pitch, it redirects the exposure away from orders and onto the services line (Finding 1). Direction: kills an existing angle.

        - **number_or_quote**: '4-hr Storage 50% / 6-hr Storage 58% / 8-hr Storage 62% / 10-hr Storage 72% ... Gas Combined Cycle 74% / Gas Combustion Turbine 60% / Gas Combustion Turbine Dual Fuel 78%'

Searched: 'ELCC saturation 4-hour battery storage capacity credit declines penetration CAISO 2026', 'battery storage forces combined cycle gas turbine deeper cycling more starts capacity factor decline study 2025 2026', 'PJM capacity accreditation 4-hour storage ELCC class rating 2026/2027'. Direction is neutral-to-negative: it does not by itself create value or destroy it, it removes a hedge the bull case implicitly assumes and makes it unfalsifiable.
