## [Verify] skeptic:demand_flexibility:The $500M/GW services annuity is

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: The central number — a "6.8 percentage-point, 10.6% relative decline in the NEWEST cohort" — is mostly a division error, and the residual is not a decline at all.

**Error 1: partial-year generation divided by a full 8,760 hours. This is 66% of the claimed effect.**
The 2020+ CC cohort (23.1 GW, 57.3% CF in 2025) includes 1.85 GW of units whose first operating year is 2025. Those units show a 5.0% capacity factor purely because they ran for a few weeks of 2025 while the denominator charges them the full year. Removing only them:
- 2020+ cohort, units fully operational for all of 2025 (fy<=2024): **21.28 GW at 61.8%**, not 57.3%.
- Arithmetic check: 23.1 x 57.3 = 1323.6; minus 1.85 x 5.0 = 9.25 -> 1314.4 / 21.28 = 61.8%. Exact.
The gap to the 2015-19 cohort (64.1%) collapses from **6.8 pp to 2.3 pp**, and relative decline from 10.6% to 3.6%.
Query: same `cap` temp table as the finding, but `WHERE c.fy BETWEEN 2020 AND 2024` (CT/CA/CS only), joined to `generation` year=2025.

**Error 2: "has already rolled over" is false — the mature series is flat.**
Restricting to the 2020-2022 vintages (15.45 GW, at least three full operating years), capacity factor by year is **61.8% (2023) / 62.1% (2024) / 61.4% (2025)**. Flat within noise. There is no rollover, no trend, no deterioration. The full-cohort series the finding implies a trend from (56.6 -> 62.9 -> 57.3 across 2023/24/25) is non-monotonic and is just the partial-year tail moving around as new units commission.

**Error 3: the 64.1% "baseline" is a composition artifact, not a physical norm.**
2025 CF by single first-operating-year: fy2015 53.5%, fy2016 62.2%, fy2017 60.0%, fy2018 65.7%, fy2019 76.1%, fy2020 54.0%, fy2021 69.2%, fy2022 62.4%, fy2023 63.0%. fy2018 alone is 19.13 of the 43.25 GW 2015-19 cohort (44%), and fy2019 adds a small very-high slice. The 2015-19 bucket is high because of two vintages. The 2020-22 mature cohort at 61.4% sits *above* fy2015, fy2016 and fy2017. Shifting the cohort boundary by one or two years reverses the sign of the "decline."

**Error 4: the comparison the finding needed is the one it did not run.** The 2015-19 cohort itself rose over the same window (62.3% in 2022 -> 65.2 -> 65.9 -> 64.1%). Both mature cohorts are flat-to-up. Nothing in EIA-923 supports utilization erosion.

Not errors: the $4.37/MWh unit conversion is arithmetically correct ($25M per GW-yr / 5.72M MWh = $4.37/MWh), and the finding's own caveat (2) is right that the aggregate fleet shows no CF decline. The finding listed commissioning-ramp contamination as caveat (1) and said it "could not separate" it. It is separable with the same two tables, and once separated the finding is gone.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **physics_errors_note**: n/a
- **already_published**: False
- **where_published**: I could not find the specific connection published. Searches for the $500M/GW figure paired with capacity-factor or fired-hours skepticism surface only GEV's own statement of the metric (130 HA machines operating, 195 under contract, ~$500M/GW over the first 20 years — restated at the Sep 2026 investor communications and in the 2025 annual report) and the general analyst spread; no note tests the metric for its implied capacity factor. So the novelty claim in the original finding is fair as far as it goes. But novelty is moot here: the finding is unpublished because it is wrong, not because it is undiscovered. The reason no one has published "new-vintage CC capacity factors have rolled over" is that, on the same public data, they have not.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The strongest surviving version of the argument — and the team should understand why it still fails — is this: even at a flat 61.8% cohort CF, GEV's $25M/GW-yr implies ~$4.37/MWh, and if flexible AI load *later* pushes new-build CC toward peaker-like duty, the hours-billed half of the annuity compresses. The physics of that is coherent and the 10-K billing language genuinely does tie services revenue to utilization.

Two things break it anyway.

**The billing term has a second trigger the finding drops mid-quote.** GEV bills on utilization "*and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event*." GER-3620 Rev P sets intervals on factored hours *or* factored starts, **whichever comes first**. A unit that runs fewer hours but starts more often — which is exactly what demand-flexible dispatch means — hits the starts-based limit instead of the hours-based one. Industry convention converts a single normal start to roughly 10-20 equivalent operating hours, LTSAs assign about 2 complete cycles to a fast-loading operation, and a trip from full load is the most severe thermal event a machine sees. Cycling raises maintenance events per MWh. The finding assumes services revenue is linear in hours; under the flexibility scenario it is invoking, the starts term binds and the event-billing leg rises. Direction is ambiguous at minimum, and plausibly *positive* to GEV services on a per-MWh basis. That is a mechanism inversion, not a haircut.

**The materiality does not clear the bar even on the finding's own arithmetic.** Substituting the corrected 3.6% relative gap for the erroneous 10.6%: $7.2B hours-billed stream x 0.036 = $258M revenue, x 0.30 assumed incremental EBITDA margin = $77.5M, x 25 = $1.94B / 266,333,581 shares = **$7.28/share = 0.77%** of $940.33. Below the task's own $10/share threshold. And that number still credits a 2.3 pp cross-sectional cohort gap as if it were causal deterioration, which the flat 2023-2025 mature-cohort series says it is not. The honest corrected figure is approximately zero. The bear extension to 50% CF has no empirical anchor left once the trend is gone — it was extrapolating a line that does not exist.

Note also that the 60% hours-billed split and 30% services EBITDA margin are undisclosed assumptions the result scales linearly in, as the finding concedes. Three assumed parameters multiplying a measurement error is not a wedge.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED on physics and on mechanism; materiality collapses below the threshold even before the mechanism problem.

**Physics.** I reproduced the finding's query exactly and got its numbers, then decomposed them. 4.5 of the claimed 6.8 percentage points come from 1.85 GW of units that first operated in 2025 being charged a full 8,760-hour denominator for a few weeks of generation (they show a 5.0% CF). Excluding units not fully operational through 2025, the 2020+ cohort runs 61.8%, not 57.3% — a 2.3 pp gap, 3.6% relative. The remaining gap is not a trend: the mature 2020-2022 cohort is flat at 61.8 / 62.1 / 61.4 percent across 2023/2024/2025. And the 64.1% "baseline" is 44% weighted to a single unusually high vintage (fy2018 at 65.7%, plus fy2019 at 76.1%); the 2020-22 cohort actually outruns fy2015 (53.5%), fy2016 (62.2%) and fy2017 (60.0%). Moving the cohort cut by one year flips the sign. The finding flagged commissioning-ramp contamination as an unresolvable caveat; it is resolvable with the same two tables, and resolving it removes the finding.

**Mechanism.** Even granting the physics, the chain to Power services revenue breaks. The finding quotes the 10-K billing term but drops "and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event." GER-3620 Rev P intervals bind on factored hours *or* factored starts, whichever comes first. Demand-flexible dispatch cuts hours and raises starts; a start counts as roughly 10-20 equivalent operating hours and LTSAs charge about 2 cycles for a fast load change. So the scenario the finding invokes pushes the event-billing leg up while pushing the hours leg down. Services revenue is not linear in fired hours, which is the load-bearing assumption of the whole $/share bridge.

**Materiality.** Recomputed with the corrected 3.6% gap: $7.2B x 0.036 x 0.30 x 25 / 266,333,581 = $7.28/share = 0.77%. Below the $10/share bar. With the flat mature-cohort series the defensible number is approximately zero, and the $21-45/share range in the finding is not recoverable.

**What survives and is worth keeping.** Three by-products are genuinely useful to the team, none of them a wedge on their own: (1) the $4.37/MWh implied-rate cross-check on management's $500M/GW is arithmetically sound and does show the metric is a baseload-duty number — a fair question to ask management, just not a short; (2) the 2020-22 mature cohort running a stable ~61-62% is a mild *positive* datapoint for the annuity, and directly contradicts the peaker-ization narrative; (3) the starts-vs-hours "whichever comes first" structure is the more interesting unexplored angle and points the opposite way — if flexible load raises cycling, GEV's maintenance-event billing and parts consumption per installed GW could rise, which would be a long-side technical argument. If the team wants to spend more time in this lens, that inversion is where to spend it.

**Recommendation: do not carry this finding into the memo.** Anyone on a judging panel who pulls EIA-923 and controls for commissioning year kills it in ten minutes, and the 5.0% capacity factor on the 2025 vintage is visible on inspection.

## [Research] research:algorithmic_efficiency

- **lens**: Rate of algorithmic and hardware energy-efficiency improvement per unit of AI capability vs. demand growth — and what a plausible range does to the 2028-2032 electricity demand forecasts underpinning GEV's 30 GW/yr plan and terminal value.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: AI's energy floor is set by memory-bandwidth-per-watt (19.4%/yr), not compute-per-watt (55.4%/yr) — the DeepSeek bear case applies the wrong exponent to the wrong workload
    - **physical_fact**: For top-performing NVIDIA datacenter GPUs, per-watt improvement rates diverge by 2.9x: FP16 compute-per-watt grows 55.4%/yr (doubling time 1.57 yr) while off-chip memory-bandwidth-per-watt grows only 19.4%/yr (doubling time 3.91 yr). Source: Del Sozzo, Fleming, Flamm & Thompson, 'How Much Progress Has There Been in NVIDIA Datacenter GPUs?', ACM Computing Surveys 37(4), arXiv:2601.20115v3 (2026), §4.1: 'the CAGRs (DTs) range from 55.4% (1.57y) to 19.4% (3.92y) for FP16 and memory bandwidth, respectively.' LLM decode — the dominant and fastest-growing AI workload — is memory-bandwidth-bound, so its energy per token tracks the 19.4% rate, not the 55.4% rate. Confirmed by controlled experiment: H100 -> H200 is the same GH100 die (identical FLOPs, identical 700W TDP) with +43.3% HBM bandwidth (3.35 -> 4.8 TB/s); MLPerf Inference v4.0 Llama2-70B offline throughput rose +42.3% (22,290 -> 31,712 tok/s), an elasticity of 0.98 to bandwidth and 0.00 to FLOPs. Energy per token at fixed 700W fell 31.4 -> 22.1 mJ/token (-29.7%), i.e. exactly the bandwidth gain.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: GEV Power segment services revenue (FY2025 $13,072M) and Power equipment revenue (FY2025 $6,420M), plus the forward multiple premium (~35x vs S&P ~22x) that capitalizes the 20 -> 30 GW/yr gas shipment plan. Direction: POSITIVE. The efficiency-driven demand-destruction risk that the market prices into GEV on shock days is quantitatively overstated by ~3x, because the applicable efficiency rate for the marginal (inference-serving) AI load is 19.4%/yr, not the 55.4%/yr compute rate or the 183%/yr pretraining-algorithmic rate that bear arguments implicitly use.
    - **direction**: long
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: Del Sozzo, Fleming, Flamm & Thompson, 'How Much Progress Has There Been in NVIDIA Datacenter GPUs?', ACM Comput. Surv. 37(4) Art. 111, arXiv:2601.20115v3, 2026
        - **number_or_quote**: 'the CAGRs (DTs) range from 55.4% (1.57y) to 19.4% (3.92y) for FP16 and memory bandwidth, respectively' (per-watt ratios, top-performing GPUs). Also Insight 7: 'computing power grew much faster than off-chip memory bandwidth'; abstract: off-chip memory size and bandwidth 'doubling every 3.29 to 3.41 years'.
        - **reproduction**: WebFetch https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.20115 (PDF saved locally); extracted with pdfplumber to scratchpad/gpu_paper.txt; search string 'perwatt' -> hit at char offset ~47009. Note the PDF has spaces stripped by the extractor.
      - - **source**: MLCommons MLPerf Inference v4.0 (Mar 2024), Llama2-70B, H100 SXM vs H200 SXM; NVIDIA H100/H200 datasheets
        - **number_or_quote**: H100 offline 22,290 tok/s -> H200 31,712 tok/s (+42.3%); server 21,504 -> 29,526 (+37.3%). Bandwidth 3.35 -> 4.8 TB/s (+43.3%). Same GH100 die, same FP16/FP8 FLOPs, same 700W.
        - **reproduction**: WebSearch 'NVIDIA H200 vs H100 Llama 2 70B inference throughput ... MLPerf'. Elasticity = 0.423/0.433 = 0.98. Energy/token = 700W / (tok/s): 31.4 mJ -> 22.1 mJ.

(c) TOTAL = $840M EBITDA/yr. (d) x25 multiple = $21.00B. (e) / 266,333,581 shares = $78.85/share = 8.39% of $940.33. This finding does not claim the whole branch; it re-weights its probability. Cross-check on magnitude: GEV's actual one-day move on the last efficiency shock was -21.52%, which at $940.33 equals $202.36/share — so the market demonstrably prices this risk far larger than $79/share on the day.
    - **novelty_check**: Searched five ways: (1) '"bandwidth per watt" OR "memory bandwidth per watt" GPU trend flat stagnant AI datacenter power demand'; (2) '"memory wall" ... why AI data center electricity demand forecasts too low inference bound investors'; (3) 'sell-side research note AI power demand "memory bandwidth" per watt efficiency floor GE Vernova Vertiv terminal value 2026'; (4) '"inference is memory bound" therefore AI electricity demand will not fall ... power stocks analyst 2026'; (5) '"H200" "H100" MLPerf throughput scaled with memory bandwidth used to argue AI power demand forecast'. FOUND PUBLISHED: the memory wall itself (Gholami et al., IEEE Micro 2024, arXiv:2403.14123 — DRAM bandwidth 1.6x/2yr vs peak FLOPS 3.0x/2yr); the generic Jevons rebuttal (IEA, Brookings, TrendForce, Global X: 'memory is the new bottleneck'); the qualitative claim that inference demand persists despite efficiency. I cannot know nobody has thought of it; I can say I could not find it published.
    - **testable_prediction**: Two dated tests. (1) MARKET TEST, live now through GEV's Q3'26 print on Oct 28 2026: on the next major training-efficiency headline (a lab claiming an order-of-magnitude cheaper frontier model), GEV should fall materially less than the -21.52% of 2025-01-27 and should retrace more than half of any drawdown within 30 trading days — because the transmission channel from training efficiency to serving power is near zero and the market has partially learned this (GEV went 330 -> ~940 after the last one). (2) HARDWARE TEST, MLPerf Inference results for Rubin VR200 (expected 2027): Rubin carries 20-22 TB/s HBM4 at 1800-2300W versus B300's 8 TB/s at 1400W — a 2.5x bandwidth step but a far larger FP4 FLOPs step. Predict Llama-class decode tokens/s per GPU scales ~1:1 with the bandwidth ratio (elasticity to bandwidth > 0.8) and shows no additional gain attributable to FLOPs.
    - **kill_condition**: Three things kill it. (1) HBM4 and successors break the trend: Rubin already delivers a one-time 1.7-1.9x step in bandwidth-per-watt (B300 5.71 -> Rubin 9.57-11.11 GB/s/W). Two consecutive steps of that size would lift the sustained rate above ~40%/yr and collapse the gap with compute-per-watt. Watch HBM5 specs. (2) Serving moves out of the memory-bound regime — processing-in-memory (arXiv:2502.07578 claims 2.9x less energy), photonic KV access (arXiv:2603.21576 claims four orders of magnitude), or a shift to small dense models at very large batch. If a future MLPerf shows decode-throughput elasticity to bandwidth below 0.5, the mechanism is broken. (3) Demand-side: if token volume growth decelerates below ~20%/yr (from Goldman's implied ~121%/yr, 24x over 2026-2030), AI load flattens regardless of the efficiency rate — the efficiency argument becomes moot and GEV's plan is at risk for a different reason.

My own flagship-to-flagship check gives a SLOWER recent rate (A100 2020 -> B300 2025: 5.10 -> 5.71 GB/s/W = 2.5%/yr) but a FASTER forward rate once Rubin lands (A100 -> Rubin: 11.1-13.9%/yr).   - - **title**: The agentic/long-context transition moves AI energy into the one component that is neither batch-amortizable nor quantizable — KV-cache streaming — while per-accelerator TDP compounds at ~34%/yr
    - **physical_fact**: Two compounding demand-side accelerants that are invisible in 'energy per query' metrics. (a) KV-CACHE: at batch 512 and context 2048, PaLM-540B's KV cache is 3 TB, three times the model's parameters, and must be read from off-chip memory once per generated token 'during which the computational core of the chip is essentially idle' (Pope et al., arXiv:2211.05102, 2022). KV bytes scale as batch x context, so unlike weight reads they are NOT amortized by batching, and unlike weights they cannot be pushed below ~4 bits. 2026 agentic contexts run 100k-1M tokens, i.e. 50-500x the 2048 studied. (b) TDP: flagship per-accelerator TDP went 400W (A100, 2020.9) -> 700W (H100) -> 1000W (B200) -> 1400W (B300, 2025.6) -> 1800-2300W (Rubin VR200, 2026-27) = 5.75x in 6.0 years = 33.8%/yr, versus the 8.6%/yr TDP CAGR Del Sozzo et al. measure for top-performing GPUs over the full history — roughly a 4x acceleration. GPU power is ~40% of total AI datacenter power (Del Sozzo et al. 2026, §4, citing ref [29]).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: GEV Power segment gas equipment orders and slot reservations (the 53 GW firm + 63 GW reservation stack, targeting 30 GW/yr output by 2030) and GEV Electrification revenue (FY2025 $9,642M, with $2.7B of data-center orders in Q2'26 alone). Direction: POSITIVE. Datacenter MW over a 3-12 month horizon is determined by installed accelerator count x TDP and by committed interconnect requests — i.e. by capex and supply — not by model efficiency. Efficiency changes tokens delivered per watt; it does not change the watts, because GPUs run pinned near TDP whenever they are saturated. This is why the DeepSeek shock had no measurable effect on GEV's subsequent order book.
    - **direction**: long
    - **evidence**:

        - **reproduction**: pdfplumber extraction to scratchpad/pope.txt, find('3TB'). The KV term scales with batch x context; the weight term scales with 1/batch. As context grows the non-amortizable term dominates.

MoE is a FLOP-saving, not a byte-saving, technique — the headline DeepSeek innovation is close to energy-neutral for serving.

PARTIALLY NOVEL: I could not find the specific quantification of flagship TDP CAGR at 33.8%/yr benchmarked against the 8.6%/yr historical rate from Del Sozzo et al., nor the argument that KV-cache bytes are the specific non-amortizable, non-quantizable residual that makes the agentic transition energy-intensive. Q2'26 signed 20 GW and converted 10 GW; predict Q3'26 signed >= 15 GW. Separately, Rubin VR200 shipping at 1800-2300W (vs B300's 1400W) should be confirmed at NVIDIA's next product disclosure — if Max-P lands at or above 2300W, per-rack MW rises again and the density leg strengthens.

(3) If context-compression techniques (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek V3.2 sparse attention, KV quantization below 4 bits) reduce KV bytes per token by more than ~5x in production serving, the non-amortizable residual shrinks and the agentic accelerant largely disappears.

- **dead_ends**:
  - THE CORPUS ACADEMIC TIER IS USELESS FOR THIS LENS — this is the most useful negative result. The 30,023 'academic' chunks (25,934 openalex + 4,089 arxiv) contain essentially zero AI-hardware or ML-efficiency literature. FTS counts across the whole academic tier: 'energy per token' = 0, 'roofline' = 0, 'arithmetic intensity' = 0, 'joules per token' = 0, 'speculative decoding' = 0, 'perf' + 'per watt' = 0, 'mixture of experts' = 2, 'algorithmic efficiency' = 1, 'KV cache' = 5, 'HBM' = 15 (and most HBM hits are EU/Korea industrial-policy documents, plus one gas-turbine burner paper). The 24 hits for 'power oscillation' are grid/HVDC/converter papers, not GPU power. The academic tier is a power-systems and wind-turbine corpus. Every number in Finding 1 came from live literature, not the corpus. Do not spend more time mining tier='academic' for AI-efficiency edge.
  - THE NAIVE JEVONS/EFFICIENCY BEAR CASE IS ARITHMETICALLY SELF-REFUTING — closed with a number. If you apply Epoch's headline 8-month halving (= 183%/yr efficiency gain) against Goldman's implied token growth of 121%/yr (24x over 2026-2030), AI datacenter load should be SHRINKING 21.7%/yr. It is not; load is growing and interconnect queues are lengthening. Epoch itself scopes the 8-month result to pretraining. Any bear argument that cites the 8-month halving, or that cites 'DeepSeek trained for $5.6M', is dead on arrival because it is a training-compute statistic with no serving-power transmission channel. Conversely: at the compute-per-watt rate (55.4%/yr) load still grows +42%/yr, and at the bandwidth-per-watt rate (19.4%/yr) it grows +85%/yr. Under EVERY published efficiency rate except the inapplicable pretraining one, demand growth dominates. The bear case therefore requires TOKEN GROWTH TO DECELERATE, not efficiency to accelerate — and needs it to fall to <=19%/yr (a 6.3x deceleration) rather than <=55%/yr (a 2.2x deceleration). That 2.9x harder bar is the whole finding.
  - I KILLED MY OWN STRONGER FRAMING. I initially had 'memory bandwidth per watt has been flat since 2020' — and the 2020-2025 flagship series does support it (A100 5.10 -> B300 5.71 GB/s/W = 2.5%/yr, with H100 at 4.79 actually WORSE than A100 and B300 worse than B200). But Rubin VR200's HBM4 delivers 20-22 TB/s at 1800-2300W = 9.57-11.11 GB/s/W, a 1.7-1.9x one-time step. So 'flat' is false going forward, and only the weaker, defensible claim survives: bandwidth-per-watt improves ~3x slower than compute-per-watt. Do not let anyone pitch the 'flat' version — it will be killed in Q&A by anyone who knows the Rubin specs.
  - THE WORKLOAD-COMPOSITION / RAMPING ANGLE COULD NOT BE QUANTIFIED. The Harvard paper in the corpus (Majumder, Yu & Xie, src:3538) shows a genuinely non-obvious result — hybrid batch+inference datacenters are SMOOTHER in aggregate than either pure workload (U-shaped variability vs inference share) while being HARDER to follow on short timescales (hump-shaped ramping). That would connect the AI workload mix to GEV's aeroderivative-vs-HA product mix and to Electrification storage. But every magnitude lives in Figures 1(a)/1(b) and Supplementary Figures 20/21/25/27, which are not in the corpus text, and the paper reports no percentages in prose. I could not derive a $/share number without inventing one, so I dropped it. If someone can get the figure data, this is the most promising unexploited item in the corpus for a load-shape angle.
  - GEV'S -21.52% DEEPSEEK MOVE WAS NOT A POWER-DEMAND REPRICING. Checked the corpus prices table directly: on 2025-01-27 GEV -21.52%, VRT -29.88%, ETN -15.56% — but NEE +1.37% and SPY -1.41%. A regulated utility with the same underlying electricity-demand exposure went UP. The selloff was confined to equipment suppliers levered to datacenter capex, i.e. the market repriced AI CAPEX, not electricity demand. This matters: it means the 'AI efficiency kills power demand' story is not actually what traded that day, and a pitch built on refuting it is attacking a strawman of the market's own behavior. Use the event as evidence of reflexive repricing risk, not as evidence of what the market believes about demand.
  - COULD NOT ACCESS the one paper most directly on-lens: 'Energy use of AI inference, efficiency pathways, and test-time scaling' (ScienceDirect S2542435126001145, Joule-family) returned HTTP 403. No paywall bypass attempted. It may contain an aggregate inference-energy projection that contradicts or supersedes my synthesis. Flagging as an open risk, not a closed question.

## [Research] research:hydrogen_blending

- **lens**: Hydrogen co-firing physics (flashback, NOx, Wobbe, derate, hardware) and its effect on DLN combustion-section and hot-gas-path life, inspection intervals, and therefore GEV's per-fired-hour / per-maintenance-event services annuity — plus the commercial reality of what "H2-ready" actually commits GE Vernova to.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The H2O-loading bridge: GE's own diluent severity formula, applied to hydrogen's combustion water, implies a 28-30% shorter HA inspection interval at GEV's advertised 50 vol% H2 — a severity factor GE has never published, and which the industry's own consensus document books as zero
    - **physical_fact**: Per unit of heat released, hydrogen produces 1.66x the water of methane (H2: 1 mol H2O / 241.8 kJ = 4.136 mol H2O/MJ; CH4: 2 mol H2O / 802.3 kJ = 2.493 mol H2O/MJ). At an H-class heat-to-air ratio of ~1.16 MJ per kg of compressor inlet air (7HA.02: ~384 MW simple cycle at 43.4% => 885 MW heat input over ~765 kg/s airflow), this puts exhaust H2O at 8.4 mol% on methane — independently corroborated at 8.3 vol% by Schonewald & Ziminsky (2007) as cited in CATF's 'Emissions and Performance Implications of Hydrogen Fuel in Heavy Duty Gas Turbines' (2023). At 50 vol% H2 (23.2% of heat from H2), incremental hot-gas water = 0.79% of compressor inlet mass flow; at 100% H2, 3.42%. GER-3620 Rev P (GE Vernova, released 2021-03-15, p.12) states the governing mechanism in GE's own words for injected water: 'Higher gas conductivity, in particular, increases the heat transfer to the buckets and nozzles and can lead to higher metal temperature and reduced part life.' GE's published diluent severity relation is S = K + (M x I), with the worked example on p.37 giving M = 0.55, K = 1 for FSX-414 stage-2/3 nozzles on a wet control curve. Applying M = 0.55 to I = 0.79 gives S = 1.44; a conservative M = 0.35 gives S = 1.28. Against the GER-3620 Fig. 36 baseline for 7HA.01/9HA.01 of 25,000 factored fired hours for both DLN combustion and hot-gas-path inspection, that is an interval of 17,400-19,500 h, i.e. 22-30% shorter. At 100% H2: S = 2.20-2.88, interval 8,700-11,400 h (54-65% shorter).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment services. Specifically (a) 'Net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability' (10-Q Note 9; -$218M in H1'26 vs -$42M H1'25) — under a contractual service agreement billed at a fixed rate per fired hour, a customer switching to H2 blends accelerates GEV's parts consumption at unchanged revenue, compressing CSA margin; and (b) Power services revenue (positive) for the transactional half of the book, where shorter intervals mean more parts sales. The sign depends on CSA-vs-transactional mix, which GEV does not disclose. Direction on CSA margin: negative. Direction on transactional parts revenue: positive.
    - **direction**: either
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: GE Vernova, GER-3620 Rev P, 'Heavy-Duty Gas Turbine Operating and Maintenance Considerations,' released 2021-03-15, p.12 (Steam/Water Injection) and p.37 (worked example)
        - **number_or_quote**: 'Higher gas conductivity, in particular, increases the heat transfer to the buckets and nozzles and can lead to higher metal temperature and reduced part life.' Worked example: 'at a steam injection rate of 2.4% on a wet control curve, M4 = 0.55, K4 = 1 ... S4 = K4 + (M4 . I4) = 1 + (0.55 . 2.4) = 2.3'
        - **reproduction**: WebFetch https://www.gevernova.com/content/dam/gepower-new/global/en_US/downloads/gas-new-site/resources/reference/GER-3620-P.pdf ; the fetch saves the PDF locally; extract text with pypdf and grep for 'steam severity' and 'K + (M'. Text saved at <scratch>
      - - **source**: GE Vernova, GER-3620 Rev P, Figure 36 'Baseline recommended inspection intervals: base load - natural gas fuel - dry'
        - **number_or_quote**: 7HA.01 / 9HA.01 DLN Combustion factored 25,000/900; Hot Gas Path factored 25,000/900; Major factored 50,000/1,800. 7HA.02 / 9HA.02: 25,000/720 and 50,000/1,440. Note the explicit qualifier in the figure title: 'natural gas fuel - dry'.
        - **reproduction**: Same extracted text; grep '7HA'. The figure title is the load-bearing detail: GE's baseline is defined ONLY for dry natural gas, and GER-3620 Rev P contains no hydrogen severity factor anywhere (grep for 'hydrogen' returns exactly 2 hits in 60 pages, both in the liquid-fuel Figure 9 discussion).
      - - **source**: Clean Air Task Force, 'Emissions and Performance Implications of Hydrogen Fuel in Heavy Duty Gas Turbines' (2023), citing Schonewald & Ziminsky 2007 and Ebacher/GE 2003
        - **number_or_quote**: 'for 100% hydrogen, moisture content in the flue gas doubles from 8.3% (vol.) with natural gas, to 16.9%'; 'Moisture diffusion can cause thermal barrier coatings (TBCs) to spall and cause accelerated corrosion or oxidation in base alloys.' Figure 7, 'Turbine HGP Component Life Factor Versus Hydrogen Content,' sourced to Jon Ebacher (GE), UNECE WP-6, Geneva 2003, plots life fraction on a 1.0-to-0 y-axis against 0-40 vol% H2.
        - **reproduction**: gev.db: SELECT text FROM chunks WHERE text LIKE '%moisture content in the flue gas doubles%' (chunk accession src:1598; sources.url = https://cdn.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/13144950/emissions-performance-implications-hydrogen-fuel-heavy-duty-gas-turbines.pdf). CAVEAT: I could NOT extract the plotted point values of Ebacher Figure 7 — it is a raster/nested-form image and pdftoppm is unavailable on this machine. I report only its axes and source, not interior values.
      - - **source**: ETN Global, 'Hydrogen Gas Turbines' report, October 2024, section 4.3.2
        - **number_or_quote**: '...will increase the moisture content in the exhaust gas. This can cause higher heat transfer to the gas turbine hot gas path components ... and may require an adaptation of the cooling system to avoid overheating of components ... the stability and life of thermal barrier coatings can be influenced. Since the water content in the exhaust gas depends mainly on the global fuel-to-air ratio and thus on the turbine inlet temperature, larger high efficiency gas turbines are likely to be more affected by this.'
        - **reproduction**: WebFetch https://etn.global/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/ETN-Global-Hydrogen-Gas-Turbines-Report-10-2024.pdf then pypdf-extract (saved as .../scratchpad/etn.txt) and grep 'water content'. The last clause is the asymmetry that matters: GEV's franchise is the highest-TIT machines, so GEV is the most exposed OEM, not the least.
      - - **source**: ETN Global 2024, Table 3 'Required gas turbine plant modifications with respect to CO2 reduction and hydrogen blend'
        - **number_or_quote**: Across all four blend bands (<=15, <=30, <=60, <=100 vol% H2) the HGP row reads 'No changes / No changes / No changes / No changes'. Same report also: 'If a diluent (e.g., water or steam) is required for NOx control, this will typically reduce the maintenance interval for the hot gas path components or lead to gas turbine power output derating.'
        - **reproduction**: grep 'Table 3' in .../scratchpad/etn.txt. This is an internal contradiction inside the industry's own consensus document: the summary table books HGP impact at literally zero for every blend, while the technical chapter says the opposite and concludes 'further research is needed to understand these effects in detail.' The zero is an assumption, not a measurement.
      - - **source**: GE Vernova product pages for 7HA and 9HA (gevernova.com/gas-power/products/gas-turbines/7ha and /9ha), accessed 2026-09-22

This makes S = 1.44 an upper bound. (2) The M = 0.55 value is specific to FSX-414 stage-2/3 nozzle material on a wet control curve; HA-class hardware differs and GER-3620 explicitly says 'Refer to unit specific documentation for HA-class' for several factors. (3) A DLN combustor purpose-designed for hydrogen (DLN 2.6e) may already carry cooling-flow margin to absorb the higher gas-side heat transfer — in which case the penalty is paid as an efficiency/output derate rather than as a shorter interval, which moves the impact from services margin to equipment performance guarantees. - **dead_ends**:
  - DERATE AT BLEND. I expected to find a quantified output/efficiency derate at moderate H2 blends that would hit GEV performance guarantees. The literature says the opposite: Ciani et al. (JGPPS 2019, doi:10.33737/jgpps/110717) demonstrate 0-70 vol% H2 on Ansaldo's GT36 'at full nominal exit temperature, i.e., without any derating,' and ETN 2024 attributes derate risk not to hydrogen itself but to the NOx abatement chosen (SCR, or diluent injection) on legacy burners. On modern DLN hardware there is no derate story. CLOSED.
  - WOBBE INDEX AS A SCREENING CONSTRAINT. I expected Wobbe limits (GE's GEI-41040 spec, +/-5%) to be a hard gate on blending. ETN 2024 kills this explicitly: hydrogen has much higher LHV per mass but 'its Wobbe Index is only slightly lower' than natural gas, so Wobbe barely moves with H2 and 'illustrates a limitation of using Wobbe Index for fuels containing hydrogen.' The real constraints are volumetric fuel flow (x1.54 at 50 vol%, x3.32 at 100%, driving skid/valve/nozzle resizing) and flame speed. Wobbe is a red herring. CLOSED.
  - NOx AS A BLEND-LIMITING ECONOMIC PENALTY. ETN 2024 shows that on an energy-normalised basis the widely-quoted NOx increase is largely an artefact: 'the normalised NOx emissions from hydrogen combustion can be quoted up to 40% higher than for natural gas without any change in the absolute amount of NOx emitted into the atmosphere.' Combined with GEV's <25 ppm dry at 100% H2 on the new B/E DLN, NOx does not generate a quantifiable financial line. CLOSED.
  - GER-3620 FIGURE 9 AS A HYDROGEN SEVERITY CURVE. This is a trap the team should be warned about. GER-3620 Rev P Figure 9 is titled 'Estimated effect of fuel type on maintenance' with axes 'Increasing Hydrogen Content in Fuel' vs 'Increasing Fuel Severity Factor,' plotting Natural Gas / Distillates / Residual (Light, Heavy). It is about the mass H/C ratio of LIQUID hydrocarbons and flame luminosity/sooting — higher H/C means less soot, less radiant flux, LOWER severity. It points the opposite way from H2 blending and must not be cited as evidence that hydrogen is benign for maintenance. GER-3620 Rev P contains only 2 occurrences of 'hydrogen' in 60 pages, both in this liquid-fuel passage. CLOSED as evidence, FLAGGED as a misreading risk.
  - PEAKER STARTS-SEVERITY ANGLE (adjacent, discovered through this lens, does not clear the bar). GER-3620 Fig. 13 gives peaking-fast start factors: starts-based combustion inspection As = 4.0 for B/E-class, 2.0 for F-class; starts-based HGP Ps = 3.5 B/E, 1.2 F-class; and notably 'Refer to unit specific documentation for HA-class' — GE does not publish HA fast-start factors. Combined with the corpus fact that ~60% of planned US gas is simple-cycle peakers and my EIA-860M cut (prime_mover 'GT' planned: 2,281 MW in 2026, 6,988 in 2027, 6,978 in 2028, 4,760 in 2029), a peaker at ~10% capacity factor hits its combustion inspection on the STARTS criterion roughly 16x earlier than on the hours criterion, and about 1.7x more often per calendar year than a baseload CC running nine times the hours. I sized the CSA margin exposure at roughly $45M/yr of unrecovered parts = ~$4.20/share and stopped: OEMs price peaker CSAs per start or per event, not per hour, so the mispricing almost certainly is not there, and the ground overlaps the team's existing fired-hours work. Reported so the team does not spend days on it.
  - GERMAN STromVKG / KWSG H2-READY TENDER AS AN ORDER WEDGE. Real and dated (9 GW in 2026, bid rounds 8 Sep and 22 Dec 2026, EU state aid approved 2 Sep 2026, H2-capability required), but I could size GEV's realistic share at only ~$3.80/share even on generous assumptions, against a domestic Siemens Energy incumbent. Kept as the dated test for finding 2 rather than as a wedge of its own.
  - EBACHER (GE, 2003) HGP LIFE-FACTOR CURVE — COULD NOT EXTRACT. The single best number in this lens would be the plotted values of CATF Figure 7, 'Turbine HGP Component Life Factor Versus Hydrogen Content,' sourced to Jon Ebacher of GE (UNECE WP-6, Geneva, 2003). I recovered the axes from the PDF text layer (life fraction 1.0 down to 0, hydrogen 0-40 vol%) and the caption, but the curve itself is a raster/nested-form image; pypdf could not isolate it and pdftoppm is not installed on this machine, so I could not read interior values. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP for the team: open https://cdn.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/13144950/emissions-performance-implications-hydrogen-fuel-heavy-duty-gas-turbines.pdf at page 14 and digitise Figure 7 by eye. If that curve shows life fraction dropping to ~0.5 or below by 30-40 vol% H2, it is GE's own number, it is far more severe than my steam-equivalent derivation (which gives ~0.70 at 50 vol%), and finding 1's confidence goes from 3 to 5.
  - ASME JEGTP 2025 HOT-SECTION MATERIALS REVIEW — PAYWALLED. asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/gasturbinespower/article/147/8/081013 returned HTTP 403 and I found no open-access mirror. I did not paywall-bypass and I do not cite its contents. It is the most likely source of a peer-reviewed metal-temperature delta in degrees for H2 vs CH4 firing; if the team has university library access, it is the highest-value single paper to retrieve.
  - OVERALL LENS VERDICT. Hydrogen co-firing does not produce a wedge on GE Vernova that clears the $10/share (1%) bar on a 3-12 month horizon. The physics is real, the mechanism is genuinely unpriced and genuinely undisclosed, and the industry's own consensus document contains a documented internal contradiction about it — but there is no installed or contracted base for it to act on. US planned hydrogen-fired turbine capacity is zero. I am reporting this plainly rather than inflating it.

## [Research] research:hot_section_materials

- **lens**: Hot-section materials physics and the supply chain beneath the ramp: TBC/superalloy life limits, GE's own factored-hours/factored-starts life-consumption algebra, and single-crystal casting capacity — tested against GEV's services accounting and the announced 20→30 GW/yr gas ramp.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: GE's own maintenance algebra charges a factored start for every ≥20% load step in ≤10 seconds — the exact signature of a behind-the-meter AI training campus — while GEV's CSAs bill per fired hour. GEV's canonical worked example for this term is an islanded arc-furnace mill, and it has now sold ~5.4 GW of 7HA into structurally identical duty.
    - **physical_fact**: GER-3620 Rev P (GE Vernova, released 2021-03-15), Figure 42, hot-gas-path starts-based criterion: Factored Starts = 0.5·N_A + N_B + 1.3·N_P + Ps·F + Σ(a_Ti−1)·T_i + Σ(a_Li−1)·L_i, where L = annual number of load steps ≥20% and a_L = exp(0.0137 × %Load Step). GE defines the trigger as "more than +/- 20% of GT rated load change in 10 seconds or less." Appendix A.3 (Example 3) works it: a 6F.03 powering an islanded electro-intensive steel mill executed 30 load steps beyond ±20%, producing 25.4 Load Step Factored Starts — i.e. 0.85 factored starts per event; a ±50% step alone costs exp(0.0137×50)−1 = 0.98 factored starts. I reproduced GE's per-row table values exactly from the formula (±20%: 6 steps→1.9 FS; ±50%: 3 steps→3.0 FS; ±95%: 1 step→2.7 FS). Figure 36 sets 7HA.02/9HA.02 HGP inspection at 25,000 factored fired hours OR 720 factored starts, whichever comes first (7HA.01/9HA.01: 25,000/900). Trip severity factors from Example A.2: a_T = 6.5 at 50% load, 8 at base load, 10 at peak — a single trip from base load consumes 7 extra factored starts.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — Contractual Service Agreement (CSA) estimated total contract cost, which flows to 'net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability' (10-Q/10-K Note 9) and to Power services operating margin. Direction: negative. GEV's own critical-accounting-estimate language names this exact variable: 'A significant estimate in determining expected revenues is estimating how customers will utilize their assets over the contract term.' CSAs are billed on utilization (per hour of usage) and at major maintenance events, but the contract PRICE is fixed at signing; if the realized duty cycle generates load-step factored starts, the starts-based HGPI limit binds long before the 25,000-factored-fired-hour limit, so outage and hot-section parts cost is incurred 2–4x faster than the fired-hours revenue accrual assumed at underwriting. Under ASC 606 cost-to-cost percentage-of-completion, the re-estimate is booked as an immediate cumulative catch-up across the elapsed portion of the affected book.
    - **direction**: short

The underlying physics is stated by GE in the same document: 'Higher operating temperatures affect the creep capability of hot gas path components which is the primary life limiting mechanism' (p.8), with peak-fire severity exponential in ΔT_fire (one hour at +100°F peak fire = six hours at base load).

## [Research] research:smr_nuclear_timeline

- **lens**: BWRX-300 SMR engineering/schedule reality vs. the market's option value in GEV. Net result: the SMR option is real but small and far out of the money on the customer's own economics. I could bound total nuclear/SMR option value at $15-32/share (1.6-3.4%), materially less than the narrative implies, and I found a published academic viability threshold (~$5,000/kWe) that the BWRX-300's four independently-sourced realized capex points (US$12,530-17,949/kW) miss by 2.5-3.6x. The regulatory/licensing leg is de-risking, not risking, which kills the obvious bear catalyst.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: GEV's entire nuclear/SMR option is worth $15-32/share (1.6-3.4%), bounded two independent ways — nuclear is not where the GEV argument is won or lost
    - **physical_fact**: GVH's announced BWRX-300 pipeline is ~15 GW gross (Darlington 4 units = 1.2 GW with FID and one basemat poured 22 Apr 2026; US-Japan TN+AL = 3.0 GW; Poland OSGE 10-24 units; Hungary up to 10 units LOI; SaskPower up to 4; Blue Energy TX up to 5 = 1.5 GW; Estonia 1-2). Of that, exactly 0.3 GW has concrete poured and 1.2 GW has an FID. GE-Hitachi Nuclear Energy Americas LLC is 60% owned by GE Vernova (10-K Exhibit 21.1, filed 2025-02-06 and 2026-01-29) — GEV books 60% of the economics, 40% is Hitachi's noncontrolling interest. GEV does not separately disclose nuclear revenue in segment reporting, so the widely-cited '$2B steady-state / 2.6% of revenue' is a sell-side estimate, not a filing number.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — nuclear equipment and services revenue, and the portion of GEV's 35x forward P/E attributable to SMR optionality. Direction: caps the upside case; a Clinch River permit or slip moves only a few dollars per share either way.
    - **direction**: kills-an-existing-angle
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: GE Vernova 10-K Exhibit 21.1, filed 2025-02-06 and 2026-01-29 (corpus chunks, kind='sec', tier='primary')

    - **materiality_dollars_per_share**: Method A (pure-play comp): 15 GW announced pipeline x $550M/GW (mid of Oklo $537M and NuScale $565M) = $8.25B gross x 60% GEV ownership of GE-Hitachi = $4.95B / 266,333,581 shares = $18.59/share = 1.98% of $940.33. Low bound 15 GW x $454M x 0.60 = $4.09B = $15.34/share (1.63%). High bound, ignoring the 40% Hitachi NCI, 15 GW x $565M x 1.00 = $8.47B = $31.82/share (3.38%). Method B (fundamental, independent): $2B/yr steady-state nuclear revenue x 15% EBITDA margin = $300M EBITDA x 60% GEV share = $180M x 25x = $4.50B / 266,333,581 = $16.90/share = 1.80%. The two methods converge within 10% at ~$17-19/share. Central estimate $18/share (1.9%); defensible ceiling $32/share (3.4%). That figure covers the ENTIRE nuclear franchise including legacy BWR fleet fuel and services, so the SMR-only slice is strictly smaller.

Sell-side frames nuclear qualitatively ('small now, big future'). I could not find the 60%-ownership haircut applied, nor the pure-play $/GW-of-pipeline comp method applied to GEV, nor any published $/share bound. I cannot know whether someone has done this internally.
    - **testable_prediction**: NRC staff recommended issuance of the Clinch River construction permit in June 2026 (several months early; review hours cut from 25,000 to 16,500) and the Commission decision is expected by December 2026. Prediction: on permit issuance GEV moves less than 3% on the news and gives most of it back within five sessions, because the event is worth ~$3-6/share on this arithmetic. Corollary: on the Q3'26 call (Oct 28 2026) management will again decline to give a standalone nuclear revenue or margin figure.
    - **kill_condition**: Killed if (a) GEV begins reporting nuclear as a separate segment or discloses SMR-specific RPO above ~$5B, meaning booked scope far larger than the comp method implies; or (b) a single BWRX-300 order lands with disclosed GEV content above ~$1.5B/GW, breaking the $550M/GW comp; or (c) GEV re-rates more than 8% on a nuclear-only headline with no other news, showing the market is capitalizing far more than $32/share.

    - **novelty**: 4
    - **confidence**: 4
    - **materiality**: 3
    - **caveats**: The 15 GW pipeline mixes FID'd units with non-binding MOUs and LOIs; counting only FID'd capacity collapses the value to ~$1.5/share, so the estimate is deliberately generous to the bull. The $2B nuclear revenue figure is sell-side, not disclosed — GEV does not break out nuclear, which is itself why no one can audit this. Pure-play comps are contaminated: Oklo and NuScale carry speculative retail premia that may not transfer to a diversified industrial, which biases my estimate HIGH (conservative for the conclusion). 25x is the mandated multiple; nuclear equipment arguably deserves less.
  - - **title**: Four independent sources put realized BWRX-300 capex at US$12,530-17,949/kW — 5.6-8.0x GE Hitachi's own advertised $2,250/kW and 2.5-3.6x the ~$5,000/kWe threshold at which the peer-reviewed literature says a colocated SMR beats grid supply for a hyperscaler
    - **physical_fact**: Li, She & Zhang (arXiv:2608.10999, 11 Aug 2026) co-optimize a BWRX-300 plus absorption-chiller plant against a 200 MWe ERCOT data center across 109 scenario runs and find: 'At 2023 mid-range reactor capital, the nuclear configurations cost 49-62% more than grid supply even with the Section 45Y production tax credit. The viable region opens near $5,000 kWe-1.' Against that threshold, four independent realized/committed BWRX-300 capex points: OPG's four-unit Darlington envelope C$20.9B / 1,200 MW = C$17.4M/MW = US$12,530/kW at 0.72; OPG unit 1 ~US$15,000/kW; the US-Japan package $40B / 3 GW = US$13,333/kW; and TVA's own filings at US$17,949/kW overnight in 2024 dollars. GE Hitachi's advertised figure is US$2.25M/MW, confirmed two ways (IAEA ARIS/Steigerwald 2023 as tabulated in Rao et al. 2026; and quoted by the World Nuclear Industry Status Report as 'US$2.25-million per megawatt').
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — nuclear equipment orders and the conversion rate of the ~15 GW announced BWRX-300 pipeline into RPO. Direction: negative. Commercial (non-government-backstopped) units do not clear a hyperscaler's own hurdle, so the pipeline beyond Darlington and the US-Japan 3 GW is unlikely to convert on the announced timeline.

Its design basis bounds it between 435 and 870 MWth (a 50% minimum-load fraction) with a ramp limit of 522 MWth/h, i.e. 1%/min (Li, She & Zhang 2026, citing the BWRX-300 design basis); IAEA ARIS-derived sources state 50-100% load following at 0.5%/min. On a 300 MWe unit that is 1.5-3.0 MW/min across a 150 MW maneuvering band — 50 to 100 minutes to traverse. Refueling is a 701-contiguous-hour outage, capping capacity factor at 0.92. By contrast GEV's own 7HA.03 is rated 430 MW with a 75 MW/min ramp and reaches full simple-cycle load in 10 minutes, turning down to zero. Absolute ramp ratio 25-50x; per-MW-installed 17.4%/min vs 0.5-1%/min. Meanwhile AI clusters swing far faster than either: 'large-scale GPU clusters can produce power fluctuations of hundreds of megawatts within only seconds' (arXiv:2509.07218v6).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment gas equipment revenue and the 20-year contractual service agreement annuity. Direction: positive/protective. Every SMR site needing firm dispatchable power before 2032 must buy a fast-ramping bridge, and GEV sells it. Equally important defensively: this bounds the 'AI data centers will go nuclear instead of gas' bear case on GEV's 116 GW gas pipeline.

(1) FATAL — the physical fact is an artifact. The "6.8-point, 10.6% relative decline in the newest cohort" does not exist. Separately, the author's evidence set contains a conflation worth naming. The Duke study's 76-126 GW of headroom is an argument about NEW CAPACITY NOT GETTING BUILT — that is a Power EQUIPMENT orders mechanism, on a 2028+ timeline, outside a 3-12 month horizon. It is not a fired-hours mechanism on the installed fleet. The finding cites it as support for a services-utilization thesis, but the two channels are separable and only the smaller one (85 curtailment hours) actually reaches the services line the finding names.

What I agree with: the $4.49/MWh implied-rate decomposition of management's $500M/GW is correct, clean, and genuinely useful. I set it at 0.60%, sourced from Duke/Norris's 85 curtailment hours per year against 5,563 baseload fired hours (1.53%), discounted by 40% for the US-exposed share of a global fleet.

The 40% US-exposure discount is itself an unverified judgment of mine and is the weakest link on my side. But note that even removing it entirely — using the full 1.53% — gives only $3.18/share. The gap to the author's number is not recoverable through my assumptions; it lives in the artifact.

Secondary assumptions, both mine and both unverifiable from disclosure: the 70% hours-elastic share of gas services revenue (author used 60%) and the 30% incremental services EBITDA margin (same as author's). ## [Research] research:memory_bound_inference

- **lens**: Memory-bandwidth wall → realized data-center electrical load → gas-turbine duty cycle → GEV services economics. The assigned hypothesis (low realized load factor ⇒ fewer fired hours ⇒ less services revenue) is WRONG on the physics and I killed it. But chasing it into GE's own maintenance-interval standard surfaced a different and larger mechanism: the memory wall makes AI load *volatile*, not just *low*, and GER-3620 Rev P charges volatility against the factored-STARTS clock, not the hours clock.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The load-step term: AI power volatility burns GEV's factored-starts maintenance clock with zero actual starts and zero extra fired hours — and <1 load step per day flips a baseload 9HA from hours-limited to starts-limited
    - **physical_fact**: GER-3620 Rev P (GE Vernova, released 2021-03-15), Figure 42, adds a load-step adder to factored starts: aL = exp(0.0137 x %load step), contributing (aL - 1) x L factored starts, applied to every load change exceeding +/-20% of GT rated load in 10 seconds or less. A +/-30% step adds 0.508 factored starts; +/-50% adds 0.984; +/-100% adds 2.935. Baseline HGP/combustion interval for 7HA.01/9HA.01 is 25,000 factored fired hours OR 900 factored starts; for 7HA.02/9HA.02 it is 25,000 FFH / 720 factored starts (Figure 36). The hours-based load severity factor Ap = 1.0 up to base load, so the hours clock cannot run faster. Separately, trip severity is 8:1 from 80-100% load and 10:1 from peak load (Figure 19). The physical driver on the IT side is the memory wall: measured on an NVIDIA H200 (700 W TDP, 4.8 TB/s HBM3e), decode draws 137-300 W (20-43% of TDP) with tensor cores >88% idle because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, while prefill draws ~90% of TDP. The prefill-to-decode swing is therefore 47-70 percentage points of rated GPU power — far above the +/-20% threshold — and it is a hardware property, not a user-behavior property.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment, 'net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability' on contractual service agreements (10-K/10-Q Note on Contract and Other Deferred Assets), and Power Services EBITDA margin. Direction: NEGATIVE near term. GEV recognizes CSA revenue on a percentage-of-completion basis against estimated LIFETIME contract cost. Load-step and trip factoring raises the number of combustion/HGP/major events expected over a 15-25 year contract without raising fired hours or actual starts. Because the exposed contracts were priced on a duty-cycle model built for baseload gas, the extra parts life consumed lands as a cumulative catch-up unfavorable revision. The same physics is POSITIVE over a 5-10 year horizon for contracts whose factoring formula includes the Rev-P load-step term, because GE LTSAs bill per factored fired hour and per factored start — that is the mechanism for management's $15M/GW-yr to $25M/GW-yr services-yield bridge. The near-term, dated, larger leg is the margin drag.
    - **direction**: short
    - **evidence**:
      - - **source**: GE Vernova, GER-3620 Rev P, 'Heavy-Duty Gas Turbine Operating and Maintenance Considerations', released 2021-03-15, Figure 42 and Appendix A.3 (60pp PDF, gevernova.com/content/dam/gepower-new/global/en_US/downloads/gas-new-site/resources/reference/GER-3620-P.pdf)
        - **number_or_quote**: aL = Exp(0.0137 x % Load Step); L = Annual Number of Load Steps >= 20%. Load steps are 'defined as more than +/- 20% of GT rated load change in 10 seconds or less.'
        - **reproduction**: I implemented aL=exp(0.0137*p) and applied (aL-1)*n to GE's own Appendix A.3 worked example (6F.03 steel-mill case, 30 load steps). My per-amplitude results match GE's published table to within 0.05 factored starts at every one of 13 amplitudes, and my total is 25.4 vs GE's stated 25.4. Script: scratchpad/ (aL lambda + GE table dict). The formula is verified against the vendor's own arithmetic.
      - - **source**: GE Vernova GER-3620 Rev P, Figure 36 ('Baseline recommended inspection intervals: base load - natural gas fuel - dry') and hours-based criterion text
        - **number_or_quote**: 7HA.01 / 9HA.01: Combustion (DLN) Factored 25000/900, Hot Gas Path 25000/900, Major 50000/1800. 7HA.02 / 9HA.02: 25000/720, 25000/720, 50000/1440. 'Ap = 1.0 up to base load.'
        - **reproduction**: Text-extracted the full 60-page PDF with pypdf to scratchpad/ger3620p.txt and grepped for '7HA','9HA','Load Factor','Part Load'. The Ap=1.0 cap is the reason the naive load-factor thesis fails and the reason the starts clock is the only clock that can move.
      - - **source**: 'The Illusion of Power Capping in LLM Decode: A Phase-Aware Energy Characterisation Across Attention Architectures', arXiv:2605.11999v1 (2026)

Independently, whole-facility simulation driven by measured H100 power traces at 0.1 s resolution found that even when 100% of nodes were concurrently utilized, facility power reached only ~73% of rated design for a colocation profile and ~80% for an LLM-inference profile, with peak-to-average ratios of 1.24-2.56 (colocation) and 1.21-2.04 (inference) across 20-80% target utilization (Vercellino et al., arXiv:2604.07345v1, Tables 3 and 4). The cited POLCA result puts inference power headroom at ~21% of TDP versus ~3% for training, enabling ~30% more effective capacity per provisioned watt. The root cause is the memory wall: decode cannot draw TDP because it is bandwidth-bound. - **dead_ends**:
  - THE ASSIGNED LENS HYPOTHESIS IS DEAD, and this is the single most useful thing I can hand the team. The brief argues: realized data-center load factors below the assumed 80-90% mean the same installed GW produces fewer FIRED HOURS and less services revenue. The physics forbids this. GER-3620 Rev P states 'Ap = 1.0 up to base load' — the hours-based load severity factor is CAPPED at 1.0 and has no value below 1. Fired hours are wall-clock hours while the machine is fired, independent of load. A turbine behind a data center drawing 60% of contracted nameplate still runs ~8,000 fired hours a year and still accrues ~8,000 FACTORED hours. Load factor can only reduce fired hours by causing SHUTDOWNS (unit commitment), not by part-loading — and a behind-the-meter unit dedicated to a 24/7 AI campus does not shut down. Do not build a short on 'low DC load factor starves GEV services fired hours.' It is wrong.
  - 'Part-load operation will show up as degraded heat rate in the EIA fleet data' — KILLED with data. Implied US combined-cycle heat rate (fuel on CT/CA/CS rows, NG) is FLAT: 7,451 / 7,402 / 7,397 / 7,419 Btu/kWh for 2022 / 2023 / 2024 / 2025. There is no part-load degradation signal in the national CC fleet. Query: SELECT sum(fuel_consumed_mmbtu), sum(net_generation_mwh) FROM generation WHERE prime_mover IN ('CT','CA','CS') AND fuel_type='NG' GROUP BY year. If anyone on the team wants to argue the US gas fleet is being pushed into part-load duty, this dataset says no.
  - 'GEV bills ACTUAL hours while cost accrues on FACTORED hours, so cycling destroys CSA margin' — this is the obvious version of the wedge and it is WRONG, or at least not established. GE LTSAs commonly bill per FACTORED fired hour (combined cycle) and per FACTORED start (simple cycle); Entergy is a documented example of exactly this split (power-eng.com, 'Long-Term Service Agreements: Weighing the Risks and Rewards'). The 10-K's 'per hour of usage' is ambiguous and does not settle it. The real fork is narrower and is what Finding 1 turns on: whether a given contract's factoring formula includes the GER-3620 Rev P LOAD-STEP adder, which appears to be a recent addition motivated by 'the advent of non-synchronous generation' and which most 15-25 year contracts on the installed base would predate.
  - The gas-equipment channel for the provisioning/load-factor short — KILLED for the 3-12 month horizon. GEV is SUPPLY-constrained, not demand-constrained: slots are effectively sold out through 2028-2030, reported lead times reach 243 weeks, and pricing is rising toward a projected $600/kW by end-2027 (up ~3x from 2019). A 10-20% reduction in MW required per unit of AI compute shortens the queue; it does not reduce bookings while demand exceeds deliverable supply. Any short thesis routed through 'AI needs less gas than people think' has no transmission mechanism to GEV revenue inside the pitch window. Route it through Electrification (MVA-priced, less supply-constrained) instead.
  - Simple-cycle peaker capacity factors — reproduced independently but adds nothing new. US NG simple-cycle (prime_mover='GT') operating capacity 161.1 GW; capacity factor 10.4% (2023), 11.3% (2024), 11.2% (2025); implied heat rate ~11,815-11,950 Btu/kWh. This confirms the team's existing ~10% peaker capacity-factor fact from an independent dataset but is not itself a wedge. Planned NG additions by prime mover (vintage 2026-07) also confirm the peaker-heavy near term: GT 2.3/7.0/7.0/4.8 GW for 2026/27/28/29 vs combined-cycle (CT+CA+CS) 1.9/4.2/9.1/8.6 GW — simple-cycle is ~60% of 2026-27 but the mix flips to combined-cycle by 2029-30.
  - The corpus 'projects' table (130 GE-linked rows) is too noisy for exposure sizing. Extraction quality is poor: capacity_mw and turbine_count are frequently 'not specified' / 'N/A', owner fields contain values like 'Elon Musk' and duplicated GEV rows, and the same project appears 3-4 times with inconsistent fields. I abandoned it and used GEV's own disclosure (~20% of the ~100 GW under contract is data-center tied) plus EIA-860M instead. Worth flagging to whoever maintains the corpus as a phase-2 extractor defect.
  - arXiv:2604.10769v1 ('Workload composition smooths aggregate power demand while sustaining short-horizon ramps in AI data centers') looked like the ideal corroboration for absolute load-step magnitudes and does not deliver — the authors normalize power by scenario-specific mean total power and report only relative temporal structure, median normalized 15-minute ramp rates, and COV. No absolute MW, no percent-of-nameplate, no event-frequency tallies. Do not spend time on it for magnitude evidence.
  - NOTE, not a dead end but a caution that cuts against Finding 1: the load-step problem has a known engineering mitigation and GEV SELLS it. Behind-the-meter vendors market UPS and BESS buffering plus staged modular capacity specifically to shield turbines from 'sudden large AI-driven load steps' and claim it will 'reduce wear, lower unplanned maintenance' (datacenterdynamics.com; bergenengines.com). If buffering is deployed at scale the factored-starts mechanism is blunted — but the volatility then monetizes through GEV's Electrification segment (grid-forming BESS, STATCOMs, synchronous condensers) instead of through Power services. For a GEV LONG this is a genuine heads-I-win/tails-I-win structure and may be the more useful way to use this research.

## [Research] research:ambient_derating_siting

- **lens**: Ambient derating and the geography of where GE Vernova's gas turbines actually go — quantified derate curves for H-class machines, fleet-weighted against where EIA says the planned US gas fleet is being built, and then followed through GE's own maintenance-interval physics (GER-3620 Rev P) into GEV's service-contract accounting.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The 34.7-hour rule: HA-class maintenance is STARTS-limited, not hours-limited, in the duty cycle GEV is actually shipping into — and GEV's own critical accounting estimate keys LTSA revenue to hours
    - **physical_fact**: GE Vernova GER-3620 Rev P (released 2021-03-15), Figure 36, p.29: 7HA.02 and 9HA.02 combustion AND hot-gas-path inspection intervals are 25,000 factored fired hours OR 720 factored fired starts, whichever comes first; major inspection 50,000 / 1,440. 7HA.01 and 9HA.01 are 25,000/900 and 50,000/1,800. The ratio 25,000/720 = 34.7 fired hours per start is the exact crossover: below a mean fired-run length of 34.7 hours the starts clock binds first, and it binds regardless of capacity factor because both clocks scale linearly with run time. For the .01 machines the crossover is 27.8 h. GER-3620 p.16 adds multipliers that only make the starts side worse: peak-load start/stop cycle factor 1.3, trip from base load 8:1, trip from PEAK load 10:1, trip from 50% load 6.5:1 (part-load cycles below 60% get a 0.5 credit). Measured against this, the realized US fleet duty cycle (computed from EIA-923 joined to EIA-860M inside the corpus) is: simple-cycle gas (prime mover GT) capacity factor 10.5% / 11.4% / 11.2% in 2023 / 2024 / 2025; combined-cycle gas-turbine side (prime mover CT) 56.3% / 57.3% / 55.6%. A peaker at 11.2% CF = 981 equivalent full-load hours per year; for its 25,000-hour clock to bind before 720 starts it would have to start fewer than 32 times a year, i.e. average 35 hours per run — physically impossible for a peaker (typical runs are 3-8 h, implying 123-327 starts/yr). Time to first hot-gas-path event is therefore 1.7-4.5 years on the starts clock versus 22.2 years on the hours clock: the starts clock binds by 5-13x. Even a 55.6%-CF combined cycle is starts-limited above 140 starts per year, which daily-cycling CCGTs exceed.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment: (1) 'net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability' on contractual service agreements, disclosed in 10-Q/10-K Note 9 — and this line is 100% Power (Q2'26 Note 9 shows contractual service agreement assets of $5,399M in Power, $0 in Electrification, $0 in Wind); (2) Power services gross margin; (3) Power segment EBITDA. Direction: negative. The transmission mechanism is GEV's own stated critical accounting estimate. The 2025 Form 10-K (filed 2026-01-29) says: 'a significant estimate in determining expected revenues of a contract is estimating how customers will utilize their assets over the term of the agreement,' and the billing basis is 'per hour of usage' plus payment 'upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.' Revenue is recognized percentage-of-completion on COSTS INCURRED. So the cost schedule is set by factored STARTS while the billings estimate is anchored to hours of usage. A peaker-duty or daily-cycling HA unit delivers a ~2-4 year parts-and-labor cycle against a ~1,000-hour billing year. When GEV re-estimates utilization and finds the customer is running short, frequent, peak-rated blocks rather than long base-load blocks, total estimated contract costs rise faster than total estimated billings and the contract takes an unfavorable cumulative catch-up.

    - **caveats**: Biggest weakness: I can establish the physics and the accounting channel, but NOT causation for the observed $218M. GEV attributed FY24's $319M to 'higher costs' generically and gives no duty-cycle breakout, so the attribution is a hypothesis with a dated test, not a demonstrated fact. Second: GER-3620's published intervals are the BASELINE recommendation; actual contracted intervals are unit- and contract-specific and GE routinely extends them on operating experience (the document says so explicitly). Third: the 34.7-hour crossover is exact only if factored hours equal actual fired hours; peak firing, water/steam injection and distillate all inflate the hours side and would push the crossover down further, so 34.7 h is a conservative upper bound for the starts-limited regime. Fourth: my 123-327 starts/yr for peakers is inferred from capacity factor divided by an assumed 3-8 h run length, not from a starts dataset — I could not find a citable US starts-per-year series (EIA-923 in the corpus is annual only, no monthly or event data). The argument survives this because even the most generous assumption (8 h runs) leaves the starts clock binding 4x sooner than the hours clock. Fifth: counter-evidence I found and did not suppress — one trade source notes that more than half of GEV's recent orders are HA-class machines that customers typically run at higher capacity factors, which would put part of the book on the hours side of the line. Sixth: direction depends on the billing basis; if CSAs are actually indexed to factored hours the whole effect flows to revenue instead of margin and the sign flips to bullish.

  - - **title**: GEV's 116 GW is ISO-rated iron, and EIA's planned-capacity numbers are generator nameplate — the fleet-weighted summer derate at the actual sites is 10.8-15.0%, which is a bullish argument for unit count, not a bearish argument about backlog quality
    - **physical_fact**: Heavy-duty gas turbine power output falls 0.5-0.9% for every 1 degC rise in ambient inlet temperature, with heavy-duty frames at the low end of that band and aeroderivatives at the high end (Giannakopoulos / Roumpedakis et al., 'Thermal Energy Storage For Gas Turbine Power Augmentation', Journal of the Global Power and Propulsion Society 3:592-608, 2019, DOI 10.33737/jgpps/110254, citing Kakaras et al. 2004 and Cole et al. 2014). ISO rating conditions are 15 degC, sea level, 60% RH. Applying 0.5-0.7%/degC plus ~1.07% per 100 m of altitude to the 51.3 GW of US gas-turbine capacity (EIA-860M prime movers CT/GT/CS, natural gas, planned_year 2026-2031, vintage 2026-07) weighted by ASHRAE-approximate state summer design dry-bulb temperatures gives a fleet-weighted summer derate of 10.76% at 0.5%/degC and 14.95% at 0.7%/degC. The geography drives it: Texas alone is 15.33 GW of the 51.3 GW (30%) at ~14% derate, Louisiana 5.66 GW at ~12%, Oklahoma 2.73 GW at ~14%, Arizona 1.68 GW at ~17%. Crucially the reported MW are NOT already site-derated: planned CT units in Louisiana, Mississippi and Arkansas are listed at 469.3-478.0 MW each and Georgia's Yates units at 482.8 MW, which is at or above the ISO simple-cycle rating of the largest 60 Hz H-class machines — EIA-860M reports GENERATOR nameplate, which is deliberately sized above the turbine's ISO output so the generator is not the limit on cold days.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment equipment revenue and Power equipment unit shipments, direction POSITIVE. A data center or a capacity-market obligation is denominated in firm summer MW; the turbine is sold in ISO GW. To hold a given firm summer MW at a hot site you must buy 1/(1-derate) times the ISO GW. This means the GW demand curve the market extrapolates from data-center MW announcements is structurally 12-18% larger than the MW arithmetic suggests, which supports GEV's 20 GW/yr (Q3'26), 24 GW (2028) and 30 GW (2030) output targets being met by real firm-MW demand rather than speculative slot reservations. It does NOT make the backlog lower quality — GEV ships and bills the iron either way.

All of them count GW and none of them distinguishes ISO GW from summer-available MW. The physics itself is textbook and known to every power engineer — what I could not find published is anyone applying it to GEV's specific 116 GW figure or computing a fleet-weighted derate from the actual geography of the EIA planned queue, or noticing that EIA's planned MW are generator nameplate and therefore at or above ISO turbine output rather than site-derated. The novelty is in the quantification and the direction call, not the mechanism.
    - **testable_prediction**: EIA-860 ANNUAL (not 860M) reports Nameplate Capacity, Summer Capacity and Winter Capacity separately for every generator. Prediction: for the hot-state gas turbine units entering service in 2025-2026 (Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Mississippi, Arizona), the ratio Summer Capacity / Nameplate Capacity will come in at 0.86-0.92, and Winter/Summer will exceed 1.15. The 2025 final EIA-860 file is released around September 2026 and the 2026 early release around June 2027. A second, faster test: ERCOT's seasonal resource adequacy (CDR) report for Summer 2027, due around December 2026, will list these units at seasonal capability well below their EIA nameplate.
    - **kill_condition**: Killed if EIA-860 annual shows Summer/Nameplate at or above 0.97 for the new hot-state units — that would mean developers are already reporting site-derated numbers and the gap is illusory. Also killed if GEV clarifies that its '116 GW under contract' is quoted at site conditions rather than ISO, or if the incremental iron is instead supplied by inlet chilling (mechanical chillers or thermal energy storage), in which case the extra MW is bought from third parties such as Mee Industries or TES/absorption vendors and GEV captures none of it.
    - **has_dated_test**: True
    - **novelty**: 3
    - **confidence**: 3
    - **materiality**: 2
    - **caveats**: This is the weakest of the two on materiality and I am not going to dress it up. Problems: (1) The extra iron is ALREADY inside the 116 GW — the derate does not create a hidden order book, it explains why the order book is as large as it is. The finding is a support for the bull case on demand durability, not a mispricing you can trade directly. (2) My state design temperatures are ASHRAE-approximate values I assigned by hand to a representative metro per state, not site-specific ASHRAE 0.4% values; this is the softest input and probably carries +/-2 degC, i.e. +/-1.4 percentage points of derate. (3) The $265/kW and $400/kW equipment prices are derived and assumed respectively, not disclosed. (4) EIA nameplate is generator nameplate, so applying a turbine derate percentage to it is not strictly like-for-like — it biases the GW-gap estimate slightly high, though in the direction that makes the reported GW even less representative of summer MW. (5) Several of the largest hot-state planned CT units I found (Richland Parish, Waterford, Franklin Farms) are Entergy projects and are Mitsubishi-linked, not GEV — so the hot-state planned GW is NOT all GEV's, and the derate applies to the industry, not uniquely to GEV. (6) The counter-mechanism is real: operators can recover most of the derate with evaporative cooling or inlet chilling instead of buying more turbines, which would collapse this finding entirely.
    - **kill_condition_note**: None

Used solely to corroborate the GER-3620 peak-fire constant Ap = e^(0.018 x delta-Tf) for B/E-class and the '+100 degF peak fire = six base-load hours' equivalence. I could not read the article text directly and flag it as second-hand.
