Not developed into a finding.
- **dead_ends**:
  - INLET CHILLING AS A GEV REVENUE LINE — DEAD. I checked whether GEV captures the inlet-cooling scope that hot-site derate creates. The corpus academic tier's inlet-cooling literature names third-party suppliers and technologies (Mee Industries fogging and wet compression, absorption chillers, thermal energy storage tanks, Stellar/TAS-class evaporative and chiller packages); nothing in the corpus or in GEV's own materials shows GEV selling inlet cooling as a product line. Worse for the angle: the JGPPS 2019 review finds inlet cooling can REDUCE net combined-cycle output because lowering turbine exhaust temperature cuts steam-cycle heat recovery ('As the turbine outlet temperature is decreased a net reduction in the overall power output is observed due to less energy recovery from the steam turbine'), and that evaporative cooling 'is not very effective in areas of humid climate' — which rules it out across most of the Gulf Coast where the planned GW actually is. No wedge.
  - THE BULLISH READING OF OVER-FIRING — DEAD, AND ITS DEATH IS WHAT MAKES FINDING 1 WORK. GER-3620 gives the peak-fire hours severity factor Ap = e^(0.018 x delta-Tf) with delta-Tf the peak firing-temperature adder in degF, so one hour at +100 degF peak fire consumes six hours of base-load hot-gas-path life. A hot-climate unit over-firing to hold contracted MW for its ~600 hottest hours a year would burn 3,600 factored hours instead of 600. I wanted this to be a bullish services-revenue finding (more billable severity). It is not, because GEV's disclosed billing basis is 'per hour of usage', i.e. plain fired hours, not FACTORED hours. The severity multiplier therefore lands on GEV's cost estimate and not on its billings — which is the same cost/revenue mismatch as Finding 1, in the same direction, and should not be counted twice. Caveat on the physics: the 0.018 constant I could verify is published for B/E-class; GER-3620 Figure 10 shows separate curves for F and H class whose exponents I could not read out of the figure (the PDF's figure text is glyph-subset encoded), so the 6x number is illustrative for H-class, not established.
  - 'THE 116 GW IS BAD BACKLOG BECAUSE OF DERATE' — KILLED WITH EVIDENCE. The obvious bear version of the ambient lens is that GEV's contracted GW overstates the real thing. It does overstate summer-available MW by 10.8-15.0% at the actual site geography, but that is not a GEV P&L problem: GEV ships and bills ISO-rated iron, the developer takes delivery, and the shortfall is the grid's problem, not the OEM's. Direction is bullish for unit count, not bearish for backlog quality. Do not pitch this as a short.
  - EIA-923 CANNOT GIVE YOU STARTS OR MONTHLY PEAKS. The corpus generation table is annual only (year, plant_id, prime_mover, fuel_type, net_generation_mwh, fuel_consumed_mmbtu). There is no month column, so you cannot measure summer-peak output directly, and there is no start-count field anywhere in EIA-860M or EIA-923. I searched the academic tier for a citable US starts-per-year series ('"starts per year" "gas turbine"', '"cycling" "starts" "peaking" "combustion turbine"', '"start" "stop" "cycles" "peaker"') and it returned nothing usable — the academic tier's maintenance hits are about SMRs and generic maintenance-strategy papers. NREL/SR-5500-55433 'Power Plant Cycling Costs' (Kumar et al., 2012) is the right document but docs.nrel.gov would not resolve from this environment. If someone wants to harden Finding 1, the missing input is a starts-per-year distribution for US simple-cycle CTs — NERC GADS, EPRI, or ERCOT/PJM unit-commitment data are the places to get it.
  - TRANSFORMER THERMAL AGEING AS AN ELECTRIFICATION WEDGE — NOT DEVELOPED, FLAGGED AS A LEAD. IEEE C57.91's Arrhenius model (FAA = exp[(15000/383)(1/383 - 1/theta_H)], insulation life halving every 6-8 degC above the 110 degC reference hot spot) implies a step-up or data-center transformer in Phoenix ambient runs a materially shorter life than in the 30 degC reference ambient, which would compress replacement cycles and feed Prolec GE and Electrification aftermarket. I did not build it because (a) data-center GSUs are usually not loaded to the reference hot spot, (b) utilities already de-rate for ambient at the specification stage, and (c) I could not construct a credible dollars-per-share chain in the time available. It is a real physics hook on a different segment if someone wants to run it down.
  - THE EPA COMBUSTION-TURBINE TSD IS QUALITATIVE. I fetched and text-extracted the full 27-page EPA 'Efficient Generation: Combustion Turbine Electric Generating Units' TSD (May 2023) hoping for a regulatory-grade derate curve. It discusses ambient effects, evaporative cooling and chilling systems in prose but contains zero percent-per-degree numbers, zero capacity factors and zero starts data. Do not cite it for a number.
  - GE'S OWN O&M DOC UNDERCUTS THE STANDARD DERATE MITIGATION — worth knowing, too small to be a finding. GER-3620 Rev P p.20 warns that inlet foggers 'inject a large amount of moisture in the inlet ducting, exposing the forward stages of the compressor to potential water carry-over', that this 'may lead to long-term degradation of the compressor due to corrosion, erosion, fouling, and material property degradation', and that water droplets 'may cause leading edge erosion... [which] may lead to an increased risk of blade failure'; the same document's Figure 28 shows a 5% airflow loss reduces output by up to 8% and raises heat rate by up to 3%. So the cheap fix for hot-site derate degrades the compressor that GEV then has to maintain under the LTSA. Real, GE-authored, and on-lens — but I could not size the dollar impact credibly and would be inventing numbers if I tried.

## [Verify] skeptic:demand_flexibility:KILL: the flexible-load literatu

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: FATAL DATA ERROR in measurement (1). The "74.0 GW of 7HA/9HA" row is not a customer project and not GEV's order book. I pulled the full row: projects.id=235, accession='src:3070', source_kind='NEWS', source_date='2026-05-23', owner='GE Vernova', project_name='H-class gas turbine fleet', location='' (blank), oem='GE Vernova', turbine_count='128', capacity_mw='74000', commitment_status='operating', commercial_operation_date='' (blank), and the attached quote is generic Motley Fool stock commentary ("investors traded the company's stock up by more than 3% on Tuesday"). It is a single aggregate row scraped from a press release.

Independent confirmation of what that number actually is: GE Vernova press release, May 26 2026, "GE Vernova's HA gas turbine fleet surpasses 4 million operating hours" (gevernova.com/news/press-releases/ge-vernova-ha-gas-turbine-fleet-surpasses-4-million) — the HA fleet "has grown to 128 units operating across 21 countries" representing "approximately 74 gigawatts of power plant capacity." So 74 GW is the GLOBAL, ALREADY-OPERATING, CUMULATIVE-SINCE-2016 HA installed base (and it is PLANT capacity, i.e. includes the steam bottoming cycle, not turbine nameplate: 74,000/128 = 578 MW/unit, consistent with 1x1 combined-cycle plant output, not the ~430 MW simple-cycle frame rating).

The finding then compares that 74 GW against "2027 planned US gas is 6.99 GW GT vs 4.15 GW CC." That is a double category error: global-vs-US and installed-since-2016-vs-planned-for-one-future-year. The two populations are not comparable in either dimension, so the stated contrast (74.0 GW HA against 0.1 GW of "50-MW simple-cycle turbines") carries no information about GEV's forward model mix.

The `projects` table cannot substitute. Excluding row 235, the GE-linked rows are 129 projects / 44.7 GW, of which 84 rows / 27.5 GW (61% of MW) have a BLANK model field — the finding's own caveat understates this, since with row 235 removed the blank-model bucket becomes the single largest category, not a minor residual. The table is also heavily duplicated: Vineyard Wind (one ~806 MW project) appears in at least six separate rows at 800-806 MW each, ~4.8 GW of phantom capacity from one asset. Status mix: 'operating' 26 rows/82.3 GW (dominated by row 235), 'announced' 52 rows/27.9 GW, 'under_construction' 26/4.4 GW, 'order' only 12 rows/4.1 GW, 'reservation' 1 row/~0 GW. A table with 4.1 GW in 'order' status cannot characterize a 116 GW contracted book either way.

What DID replicate: the EIA-860M recompute is correct. vintage='2026-07', Planned, energy_source='NG': 2026 GT 2.28 vs CC(CA+CS+CT) 1.92; 2027 GT 6.99 vs 4.15 (62.7% simple-cycle); 2028 GT 6.98 vs 9.12; 2029 GT 4.76 vs 8.64; 2030 GT 0.49 vs 17.64. Prime-mover classification (CT/CA/CS = combined cycle, GT = simple cycle) is correct. But a unit-size cut weakens the "peaker" reading the finding inherits: of 18.7 GW of planned GT 2027-29, 5.95 GW sits in 12 units >=350 MW (heavy frames running simple cycle, plausibly HA/F-class) and only 5.55 GW is in the 111 units <100 MW that are genuinely aeroderivative peakers. "Simple-cycle" and "peaker" are not the same population.

Secondary: the two curtailment numbers are presented as one result when they are different quantities. 85 hours/yr is the count of hours in which SOME curtailment occurs; the review paper's "22 hours/year" is the energy-equivalent of 0.25% of annual flexible-load hours (0.0025 x 8760 = 21.9). Calling the second an independent restatement of the first conflates event-hours with equivalent-full-curtailment-hours — a factor of ~3.9. The finding's prose elsewhere gets this right ("Nearly 90% of hours ... retain at least half of the new load"), so it is an exposition error, not a conclusion error, but the team must not quote both side by side.
- **mechanism_sound**: True
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The flexibility premise is saturated: Norris et al., "Rethinking Load Growth" (Nicholas Institute, Duke, 2025) and its 76 GW / 0.25% headroom result were covered by Utility Dive, Latitude Media, Smart Energy International and Daily Energy Insider, and EPRI's DCFlex / Flex MOSAIC work is explicitly marketed on shortening interconnection timelines. The finding concedes this and self-scores novelty 2, which is honest.

The claimed novel step — "nobody has checked GEV's model mix against the US peaker-heavy planned mix" — is not established as novel either, because the check as performed was not a valid check (see physics_errors). The underlying true fact it was reaching for, that GEV's gas franchise is H-class heavy-duty, is stated by GEV itself in every investor deck and in the 20 GW/yr HA output ramp, and the 74 GW/128-unit fleet figure has been carried by GE Vernova IR, Turbomachinery Magazine, Petroleum Australia and Motley Fool since May 2026. There is no unpublished disaggregation here; there is a corpus row that was misread as one.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The conclusion is probably still right, but not for any reason this finding supplies — and one leg of its stated reasoning is self-contradictory.

(a) The conclusion survives on filings alone. Equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred against contracts already signed; 53 GW is firm backlog and the FY26 $45.5-46.5B guide converts work in hand. Nothing in the flexible-load literature can reach FY26 Power equipment revenue. That argument needs no projects table and no model mix. The team should keep the conclusion and delete the evidence.

(b) The finding's own reasoning breaks on its own test. It says a flexible-load thesis "must express itself through NEW orders, which is a 2028+ observable." That is false: GEV reports orders and gas backlog/slot-reservation totals EVERY quarter, and the finding's own testable prediction is that those quarterly figures will be flat or up on Oct 28 2026. So orders are an in-horizon observable, and the correct statement is much weaker — not "untestable," but "very likely to print as a non-event because the 116 GW position is contractual." That distinction matters: a non-event prediction that is near-certain ex ante has almost no information value in a pitch, which is a different and smaller claim than "the bear case cannot be tested."

(c) The materiality arithmetic is not defensible even as an error-size estimate. It capitalizes a one-time backlog haircut at 25x as if it were a perpetual EBITDA stream — a 10% impairment of a finite 53 GW book is a level effect on a fixed pool of future revenue, not an annuity, so 25x overstates it by roughly an order of magnitude. The $1,200/kW HA equipment price and the 10% impairment rate are both asserted without source. The headline "$89.5/share of avoided error" is therefore a number the team must not put in front of a Citadel judge; strike it and describe the avoided error qualitatively.

(d) Residual risk the finding acknowledges but the team should weight higher: the kill is horizon-scoped only. Duke's authors argue flexibility can defer generation capex, and slot reservations are non-binding by construction. If reservation-to-firm conversion slows for any reason in Q3'26, the equipment story reopens inside the horizon, contradicting (b)'s framing.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED as evidence; the conclusion may be salvageable, the supporting measurement is not.

The central technical number is a data-extraction artifact. projects.id=235 ("7HA and 9HA ultra-high-efficiency turbines", 74,000 MW, 128 units) has owner='GE Vernova', commitment_status='operating', blank location and blank COD, and derives from a May 2026 news item. Independently confirmed against GE Vernova's own May 26 2026 press release: 74 GW / 128 units is the GLOBAL ALREADY-OPERATING HA fleet across 21 countries since 2016, measured as plant capacity (578 MW/unit = 1x1 combined-cycle plant output, not frame nameplate). It is not GEV's order book, not forward-looking, and not US. Comparing it to US planned 2027 gas capacity is a global-vs-US and installed-vs-planned category error, so the finding's headline contrast (74 GW HA vs 0.1 GW simple-cycle) is void.

Remove that row and the `projects` table supports no model-mix conclusion at all: 129 GE-linked rows / 44.7 GW, 84 of them (27.5 GW, 61% of MW) with a blank model, only 4.1 GW in 'order' status, and obvious duplication (Vineyard Wind's single 806 MW project occupies at least six rows). The finding's caveat flagged the blank-model problem but treated it as secondary; with row 235 excluded it is the dominant category.

What replicated: the EIA-860M planned-capacity recompute is exactly right year by year and the prime-mover classification is correct. A unit-size cut I ran adds a caveat the finding missed — 5.95 GW of the 18.7 GW planned GT for 2027-29 is in units >=350 MW, i.e. heavy frames in simple cycle, so "simple-cycle" overstates "peaker." Separately, the 85 hours/yr and 22 hours/yr figures are different quantities (event-hours vs energy-equivalent hours, ~3.9x apart) and must not be quoted as one result.

The mechanism leg holds, but for reasons independent of the evidence offered: revenue recognized over time on costs incurred against a 53 GW firm backlog means no flexible-load mechanism can reach FY26 Power equipment revenue. That argument stands on the 10-K alone. However the finding's stated reason — that flexibility could only show up in orders, "a 2028+ observable" — is wrong, since orders and the backlog/reservation total print quarterly, as the finding's own Oct 28 prediction presupposes. The correct claim is the weaker one: the equipment print will almost certainly be a non-event, which is near-certain ex ante and therefore carries little pitch value.

Novelty is genuinely ~2 and self-reported as such. Materiality is not usable: capitalizing a one-time backlog haircut at 25x treats a level effect as an annuity and overstates the avoided error by roughly an order of magnitude, on top of two unsourced inputs ($1,200/kW, 10% impairment).

Recommendation to the team: keep the one-line conclusion (do not build an equipment-line bear case on load flexibility within 3-12 months; it dies on the contracted position), sourced to the 10-K revenue-recognition language and the 53 GW firm backlog. Delete the 74 GW comparison, the projects-table model mix, and the $89.5/share figure entirely — any one of them is a fatal Q&A liability. Redirect the flexible-load lens to the services line as the finding itself suggests.

## [Research] research:transformer_hvdc_supply

- **lens**: Transformer and HVDC physics, materials and lead times — the Electrification segment. I ended up following the materials/lead-time thread into an area the team has not worked: the April 2026 Section 232 restructuring, which changed the tariff BASE from metal-content value to full customs value. That change interacts with a physical fact about transformers (they are ~68-80% metal by mass but metal is only ~10% of a 2026 selling price) in a way that is specific to GE Vernova's stated Prolec revenue-synergy strategy ("leverage global factory footprint to sell into North America"). I could not turn GOES supply, amorphous cores, or data-center harmonic derating into quantified wedges and report those as dead ends.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: GEV's Prolec revenue synergy is an IMPORT strategy, and the Section 232 tariff base flipped from metal-content value to full customs value on 6 Apr 2026 — which raises the effective duty on an imported transformer roughly 3x, with a second step on 1 Jan 2028
    - **physical_fact**: A liquid-immersed power transformer is metal-dominated by MASS but metal-cheap by VALUE, and the 2019-2026 price escalation widened that gap. Mass composition (LCA of liquid-immersed transformers, Global Energy Interconnection 2025, ScienceDirect S1674927825001145): steel 55.11%, transformer oil 24.52%, copper 12.67% — i.e. ~68% metal by weight (a 400 MVA EHV unit checks higher, ~80%, once tank/structural steel is counted). Value build for a representative 100 MVA power transformer: ~130 t total mass -> 71.5 t steel (39 t GOES core at ~$3,300/t = $129k; 32 t structural at ~$1,100/t = $35k), 16.5 t copper at ~$11,000/t = $182k, 32 t oil at ~$2,000/t = $64k. Total metal value ~$346k against a 2026 unit price of ~$3.5M (~$35/kVA, consistent with Wood Mackenzie's +77% power-transformer price escalation since 2019) = metal is ~9.9% of price. Under the pre-April-2026 rule (50% Section 232 on the declared metal CONTENT value) the effective duty was therefore ~5% of the article's value. Under Proclamation 11021 (effective 6 Apr 2026) duty applies to the FULL customs value; the 0% escape hatch requires applicable metal to be under 15% of product WEIGHT, and the 10% tier requires metal at least 95% US-melted/poured. A transformer fails the weight test by ~4.5x and cannot pass the US-metal test (Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works is the only US GOES producer; roughly 80% of US GOES demand is imported). The physics of the product locks it into the 15-25% tiers with no compliance path.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment is unaffected. This hits ELECTRIFICATION SEGMENT EBITDA (cost of revenues line), and specifically the Power Transmission / transformer sub-line, NEGATIVELY. Mechanism: GEV's stated Prolec revenue synergy is explicitly to import — the Q2'26 deck lists 'Leverage global factory footprint to sell into North America' as the lead commercial synergy, and Strazik said on the 22 Jul 2026 call that GEV booked '$800 million in orders for transformers in the US that will be fulfilled by our global factories, something we could not do when we did not fully own Prolec.' Every dollar of that channel is an import. Pre-6-Apr-2026 those imports carried ~5% effective duty (LPTs) to ~15% (distribution class, where metal is a larger share of price); from 6 Apr 2026 they carry 25% of full customs value for HTS 8504.21/.22 (units up to 10,000 kVA, Prolec's volume core) and 15% for 8504.23/8504.34 (over 10,000 kVA) under the Annex III / Proclamation 11032 transitional band, which expires 31 Dec 2027 and reverts to 25%. For USMCA-qualifying Mexican origin (Prolec's Monterrey plant, the largest transformer facility in the Americas, 5-1200 MVA to 800 kV), the June 2026 proclamation applies '25 percent ... only to the non-U.S. content of the product' with the proviso that 'the total effective duty ... shall not be less than 15 percent ad valorem' — so the rate is 15% only if US content is at least ~40% of value, which a Monterrey-built transformer cannot reach because its GOES, magnet wire, bushings and tap changers are not US-origin.
    - **direction**: short

Base case for US-delivered, non-US-built Electrification revenue at the 2028 run-rate: $2.0B/yr (low $1.5B, high $3.0B). STEP 2 — duty delta vs the pre-6-Apr-2026 metal-content basis. Large units (8504.23): old effective ~5% (50% x ~9.9% metal value share) -> 15% now -> 25% from 1 Jan 2028 = +10 pts today, +20 pts in 2028. Distribution/medium units (8504.21/.22, metal ~30% of price): old effective ~15% -> 25% since 6 Apr 2026 = +10 pts, already live. Blended 2028 delta: +15 pts of customs value. STEP 3 — gross incremental duty 2028 = $2.0B x 15% = $300M/yr. STEP 4 — recovery. GEV cites 'contractual protections' and 'pursuing the recovery of certain tariffs'; assume 50% recovered on orders priced after Apr 2026 and 0% on the ~$24-28B of Electrification equipment backlog priced before it. Net unrecovered EBITDA drag = $200M/yr. STEP 5 — per share: $200M x 25 = $5.0B enterprise value / 266,333,581 shares = $18.77/share = 2.00% of $940.33. RANGE: $100M -> $9.39/share (1.00%); $400M -> $37.54/share (3.99%). At GEV's own ~35x forward multiple the base case is $26.28/share (2.79%).   - - **title**: Because Section 232 now taxes the article and not the metal, a US-built transformer carries a 12-21 point structural cost advantage over an identical imported one — and Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and Eaton's new US plants start producing in 2027, exactly when GEV's import channel is scaling and the 15% band expires
    - **physical_fact**: Section 232 reaches imports, not domestic manufacture. A transformer BUILT in the US pays duty only on its imported inputs: GOES at 50% under Annex I-A on ~$129k of core steel in a representative 100 MVA unit, plus copper, against a ~$3.5M selling price — an effective ~3-4% of article value. The same unit IMPORTED pays 15-25% of full customs value. The gap is 12-21 points of revenue on a segment guided to an 18-20% EBITDA margin, i.e. the duty differential alone is comparable to the entire margin. GEV cannot close this inside the horizon for two physical reasons. (1) Plant build-and-qualify time: Siemens Energy announced its Charlotte NC large-power-transformer plant and targets production in early 2027 — roughly 3 years door to door; Hitachi Energy announced Gallman, Mississippi ($528M) only on 15 Sep 2026, so it produces at the end of the decade. A transformer plant is not a fast asset: it needs winding bays, a vapor-phase drying autoclave (4-5 day cycle per unit), an oil-processing plant, and an impulse/short-circuit test bay, then customer qualification. (2) Input constraint: the domestic-content path runs through Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works, the sole US GOES producer, from which roughly 80% of US GOES demand must instead be imported — and Cliffs has now entered transformer manufacturing itself ($150M three-phase distribution transformer plant at Weirton WV, targeted online H1 2026), so the only US GOES source is also a competitor with first call on its own steel.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: ELECTRIFICATION segment EBITDA margin and Electrification equipment ORDERS/share, NEGATIVE, from 2027. This is the pass-through test for Finding 1. As long as domestic transformer capacity is short (Wood Mackenzie models a ~30% national power-transformer supply deficit in 2025 narrowing below 10% only by 2030), GEV can price the duty through because the customer has no domestic alternative — which is exactly what management means by 'contractual protections' and 'solid pricing'. The moment Siemens Charlotte (early 2027), Eaton South Carolina ($340M, 2027) and Hitachi's US program (~$1.5B, plus CA$270M at Varennes Quebec to nearly triple LPT output) have qualified domestic product in the market, a US buyer can source a tariff-free unit. GEV then chooses between eating 12-21 points on imported units or losing the volume. Note the asymmetry in committed capital: Hitachi Energy has announced roughly $1.7B of North American transformer capacity versus GEV/Prolec's announced ~$300M+, part of which (the $85M single-phase pad-mount doubling) is in MEXICO, on the wrong side of the border for this regime.

Practitioner sources give only qualitative guidance and one fleet fact (colos standardize on 2.5 MVA dry-type units per hall). ## [Verify] quant:demand_flexibility:Starts-limited maintenance inver

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: CENTRAL: $11.24/share pre-tax (1.19% of $940.33); $8.88/share after-tax at 21% (0.94%). I reject the original's 25x-on-annual-charge framing — see below.

STEP 1 — PHYSICAL QUANTITY (restating the fact with the number the original omitted). GER-3620 sets combustion/HGP inspection at min(25,000 factored fired hours, 900 factored starts). The crossover is therefore 25,000/900 = 27.8 FIRED HOURS PER START. A unit averaging more than 27.8 fired hours per start is hours-limited; below that it is starts-limited and maintenance falls due earlier than an hours-based cost model predicts. This single ratio is the whole mechanism and the original never computed it.

STEP 2 — WHERE THE FLEET ACTUALLY SITS (my own computation, gev.db tables `generation` (EIA-923) + `generators` (EIA-860M vintage 2026-07, sheet='Operating', energy_source='NG'); equivalent full-load hours = annual net generation MWh / operating nameplate MW):
  CC combustion turbines (CT): 190,191 MW / 1,231 units. EFLH 4,722 (2022) -> 4,935 (2023) -> 5,019 (2024) -> 4,873 (2025).
  CC steam side (CA): 116,494 MW. EFLH 3,850 -> 4,182 -> 4,230 -> 4,067.
  Simple-cycle (GT): 161,610 MW / 2,327 units. EFLH 893 -> 906 -> 989 -> 974.
  At 40-80 starts/yr (typical CC duty), CT units sit at 60-120 fired hr/start = 2-4x CLEAR of the 27.8 crossover; a CC unit would need >175 starts/yr at current hours to flip. At 150-300 starts/yr (peaker duty), GT units sit at 3-6 fired hr/start = 5-9x deep on the starts-limited side — but they have been there for four straight years with no trend. CONCLUSION: the crossover is real, peakers live on the wrong side of it, but NOTHING in the data shows the serviced fleet CROSSING the line in 2022-2025. The mechanism requires a transition and I cannot find one.

STEP 3 — AFFECTED LINE, with a revision series the original did not have. From 10-Q/10-K Note 9 (gev.db chunks, kind='sec'), "net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability" on contractual service agreements, by period:
  Q1'25 +$29M FAVORABLE | H1'25 -$42M (so Q2'25 = -$71M) | 9M'25 ~ -$3xM (text truncated at "$3"; implies Q3'25 roughly FAVORABLE $6-12M) | FY2025 -$151M (so Q4'25 ~ -$115M) | Q1'26 -$89M | H1'26 -$218M (so Q2'26 = -$129M).
  Four consecutive deteriorating quarters starting Q4'25, monotone in the last three: -115, -89, -129. This is stronger trend evidence than the original's two half-year points, and it dates the inflection to Q4'25, not H1'26.

STEP 4 — THE DISCLOSED LEVER. FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-01-29): net LTSA balance $3.4B "represents approximately 4% of our total estimated life of contract billings"; contracts "approximately 29% complete"; "one percentage point would increase or decrease the long-term service agreements contract assets balance by $0.2 billion." Two routes to lifetime billings L: (A) $3.4B/0.04 = $85B; (B) back out of the sensitivity, $0.2B = 0.01 x L x 0.29 -> L = $69B. They disagree because "approximately 4%" is rounded. I carry L = $70B, the value the sensitivity arithmetic actually implies (the original used the stale FY2024 $3.5B/~5% figure and landed on the same $70B by luck). That is a repricing of the entire services annuity and GEV would be forced to disclose it explicitly and restate the sensitivity. It is a tail, not a case.

The range is therefore $5.62 to $22.47/share pre-tax (0.60% to 2.39%) — and note that even the DOUBLED tail does not reach the original's $33.0 headline. To get there you need the 25x multiple, which is the step I reject.

## [Verify] skeptic:load_oscillation_stability:GEV does sell the mitigation har

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: Three defects, one of them load-bearing.

(1) LOAD-BEARING: the claim that "the physics selects for its product class over lithium BESS" is not supported and is arguably backwards. The binding requirement in ERCOT/LIPA/ATC is on POWER-stage rating and closed-loop control bandwidth (sub-cycle to seconds, 0.1-55 Hz), not on storage chemistry. A grid-forming lithium BESS already meets both. Published, peer-reviewed work says so explicitly: "Strengthening Data Center Operations Using Grid-Forming Battery Energy Storage as a Line-Interactive Uninterruptible Power Supply" (Int. J. Electrical Power & Energy Systems, S0142061526000803, 2026) reports ~89% and ~78% attenuation of fast active-power oscillations for 1-cycle and 6-cycle load steps; arXiv:2602.01013 "Mitigating Data Centers Load Risks and Enabling Grid Support Functions through Grid-Forming Control" shows 8x5 MW GFM-BESS tracking the data-center power reference "within milliseconds." Energy over-specification is not a disqualifier when the energy is already bought for another reason: the data center purchases the BESS/UPS for ride-through and outage backup regardless, so the oscillation-damping function rides free on capex already committed to a different vendor channel. The correct selector for supercapacitors is CYCLE LIFE under continuous high-rate micro-cycling and $/kW of the power stage, not "four orders of magnitude of excess energy." The finding never establishes that, and until it does, the technology-selection premise fails.

(2) Order-of-magnitude slip: a 150 MW / 4 h lithium system is 600 MWh against a ~0.21 MWh duty (150 MW x 5 s), a ratio of ~2,860 — about 3.5 orders of magnitude, not "roughly four." Same on the 10 MW basis (40 MWh vs 0.014 MWh = 2,880x). Directionally fine, overstated by ~3x.

(3) Synchronous condensers are mis-assigned to this duty. A sync-con supplies inertia and short-circuit strength at the system level; it does not actively cancel a load's emitted 0.1-55 Hz power variation at the point of interconnection, which is what the ERCOT/LIPA/ATC specs measure. Bundling sync-cons into "the mitigation hardware for this spec" inflates the apparent GEV product overlap. The finding's own evidence undercuts it: the $1.6B Saudi sync-con order is renewables/system-strength driven.

VERIFIED CORRECT, independently: ERCOT's 10 MW peak-to-peak over a rolling 5-second window evaluated across 0.1-55 Hz (ERCOT LEL/SSO Power Variation Consideration deck, ercot.com/files/docs/2026/02/19/ERCOT-LEL-SSO-Power-Variation-Consideration.pdf; also applies to EXISTING loads per LLWG 6/19/26). FACTSFLEX GFMe: grid-forming double-star MMC STATCOM, +/-300 MVAr, supercapacitor storage, "immediately deliver or absorb 150 MW (example) of power for several seconds," announced 2024-08-28 (gevernova.com FACTSFLEX pages). Energy arithmetic 10 MW x 5 s = 50 MJ = 0.0139 MWh is right. Corpus check reproduces the 10-Q figures exactly: Q2'26 Power Conversion & Storage $539M, H1'26 $1,016M, smallest Electrification sub-segment; Electrification segment EBITDA margin 18.4%.
- **mechanism_sound**: True
- **already_published**: False
- **where_published**: The specific financial claim — that GEV's PC&S sub-segment is too small for the AI grid-stability theme to move the stock, and that the headline sync-con order is Saudi renewables rather than AI — I could not find in any sell-side note, trade publication or investor write-up. That part holds.

But the finding's NOVELTY FIELD overreaches. It claims the power-spec-vs-energy-spec observation "I could not find published anywhere." The frequency-domain framing of the constraint is exactly the contribution of arXiv:2605.01173 (Penn State turbine-fatigue paper), which the finding itself cites. Hybrid supercapacitor+BESS sizing for datacenter ramp/fluctuation mitigation is an existing published line of work (surfaced in search of renewable-powered computing-center storage literature), and the power-vs-energy split is standard hybrid-ESS sizing doctrine. Adjacent published work the team should know about: arXiv:2601.12686 (Best Practices for Large Load Interconnections, North American data centers), arXiv:2605.14109 (Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers under Connect-and-Manage), arXiv:2510.03867 (Data Center Low-Voltage Ride-Through), arXiv:2603.09110 (SMR-powered data center dynamic stability), keentelengineering.com ERCOT LLIS and SPP HILL guides (commercial consultancies already selling compliance advice). Novelty should be marked down from 3 to ~2: the physics framing is in the literature; only the GEV-specific sizing is not.

No paywall was bypassed; ScienceDirect S0142061526000803 was read only at abstract/summary level.
- **refuted**: False
- **strongest_counterargument**: The finding may be scoping GEV's exposure to the wrong product line, and in doing so UNDERSTATES the offset it is trying to kill. It sizes only compliance hardware inside Power Conversion & Storage ($2.1B/yr run-rate). But the mechanism by which large-load power-variation rules reach GEV's P&L is not mainly "sell a STATCOM per campus" — it is that stricter interconnection study requirements push each gigawatt campus toward a larger transmission-class scope: AC substation solutions, HVDC, switchgear, transformers. Those sit in Grid Systems Integration ($806M/qtr) and Power Transmission ($1,877M/qtr), together ~5x PC&S, and that is precisely where GEV reported Q2'26 Electrification orders +66% organic. If the ERCOT/LIPA/ATC rule set adds even $50-100M of incremental substation/HVDC scope per GW across ~10 GW/yr, the revenue line is $0.5-1.0B/yr, not $132M — roughly $9-17/share at 18.4% and 25x, which crosses the wedge bar and flips the sign of the conclusion. Second counterargument, weaker but real: the finding's own caveat 4 — generator-to-synchronous-condenser conversion sits in GAS POWER SERVICES, not Electrification. That matters more than the finding realizes, because a converted unit stops accruing factored fired hours (which is how GEV bills services) while earning a conversion project plus a different, rotating-machine service scope. That is a direct interaction with Finding 1's fired-hours thesis, and it is unquantified in both findings.

Rebuttal to both: neither has a dated test before Oct 28 2026, and GEV does not disclose per-campus scope or conversion revenue, so neither is falsifiable on the team's horizon.
- **verdict_summary**: NOT REFUTED as a conclusion, but the stated reason is partly wrong and the novelty claim is overstated.

What survives: every checkable number reproduces. ERCOT 10 MW / 5 s / 0.1-55 Hz confirmed from the primary ERCOT LLWG deck. FACTSFLEX GFMe +/-300 MVAr, 150 MW for several seconds, supercapacitor, confirmed from GE Vernova's own product pages. Corpus reproduces PC&S $539M Q2'26 / $1,016M H1'26 and the 18.4% Electrification margin exactly. The materiality arithmetic is correct end to end: $600M TAM x 22% = $132M revenue, x18.4% = $24.3M EBITDA, x25 = $607M, /266,333,581 = $2.28/share = 0.24%; aggressive case $6.22/share = 0.66%; the $590M-incremental-revenue break-even for $10/share (= 28% of the whole sub-segment) checks. Both cases sit below the $10/share bar, so the finding's function — killing the "GEV sells the fix, so it nets out" rebuttal — holds.

What breaks: the central physics premise, that the seconds-timescale power spec selects supercapacitor STATCOM over lithium BESS. Two independent 2026 papers show grid-forming lithium BESS meets the same duty (89%/78% attenuation of fast oscillations; millisecond reference tracking), and a data center buys that BESS anyway as line-interactive UPS, so the compliance function is a free rider on someone else's capex. The real supercap advantage is cycle life, which the finding never argues. Also: "four orders of magnitude" is ~3.5; synchronous condensers do not serve this spec and should be removed from the product-overlap claim.

Net effect on the team's conclusion: the correction makes the finding MORE negative for GEV, not less — the hardware attach is likelier to land behind the meter with Vertiv/Eaton/Schneider/Tesla/Fluence than with GEV's transmission-class Grid Solutions channel, and a +/-300 MVAr transmission-class FACTS unit is scope-mismatched to a single-campus compliance need. So keep the finding, rewrite the physics paragraph, drop novelty 3 to 2, keep confidence 4, keep materiality 2.

Before using it: (a) re-source the $1.6B Saudi quote from the actual Q3 2025 transcript, since the corpus filing_date is an ingest artifact; (b) label the 0.2 MW/MW attach ratio and $300/kW as unsourced estimates every time the number appears — the $/share scales linearly in both; (c) test the Grid Systems Integration / Power Transmission scope-per-GW channel before concluding GEV captures nothing, because that is where the offset could actually exceed $10/share.

Does it pass "so what" at $250B? As a standalone wedge, no — 0.24-0.66% is noise. As a defensive kill of the natural rebuttal to Finding 1, yes, and that is how the team should deploy it: one paragraph in the risks/rebuttal section, not a pillar.

INDUSTRY PRICING ALREADY HANDLES STARTS. LTSAs are priced per fired hour, per start, per planned maintenance event, or per calendar year. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS REMAIN UNEXCLUDED. Prolec GE closed in the same period (the same Note 9 attributes the $14,088M contract-liability move partly to Prolec); tariffs and input-cost inflation are untested. GEV does not disclose the cause.

WHAT THE TEAM SHOULD KEEP: (1) The corrected CSA rollforward series — revenue-over-billings +$187M (H1'25) -> +$297M (H1'26), revisions $42M -> $218M, against a FLAT CSA asset balance (~$5.4B throughout). (3) The scope-inflation variant (fixed per-event billing vs cycling-driven parts fallout) is the only version not refuted — but it is unsized and its precondition is currently absent from the data.

SCORING: physics real but derivation errors and unverified primary intervals; mechanism broken by disclosed contract terms; empirical premise contradicted by corpus data; materiality overstated ~3x by an invalid capitalization. Do not pitch. Keep the Oct 28 listening post.

## [Verify] skeptic:load_oscillation_stability:AI-training torsional fatigue is

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: The cited source numbers appear faithfully transcribed, but they are misused in three ways.

(1) RESONANCE-COINCIDENCE SMUGGLING. The 23x amplification (0.042 pu -> 0.993 pu) is not a property of "a realistic AI training profile." It is the difference between a profile with and without a spectral line sitting exactly on the machine's 12 Hz torsional mode. Electranix's 100 MW generic machine was given a 12 Hz mode and then driven at 12 Hz. The finding's own caveat (6) concedes GEV has not published 7HA/9HA single-shaft torsional signatures, so the coincidence is assumed, not demonstrated. The honest "realistic, non-resonant" number is 0.042 pu -- the one that should anchor a fleet-wide base case. Using 0.993 pu fleet-wide is citing a tuned stress-test as an operating number, which is exactly the error the task warns about.

(2) THE DAMAGE FUNCTION IS A CLIFF, NOT A SLOPE -- and this is fatal to the dollar chain. Steel shaft/rotor alloys have a high-cycle fatigue endurance limit (~10^6-10^7 cycles); below it essentially no life is consumed (infinite life), above it life is consumed fast. ERCOT's own MCTV method the finding cites USES this framework explicitly: Endurance Limit = 0.1 pu. So at the finding's realistic non-resonant 0.042 pu the accrued damage is ~ZERO, not 10%. At the resonant 0.993 pu -- ~10x the endurance limit -- you are in low-cycle territory and at 3.79e8 cycles/yr (I reproduce that arithmetic: 12 x 31.56e6 s = 3.787e8) the shaft fails in hours to days, not via a gradual 10% maintenance-cost uplift. There is no physical regime that produces "10% higher lifetime maintenance cost spread smoothly across 20% of the book." The finding's step 3 assumption is not merely unmeasured (which it admits); it is inconsistent with the fatigue physics it rests on.

(3) INDEPENDENT RE-DERIVATION CONTRADICTS IT. The one paper that actually closes the S-N / Goodman loop -- "Assessing Risks of Hydro-Generator Shaft Fatigue from Data Center Load Oscillations", arXiv:2607.14412 (2026) -- finds for realistic data-center load oscillations: GC-7 (60 MVA) alternating torque 0.089 pu, tau_a 4.05 MPa, fatigue safety factor n = 5.9; GC-19 (715 MVA) 0.116 pu, tau_a 6.8 MPa, n = 3.8. Both "within the Goodman safe region," and its conclusion is that 5-6% peak-to-peak active power oscillations "remain below the high-cycle fatigue limit." Safety factors of 3.8-5.9 mean the realistic case consumes no measurable life. (Caveat: hydro sets, not HA gas trains -- but it is the same shaft-fatigue framework, and the larger 715 MVA machine, closer to HA scale, is safe too.) Corroborating industry yardstick surfaced in the same search: limiting sudden generator output change to <0.5 pu keeps loss of life under ~0.01% PER EVENT. That is the calibration scale the finding is missing -- and it is four orders of magnitude away from a 10% lifetime cost uplift.

Net: the mechanism is real at the tail (resonant, low-impedance co-located, undamped), and the three ERCOT/Dominion field events are real. But the finding converts a rare tail risk into a fleet-wide mean, which is a category error, not a calibration quibble.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **physics_errors_2**: unused
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: Partially. The PHYSICS and its financial salience are published and have reached retail investor media: Investor's Business Daily, 2026-07-29, on AI data-center turbines "suffering early deaths," quoting Ray Chaudhuri (author of arXiv:2605.01173). The academic literature is dense and current: arXiv:2508.14318 (Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA, power stabilization, 0.2-3 Hz FFT energy, 7->100 Hz shaft torsional band), arXiv:2605.01173 (Penn State + Tesla, 35-84 MW standalone allowable per bus collapsing to 6-13 MW with 12 co-located DCs), and arXiv:2607.14412 (hydro shaft fatigue, Goodman safety factors) -- the last of which the finding did NOT cite and which cuts against it. ERCOT's LLWG work and the Feb 2026 10 MW / 5 s draft limit are public. FERC Order RD26-7-000 and the Dec 31 2026 NERC deadline are public.

What I could NOT find published is the specific accounting link: "GER-3620 factored fired hours contains no torsional factor, therefore this wear mode is unpriced in GEV's $85B life-of-contract LTSA billings." I found no sell-side note or trade article making it. I also independently confirm the disclosure asymmetry in the corpus: chunks kind='sec' returns 0 hits for "torsional", 0 for "subsynchronous", 0 for "sub synchronous", 3 for "oscillation" (none GEV), against 16 / 23 / 13 / 377 across all kinds. So the framing is plausibly novel; the underlying risk is not, and an IBD-level article means it is not an information edge the market has never seen.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The materiality arithmetic double-counts, and correcting it puts the base case below the task's own $10/share bar -- before any physics discount.

Reproducing the finding's own chain: exposed billings 0.20 x $85B = $17.0B; 10% cost uplift = $1.70B of LIFETIME margin destruction. That $1.70B is the ENTIRE, UNDISCOUNTED damage. It equals $1.70B / 266,333,581 = $6.38/share = 0.68% of $940.33. That is the ceiling.

The finding then reports $12.09/share by taking the remaining 71% ($1.207B), amortizing it over 10.7 years ($112.8M/yr), and capitalizing that at 25x to get $2.82B -- which is 2.34x the entire remaining damage it was derived from. A 25x multiple is a perpetuity proxy; it cannot legitimately be applied to a finite, self-terminating 10.7-year stream that has already been fully sized. Discounting the $112.8M/yr stream properly at 9% over 10.7 years gives $0.75B ($2.83/share); adding the $400M catch-up ($1.50/share) gives $4.34/share = 0.46%. Even undiscounted-ceiling treatment gives $6.38/share = 0.68%. The bear case falls the same way: $5.10B lifetime = $19.15/share = 2.04%, not 3.86%.

So on the finding's OWN assumptions the base case is $4.34-6.38/share, i.e. below the $10 threshold and inside the noise band of a $250B company that already books +/-$218M of LTSA revisions in a half-year for ordinary reasons.

Three mechanism breaks compound this, each independently serious:

(a) WRONG BOOK. The $85B of life-of-contract billings, 29% complete on average, is the LEGACY installed fleet -- F-class and earlier, contracted over decades, serving utilities. The AI/data-center exposure sits in the 116 GW BACKLOG, which has not shipped. Management's own split is that ~80% of gas turbine buyers are still utilities and incumbents. In the corpus, GE-linked project CODs cluster at 2028-2030 or are blank (106 of 130 GE-linked projects, ~106 GW, carry no COD). You cannot apply a 20% data-center share of a FUTURE backlog to a book whose value is already 29% earned on PAST units. Real near-term exposure is a small fraction of 20%.

(b) WRONG TEST. Prediction (1) -- Q3'26 nine-month LTSA revisions worse than -$300M on Oct 28 -- cannot be evidence for this mechanism, because essentially no torsionally-coupled AI-adjacent HA units are in commercial operation yet accruing damage. If that number does come in bad, inflation, labor, scope and outage-cost escalation explain it, and the finding would be right for the wrong reason. Conversely, ASC 606 cumulative catch-ups require a REVISED COST ESTIMATE; auditors do not let you re-estimate decades of future maintenance cost off an unpublished resonance hypothesis, so the catch-up leg has no realistic trigger in the pitch horizon.

(c) SIGN AMBIGUITY IS WORSE THAN STATED. GEV bills services per fired hour AND "upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event." A torsional-induced forced outage IS a major maintenance event. On transactional (non-LTSA) units, faster degradation is straightforwardly MORE revenue. And the tail-risk version -- a snapped shaft at a co-located site -- is a discrete, insurable, liability-capped, likely excluded-scope event (industry LTSAs standardly carve out third-party- and customer-caused damage), not a margin bleed. The physics, correctly applied, points to a rare catastrophic-event distribution, which is exactly the shape a 25x EBITDA multiple cannot price and a 3-12 month horizon cannot capture.

Finally: the ISO counter the finding already flags is the base rate, not the alternative. ERCOT binds the LOAD (10 MW in a sliding 5 s window), NERC's FERC-directed standards are due Dec 31 2026, and vendors (Tesla, GPU-side smoothing, STATCOM/BESS) are selling the mitigation now. The compliant steady state has alternating torque back at ~0.04-0.12 pu -- below the endurance limit, zero damage. The exposure window is closing as the exposed fleet is still being built, which is the wrong ordering for a short.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED as a tradeable wedge; keep as a qualitative risk-factor talking point only.

The physics is real but is applied at the wrong point on the damage curve. Shaft torsional fatigue is an endurance-limit phenomenon -- a cliff, not a slope. ERCOT's own MCTV method sets that limit at 0.1 pu. The finding's realistic non-resonant number is 0.042 pu (below it, zero damage), and the 0.993 pu headline requires a load spectral line landing exactly on a machine torsional mode that GEV has never published for 7HA/9HA. The one paper that actually completes the S-N/Goodman conversion (arXiv:2607.14412, 2026, not cited by the finding) computes fatigue safety factors of 3.8-5.9 at 0.089-0.116 pu alternating torque for realistic data-center oscillations and concludes they sit below the high-cycle fatigue limit. So the "+10% lifetime maintenance cost" assumption -- which the whole $/share result scales linearly on, as the finding admits -- has no physical regime supporting it.

The mechanism does not reach the named line on the stated horizon. The $85B life-of-contract book is the legacy utility-served fleet (29% complete); the AI exposure is in the unshipped 116 GW backlog with CODs at 2028-2030. ASC 606 catch-ups need a revised, auditable cost estimate, which a resonance hypothesis will not produce by Oct 28. And a torsional forced outage is itself a billable major maintenance event, with the tail case likely outside LTSA scope.

The dollars do not clear the bar even on the finding's own inputs. Its lifetime damage is $1.70B = $6.38/share ceiling (0.68%); the reported $12.09 comes from capitalizing a finite 10.7-year amortization of that same $1.70B at 25x, producing $2.82B -- 2.34x the damage being capitalized. Properly discounted: $4.34/share (0.46%). Bear case corrects from 3.86% to 2.04%.

WHAT THE TEAM SHOULD SALVAGE (this is the genuinely useful residue, and it is not a short):
1. The disclosure asymmetry is real and verified in-corpus: zero "torsional" / "subsynchronous" in GEV SEC filings while gevernova.com/consulting sells SSTI analysis and a Torsional Stress Relay. That is a legitimate slide, framed as "an emerging risk not yet in the risk factors," not as a valuation adjustment.
2. The sign is arguably POSITIVE and that is the more defensible, more novel pitch: GEV sells the mitigation. SSTI studies, torsional stress relays, STATCOM/synchronous condensers, grid software, power conversion, and BESS all sit in ELECTRIFICATION (~$9B/yr, the fastest-growing segment). If ERCOT codifies the 10 MW / 5 s limit and NERC files by Dec 31 2026, every large co-located load needs measurable compensation hardware and interconnection studies. That reaches "Electrification orders" with a POSITIVE sign, has the same dated catalysts (ERCOT revision request; NERC Dec 31 2026 filing under FERC Order RD26-7-000), and is a far cleaner chain than an unpriceable fatigue-to-LTSA-cost conversion. Materiality is still unquantified and would need its own work -- do not pitch it until it is.
3. If the team keeps any short exposure to this idea, scope it to the tail: behind-the-meter co-located gas + AI load in jurisdictions with no binding limit, pre-standard, a handful of sites -- and price it as event risk, not margin drift.

Confidence in this refutation: moderate-to-high on the arithmetic (deterministic, reproduced above) and on the book-composition break; moderate on the physics, since no one has published an HA-class-specific torsional signature, so the resonance coincidence is unproven in BOTH directions.

For a 500 MW campus with a 20% residual: 100 - 10 = 90 MW => 0.18 MW/MW. For 1 GW at 20% residual: 190/1000 = 0.19. Note the structural point: you have to push the attach ratio past 0.80 MW/MW — meaning essentially the entire campus TDP is uncontrolled seconds-timescale swing that hardware must absorb — before Scenario A alone clears $10/share. ## [Research] research:partload_cycling_thermo

- **lens**: Part-load thermodynamics, cycling, and factored-hours economics of H-class turbines — specifically GE's own GER-3620 Rev P maintenance-factor algebra (factored hours vs factored starts, trip severity, and the load-step term added in 2021), mapped onto GEV's fired-hour-billed contractual service agreements and onto the realized/planned US gas duty mix from EIA-860M and EIA-923.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: The 7HA.02 has a 720-factored-start maintenance budget — 20% tighter than the 7HA.01 and 42% tighter than the 7F.04 — and GEV is selling it into a duty mix that is 56% simple-cycle peaking, where starts (cost) bind but hours (revenue) do not
    - **physical_fact**: GER-3620 Rev P, Figure 36, p.33: 7HA.02 and 9HA.02 baseline inspection intervals are 25,000 factored fired hours / 720 factored fired starts for BOTH combustion and hot-gas-path, and 50,000 / 1,440 for major. The 7HA.01 and 9HA.01 get 25,000/900 and 50,000/1,800; the 7F.04 gets 32,000/1,250 (HGP); the 6F.03 gets 32,000/900. The break-even operating profile (where the two clocks bind equally) is 25,000/720 = 34.7 fired hours per start for a 7HA.02, vs 27.8 for a 7HA.01 and 25.6 for a 7F.04. GER-3620 Figure 22 (p.17) reference profiles: Continuous = 8,200 h/yr, 21 starts/yr (390 h/start); Cyclic = 4,800 h/yr, 300 starts/yr (16 h/start), starts MF 1.0; Peaking = 600 h/yr, 150 starts/yr (4 h/start), starts MF 1.7. Both cyclic and peaking profiles sit far BELOW the 34.7 h/start break-even, so the starts clock binds. A 7HA.02 on GE's own Peaking profile reaches 720 factored starts in 720/(150x1.7) = 2.8 years having accumulated only 600x2.8 = 1,700 fired hours — 6.8% of its 25,000-hour budget. On GE's Cyclic profile it reaches 720 starts in 2.4 years at 11,520 fired hours, i.e. 54% fewer fired hours of revenue per hot-gas-path event than the baseload case.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — long-term (contractual) service agreement estimated profitability, i.e. the 'net unfavorable revisions to estimated service-contract profitability' line (10-Q Note 9) and the underlying Power services margin rate. Direction: negative. GEV recognizes CSA revenue percentage-of-completion on a cost-to-cost basis while 'billing terms for these arrangements are generally based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event' (FY2025 10-K, filed 2026-01-29). Revenue therefore indexes to fired hours; cost indexes to whichever of factored hours or factored starts binds first. As the duty mix shifts to peaking and grid-following, the starts clock binds, so outage cost per fired-hour of billing rises. The mismatch shows up as a downward revision to total estimated contract profitability, recognized as a cumulative catch-up.

    - **physical_fact**: GER-3620 Rev P, Figure 42 (p.38), starts-based hot-gas-path criterion: Factored Starts = 0.5*N_A + N_B + 1.3*N_P + Ps*F + SUM(aT_i - 1)*T_i + SUM(aL_i - 1)*L_i, where L = annual number of load steps >= 20% and aL = exp(0.0137 x %Load Step). GE defines the trigger on the same page: 'power generating units are more often considered to contain large load steps, defined as more than +/- 20% of GT rated load change in 10 seconds or less.' Per-event penalty: +/-20% step = exp(0.274)-1 = 0.315 factored starts; +/-50% = 0.984; +/-70% = 1.61; +/-95% = 2.67. GE's own worked example, Appendix A.3 (p.44), is a 6F.03 powering an arc-furnace island 'not interconnected to the national grid': 30 load steps beyond +/-20% produce 25.4 load-step factored starts, i.e. 0.85 factored starts per event on average. Against the 7HA.02's 720-start HGP budget, 2.3 such events per day consumes the entire interval in one year. Trips are worse: Figure 19 (p.15-16) gives a trip severity factor of 8:1 from 80-100% load, 10:1 from peak, 2:1 from FSNL, applied as adders (startup plus trip from base load = 8 total cycles). Off-frequency operation (p.22) adds: 'one hour of operation at 105% speed is equivalent to two hours at rated speed', and 'When frequency deviation withstand requirements are combined with active power response requirement (also known as governor response), a start-based penalty may be incurred.' The AI load that supplies these steps: Choukse et al. (Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA), arXiv:2508.14318, report GPU power dropping between compute and communication phases 'ranging from once per second or less, to once every tens of seconds', 'aggregate power consumption can oscillate by tens of megawatts within a single datacenter', with FFT energy concentrated at 0.2-3 Hz; Hossain et al., arXiv:2605.01173 (2026), state 'At the beginning of a training cycle, the power consumption can increase by up to 70% of the power rating in a short time'; and NERC/ERCOT data show large electronic loads losing 17% to 95% of pre-disturbance consumption within milliseconds of a normally cleared fault, with 26 such ERCOT ride-through events between January 2023 and September 2025 and a ~1,500 MW single-event data-center load loss in the Eastern Interconnection on July 10 2024.

Direction: negative. For an islanded or behind-the-meter turbine the campus's load step IS the machine's load step, because there is no grid to absorb it — GE's own example is explicitly an island. Each qualifying step burns 0.32-2.7 factored starts against a 720-start budget that the CSA pricing model almost certainly built from a baseload profile, so the hot-gas-path outage arrives years early, GEV supplies the parts and labor, and the fired-hour billing clock has barely moved.

  - - **title**: KILL: part-load operation of an H-class combined cycle consumes ZERO extra factored hours down to 80% load, and part-load start cycles below 60% carry a maintenance factor of 0.5 — the generic 'cycling wears turbines out, GEV eats the cost' argument is false as usually stated, and the real exposure is narrower than the team would otherwise assume
    - **physical_fact**: GER-3620 Rev P, p.12: 'in heat recovery applications, where steam generation drives overall plant efficiency, load is first reduced by closing variable inlet guide vanes to reduce inlet airflow while maintaining maximum exhaust temperature. For these combined cycle applications, firing temperature does not decrease until load is reduced below approximately 80% of rated output.' Combined with Figures 39 and 41 (pp.37-38), where the hours-based load severity factor is 'Ap = 1.0 up to Base Load', this means a combined-cycle H-class turned down from 100% to 80% accrues factored hours at exactly 1.0x — no penalty at all. And GER-3620 Figure 20 (p.16) goes the other way: 'two operating cycles to maximum load levels of less than 60% would equate to one start to a load greater than 60% or, stated another way, would have a maintenance factor of 0.5.' Part-load cycling EXTENDS the starts-based interval. By contrast a simple-cycle non-DLN machine at 80% load loses 'over a 200 degF reduction in firing temperature' — it gets easier too. The mechanisms that actually consume life are therefore a short, specific list: trips (8:1 from base, 10:1 from peak), peak firing (starts factor Ap = exp(0.009 x peak firing temperature adder in degF)), peaking-fast starts (F-class HGP factor Ps = 1.2, rotor Fs = 2.0, and the rotor hot-start factor 4.0 for a peaking-fast start with downtime <= 1 hour), non-premix combustion modes (maintenance factor of 10 for DLN-1/1+ extended lean-lean and DLN 2.0/2+ extended piloted premixed), rapid/forced/crank cooling (rotor factor 4.0, same as a cold start), off-frequency operation (105% speed = 2x), and >=20% load steps in <=10 seconds.
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: Power segment — CSA estimated profitability. Direction: this KILLS a bearish angle and therefore BOUNDS the downside on that line. It says the several hundred GW of grid-connected combined-cycle capacity that will merely run at lower average load because renewables and data centers reshape the net-load curve does NOT, on GE's own algebra, accelerate GEV's service cost at all. The GER-3620 load-step term requires a >=20% change in <=10 SECONDS, which is a much slower and rarer class of event (job start/crash, cluster drain, ride-through trip). The middle band — job starts, job crashes, checkpoint stalls, planned drains — is where the answer is, and I could not find it published. Meta's Llama-3 405B run reportedly had 419 unexpected interruptions over 54 days on one 16k-GPU job (~7.8/day), but I read that only in secondary coverage, not in arXiv:2407.21783 itself, and a single job's interruption need not be >=20% of a whole campus's turbine load. ## [Verify] quant:grid_alternatives:The HA fleet's fired-hour clock

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: REBUILD, step by step.

STEP 1 — Physical fact (I verified this, it holds).
Interval 1: 2023-09-07 (2.0M h, ~80 units in commercial op) to 2025-03-06 (3.0M h, 116 units). I counted 546 days = 1.4948 yr. Mean operating units (80+116)/2 = 98. 1,000,000 / (98 x 1.4948) = 6,826 h/unit-yr.
Interval 2: 2025-03-06 (116) to 2026-05-26 (4.0M h, 128 units). 446 days = 1.2211 yr. Mean units 122. 1,000,000 / (122 x 1.2211) = 6,713 h/unit-yr.
Agreement 1.7%. I reproduce ~6,750 h/unit-yr. This part of the finding is sound and is genuinely a nice piece of reverse-engineering.

STEP 2 — The comparator, and where I break with the original. UNITS ERROR.
I re-ran the corpus queries and they reproduce exactly: generators (vintage 2026-07, Operating, NG) CA 116.4 + CS 21.8 + CT 190.1 = 328.3 GW; generation 2025 NG CA 473.8 + CS 103.0 + CT 926.7 = 1,503.5 TWh; CF = 1,503.5 / (328.3 x 8.760) = 52.3%; 0.523 x 8,760 = 4,581 h.
But 4,581 h is EQUIVALENT FULL-LOAD HOURS, not operating hours. GEV's 6,750 is SYNCHRONIZED OPERATING hours at whatever load. A CC unit online 6,100 h/yr at 75% average load has a 52.3% capacity factor. Comparing 6,750 synchronized hours to 4,581 EFLH is a category error, and it is the entire source of the claimed 1.474x duty advantage.
The correction matters twice over, because GER-3620 factored fired hours are counted per fired hour (with start/trip/peak multipliers), not per MWh — so the maintenance clock runs on operating hours on BOTH sides of the comparison.
Defensible substitute: US CC average part-load factor when synchronized = 0.75 (US CC fleet cycles; annual mean load 70-80% when online). Comparator operating hours = 4,581 / 0.75 = 6,108 h/yr.
Corrected duty ratio = 6,750 / 6,108 = 1.105x, not 1.474x.

STEP 3 — Physical quantity to revenue line.
Line: Power segment services revenue (Gas Power), direction up. Both 10-K billing triggers (per hour of usage; occurrence of a major maintenance event) are linear in fired hours, so I keep the original's linear mapping.
Management's $500M/GW over 20 yr = $25.0M/GW-yr, assumed to correspond to the measured 6,750 h/yr duty. Implied rate = $25.0M / 6,750 = $3,704 per GW-operating-hour.
At the corrected comparator duty of 6,108 h/yr: 6,108 x $3,704 = $22.62M/GW-yr.
DELTA = $25.00 - $22.62 = $2.38M/GW-yr. (Original claimed $8.04M/GW-yr.)

STEP 4 — Annual EBITDA delta.
Case A, installed base 74 GW: 74 x $2.38M = $176M incremental services revenue/yr.
Case B, 74 GW installed + 53 GW firm equipment backlog = 127 GW at maturity: 127 x $2.38M = $302M/yr.
Incremental services EBITDA margin: I substitute 28% for the original's 30%. Justification: Power is guided 17-19% blended segment EBITDA on ~$16B; services is ~half of Power revenue; solving a blend of ~9-10% equipment and ~27-28% services reproduces the guided 18%. 30% is the top of the defensible band, not the centre. This is still an assumption, not a disclosure.
Case A EBITDA: $176M x 0.28 = $49.3M.
Case B EBITDA: $302M x 0.28 = $84.6M.

STEP 5 — Multiple, shares, price.
25x as instructed (note: GEV actually trades ~35x EV/EBITDA on FY26, so 25x is conservative here; at 35x every figure below rises 40%).
Case A: $49.3M x 25 = $1,232M / 266,333,581 = $4.63/share = 0.49% of $940.33.
Case B: $84.6M x 25 = $2,115M / 266,333,581 = $7.94/share = 0.84% of $940.33.

MY ANSWER: $4.6 to $7.9 per share, i.e. 0.5% to 0.8%. Below the team's own $10/share bar.

Cross-check on the original's own inputs: using its 1.474x ratio and 30% margin I get $16.76 (74 GW) and $28.75 (127 GW) — so the original's arithmetic is internally correct to the cent. The disagreement is entirely in the comparator, not the algebra.
- **agrees_with_original**: False
- **where_it_differs**: Three places, in descending order of impact.

1. THE COMPARATOR IS A UNITS ERROR (worth ~70% of the claimed value). The original compares GEV's 6,750 SYNCHRONIZED OPERATING hours against 4,581 EQUIVALENT FULL-LOAD hours derived from a 52.3% capacity factor. These are not the same quantity. A US CC unit at 52.3% CF is typically online ~6,100 h/yr at ~75% average load, not 4,581 h/yr. Converting properly collapses the duty ratio from 1.474x to ~1.105x and the per-GW delta from $8.04M to $2.38M. This single correction takes $16.8-28.7/share down to $4.6-7.9/share. The original's caveat (1) flags the running-hours-vs-factored-hours distinction on the GEV side but never notices the EFLH problem on the EIA side, which is the larger error and runs the opposite way.

2. MARGIN. I use 28% incremental services EBITDA rather than 30%. 30% is the top of the band that reconciles with Power's guided 17-19% blended margin. Minor: -7%.

3. THE DELTA IS NOT A DELTA VS CONSENSUS. This is the structural objection and the original half-admits it in its last sentence. The construct prices the difference between the true duty and a counterfactual duty. That is only worth money if the market embeds the counterfactual. Management stated $500M/GW-over-20-years publicly at Morgan Stanley Laguna on 2026-09-16, six days before this analysis; sell-side models are built off that guidance, not off EIA fleet-average CF. So the measured duty is confirmatory of a number already in consensus, and the incremental information content is closer to zero than to $4.63. I would not put this in a pitch as a valuation line. I would put it in as a DEFENSIVE exhibit — evidence that management's $25M/GW-yr is arithmetically reachable — which is a real but unmonetizable use.

4. GEOGRAPHIC MIX, not quantified by either of us. 128 units across 21 countries. The thesis the team is actually pitching is a US data-center thesis. A global 6,750 h/yr average that includes Middle East and Asian baseload units tells you very little about US HA duty, which is the number that matters. The original lists this as open risk (4) but does not discount for it. I would discount the US-facing version further.
- **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: The counterfactual duty cycle the comparison is drawn against — concretely, the average part-load factor used to convert the US CC fleet's 4,581 equivalent full-load hours into actual synchronized operating hours. I use 0.75, giving a 6,108 h/yr comparator. The original implicitly uses 1.00 (treating EFLH as operating hours), giving 4,581 h/yr. Every dollar of the $/share figure is the gap between 6,750 and that comparator, so this one number is a ~3.4x lever on the answer. The 28% incremental EBITDA margin is the second lever but only ~1.5x across its plausible range.
- **sensitivity**: Sensitivity on the part-load factor (the key assumption), at 25x and 28% margin, 74 GW / 127 GW:

- 0.65 (comparator 7,048 h/yr): delta is NEGATIVE. The HA fleet would be running LESS than the US CC fleet and the thesis inverts to a short-side argument. -$3.6 / -$6.2 per share.
- 0.70 (6,544 h/yr): delta $0.76M/GW-yr. $1.5 / $2.5 per share. Noise.
- 0.75 (6,108 h/yr) BASE: $4.6 / $7.9 per share.
- 0.80 (5,726 h/yr): delta $3.79M/GW-yr. $7.4 / $12.6 per share.
- 0.85 (5,389 h/yr): delta $5.04M/GW-yr. $9.8 / $16.8 per share.
- 1.00 (4,581 h/yr, the original's implicit assumption): delta $8.04M/GW-yr. $15.6 / $26.8 per share.

Halving my assumed delta ($2.38M -> $1.19M/GW-yr): $2.3 / $4.0 per share. Doubling it ($4.76M/GW-yr, roughly a 0.82 part-load factor): $9.3 / $15.9 per share.

Second-order sensitivities: swapping 28% margin for 20% gives $3.3 / $5.7; for 35% gives $5.8 / $9.9. Swapping 25x for GEV's actual ~35x EV/EBITDA gives $6.5 / $11.1 at base. Even stacking the two most favourable non-duty assumptions (35% margin, 35x, 127 GW) on my corrected duty ratio only reaches $13.9/share — so the finding cannot be rescued to "material" without restoring the EFLH error.
- **materiality_verdict**: immaterial

## [Research] research:academic_blind_mine

- **lens**: Blind mining of the corpus academic tier (30,023 chunks: 25,934 OpenAlex + 4,089 arXiv), extended into live arXiv/EPRI/ASPLOS literature where the corpus pointed. Honest assessment of the tier: it is ~80% off-topic noise for a financial wedge. The 'services' angle (68 OpenAlex sources) is almost entirely unrelated (remanufacturing, telerehabilitation, blockchain-as-a-service, ResFinder genotypes). 'technical_turbine' (63) and 'gas_turbine_supply' (145) are dominated by additive-manufacturing and hydrogen-combustion reviews with no maintenance-interval economics — FTS for '"factored" "fired hours"', '"hot gas path" "inspection interval"', '"thermal barrier coating" "spallation"' returned ZERO academic hits. The real signal is concentrated in the 42 arXiv 'datacenter_demand' papers (2025-2026), which are genuinely unmined and led to the GPU-power-physics thread below. Two findings survived; five angles killed with evidence.
- **findings**:
  - - **title**: Memory-bound decode physically caps GPU draw below TDP, so measured data-center peak is 62-80% of the nameplate that drives interconnection requests and therefore GEV's gas procurement
    - **physical_fact**: On an NVIDIA H200 SXM (700 W TDP), LLM decode draws only 137-300 W (19.6-42.9% of TDP) and the configured power cap NEVER triggers, because memory-bound decode saturates HBM bandwidth while SM clock stays pinned at ~1830 MHz (Ma, Afzal, Eitzinger & Wellein, arXiv:2605.11999v1, May 2026). This propagates to the facility: a 10 MW AI colocation centre at 80% node utilisation has mean power 5.91 MW and max 7.32 MW — 'maximum power only reached ~7.30 MW, or approximately 73% of the data center rated power design' (Vercellino et al., arXiv:2604.07345v1, Apr 2026). EPRI's measured facility data agree independently: peak utilisation relative to nameplate is 62-80%, and the average annual load factor relative to nameplate is 75% for a >75 MW single-tenant hyperscale facility, 57% for colocation (EPRI, Powering Intelligence 2026, Feb 2026, p.15). EPRI also defines nameplate as the number that 'corresponds to what the data center requests for service interconnection' — so the procurement chain is keyed to a number ~25-38% above realised peak. Microsoft Azure production data closes the loop: a DGX-A100 rated 6500 W 'never exceeded 5700 W' across all workloads, and POLCA can 'deploy 30% more servers in existing clusters with minimal performance loss' (<2% low-priority throughput decline) (Patel et al., ASPLOS '24, DOI 10.1145/3620666.3651329).
    - **mechanism_to_gev_line**: GEV Power segment gas-turbine EQUIPMENT revenue and the GW output target (20 GW/yr from Q3'26, 24 GW 2028, 30 GW 2030), via conversion of the 63 GW of slot reservations into firm orders. Utilities and developers size firm generation procurement off data-center nameplate/interconnection requests; realised peak is 62-80% of that. BOTH billing triggers are proportional to fired hours, so the services annuity is roughly linear in duty cycle. Independent corroboration of the regime: the US natural-gas combined-cycle fleet ran at 53.1% / 54.4% / 52.6% capacity factor in 2023/2024/2025 (EIA-923 + EIA-860M via corpus), i.e. 4,604-5,053 equivalent full-load hours — flat, and DOWN in 2025 despite the AI narrative.

The fired-hours series says a material part of the gap is instead a permanent DUTY-CYCLE deficit: at 69% utilisation the hours-proportional annuity tops out near $18.9M/GW-yr. Maturity can close $15M -> $18.9M; it cannot close $18.9M -> $25M.

- **dead_ends**:
  - AI-datacenter forced oscillation as a GEV Electrification product opportunity — KILLED ON MATERIALITY, and this is the most useful negative result here. Ko & Zhu (arXiv:2508.16457v2, IEEE Trans. Power Systems) is the most striking paper in the tier: AI datacenter load has a dominant ~1 Hz power-spectral peak, and at only 11.5% penetration (7 x 1 GW sites, 20% of each site's capacity fluctuating) on the WECC 179-bus system it drives SUSTAINED generator-bus frequency oscillations of ~0.2 Hz peak-to-peak, rising above 0.4 Hz p-p at reduced inertia, by resonating with unstable electromechanical modes at 0.757 / 0.852 / 0.995 / 1.06 / 1.44 / 1.83 Hz. Coherence between datacenter demand and system frequency exceeds 0.6 at 1 Hz. The paper's only two effective mitigations are datacenter-side fluctuation suppression (50-90%) and improved system damping (20-80%) — both things GEV Electrification sells (power conversion, grid-forming storage, synchronous condensers). But size it: suppressing 70% of a 200 MW fluctuating component at 1 Hz needs ~140 MW of POWER-rated (not energy-rated) buffering — only ~19 kWh of energy. At ~$200/kW that is ~$28M per GW of datacenter. Across ~50 GW of US datacenter build to 2030 that is a ~$1.4B five-year market, ~$280M/yr; at a generous 20% GEV share and 15% margin that is ~$8M/yr EBITDA = $0.8/share. Two orders of magnitude below the $10/share bar. Beautiful physics, no trade. Do not spend more time here.
  - Transformer thermal-aging acceleration under data-center duty (Prolec GE / Electrification replacement cycle) — KILLED BY DESIGN PHYSICS, not by lack of data. Hypothesis: near-continuous ~90-95% loading raises hot-spot temperature, and IEEE C57.91 Arrhenius aging roughly doubles per 6-7 degC (F_AA = exp(15000/383 - 15000/(theta_H+273)) gives 2.71x per 10 degC), so data-center transformers would age 5-20x faster than utility-average duty and create an outsized replacement market. It fails because Uptime Tier III/IV data centers are built 2N: each transformer must carry the entire load alone, so in normal operation it runs at or below ~50% of rating. Hot-spot rise scales roughly as K^1.6, so data-center transformers run COOLER than the utility average, not hotter. The residual real effect runs the other way and is a volume, not a physics, story — 2N means ~2-2.5x the transformer MVA purchased per MW of IT load — which the industry already understands. Corpus FTS for '"harmonic" "transformer" "derating"' in the academic tier returned zero hits.
  - Wind blade failure-rate physics as a driver of Wind segment provisions — NO DATA IN THE CORPUS. The academic tier holds 103 OpenAlex + 26 arXiv offshore-wind sources and 88 onshore, but FTS for '"blade" "failure rate" "per turbine" "year"', '"blade failures" "percentage" "fleet"', '"warranty" "wind turbine" "failure rate"' and '"upscaling" "blade" "mass" "scaling exponent"' all returned ZERO academic hits. The only quantified item available is leading-edge erosion costing 'a few percent' of annual energy production (Bak et al. 2020, cited in a Wind Energy Science discussion comment, corpus chunk 224519) — a customer-economics number, not a GEV provision number. A Wind wedge cannot be built from this corpus without external failure-rate data.
  - GER-3620 / factored-fired-hours maintenance economics in the academic tier — ABSENT. FTS for '"factored" "fired hours"', '"hot gas path" "inspection interval"', '"creep" "rotor" "life consumption"', '"thermal barrier coating" "spallation"' and '"ramp rate" "MW per minute" "gas turbine"' returned ZERO hits in tier='academic'. '"equivalent operating hours"' returned only four chunks, all from one low-quality review that mentions EOH as a KPI with no numbers. Academic literature does not carry OEM maintenance-interval economics; that lives in GE/Siemens/MHI technical papers and user-conference proceedings (the corpus does have useful commentary-tier user-conference coverage — chunks 250670, 250673, 250647 — including an HA plant ramping 350->1160 MW at 80 MW/min). Any factored-hours argument must be sourced outside the academic tier.
  - Kuramoto phase-locking of co-located training jobs (arXiv:2607.19638v1, Jul 2026) — NO TRADEABLE NUMBER. Conceptually the highest-upside paper in the tier: if a facility's own power-management stack phase-locks independent training jobs, aggregate fluctuation grows linearly in job count rather than as sqrt(N), and a site swings coherently against its own interconnection agreement. But it is pure theory — it derives that the throttling coupling is repulsive to leading order and turns attractive only when control-loop dead time exceeds half an iteration period, and it explicitly states the prediction 'is falsifiable by a two-job co-capped measurement, which we specify.' No measured coupling constant, no observed locking event, no facility data. Nothing to size today; worth re-checking in 2027 if anyone runs the experiment.
  - The academic tier's 'services' angle (68 OpenAlex sources) is essentially noise for this purpose — the corpus keyword harvest pulled in telerehabilitation for stroke, ResFinder 4.0 genotype prediction, smoking-cessation text messaging, FASER's physics reach for long-lived particles, and NutBaaS blockchain-as-a-service. Large parts of 'turbine_pricing' are equally off-topic (OECD Economic Surveys: New Zealand 2024; road-construction delay in Woliso-Ambo, Ethiopia). The team should not budget further blind-mining time against those angles; the yield is concentrated in the 42 arXiv 'datacenter_demand' papers and essentially nowhere else in the academic tier.

(b) The headroom only matters on constrained import paths into data-center load pockets. I could not find a published figure for total constrained transfer capability into US data-center load pockets; I assume 40 GW and flag it as my weakest input. 40 GW x 10% = 4 GW of incremental import headroom.
(c) Import headroom is energy headroom, not accredited firm capacity. A hyperscaler buys firm 24/7 supply. I assume 50% converts to firm capacity that a utility would otherwise have met with new gas -> 2.0 GW displaced. This is my base case, one-fifth of the original's assumed 10 GW.

STEP 2 — GW -> GEV REVENUE LINES. The original assumed equipment is "roughly half" of Power segment revenue and derived $450M/GW. The filings say otherwise. From data/financials/gev_segments.csv (XBRL RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax, FY2025): Power segment $19,767M, of which Product $6,420M (32.5%) and Service $13,072M (66.1%). Gas Power subsegment $16,006M. Backing nuclear/hydro/steam product out, gas equipment revenue is roughly $4.5B. Against a ~13 GW 2025 shipment rate that is ~$346M/GW recognized. Newer order vintages are priced higher, so I use $400M/GW for displaced future orders — still 11% below the original's $450M.

STEP 3 — MARGINS, REBUILT FROM THE SEGMENT DATA. Management is explicit that services carry the margin. Holding services at 20% gives services EBITDA of $2,614M, leaving $288M on $6,420M of product = 4.5% equipment EBITDA margin. The original's 12% equipment margin is not supportable on today's mix; I use 10% as a forward-vintage number that is already generous to the bear. Services margin I set at 20% (implied), not the original's 30%.

STEP 4 — SERVICES ANNUITY. Management's Laguna figure is ~$500M per GW of HA over 20 years = $25M/GW-yr; today's realized yield is ~$15M/GW-yr. I use $20M/GW-yr.

Equipment: 2.0 GW x $400M/GW = $800M revenue, recognized over 3 years = $266.7M/yr x 10% = $26.7M/yr EBITDA.
Services forgone: 2.0 GW x $20M/GW-yr = $40M/yr revenue x 20% = $8.0M/yr EBITDA.

STEP 6 — TO $/SHARE. $34.7M x 25 = $866M / 266,333,581 shares = $3.25/share = 0.35% of $940.33.

- **where_it_differs**: Four differences, all pushing the number down, and I agree with the qualitative conclusion while rejecting the size.

The original's 10 GW is a number picked to make the answer interesting.

2. EQUIPMENT REVENUE PER GW. The original used $450M/GW "implied by Power segment ~$16B revenue with equipment roughly half of segment revenue."
