## [Verify] skeptic:storage_vs_peakers:Storage does NOT contest the pea

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: Two distinct problems, one of them a real units/label error.

(1) UNITS ERROR, load-bearing. The claim "the national simple-cycle peaker fleet's fired hours went UP from 869 h/yr in 2022 to 926 h/yr in 2025" is not fired hours. I reproduced the exact numbers from the corpus (US prime_mover='GT': 151.7 TWh / 174.5 GW = 868 h in 2022; 164.0 TWh / 177.0 GW = 926 h in 2025, vintage-matched nameplate 2023-01 and 2026-01) and the arithmetic is net_generation_MWh / nameplate_MW — that is EQUIVALENT FULL-LOAD HOURS, not fired hours. A peaker on line at 60-90% of nameplate accumulates roughly 1.1-1.7x more clock fired hours than EFLH, and every start adds hours-equivalent severity factors on top. This matters precisely because the finding's stated payoff is to "redirect the exposure onto the services line," and GE bills services on FACTORED fired hours and on starts (GER-3620 Rev P: 25,000 FFH or 900/720 starts). An energy-derived proxy cannot distinguish "same MWh in fewer, deeper runs" (fired hours and starts DOWN, EFLH flat) from "same MWh in more, shallower runs" (fired hours and starts UP). The metric is blind to exactly the variable the mechanism runs on. Supporting check: national GT fleet implied heat rate barely moved, 12,022 -> 11,908 Btu/kWh (2022->2025), which is weakly against a cycling-intensification story but is also confounded by fleet turnover.

(2) The inference from the ELCC percentages is not the decision variable. Even taking 4-hr storage 50% vs Gas CT 60% as correct, a ratio of accreditation percentages per NAMEPLATE MW does not determine what a developer builds. The procurement variable is $ per accredited kW-yr (or kW-month), i.e. capex/ELCC plus energy-and-ancillary revenue offset. The finding never computes it. I could NOT independently verify the PJM 2026/27 class-rating values themselves — the web-search budget for this session was exhausted before I could search, and the PJM ELCC URL I tried (pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/planning/res-adeq/elcc/elcc-class-ratings.pdf) returns Page Not Found. So I am neither confirming nor contradicting 50/58/62/72 and 60/78/74/95; the team must re-pull that PDF themselves. One structural caveat if they do: PJM's 2026/27 ratings are MARGINAL ELCC under the accreditation reform, so the storage number is already saturated at expected penetration by construction — which makes the "it will fall further" prediction less automatic than stated.

(3) The cross-section reads the opposite way once disaggregated. Reproducing the state split myself (generators vintage-matched nameplate joined to generation by state, prime_mover='GT'): CA 935 -> 596 EFLH (-36.3%), NV 522 -> 220 (-57.8%), GA 578 -> 398 (-31.2%), AZ 486 -> 379 (-22.0%), FL 580 -> 504 (-13.1%) — i.e. the storage-dense and solar-dense states all fell hard. The national RISE is carried by TX (2,090 -> 2,254, +7.8%, no capacity market, no ELCC, extreme load growth), IL (+65.6%) and OH (+25.3%), where coal retirement and load growth dominate. Note my CA figure (-36.3%) differs materially from the finding's (-23.3%), which used an undocumented CCGT-ratio control. US ex-TX EFLH does still rise (758 -> 796), so the national claim survives in weak form, but the finding's own admitted load-growth confound (its caveat 3) is not a side issue — it is the whole result.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The specific move the finding claims is unpublished — "compare a new gas peaker against 4-hour BESS under an ELCC accreditation framework rather than under full qualifying capacity" — is published and is already sitting in the team's own corpus, untouched. Clean Energy States Alliance / Strategen Consulting, "Battery Storage for Fossil-Fueled Peaker Plant Replacement: A Maine Case Study" (corpus sources.id=2959, https://www.cesa.org/wp-content/uploads/Battery-Storage-for-Fossil-Fueled-Peaker-Plant-Replacement-A-Maine-Case-Study.pdf). It runs the identical two-scenario structure — current Qualifying Capacity, where a 2-hr BESS is fully accredited, versus a prospective ELCC framework — against a new F-frame peaker (153.8 MW at 15% CF) and reports net cost in $/kW-month.

Its numbers are worth the team's attention because they cut BOTH ways and are sharper than anything in the finding. Exclusive of health/societal costs (Table 2): New F-Frame $1.87, BESS 4-hr $2.63 under QC and $2.42 under ELCC, BESS 2-hr $3.12 under ELCC versus negative $(0.54) under QC. So on private economics the new gas peaker is the CHEAPEST new-build option under both accreditation regimes — which supports the finding's conclusion far better than the finding's own evidence does, while simultaneously destroying its novelty claim. Only when societal/health costs are internalised (Table 4) does the F-Frame move to $3.10 and 4-hr BESS win. The report's own framing, that moving from QC to ELCC is what makes 4-hour rather than 2-hour BESS the "future-proof" build, is also the published version of the finding's duration argument. Also note Appendix C: under a higher-BESS-cost scenario the F-Frame gap widens to $1.87 vs $4.85-5.06.

The finding already concedes the general "ELCC saturates" literature (Ascend Analytics, Advanced Energy United, E3 2020, arXiv:2303.09560). Between that and CESA/Strategen, the residual novelty is only "nobody ran the displacement test against realised US peaker utilisation" — and that test, as shown above, is built on a mislabelled metric and reverses on disaggregation.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The conclusion is probably right even though this evidence chain does not establish it, and the team should not over-correct. Three points survive. First, US ex-Texas simple-cycle EFLH still rose (758 -> 796 h/yr, 2022 -> 2025) across a period when operating battery capacity went 8.9 -> 53.3 GW, so at national scale there is genuinely no displacement signal yet, however much the cross-section muddies the causal story. Second, and much more important for a 3-12 month horizon: GEV has 53 GW of FIRM equipment backlog plus 63 GW of paid slot reservations, and the Greenville slots are sold into 2028-2030. Substitution at the development stage cannot reach revenue GEV has already contracted, so over the pitch horizon the storage bear case is mechanically unable to bite regardless of who is right about ELCC. That makes the finding true-but-vacuous rather than false-and-dangerous. Third, CESA/Strategen's own private-economics table ($1.87 F-Frame vs $2.42 4-hr BESS under ELCC) is independent third-party support for "gas peaker still wins on cost per accredited kW-month" — stronger evidence than anything the finding offers, and the team can cite it. If the team wants this defensive point in the memo, cite Strategen Table 2 and the PJM class-rating PDF directly and drop the fired-hours regression entirely.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED as a wedge; the underlying conclusion is likely true but is not established by this evidence, is already published, and fails the task's own four criteria.

PHYSICS: one real units error. "Fired hours 869 -> 926 h/yr" is net_generation_MWh/nameplate_MW, i.e. equivalent full-load hours, not fired hours (I reproduced 868 and 926 exactly from the corpus). Since GEV bills services per FACTORED fired hour and per start, an energy-derived proxy is blind to the exact variable the mechanism needs — it cannot tell fewer-deeper runs from more-shallower runs. The ELCC percentages themselves I could NOT verify (session web-search budget exhausted; the PJM URL I tried 404s) — unverified, not wrong. Disaggregating the fleet data reverses the read: CA -36.3%, NV -57.8%, GA -31.2%, AZ -22.0% EFLH, with the national rise carried by TX (+7.8%), IL (+65.6%) and OH (+25.3%) — load growth and coal retirement, not an absence of displacement. The finding's admitted confound is the whole result, not a caveat.

MECHANISM: breaks in three places. (a) Wrong population — utilisation of the installed 178 GW US simple-cycle fleet does not test whether NEW capacity procurement picks batteries or turbines, and GEV's revenue comes only from new units and their attached service contracts. The right population is the planned queue, where the finding's own data shows planned BA 61.9 GW against GT 21.1 GW (2.9x), a fact it dismisses by assertion ("coexist with rather than replace"). (b) Wrong market — PJM accreditation does not govern the marginal data-center turbine order, much of which is ERCOT (no capacity market, no ELCC at all) or behind-the-meter bridge power; and ERCOT/TX is the single datapoint that moves against the finding. (c) Percentages are not the decision variable — $/accredited kW-yr is, and the finding never computes it, while a published study that does compute it exists.

MATERIALITY: circular, and therefore not materiality at all. The $18.87/share is the size of a bear case the analyst himself parameterised: 116 GW x 45% US x 60% peaker-duty x 30% at risk. The 30% is an unsourced choice. At 10% it is $6.3/share and fails the $10 floor; at 50% it is $31/share. The chain measures an assumption, not a physical or market quantity. The finding's own scoring (materiality 2, novelty 3, direction "kills-an-existing-angle") effectively concedes this. Criterion 2 requires a mechanism reaching a named GEV line WITH a direction — "no change, downside that does not materialise" is not a direction, and at a $250B market cap a defensive note that removes an in-house bear case is a risk-section paragraph, not a wedge.

TESTABLE PREDICTION: the strongest part of the submission. The PJM 2028/29 class-rating test and the EIA-923 FY26 fired-hours test are both properly dated with real kill conditions. But the EIA-923 test inherits the units error — it will measure EFLH, so a pass or fail tells the team nothing about GEV's per-fired-hour services billing.

WHAT THE TEAM SHOULD ACTUALLY TAKE: (1) Delete the state-level OLS from any draft — the agent correctly flags it as non-significant, and my recomputation gives a different CA coefficient anyway. (2) Replace the fleet-utilisation leg with CESA/Strategen Table 2 (sources.id=2959), which is third-party, published, and says the new gas peaker is the cheapest new-build per accredited kW-month under both QC and ELCC ($1.87 vs $2.42-2.63 for 4-hr BESS) — stronger than what the finding built. (3) Keep the PJM class-rating exhibit only after re-pulling the PDF and confirming the numbers, and label them as PJM marginal ELCC, one RTO's administrative methodology. (4) Redirect the real analytical effort to the services line, where the finding itself says the money is — but using starts and factored fired hours, not MWh/MW.

## [Verify] quant:algorithmic_efficiency:The agentic/long-context transit

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: REBUILD FROM PHYSICS TO PRICE.

STEP 0 — What the physical facts actually license.
(a) KV-cache: Pope et al. (arXiv:2211.05102, 2022) — at batch 512 / context 2048, PaLM-540B's KV cache is 3 TB, 3x the parameter bytes, re-read from off-chip memory once per generated token. KV bytes scale as batch x context, so batching does NOT amortize them (unlike weight reads, which scale 1/batch), and KV resists sub-4-bit quantization. I accept this as a correctly-cited, real result.
(b) TDP: A100 SXM 400W (2020-09) -> H100 700W -> B200 1000W -> B300 1400W (2025-06) -> Rubin VR200 ~1800-2300W (2026-27). I recompute the CAGR myself: (2300/400)^(1/6.0)-1 = e^(ln(5.75)/6)-1 = e^0.29153-1 = 33.8%/yr. Confirmed. Using the last SHIPPED part (B300, 4.75 yr): (1400/400)^(1/4.75)-1 = e^(1.2528/4.75)-1 = 30.2%/yr. Both are real; the Rubin endpoint is pre-launch reporting, not a datasheet.

MY FIRST SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION (unit error in the original): per-accelerator TDP growth does NOT by itself imply datacenter MW growth. Datacenter MW = (accelerators deployed) x (TDP). Rising TDP with a fixed MW budget means FEWER chips, not more megawatts. The binding constraint on 2026-2030 AI datacenter MW is interconnection queue position, transformer/turbine lead time and hyperscaler capex — all supply- and capital-constrained, not chip-TDP-constrained. So the TDP leg does not reach GEV's gas turbine GW line at all. It reaches, at most, Electrification content-per-MW (density -> more power conversion, busway, 800VDC). I therefore refuse to let the TDP CAGR carry the Power-segment argument, and I price its Electrification path separately and small (below).

The KV-cache leg is the one that legitimately touches Power. Its logical content is: "algorithmic efficiency does not reduce AI electricity demand." That is a DEFENSE OF THE BASE CASE, not an incremental earnings driver. It creates no new GW. It only reduces the probability of one specific bear branch (an efficiency shock collapsing the gas order book).

STEP 1 — Define the branch the finding re-weights.
Branch: GEV gas equipment output reaches ~30 GW/yr by 2030 (management target) versus stalling at ~20 GW/yr (the Q3'26 starting run-rate). Delta = 10 GW/yr of output.

STEP 2 — Equipment revenue line (GEV Power segment, product/equipment revenue).
10 GW/yr x $310M/GW = $3,100M/yr incremental equipment revenue.
Assumption check on $310M/GW: this is $310/kW for GE's equipment island. FY2025 Power *product* revenue was $6,420M (csv, OperatingSegments;Product;PowerSegment) against roughly 14-16 GW of gas shipments plus steam/nuclear/hydro/upgrades, implying $300-400M/GW for the gas slice. $310M/GW is defensible. I keep it.

STEP 3 — Equipment margin. THE ORIGINAL USED 15%. I SUBSTITUTE 12%.
Justification: FY26 guidance of 17-19% Power segment margin is a BLENDED figure dominated by the $13,072M services book (csv), which carries roughly 25-30% margins. Backing out, equipment-only margin inside Power is in the high single digits to low teens. Pricing 2030-delivery slots today, against a Greenville ramp with unabsorbed fixed cost, 12% is the defensible number and 15% is the bull end.
$3,100M x 0.12 = $372M EBITDA/yr.

STEP 4 — Services revenue line (GEV Power segment, service revenue).
Incremental installed base under the branch, accumulated 2026-2030: 5 yr x 10 GW = 50 GW.
Yield per GW-year: management says ~$500M/GW over 20 years = $25M/GW-yr; TODAY'S REALIZED yield on the installed base is ~$15M/GW-yr. The original used the forward $25M. I substitute the midpoint $20M/GW-yr, because the gap between $15M and $25M is precisely the unresolved question (and the -$218M H1'26 unfavorable contract-profitability revisions argue against assuming the forward number lands).
50 GW x $20M/GW-yr = $1,000M/yr incremental services revenue.
Services margin 30% (consistent with Power's blended 17-19% given equipment at 12%): $1,000M x 0.30 = $300M EBITDA/yr.

STEP 5 — Total branch EBITDA delta = $372M + $300M = $672M/yr at full run-rate (~2031).

STEP 6 — Multiple and present value.
25x per instruction: $672M x 25 = $16,800M enterprise value.
/ 266,333,581 shares = $63.08/share = 6.71% of $940.33.
I ALSO show the discounted version, because this run-rate does not exist until ~2031 and a 25x multiple on a 2031 number double-counts growth: at 9% WACC over 5 years, factor 0.65 -> $10,920M / 266,333,581 = $41.00/share = 4.36%.
(Note: 25x is if anything conservative versus GEV's own ~33x EV/EBITDA on FY26 numbers; I am not disputing the multiple.)

STEP 7 — THE CRITICAL STEP THE ORIGINAL GLOSSED: attribution.
$63.08 (or $41.00) is the value of the WHOLE 30-vs-20 GW branch. This finding does not own that branch — the AI-demand thesis, the reservation stack and Finding 1 own it. This finding's marginal contribution is the removal of one bear objection: "algorithmic efficiency will collapse AI power demand." The empirical price for that objection is observable: the DeepSeek-V3/R1 shock (Jan 2025) knocked GEV roughly 20% in days and the stock fully recovered within months. The market prices this risk EPISODICALLY, not persistently — meaning the standing probability weight on the efficiency-shock branch is small, not 15 points.
I assign 10 percentage points of probability shift, not the original's 15.
Undiscounted: 0.10 x $63.08 = $6.31/share = 0.67% of $940.33.
Discounted: 0.10 x $41.00 = $4.10/share = 0.44%.

STEP 8 — The Electrification leg, priced separately (this is where TDP actually belongs).
Q2'26 datacenter orders $2.7B; annualize conservatively at ~$8B/yr of datacenter-linked Electrification orders. Assume rack-density escalation raises GEV content per MW by 10%: $800M revenue x 15% margin = $120M EBITDA x 25 = $3,000M / 266,333,581 = $11.26/share. BUT this requires GEV to hold share through the 800VDC transition, which is untested (the original's own caveat 6 concedes this). At a 30% probability of GEV capturing that content: $3.38/share. I do not add this to the Power number with confidence; I flag it as the more interesting unexplored path.

MY NUMBER: $6.31/share undiscounted, $4.10/share discounted. Call it $4-6/share, ~0.45-0.67% of the reference price. Plus an optional, poorly-supported $3.38/share Electrification density leg. Total generous ceiling ~$9.70/share.
- **agrees_with_original**: False
- **where_it_differs**: Four differences, three of which reduce the number and one of which is a structural objection.

1. UNIT ERROR (structural). The original lets a 33.8%/yr per-accelerator TDP CAGR carry the argument that AI datacenter megawatts keep growing. Per-chip TDP is watts per accelerator; total load is accelerators x TDP. Higher TDP at a fixed MW budget means fewer chips, not more MW. Datacenter MW over a 3-12 month horizon is set by interconnection queues, capex commitments and equipment lead times — all of which the original itself concedes in the mechanism paragraph ("determined by ... capex and supply"). That concession destroys the TDP leg's relevance to gas GW: if MW is capex- and supply-determined, then neither TDP nor efficiency moves it, and the TDP statistic is decoration. TDP's real home is Electrification content-per-MW, which the original explicitly declines to test (its caveat 6) and assigns no dollars.

2. EQUIPMENT MARGIN 15% -> 12%. The original's 15% is not reconcilable with the segment mix in gev_segments.csv: Power FY2025 was $6,420M product / $13,072M service, and the FY26 17-19% segment margin guide is dominated by the services half. Equipment-only margin must sit well below the blended figure. This alone cuts the branch EBITDA by $93M/yr.

3. SERVICES YIELD $25M -> $20M/GW-yr. The original uses management's forward 20-year average while acknowledging in its own setup that today's realized yield is ~$15M/GW-yr, and while the H1'26 10-Q shows -$218M of net unfavorable service-contract profitability revisions versus -$42M a year earlier. Taking the forward number as given is exactly the assumption the filings are currently contradicting. $20M is the honest midpoint. Cuts branch EBITDA by another $75M/yr.

4. ATTRIBUTION 15 points -> 10 points, and a discounting step the original omits entirely. The original applies 25x to a ~2031 run-rate with no present-value adjustment — that double-counts the growth the multiple already embeds. More importantly, the 15-point probability shift is asserted without an anchor. I anchor it to the DeepSeek episode: the market priced the efficiency-shock objection violently for days and then unpriced it entirely. A risk the market only prices episodically does not carry 15 standing points.

Net: original $11.83/share; mine $6.31 undiscounted, $4.10 discounted. The original clears its own $10 bar; mine does not.

WHERE I AGREE: the Pope et al. KV-cache result is correctly quoted and correctly interpreted (KV bytes scale batch x context and are genuinely non-amortizable and quantization-resistant — this is real and most people arguing about AI efficiency miss it). The 33.8%/yr arithmetic is correct as computed. The MoE observation is sharp and I verified the logic: 671B/37B = 18.1x sparsity cuts FLOPs, but at serving batch the router touches most experts, so HBM bytes approach the full parameter set — MoE is a FLOP-saving not a byte-saving technique, and is close to energy-neutral for serving. That is the single best idea in the finding and it is buried in an evidence footnote rather than being the headline. The original's own novelty self-assessment (rating itself 2/5, warning the team a Citadel judge has heard the density story) is honest and I endorse it.
- **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: The probability-attribution weight — how many percentage points of probability this finding shifts onto the 30-GW-by-2030 branch. Everything else in the chain is a second-order haircut; this single coefficient is a linear multiplier on the entire result and it is pure judgment with no data behind it.

The finding produces no incremental gas turbine, no incremental order, and no incremental dollar of revenue. Its entire economic content is the removal of one bear objection ("algorithmic efficiency collapses AI electricity demand"). So its value = P(objection would otherwise have been priced) x (value of the branch it protects). The branch is worth $63.08/share undiscounted, $41.00 discounted. I use 10 points; the original used 15. Neither of us can defend the number from evidence — the only empirical anchor available is the DeepSeek episode of January 2025, where the market priced this exact objection hard and then completely unpriced it within months, which argues the standing weight is low and episodic.

Secondary driver (co-equal in mechanical leverage, but better anchored): the 10 GW/yr branch size. It scales the answer identically and is at least tied to a stated management target versus a current run-rate, so it is arguable from documents. The probability weight is not.
- **sensitivity**: SENSITIVITY ON THE KEY ASSUMPTION (probability shift, base 10 points), undiscounted branch value $63.08/share:
- Halved to 5 points: 0.05 x $63.08 = $3.15/share = 0.34% of $940.33.
- Base 10 points: $6.31/share = 0.67%.
- Doubled to 20 points: 0.20 x $63.08 = $12.62/share = 1.34%.
On the discounted branch value ($41.00/share): halved $2.05 (0.22%), base $4.10 (0.44%), doubled $8.20 (0.87%).

Reading: the finding clears the $10/share bar in exactly ONE corner of the space — you must simultaneously (a) skip present-value discounting of a 2031 run-rate, and (b) double my attribution weight to 20 points, i.e. claim that one in five units of GEV's AI-demand risk premium hinges specifically on the algorithmic-efficiency objection. Under the discounted treatment it cannot clear $10 even at 20 points. That is a fragile result.

SECONDARY SENSITIVITY — branch size (10 GW/yr base), holding probability at 10 points:
- 5 GW/yr: EBITDA delta $336M -> $8,400M / 266,333,581 = $31.54/share branch -> $3.15/share attributed (0.34%).
- 20 GW/yr: EBITDA delta $1,344M -> $33,600M -> $126.16/share branch -> $12.62/share attributed (1.34%).

THIRD SENSITIVITY — services yield, the one input the filings are actively arguing about (branch value, undiscounted, full 100% attribution):
- $15M/GW-yr (today's realized): services EBITDA $225M; total $597M; x25 = $14,925M = $56.04/share branch.
- $20M/GW-yr (my base): $63.08/share branch.
- $25M/GW-yr (management forward): services EBITDA $375M; total $747M; x25 = $18,675M = $70.12/share branch.
- $70M/GW-yr (the Jefferies 2030s claim): services EBITDA $1,050M; total $1,422M; x25 = $35,550M = $133.47/share branch -> $13.35/share attributed at 10 points.

## [Verify] skeptic:grid_alternatives:The HA fleet's fired-hour clock

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: Three errors, one of them fatal.

**(1) FATAL — units mismatch in the headline 1.474x ratio.** The finding compares GEV's *commercial operating hours* (hours synchronized, load-independent) against the US fleet's *equivalent full-load hours* (net generation / nameplate = capacity factor x 8760). These are not the same quantity and the comparison is invalid. I reproduced the EIA side exactly from the corpus (328.2 GW CT+CA+CS NG block, 1,503.5 TWh in 2025 -> 52.3% CF -> 4,580 EFLH; 2024 4,731; GT 161.1 GW / 157.4 TWh -> 977 h) — the EIA arithmetic is right, it is simply the wrong variable. GER-3620 factored fired hours count hours *fired*, not load-weighted; a plant at 60% load accrues full fired hours. So the correct denominator is US CC *operating* hours = EFLH / (average online load factor).
I bounded the load factor independently from the same corpus table: 2025 US NGCC implied heat rate = sum(fuel_consumed_mmbtu)/sum(net_generation_mwh) = 7,419 Btu/kWh (2024: 7,397; 2023: 7,402) versus a fleet full-load design heat rate of roughly 6,800-7,000 for an F/G/H mix. That 6-9% realized degradation implies substantial part-load and start-up operation, i.e. online load factor ~0.70-0.90. US CC operating hours are therefore ~5,089-6,543 h/yr, central ~5,725 — not 4,580. The gap collapses from 1.474x to roughly 1.08x central, with a range that includes 0.89x (HA running *less* than the US fleet).

**(2) The 6,750 h/unit/yr figure is at the top of its true range, and the claimed "two intervals agree within 1.7%" is spurious precision.** I confirmed both press-release endpoints by WebFetch: 2M / 88 units / "over 80 in commercial operation" / 47 GW at 2023-09-07, and 4M / 128 units / 21 countries / ~74 GW at 2026-05-26. But GEV files a *better* series in its own 10-K/10-Qs that the finding never used — corpus chunks, tier=primary, kind=sec, FTS '"HA-Turbines" "installed base"':
  2024-03-31: 94 units, "over two million" h
  2024-06-30: 100 units, ~2.5M h
  2024-09-30: 106 units, ~2.7M h
  2024-12-31: 115 units, ~2.9M h
  2025-12-31: 126 units, ~3.6M h
The clean calendar-year interval (12/31/24 -> 12/31/25) gives 0.7M h / ((115+126)/2 x 1.0 yr) = **5,809 h/unit/yr (66.3%)**, 14% below the claimed 6,750. The 0.1M rounding band puts the true value at 4,979-6,639, which overlaps 6,750 only at its very top edge. So the real uncertainty is roughly +/-15%, not +/-1.7%. The two press-release intervals agree with each other because they share the same announcement-lag bias, not because the measurement is precise.

**(3) The "major inspection crosses in 2.78 years" timing is wrong by ~3.5x.** The finding takes mean accumulated hours = 4.0M/128 = 31,250 and divides (50,000-31,250)/6,750 = 2.78 yr. That treats the denominator as frozen. GEV is adding ~18 units/yr to the installed base (94 -> 126 over 21 months) and ramping toward 20 GW/yr, so new zero-hour units dilute the mean faster than accumulation raises it. Iterating at 6,200 h/yr and +18 units/yr: mean goes 31,250 -> 32,833 -> 34,749 -> 36,899 -> 39,220 -> 41,670 over five years, i.e. ~+1,700/yr, reaching 50,000 around 2036, not Q1-Q2 2029. The mean is also the wrong statistic for timing an outage *wave* — that requires the vintage distribution, which the finding acknowledges but does not use.

**(4) Denominator inconsistency.** 74 GW / 128 units = 578 MW/unit, which is combined-cycle *plant* capacity including the steam turbine, not gas-turbine capacity (128 x ~430 MW = 55 GW). The finding applies a $/GW rate to 74 GW of plant capacity and then adds the 53 GW firm equipment backlog, which is gas-turbine GW. That inflates the base by ~34%.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: Partially, and I could not complete an independent novelty check — this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could run one, so I am reporting only what I can verify.

The finding itself honestly discloses that the qualitative claim is published: StockStory's GEV research page states that with a large contracted fleet and only part of it running, a services wave compounds once units reach their first major outage cycle mid-decade. So "a services wave is coming" is public.

What I *can* add is more damaging than a novelty problem: the specific quantitative input is disclosed by GEV itself, in the FY2025 10-K filed 2026-01-29 (corpus, tier=primary, kind=sec). Note 2 / critical accounting estimates says that a significant estimate in determining expected CSA revenue is "estimating how customers will utilize their assets over the term of the agreement," and that GEV "generally use[s] historical utilization trends in developing our revenue estimates." The measured 5,800-6,800 h/yr *is* the historical utilization trend GEV already uses. The $88.5B services RPO is stated at the transaction price, which already embeds that estimate. So the finding is recovering an input management has already applied, not supplying one the market lacks.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The best defense of the finding is on point (2), the duty-cycle number itself, and it is genuinely decent: GEV's SEC hours figures are rounded to 0.1M, so the FY2025 delta of "2.9M -> 3.6M" is really anywhere in 0.6-0.8M. If the true values were 2.851M and 3.649M, the implied rate is 6,622 h/unit/yr — which reconciles almost exactly with the two press-release intervals (6,826 and 6,713). Two independent methods landing on ~6,700 inside the rounding band is a real argument, and I should not claim the SEC series refutes 6,750 outright. It shows the number is uncertain at +/-15% and that the central estimate is below 6,750, not that 6,750 is impossible.

There is also a legitimate residual claim buried in here: HA units genuinely are high-duty machines, and the contract-acceleration effect (a fixed-value CSA earned over 14 years instead of 20) is a real positive NPV and cash-timing effect that nobody has quantified. That is worth something — but it is a discount-rate argument worth low single-digit dollars per share, not the revenue-uplift argument the finding makes.

What the counterargument cannot rescue is the comparison. Even granting 6,750 h/yr for the HA fleet, the US CC benchmark must be restated from 4,580 EFLH to ~5,089-6,543 operating hours, and the 1.474x gap does not survive that under any load-factor assumption I can defend.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. The measurement idea is clever and the EIA arithmetic reproduces exactly, but the central comparison is a unit error and the mechanism is broken by GEV's own accounting policy.

**Physics.** The 1.474x "duty gap" compares GEV running hours to EIA equivalent-full-load hours — different quantities. Restating the US fleet to operating hours (EFLH 4,580 / online load factor 0.70-0.90, where I bounded the load factor from the fleet's own 7,419 Btu/kWh implied 2025 heat rate versus ~6,800-7,000 design) gives 5,089-6,543 h/yr. Against an HA fleet at 5,809 h/yr (GEV's own 10-K series, calendar 2025, which the finding never used) to 6,750 (press releases), the ratio is ~1.08x central and spans 0.89x-1.33x. The gap may be zero. Separately, the "major inspection wave crosses in 2.78 years" is wrong by ~3.5x because it freezes the unit count while GEV adds ~18 units/yr, which pulls the fleet mean *down*; iterated properly the mean reaches 50,000 h around 2036, not 2029.

**Mechanism.** Three independent breaks, any one sufficient.
(a) *Revenue is cost-driven, not hour-driven.* FY2025 10-K: CSA revenue is recognized "using the percentage of completion method, which is based on costs incurred relative to our estimate of total expected costs." Per-hour billing is a *billing* term; the 10-K says explicitly that the difference between revenue (costs incurred) and billings (contractual) "result in changes to our contract asset or contract liability positions." Fired hours move the contract asset, not the P&L line the finding names.
(b) *CSAs cap out on events and hours.* The corpus contains an actual GE CSA (Ravenswood, tier=primary, kind=sec, filed 2025-09-24 and 2026-03-02): it expires "at the earlier of the fourth major outage or 225,000 operating hours, or October 3, 2036." Higher duty does not buy more lifetime contract value — it delivers the same value sooner and brings the renewal/repricing decision forward. That is a timing/NPV effect, not the ~32% revenue uplift the materiality assumes.
(c) *The sign is not established.* The 10-K says utilization "impacts both the amount of customer payments we expect to receive and our estimate of future contract costs." Higher-than-assumed duty raises both sides. The H1'26 net unfavorable service-profitability revisions of -$218M (vs -$42M H1'25) are evidence the cost side has lately been winning, which would make this finding *short*, not long.

**Materiality, corrected.** Rebuilding the chain with operating-hours-to-operating-hours and the gas-turbine GW denominator (55 GW, not 74 GW plant GW): delta $1.92M/GW-yr -> $105M revenue -> $32M EBITDA x25 / 266,333,581 = **$2.97/share, 0.32%**. On the full 127 GW mature base: $6.85/share, 0.73%. Only by stacking every favorable assumption simultaneously (HA at 6,750, US at 5,089, and the inflated 127 GW plant-capacity base) do you reach $22.00/share — and that version still values a counterfactual nobody forecasts and GEV does not use. Against the finding's stated $16.75-28.74/share, the defensible figure is below the $10/share bar.

**So-what at $250B.** The finding values the question "what if the HA fleet ran at the US combined-cycle fleet average?" No analyst, and not GEV, assumes that. GEV states it sets CSA revenue estimates from historical utilization trends — the very trend being measured. The finding recovers management's input rather than correcting the market's.

**Salvage for the team (one line each, both small):** the contract-acceleration NPV effect from CSAs terminating at the earlier of N major outages / an hours cap / a calendar date is real and, as far as I can tell, unquantified — but it is a discount-rate argument worth low single digits per share. And the 10-K HA installed-base/operating-hours series (94/2.0M through 126/3.6M) is a genuinely useful clean dataset the team should keep; note the disclosure appears to have been dropped from the 2025 and 2026 10-Qs in this corpus, so the FY26 10-K in late Jan/early Feb 2027 may be the next datapoint. Worth confirming against EDGAR directly, since corpus absence is not proof of non-disclosure.

**Data-quality note for the team:** corpus sources.id=1647 (the 3M-hours article) carries published='2024-09-20', which is wrong — WebFetch of the same Yahoo URL shows it updated 2025-03-10, and GEV's SEC series (2.9M at 2024-12-31) confirms the 3M crossing was early 2025, not September 2024. The finding's 2025-03-06 date is correct; the corpus metadata is not. Other date-differencing work against this table should be re-checked.

STEP 1 — PHYSICS (reproduced, confirmed).
H2: 1 mol H2O / 241.8 kJ = 4.136 mol H2O/MJ. CH4: 2 mol H2O / 802.3 kJ = 2.493 mol H2O/MJ. Ratio 1.659x; incremental dm = 1.643 mol H2O/MJ. At q = 1.157 MJ heat per kg compressor inlet air (7HA.02: 885 MW heat input / 765 kg/s air), incremental hot-gas water as % of inlet mass flow I = heat_frac_H2 x q x dm x 18.015/10.
  10 vol% H2 -> heat frac 0.032, I = 0.111%, S = 1+0.55I = 1.061 -> interval 23,562 h (-5.8%) -> EVENT FREQUENCY +6.1%
  50 vol% H2 -> heat frac 0.232, I = 0.793%, S = 1.436 -> interval 17,408 h (-30.4%) -> EVENT FREQUENCY +43.6%
  100 vol% H2 -> I = 3.424%, S = 2.883 -> 8,671 h (-65.3%) -> EVENT FREQUENCY +188.4%
CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL: a 30.4% shorter interval is a 43.6% increase in inspection events per fired hour (1/0.696 - 1), not 30%. The original used 30% and understated frequency by a third.

STEP 2 — EXPOSED BASE.
126 HA units x ~400 MW = 50.4 GW installed.

STEP 3 — AFFECTED FINANCIAL LINE (rebuilt; this is where I depart from the original).
Under a CSA billed per fired hour, H2 blending does NOT change revenue — it changes COST. The original multiplied the 30% by the $15M/GW-yr REVENUE yield, which treats a revenue figure as an EBITDA delta. Correct treatment: apply the frequency increase to the event-driven portion of service COST.
  Services revenue yield, realized today: $15M/GW-yr (mgmt, Morgan Stanley Laguna 9/16/26) -> HA services revenue ~$756M/yr, which is a sane ~9% of Power's ~$8B services book (young fleet; legacy 7F/9F carries the rest). Cross-checked against Power segment scale in data/financials/gev_segments.csv.
  Services gross margin assumed 25% (SUBSTITUTED — GEV does not disclose services-only margin; FY26 Power segment guide is 17-19% and services is the higher-margin half, so 25% is defensible and conservative-to-mid).
  Cost = 0.75 x $15M = $11.25M/GW-yr. Event-driven share (parts, HGP hardware, outage labor) assumed 85%; remainder (monitoring, remote diagnostics, admin) is fixed. Event-driven cost = $9.56M/GW-yr.

STEP 4 — EBITDA DELTA -> $/SHARE (x25 / 266,333,581 shares; % of $940.33).
  (a) VERIFIED EXPOSURE TODAY — Daya Bay 2x9HA.01, 1.34 GW at 10 vol% H2 under a 25-yr GEV LTSA: 1.34 x $9.56M x 6.1% = $0.8M/yr -> $0.07/share -> 0.008%.
  (b) 10% of HA fleet blending at 50%: 5.04 GW x $9.56M x 43.6% = $21.0M/yr -> $1.97/share -> 0.21%.
  (c) 25% of fleet at 50%: $52.6M/yr -> $4.93/share -> 0.53%.
  (d) 100% of fleet at 50% (physically implausible by 2027): $210M/yr -> $19.73/share -> 2.10%.
  (e) Absolute upper bound, 100% of fleet on 100% H2: $908M/yr -> $85.21/share -> 9.06%. This case cannot occur: GEV's validated 100%-H2 DLN combustor is B/E-class only, not HA.
  BREAK-EVEN: you need 50.7% of the entire HA fleet blending at 50 vol% H2 to reach $10/share. Nothing close to that exists or is contracted.

HEADLINE ANSWER for a 3-12 month horizon: $0.07/share (0.008%). Even the generous 10%-adoption scenario is $1.97/share (0.21%).
These are GROSS of two offsets that both cut further: (i) only the CSA half of the book has this sign — the transactional half sees the same physics as INCREASED parts revenue, a positive; (ii) CSA-vs-transactional mix on the HA fleet is undisclosed, so the true net could be near zero or positive.

- **where_it_differs**: I agree with the conclusion (not a wedge) and with the physics, but the original's arithmetic is wrong in two offsetting ways that happen to land in the same place.

1. REVENUE-AS-EBITDA ERROR. The original computed "1.34 GW x $15M x 6% = $1.2M/yr EBITDA impact." That multiplies the REVENUE yield by the severity factor and books the result as EBITDA. Under a fixed per-fired-hour CSA, revenue does not move at all; only cost does. The correct base is event-driven service cost (~$9.56M/GW-yr on my 25% margin / 85% event-share assumptions), not $15M/GW-yr of revenue.

2. INTERVAL-SHORTENING vs EVENT-FREQUENCY ERROR. "A 30% interval shortening raises parts consumption ~30%" is wrong. Events per fired hour scale as 1/(1-0.304) = 1.436, i.e. +43.6%. The original understated the physical driver by a third.

These cancel (cost base 36% lower, frequency 45% higher), so my numbers land within ~10% of theirs: base case $0.07 vs their $0.11/share; 10%-fleet case $1.97 vs their $2.13; 25% case $4.93 vs their $5.32; 100%-at-50% case $19.73 vs their $21.29. Same verdict either way, but the team should use my chain because theirs would not survive a judge asking "why is a revenue number your EBITDA number?"

3. ASSUMPTIONS I SUBSTITUTED because the original left them implicit: services gross margin 25% (GEV discloses no services-only margin); event-driven share of service cost 85%. Both are stated, both are mine, neither is disclosed by GEV.

4. I also made explicit what the original only gestured at: the break-even is 50.7% of the HA fleet blending at 50 vol%. Everything else is second-order. The cost-base assumptions (25% margin, 85% event share) are linear and modest.

Adoption is the whole answer, and adoption is verifiably near zero: 1.34 GW at 10 vol% (Daya Bay), which is 2.7% of the fleet at a blend producing a 6.1% frequency effect. The finding is a correct piece of physics attached to a business that is not happening. Note the second-order issue that could flip the sign entirely: the CSA-vs-transactional mix, which GEV does not disclose — on the transactional half this identical physics is a parts-revenue POSITIVE of the same magnitude. So the sign of the net effect is genuinely unknown, not merely small.

## [Verify] skeptic:hydrogen_blending:The empirical kill: hydrogen opt

- **physics_sound**: True
- **physics_errors**: I re-ran every generators query independently against gev.db and the numbers reproduce exactly. Planned sheet, vintage 2026-07: SUN 123,181 MW (n=1078), NG 69,677 MW (n=491), MWH 65,262 MW, H2 50 MW (n=1). The single H2 planned row is plant_id 69099, 'Orion - Helion', WA, prime_mover 'OT', 50 MW, planned 2028, status '(L) Regulatory approvals pending'. Confirmed: it is a fusion pilot, not a hydrogen turbine, and prime_mover 'OT' (not CT/CA/GT) proves it is not a combustion turbine. Ratio 50/69,677 = 0.072%, as stated.

THREE DEFECTS, none fatal to the conclusion:

(1) REPRODUCIBILITY ERROR. The finding says "only two distinct plant_ids have ever carried energy_source='H2'." That is wrong. `SELECT count(distinct plant_id) FROM generators WHERE energy_source='H2'` returns 4, not 2. The four are: 66599 Dark Sky Energy Center (CA, FC, 0.3 MW), 62423 Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (NY, FC, 1.5 MW), 69099 Orion-Helion (WA, OT, 50 MW), 69358 Calistoga Resiliency Center (CA, FC, 8 MW). The "2" figures in the evidence block are per-sheet distinct counts (Operating p=2, Planned p=2) which the author incorrectly collapsed into a union. Also the finding says "Operating H2 ... is 8 MW, Calistoga" — Operating actually contains two plants (Calistoga 8 MW + Regeneron 1.5 MW). A judge who re-runs the query gets a different number than the memo claims. Direction of error is harmless (4 tiny fuel-cell/fusion plants instead of 2 still means zero H2 turbines) but it must be corrected before anything is written down.

(2) THE HEADLINE EVIDENCE ANSWERS A STRAWMAN. The finding's own caveat concedes it: EIA's energy_source records the PRIMARY fuel at registration, so a turbine built for 30-50 vol% H2 co-firing registers as 'NG'. I confirmed there is no blend code anywhere in the schema — the full energy_source list for vintage 2026-07 is NG/SUN/DFO/WAT/LFG/WND/MWH/BIT/SUB/GEO/WDS/OBG/BLQ/RFO/NUC/MSW/OG/KER/WH/AB/RC/LIG/PC/BFG/OBL/PUR/PG/WC/OTH/WO/JF/OBS/WDL/TDF/SGC/H2/SLW/SGP, with no hydrogen-blend or dual-fuel-H2 field. The dataset is therefore STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of registering hydrogen readiness. Proving "no US generator plans to fire predominantly hydrogen" is proving something no hydrogen bull has ever claimed — the bull case was always readiness-as-priced-option, not H2 as primary fuel. The query is clean and the arithmetic is right; it just does not bear on the proposition it is presented as killing.

(3) A STRONGER PHYSICAL ARGUMENT WAS AVAILABLE AND MISSED. The finding cites ETN's 'Considerable' modification band (<=60 vol% H2: piping replaced, gaskets and valves replaced, combustor H2-compatibility checked) and notes it books "HGP: No changes" — then does nothing with that. That line is the actual kill, and it is mechanical rather than statistical: H2-readiness is a fuel-skid, piping and combustor-liner specification, and by ETN's own table it does not touch the hot gas path. GEV's services annuity bills on factored fired hours against GER-3620 Rev P intervals (25,000 FFH combustion/HGP, 50,000 FFH major), and those intervals are set by HGP metal temperature and cyclic duty. A modification that explicitly changes no HGP hardware cannot move the maintenance-interval clock, so it cannot move services RPO in either direction. Note the sign for the team: if a unit ACTUALLY fired high-H2, the physics runs the other way — higher flame temperature and higher burning velocity raise NOx and hot-section thermal load, which would INCREASE factored hours and therefore increase services revenue per operating hour. Hydrogen firing, were it real, would be a services tailwind, not a liability. Nothing is firing it, so the value is zero either way, but the finding has the sign of the hypothetical backwards by implication when it frames H2 as a retrofit/warranty liability tail.

MATERIALITY ARITHMETIC CHECKS: 2 GW x $450/kW = $0.9B; $0.9B/4yr = $225M/yr x 18% = $40.5M EBITDA; x25/266,333,581 = $3.80/share; /$940.33 = 0.40%. Arithmetic correct. $450/kW is a defensible turbine-island-only figure (full CCGT EPC is roughly $1,200-2,400/kW in 2026; OEM scope is a fraction) but it is the author's estimate, as admitted.

BROKEN DATED TEST. Prediction (1) says Bundesnetzagentur will name GE Vernova on under 25% of awarded StromVKG gas capacity. Bundesnetzagentur capacity auctions award to PROJECT DEVELOPERS, not to turbine OEMs. The award notice names the bidding entity and the site; OEM selection is a subsequent private procurement decision that is typically announced months to years later, if at all. So there is no observable "GEV share of awarded capacity" in the auction results, and the prediction cannot be scored on the stated date. Prediction (2) — that GEV will not quantify a hydrogen backlog share on the Oct 28 2026 call — is observable but is a prediction of continued silence, which is nearly unfalsifiable and has never been otherwise. The genuinely scorable test is the weakest-stated one: EIA-860M vintages through Jan 2027 continuing to show zero planned hydrogen-fired turbines.

MECHANISM REACHES THE LINE, BUT ONLY AS A NULL, AND FOR A REASON NOT GIVEN. The finding asserts no hydrogen retrofit liability sits in Power's contract-loss provisions. That is right, but the stated reason ("there is nothing to disclose") is the weak version. The accounting reason is stronger: H2-readiness is sold as a PRICED OPTION inside the equipment scope, not as a fixed-price future conversion obligation. Under ASC 606 an onerous-contract / contract-loss provision arises only when estimated costs to complete exceed consideration on that contract. A capability spec that the customer paid for at order does not create that condition, and a conversion the customer has not yet bought is not a performance obligation at all. So even if the US were building thousands of H2-ready MW, the 2027 provision exposure would still be ~$0 — the mechanism is null for a contract-structure reason that is independent of the EIA data, which means the EIA query is not load-bearing for half the finding's own claim.

THE "SO WHAT" AT $250B. The finding scores its own materiality 2 and says do not spend memo space. That is self-consistent and I agree. But note its value is bounded by whether the team had a hydrogen leg at all — hydrogen is not on the brief's already-worked-to-death list, so this may be killing an angle nobody was going to pitch. The kill is worth roughly one paragraph of a Q&A prep sheet ("if a judge asks about hydrogen optionality: EIA-860M shows zero planned H2-fired turbines in the US, the only H2 planned row is a 50 MW Helion fusion pilot mis-coded, and the ETN readiness band explicitly changes no hot-gas-path hardware so it cannot move the services annuity"), not a memo section.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY REFUTE IT. If GEV is selling H2-readiness as a priced hardware option at a positive margin on a meaningful share of the 116 GW, that is a real revenue line the EIA query cannot see, and it would be an upside leg rather than a nothing. I could not test this — GEV does not disclose attach rate or option pricing, and my search budget ran out before I could look for trade-press estimates. The team should treat "H2-readiness attach rate and price premium on HA orders" as an OPEN question, not as answered by this finding. The finding's correct claim is narrower than its title: hydrogen as a FUEL is worth zero to GEV in the US through 2030. Hydrogen-readiness as a PRODUCT FEATURE is unmeasured.
- **verdict_summary**: NOT REFUTED, BUT DOWNGRADE AND DO NOT PITCH. Every database number reproduces exactly against gev.db, with one correction: four distinct plant_ids have ever carried energy_source='H2' (Dark Sky 0.3 MW FC, Regeneron 1.5 MW FC, Helion Orion 50 MW OT, Calistoga 8 MW FC), not two — the author collapsed per-sheet counts into a union. The 50 MW / 69,677 MW planned ratio and the $3.80/share sizing are arithmetically correct.

The conclusion (hydrogen is worth under $4/share in either direction; cut it) is right. The evidence offered for it is weaker than presented. The EIA energy_source field records primary fuel only and there is no blend code anywhere in the schema, so the query is structurally incapable of detecting H2-readiness — it proves nobody plans to fire hydrogen as a primary fuel, which no hydrogen bull ever claimed. The finding admits this in its caveats and then titles itself as an "empirical kill" anyway.

The strongest argument was in the finding's own evidence and went unused: ETN's readiness band books "HGP: No changes," so H2-readiness touches fuel skid, piping, valves and combustor liners but not the hot gas path — and GEV's services annuity bills on factored fired hours against GER-3620 Rev P HGP-driven intervals. Readiness therefore cannot move services RPO by construction, no dataset required. Note the sign correction: if a unit actually fired high-H2, higher flame temperature and burning velocity would raise hot-section thermal load and INCREASE factored hours, making it a services tailwind, not the liability the finding implies.

One of the two dated tests is broken: Bundesnetzagentur StromVKG auctions award to developers, not turbine OEMs, so "GEV named on under 25% of awarded gas capacity" is not observable from the auction results. The scorable test is the residual one — EIA-860M through Jan 2027 continuing to show zero planned H2-fired turbines.

Novelty is UNVERIFIED: this session's web search budget was exhausted before I could check trade press or sell-side. Do not represent the novelty claim as confirmed.

OPEN QUESTION THE FINDING DOES NOT CLOSE: H2-readiness sold as a priced option on HA orders is a revenue line the EIA query cannot see, and GEV discloses no attach rate or premium. The defensible claim is narrow — hydrogen as a FUEL is worth zero to GEV in the US through 2030. Scores: novelty 2 (down from 3), confidence 4 on the narrow claim, materiality 1 (down from 2). Use as one Q&A prep paragraph; do not give it memo space.

TAIL 1 TOTAL: $0.61/share (0.065% of $940.33).

## [Verify] skeptic:algorithmic_efficiency:The agentic/long-context transit

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: FIVE errors, two of them fatal.

(1) STRESS-TEST NUMBER CITED AS OPERATING NUMBER. The 3TB KV cache is Pope et al.'s MULTIHEAD-ATTENTION worst case — the strawman the paper exists to demolish. Table 1 of the same paper: "Maximum context lengths supported for different attention variants of PaLM 540B on 64 chips" — Multihead 1,320 (batch 128) / 330 (batch 512); Optimized multiquery 43,000 / 10,700. The abstract's own headline: multiquery "enables scaling up to 32x larger context lengths." The finding quotes the motivating sentence on p.2 and omits the result on p.6. This is precisely the error the brief warned about.

(2) THE 3TB IS ALREADY INT8, WHICH DESTROYS THE "CANNOT GO BELOW 4 BITS" CLAIM. Independent re-derivation from PaLM architecture (118 layers, 48 heads, head_dim 256 -> KV dim 12,288/layer): KV bytes/token = 2 x 118 x 12,288 x bytes_per_elem. At bf16 (2B) = 5.80 MB/token -> 512 x 2048 x 5.80MB = 6.08 TB. At int8 (1B) = 2.90 MB/token -> 3.04 TB. The paper's "3TB" matches int8 ONLY. (The paper's own abstract confirms int8 quantization is in use.) So the "3x the model's parameters" comparison puts an int8 KV cache against bf16 parameters (1.08 TB) — an inconsistent-units comparison that inflates the ratio ~2x. And the finding argues KV "cannot be pushed below ~4 bits" against a baseline that is already at 8.

(3) THE KILL CONDITION ALREADY FIRED, IN 2024. No frontier 2026 model uses MHA. Recomputed KV bytes/token: PaLM-540B MHA bf16 = 5.80 MB. Llama-3-70B GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads x 128) bf16 = 0.328 MB = 17.7x less. DeepSeek-V3 MLA (61 layers, kv_lora_rank 512 + rope 64 = 576 elems/token/layer) = 70.3 KB bf16 / 35.1 KB fp8 = 165x less than PaLM MHA. The finding's kill condition (3) says the angle dies "if context-compression techniques (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek V3.2 sparse attention, KV quantization below 4 bits) reduce KV bytes per token by more than ~5x in production serving." MLA delivers 165x and shipped in Dec 2024. The finding wrote its own kill condition, named the exact technique that triggers it, and did not check whether it had already fired. arXiv listing confirms MLA is now a mainstream 2026 primitive (RedKnot-MLA 2609.07008, Instella-MoE 2609.00791, VideoMLA 2605.30351 at "92.7% reduction in per-token KV memory", Through the Bottleneck 2607.23054 at "81% KV-cache reduction").

(4) TDP BENCHMARK IS APPLES-TO-ORANGES AND USES A WRONG ENDPOINT. The finding benchmarks its 33.8%/yr against Del Sozzo et al.'s 8.6%/yr. But (a) Del Sozzo's OWN B300 endpoint is 1100W, not 1400W — paper text: "the TDP of the selected NVIDIA GPUs grew by a much slower 8.6% every year (8.45y DT), as the 170.9W (Tesla C870) evolved into the 1100W (Blackwell Ultra B300)", with footnote 1 stating they "extrapolate and approximate the TDP and release price of a single B300 GPU from the available information for its HGX version." (b) 8.6% is an 18-year REGRESSION SLOPE (2007-2025); its endpoint-to-endpoint rate is (1100/170.9)^(1/18)-1 = 10.9%/yr. (c) Recomputing the recent window on the paper's own value: (1100/400)^(1/5.1)-1 = 21.9%/yr. Honest acceleration is ~2x, not "roughly 4x." Comparing a 5-point endpoint ratio to a long-run regression slope manufactures acceleration from any convex series. The finding's 33.8% also depends entirely on an unshipped 2300W Rubin Max-P rumor; the 1800-2300W spread is itself 28% uncertainty on the endpoint.

(5) FATAL INTERNAL CONTRADICTION — LEG (a) REFUTES LEG (b). Leg (a) asserts the KV cache is loaded from off-chip memory per token "during which the computational core of the chip is essentially idle." Leg (b) asserts "GPUs run pinned near TDP whenever they are saturated." These describe THE SAME PHASE of THE SAME WORKLOAD. If KV-cache streaming is the binding constraint, decode is memory-bound and the chip draws materially BELOW TDP — that is what "essentially idle" means in power terms. The finding concedes this in caveat (5) and then retains the density leg anyway. You cannot invoke core idleness to prove energy intensity and simultaneously deny it to prove power draw. Whichever leg you keep, you lose the other.

Verified-correct items: the 40% GPU share of AI datacenter power is correctly attributed (Del Sozzo ref [29] = Emberson & Cottier, Epoch AI 2025). The arithmetic (2300/400)^(1/6)-1 = 33.8% is correct as arithmetic; it is the inputs and the benchmark that fail.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The framing is consensus, and it is already sitting in the team's own corpus commentary tier. FTS hits in chunks: '"Jevons" "data center"' returns a chunk explicitly naming "Jevons Paradox ... If AI becomes more efficient" applied to datacenter demand. '"rack density" "power"' returns PUE discussion, "next-generation designs approaching 1 MW" per rack, "traditional AC architectures encounter practical limitations ... Developers are responding wi[th]" (the 800VDC transition), and "hyperscale AI facilities typically contract for power capacities exceeding 100 MW ... scale to the gigawatt level." '"800VDC"' returns Eaton coverage ("Eaton is developing technolog[y]") and a Sept 17 2026 Merge4 Energy launch built on "800VDC solid-state circuit breakers." So the rack-density/800VDC leg, the Jevons leg, the training-to-inference-shift leg and the 100MW+ contracting leg are all published and in the corpus.

The finding's own novelty_check concedes this and self-rates novelty 2/5, noting "the density story in particular is close to consensus among power-equipment bulls, and the team should assume a Citadel judge has heard it." That self-assessment is correct.

The one component I could not find published — KV-cache bytes as the specific non-amortizable, non-quantizable residual — is unpublished because it is FALSE for 2026 serving stacks (see physics_errors 1-3). An unpublished wrong claim is not novelty.

Note: I could not run WebSearch (session budget 200/200 exhausted before this task). I substituted direct arXiv API fetches and corpus FTS. I therefore cannot rule out a sell-side note making this exact KV-cache connection, but given the claim is architecturally obsolete, that is immaterial.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The steelman, which the team should keep as a DEFENSIVE line and not as a wedge: GEV's order book has been empirically insensitive to AI-efficiency news. DeepSeek-R1 (Jan 2025) was the cleanest natural experiment available — a credible order-of-magnitude efficiency claim — and it produced no observable deceleration in GEV gas bookings or slot reservations in the following quarters. That is an actual fact about the tape, it does not depend on any of the broken physics above, and it answers a judge who asks "what happens to your thesis if inference gets 10x cheaper?" The correct answer is structural rather than physical: datacenter MW over a 3-12 month horizon is set by committed capex, interconnect queue position and equipment lead times, all of which are contracted years ahead and do not reprice on a model release. Del Sozzo's own Insight 8 supports this — improvement-per-watt grew faster than improvement-per-dollar, meaning DOLLARS, not watts, are the binding input.

But notice what this argument does NOT need: it does not need KV-cache physics, it does not need a TDP CAGR, and it does not need agentic token multipliers. It is a contracting-and-lead-time argument wearing a physics costume. Strip the costume and it is one defensive sentence worth $0/share of incremental thesis. The second-strongest point is that the finding's caveat (6) is the actually-interesting unexamined question — whether GEV holds share in the 800VDC/medium-voltage transition — and the corpus shows Eaton and well-funded startups contesting exactly that layer. That is a share question, not a demand question, and it deserves its own investigation rather than being a footnote here.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. Both the physics and the mechanism fail independently; either failure alone is sufficient.

PHYSICS. The central number is the wrong number. The 3TB KV cache is Pope et al.'s multihead-attention MOTIVATING case, which the same paper then fixes — Table 1 shows optimized multiquery supports 43,000-token context versus multihead's 1,320 on identical hardware, a 32x improvement, and the abstract says so. My independent re-derivation from the PaLM-540B architecture (118 layers x 48 heads x 256 head-dim) gives 5.80 MB/token at bf16 = 6.08 TB, and 3.04 TB at int8 — so the paper's 3TB figure is ALREADY int8-quantized, which guts the "cannot be pushed below 4 bits" premise, and its "3x parameters" ratio compares int8 KV against bf16 weights. Worse, the finding's own kill condition (3) fires on >5x KV-byte reduction from MLA or sparse attention; DeepSeek-V3's MLA delivers 35.1 KB/token at fp8 versus PaLM MHA's 5.80 MB = 165x, and shipped in December 2024. The finding named the technique that kills it and never checked. The TDP leg is separately mis-benchmarked: Del Sozzo et al.'s own B300 endpoint is 1100W (explicitly extrapolated from HGX, footnote 1), not 1400W, and their 8.6% is an 18-year regression slope whose endpoint rate is 10.9%/yr; the honest recent-window figure on their own data is 21.9%/yr, so the acceleration is ~2x, not 4x, and the 33.8% depends on an unshipped Rubin rumor with a 28% spread. Finally, the two legs contradict each other: leg (a) needs the core "essentially idle" during KV streaming, leg (b) needs GPUs "pinned near TDP." Same phase, same workload. Keeping one kills the other.

MECHANISM. A unit error sits at the joint. TDP is PER-DEVICE power; datacenter load is FLEET power = chips x realized utilization power, and chips shipped is set by capex, HBM supply and fab allocation. Rising per-chip TDP at fixed capex concentrates the same MW into fewer, denser racks — it does not conjure MW. Del Sozzo's Insight 8 (improvement-per-watt outpacing improvement-per-dollar) says dollars, not watts, are binding. Then the chain fails on GEV's own accounting: equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred, so gas GW signed in 2026 become RPO, not revenue, inside a 3-12 month horizon; and services bill per FIRED HOUR and per OUTAGE EVENT, so HA units delivered in 2029-30 contribute exactly zero fired hours in the window. The materiality chain takes a 2030 steady-state EBITDA, multiplies by 25x, and discounts nothing.

MATERIALITY IS ASSERTED, NOT DERIVED. The finding concedes it shares Finding 1's branch and must not be summed with it, then claims a standalone "roughly a 15-point probability shift = $11.83/share." The 15 points has no derivation, no base rate, and no sensitivity. It is a number chosen to clear the stated $10 bar — it lands at $11.83, 18% above the threshold, which is itself a tell. Strip the unsupported probability and the incremental contribution over Finding 1 is $0/share. This is a supporting argument for another finding, not a wedge.

DATED TEST IS NON-DIAGNOSTIC. "Q3'26 gas GW signed >= 15" on Oct 28 2026 tests GEV order momentum, which would pass or fail identically under any demand narrative — including ones that contradict this mechanism entirely. A test that cannot distinguish your hypothesis from its rivals is not a test. The Rubin TDP check IS diagnostic but has no committed date and resolves on NVIDIA's schedule.

SO-WHAT AT $250B. "AI datacenter load keeps growing, and efficiency gains do not reduce it" is the consensus reason GEV trades at ~35x forward versus the S&P's ~22x. It is the price. A Citadel judge has heard the Jevons framing and the rack-density story; both are already in this team's own corpus commentary tier alongside Eaton's 800VDC positioning.

RECOMMENDATION. Drop entirely. Salvage exactly two sentences: (i) the DeepSeek natural experiment as a defensive rebuttal to an efficiency objection, and (ii) caveat (6) — whether GEV holds share in the 800VDC transition — promoted to its own research question, since that is a share fight with named contestants and is genuinely untested.

PROCESS NOTE. WebSearch was unavailable (session budget 200/200 exhausted at task start). I verified via direct arXiv API fetch, independent arithmetic re-derivation, full-text inspection of both source papers in the scratchpad, and corpus FTS. The refutation rests on the primary sources' own text and on arithmetic, not on search.

## [Verify] quant:hot_section_materials:GER-3620 Rev P publishes estimat

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: REBUILD FROM SCRATCH (hot_section_materials / HA parts-life).

STEP 1 — Installed HA capacity. 126 HA units (FY25 10-K). Model mix 7HA.01 ~290MW, 7HA.02 ~384MW, 9HA.01 ~448MW, 9HA.02 ~571MW. ASSUMPTION (GEV discloses no HA GW): 0.40 GW average -> 126 x 0.40 = 50.4 GW. I adopt the original's figure because it is defensible and I can't improve on it.

Management (Morgan Stanley Laguna, 16 Sep 2026): ~$500M of services revenue per GW over the first 20 years. 50.4 GW x $500M = $25.2B lifetime, = $1,260M/yr lifetime-average. That 5.8% share is a plausible sanity check on a ~7,000-unit installed base that is mostly legacy F/E. The $25M/GW-yr lifetime average is the correct basis for a LIFETIME cost estimate, which is what ASC 606 actually books, so I keep it here.

STEP 3 — Lifetime CSA cost. ASSUMPTION: 25% contract margin (I substitute 25% for the original's 22%; Power segment EBIT margin FY25 = $2,902M / ($6,420M product + $13,072M service) = 14.9%, and services carry materially above-segment margin, so 25% at the contract level is the defensible mid-point). Lifetime cost = 0.75 x $25.2B = $18.9B = $945M/yr.

STEP 4 — Hot-gas-path parts share of CSA cost. ASSUMPTION: 50% (I substitute 50% for the original's 55%; LTSA cost stacks typically run parts 50-60%, labor 25-30%, balance outage services/logistics, and I take the low end). = $472M/yr.

STEP 5 — New-casting purchases vs repair within HGP spend. ASSUMPTION: 55% new / 45% repair (original used 60/40). New-part purchases = $260M/yr; repair = $212M/yr.

STEP 6 — The physical shock. Every legacy class published in GER-3620 Rev P Appendix D (Figs D-1..D-8) replaces Stage-1 buckets / Stage-1-2-3 nozzles / Stage-1 shrouds at 3 HGPI. If HA stage-1 hardware, at the highest firing temperature GE has fielded, achieves only 2 HGPI, the new-casting purchase rate goes from 1/3 per interval to 1/2 per interval = x1.5. Delta = 0.5 x $260M = +$130M/yr of permanent CSA cost.

STEP 7 — EBITDA delta. A CSA cost increase flows ~1:1 to Power services EBIT/EBITDA. Annual EBITDA delta = -$130M/yr (steady state, today's 50.4 GW HA base).

STEP 8 — Capitalize. $130M x 25x = $3,250M. Keeping 25x: GEV trades ~35x forward earnings and this is the highest-quality annuity line, so 25x on EBITDA is if anything conservative; I do not raise it because the shock is a cost item on an unproven assumption, not a proven run-rate.

STEP 9 — Per share. $3,250M / 266,333,581 = $12.20/share = 1.30% of $940.33.

STEP 10 — Scaled to the built-out HA book. Shipping 20 GW (2026) / 22 / 24 GW, not all HA and not all under CSA; a ~120 GW HA base by ~2030 is the reasonable upper bound (x2.38). Delta = $310M/yr -> $7,750M -> $29.10/share = 3.09%.

STEP 11 — The ASC 606 one-time catch-up (WHERE I DIVERGE MOST). Lifetime cost increase on today's base = $130M x 20 = $2.6B. Catch-up = lifetime margin reduction x percent-complete. The HA sub-book is YOUNG: average unit has run ~28,600 hours (3.6M / 126) of perhaps ~160,000 lifetime contract hours, and cost-to-cost progress is on the same order, so I use 18% complete, NOT the ~50% the original used. $2.6B x 18% = ~$468M one-time pre-tax charge = $1.76/share of book value (no multiple — it is a true one-timer, already counted inside the $12.20 capitalized figure and not additive to it).

INDEPENDENT ANSWER: $12.20/share (1.30%) on today's installed HA base; $29.10/share (3.09%) if you capitalize the ~2030 HA book. Headline range $12-29/share. One-time accounting catch-up if it breaks: ~$468M, $1.76/share of book.
- **agrees_with_original**: True
- **where_it_differs**: Same direction, same mechanism, same order of magnitude, but lower on both ends and materially lower on the one-timer.

1. Range: mine is $12.20-29.10/share vs the original's $15.21-33.40. The gap is entirely parameter choice in steps 3-5: I used 25% CSA margin / 50% HGP share / 55% new-casting share vs the original's 22% / 55% / 60%. Product of the three: mine 0.75 x 0.50 x 0.55 = 0.206 of revenue; theirs 0.78 x 0.55 x 0.60 = 0.257. Ratio 0.80, which is exactly the $12.20/$15.21 gap. Neither set is verifiable; the original sits at the aggressive end of every one of the three.

2. THE REAL ERROR — the ASC 606 catch-up. The original takes "~50% complete" and gets $1.6B / $6.08 per share. That 50% comes from GEV's disclosure that ~1,800 units under LTSA have ~10 years average remaining life — a statistic about the WHOLE LTSA book, which is dominated by 20-year-old F and E class. The HA sub-book is the youngest part of it: 126 units averaging 28,600 hours, with 51 more still in RPO and 43 mid-commissioning. Applying the fleet-wide 50% to the HA sub-book overstates the catch-up by roughly 3x. My 18% gives ~$468M / $1.76 per share. The original then describes this as "$6.08/share of one-quarter book-value hit ON TOP," which is also double-counting — the catch-up is the present recognition of part of the same lifetime cost stream already capitalized in the $15-33 figure. It is not additive.

3. Revenue basis. The original applies management's $25M/GW-yr (a 20-year AVERAGE) to today's installed base and calls the result today's revenue. That is wrong as a revenue statement — today's realized yield is ~$15M/GW-yr, so actual HA services revenue today is ~$756M, not $1,260M. It happens not to matter for the answer, because the correct thing to cost out IS the 20-year lifetime, and $25M/GW-yr is the right lifetime number. The original got the right answer by a route it did not justify.

4. Verified against real segment data: FY2025 Power services revenue $13,072M and Power EBIT $2,902M (gev_segments.csv). The implied HA services share (~5.8% of Power services at realized yield) is plausible, so the 50.4 GW estimate does not blow up against the actuals. The original never ran this check.
- **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: The 3-HGPI-to-2-HGPI severity step — i.e. that HA stage-1 buckets, nozzles and shrouds achieve one fewer hot-gas-path interval than every legacy class GER-3620 Rev P publishes. Everything else in the chain is a multiplier on a plausible range; this one is the entire thesis, it is binary, and it is unobservable. GEV has rig, lead-unit and accelerated-test data on HA hardware that nobody outside the company can see, and no HA unit in the fleet is anywhere near the 75,000-hour scrap point that would settle it. The second-order driver is the compound of the three unverifiable cost-stack ratios (contract margin x HGP share x new-casting share), which together move the answer ~25% between my parameter set and the original's.

Secondary but load-bearing: the 50.4 GW installed-HA estimate, which is linear in the answer and which GEV does not disclose at all.
- **sensitivity**: SEVERITY (the key assumption), halved and doubled:
- Half the shortfall — HA achieves 2.5 HGPI instead of 3. Replacement rate 1/2.5 = 0.400 vs 0.333 = x1.20. Delta = 0.20 x $260M = +$52M/yr. x25 / 266.3M = $4.88/share = 0.52%. BELOW the $10/share wedge floor — the finding dies.
- Double the shortfall — HA achieves 1.5 HGPI. Rate 1/1.5 = 0.667 vs 0.333 = x2.0. Delta = +$260M/yr -> $24.41/share = 2.60%.
So the honest severity band on today's installed base is $4.88 to $24.41 per share, and the lower half of that band is not a wedge at all.

INSTALLED HA GW (linear), halved and doubled:
- 25.2 GW: +$65M/yr -> $6.10/share = 0.65%. Also below the floor.
- 100.8 GW: +$260M/yr -> $24.41/share = 2.60%. (100 GW is roughly the 2029-30 fleet, so this doubles as the forward case.)

CROSS: half-severity AND half-GW = $2.44/share, i.e. noise. Full-severity AND 120 GW forward book = $29.10/share = 3.09%, the realistic ceiling.

The distribution is unattractive: the base case clears the $10 floor by 22%, and a single one-notch softening of ANY of the three main assumptions pushes it under.
- **materiality_verdict**: marginal

- **where_it_differs**: I get $8.71/share vs the original's $23.84 — 2.7x apart. The math is not in dispute: when I feed their inputs into my chain I reproduce $23.81, so the entire gap is assumptions.

   (b) They treated all planned GT capacity as HA-class. It is not. Of 21.6 GW planned GT 2026-30, only 7.93 GW is >=300MW; 6.53 GW is under 200MW (aeroderivative and small frame). The $25M/GW-yr yield is an HA number and does not apply to LM2500/LM6000 or old frames.

2. FLOW-THROUGH. They used 80%, I use 65%. Their own physics says the outage cadence stretches 3.05 -> 3.53 years under peaking duty, which is a 16% reduction in annual cost. They asserted cost is unchanged and then modeled 80% drop-through; those two statements are inconsistent with each other.

3. THE "INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK" IS NOT INDEPENDENT. 4. MECHANISM TIMING, in their favour but they got it backwards. The 10-K says revenue is recognized cost-to-cost against an ESTIMATE of total expected customer payments. So fewer fired hours do not reduce quarterly recognized revenue directly; they force a downward revision to estimated total contract revenue, landing as a lumpy cumulative catch-up. The steady-state economics are as modeled, but there is no smooth annual line for the market to observe — which makes this harder, not easier, to trade on a 3-12 month horizon.

5. AGREEMENTS. The 19.0% fired-hour ratio is correct and I reproduced it from the raw tables. The 10-K billing language is verbatim correct. The novelty claim is credible — I found no published version of this connection in the corpus either (their academic-tier search returning zero rows matches my experience). The physics is sound; the sizing is not.
- **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: Two assumptions dominate, and both are undisclosed by GEV.

PRIMARY: the share of the 116 GW cohort that is genuinely HA-class, US-sited, and in peaker/cycling duty. My 27% vs the original's 60% is more than half the total disagreement. It is the only link where hard data exists (EIA-860M Planned, which I cut myself), and the data says the original is roughly 2x too aggressive — chiefly because most planned simple-cycle capacity is aeroderivative and small-frame, not HA, and because the pipeline reverts to combined cycle by 2030.

SECONDARY AND MORE FRAGILE: the 50% fired-hour-driven share of services billing. GEV discloses that billing rests on two bases (per hour of usage, and major maintenance events) and never splits them. 50% is a coin flip dressed as an estimate. The original's justification for it is worse than no justification, because it borrows a contract-type statistic and relabels it as a billing-basis statistic. The entire thesis is linear in this number and nobody outside GEV knows it. If a single question gets asked of IR, it should be this one: what fraction of HA CSA billings is indexed to actual fired hours rather than to factored/equivalent operating hours or to outage events?

CEILING: take everything bullish at once — $1.4B nuclear EBITDA-generating revenue at 20% margin plus a doubled SMR ramp, no discount, no NCI haircut — and you get ~$39/share (4.2%). That is the defensible maximum, not a base case.
