- **sensitivity**: Halving the SMR ramp (3.9 GW -> 1.95 GW delivered): total falls to $14.39/share (1.53%). Doubling it (3.9 -> 7.8 GW, i.e. assuming the US-Japan and Poland tiers both land in full): total rises to $21.07/share (2.24%).

That is a 4x swing in the driving physical assumption producing a $6.68/share, 0.71-percentage-point move in the answer. The estimate is remarkably insensitive, and that insensitivity IS the finding — you cannot construct a version of the nuclear story that matters to a $940 stock without abandoning arithmetic.

Stress the other levers: dropping to zero discount on the SMR piece adds $3.02 ($19.64 total). Removing the 60% NCI haircut entirely adds ~$11 ($27.7 total). Cutting the multiple from 25x to 15x takes the total to $9.97. Doing all three bullish moves at once plus a doubled ramp gets to ~$39/share (4.2%), which I would call the outer ceiling. The original's $32 ceiling is within this and is defensible.

For the tradeable event specifically: a Clinch River construction permit converts 0.3 GW from the 40% tier to the ~90% tier. On my arithmetic that is 0.3 x 0.5 probability delta x $4.25B/GW / 15 yrs x 12% x 0.60 x 25 x 0.596 = ~$0.05/share of mechanical value. Even allowing a large sentiment/derisking multiplier on the whole US pipeline, the honest range is $2-6/share. That is 0.2-0.6% of price.
- **materiality_verdict**: immaterial

## [Verify] skeptic:algorithmic_efficiency:AI's energy floor is set by memo

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: THREE ERRORS, ONE OF THEM FATAL TO THE LOAD-BEARING EVIDENCE.

(1) FATAL — the "controlled experiment" pairs a 1,000W throughput number with a 700W power number. The finding states: "H100 -> H200 is the same GH100 die ... identical 700W TDP ... MLPerf Inference v4.0 Llama2-70B offline throughput rose +42.3% (22,290 -> 31,712 tok/s), an elasticity of 0.98 to bandwidth and 0.00 to FLOPs. Energy per token at fixed 700W fell 31.4 -> 22.1 mJ/token (-29.7%)." NVIDIA's own MLPerf v4.0 writeup says the opposite (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-h200-tensor-core-gpus-and-nvidia-tensorrt-llm-set-mlperf-llm-inference-records/): the 700W H200 delivered "up to 28% better Llama 2 70B inference performance" than H100, and separately "NVIDIA also made submissions using H200 with a custom thermal design, enabling the GPUs to run at a higher 1,000 W TDP. This unlocked 11% and 14% more performance in the server and offline scenarios, respectively, enabling total speedups of 43% and 45% compared to H100." The +42-45% numbers the finding uses ARE the 1,000W custom-thermal submission. The finding's own caveat #5 says "I used the 700W comparison" — it did not. This is precisely the stress-test-config-quoted-as-operating-config error.

Corrected iso-power arithmetic (back out the custom-thermal uplift): offline 1.45/1.14 = +27.2%; server 1.43/1.11 = +28.8%. Against +43.3% bandwidth (3.35 -> 4.8 TB/s):
  - Elasticity of decode throughput to bandwidth = 0.272/0.433 = 0.63 (server 0.66), NOT 0.98. Since H100 and H200 have identical FLOPs, the ~35% of the bandwidth gain that does NOT convert is evidence that decode is only PARTLY bandwidth-bound — the exact opposite of the finding's "elasticity 0.00 to FLOPs" framing.
  - Energy/token at true 700W: 700 / (22,290 x 1.272) = 24.7 mJ/tok vs H100's 31.4 mJ/tok = -21.4%, not -29.7%, and materially LESS than the bandwidth gain, not "exactly the bandwidth gain."
  - At the 1,000W config the finding actually quoted: 1000W / 31,712 tok/s = 31.5 mJ/token vs H100's 31.4 mJ/token — energy per token improved by ZERO. The single datapoint the finding built its energy-floor claim on, read with its own power number, shows no energy-per-token improvement at all.

(2) CONCEPTUAL — "energy floor is set by memory-bandwidth-per-watt" holds bytes-per-token constant, and it is not. Energy/token ~ (bytes moved per token) / (bandwidth per watt). The denominator grows at the cited 19.4%/yr; the NUMERATOR has been falling fast and independently: weight quantization FP16->FP8->FP4 (a 4x byte reduction that costs zero bandwidth progress and is the real content of the "compute-per-watt" FP4 headline numbers), GQA/MQA/MLA KV compression, speculative decoding (many tokens verified per weight-load pass), and distillation to smaller models at fixed capability. Bandwidth-per-watt is one multiplicative term, not a floor. Independent end-to-end measurement contradicts the 19.4% claim directly: Epoch AI's LLM inference price series (https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends) finds price per token at FIXED capability falling 9x-900x per year across six benchmarks, with GPT-4-level science QA at 40x/yr. Even allowing generously for margin compression and chip-cost effects, a 19.4%/yr serving-efficiency rate is not reconcilable with that series.

(3) SOURCE MISUSE — the Pope et al. citation is the problem statement of a paper whose contribution is solving it. Verified from the local extraction of arXiv:2211.05102: the 3TB figure is the MULTI-HEAD attention case, and the same paper's abstract says "the lower memory requirements of multiquery attention ... enables scaling up to 32x larger context lengths," its method section says the key design goal is "to minimize the memory time of repeatedly loading the KV cache that dominates the inference cost," and its headline result uses int8 weight quantization. Citing the 3TB number as evidence that KV bytes are an irreducible floor inverts the paper.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY SOUND: the Del Sozzo et al. paper is real and the quote is transcribed correctly. I verified arXiv:2601.20115 exists (Del Sozzo, Fleming, Flamm, Thompson; submitted 2026-01-27, v3 2026-05-29) and found the sentence verbatim in the extracted text: "the CAGRs (DTs) range from 55.4% (1.57y) to 19.4% (3.92y) for FP16 and memory bandwidth, respectively," plus the Fig.4 annotations "2.02E-03 TFLOPS/W w/o Sparsity - CAGR: 55.4%" and "4.49E-01 GB/s/W GDDR and HBM - CAGR: 19.4%". But these are log-linear regressions fitted over roughly 2007-2025 across the whole NVIDIA datacenter line, spanning the one-time GDDR->HBM transition. The paper nowhere proposes them as forward discount rates for 2026-2030 AI load, and the finding's own caveat concedes its flagship-to-flagship check gives 2.5%/yr on one pairing and 11-19%/yr on another — a 7x spread that makes the "2.9x divergence" headline an artifact of endpoint selection.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The load-bearing IDEA is published; only the specific citation is new. The finding's own novelty_check concedes it found already published: the memory wall itself (Gholami et al., IEEE Micro 2024, arXiv:2403.14123 — DRAM bandwidth 1.6x/2yr vs peak FLOPS 3.0x/2yr, which is the same divergence claim with different constants); the generic Jevons/"memory is the new bottleneck" rebuttal from IEA, Brookings, TrendForce and Global X; and the qualitative claim that inference demand persists despite efficiency gains. That is the entire mechanism. What is new — using the Del Sozzo per-watt split as the discount rate, and the H100->H200 pairing — is a citation choice and a datapoint, and the datapoint is wrong (see physics_errors). An investment wedge cannot rest on novelty of footnote when the argument is the consensus post-DeepSeek rebuttal that every power-equipment bull ran in Feb 2025.

HONESTY CAVEAT ON MY OWN SEARCH: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could run independent novelty queries, so I could not search sell-side or trade coverage myself. I am relying on the finding's own admissions plus my prior that the "inference is memory-bound, so AI power demand is sticky" argument was extremely widely circulated in 2025-2026. Treat the novelty score as an upper bound, not a verified floor. The team should re-run the novelty searches with budget available.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The strongest surviving version of the argument — and the team should know it exists even though it is not this finding — is the DIRECTIONAL claim without the fake precision: "training-efficiency headlines have near-zero transmission to serving power, and the market has repeatedly mispriced that." The corpus price data supports the mispricing half cleanly. On 2025-01-27 GEV fell 420.49 -> 330.00 (-21.52%) while VRT fell -29.9% and ETN -15.6%, but NEE rose 72.83 -> 73.83 (+1.37%) and SPY fell only -1.41%. A regulated utility with the same underlying power-demand exposure went UP the same day, which does isolate the selloff to AI-datacenter equipment sentiment rather than to any revision in power demand. And DeepSeek R1's headline was a training-cost claim, which genuinely does not bind serving energy.

But that argument is (a) qualitative, (b) already the consensus rebuttal, and (c) not what this finding claims. This finding claims a specific numeric efficiency rate (19.4%/yr) is the correct one, that the bears' rate is 3x too high, and that a controlled H100/H200 experiment proves an energy-per-token floor. All three of those specific claims fail.

A second counterargument the team should weigh AGAINST the finding: its own proposed market test is not discriminating, and the historical episode it is calibrated to actually contradicts it. The finding predicts GEV "should retrace more than half of any drawdown within 30 trading days." In the 2025 episode GEV closed 382.94 on 2025-01-30 — more than half the retrace inside THREE trading days — and then fell to 303.00 by 2025-03-27, well BELOW the DeepSeek-day trough of 330.00. A test that both passes in 3 days and is then invalidated by a lower low two months later is not a test.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. Kill it, but keep one number from the wreckage.

(1) PHYSICS — the load-bearing evidence is wrong, not merely weak. The "controlled experiment" (same die, same 700W, +42.3% throughput, elasticity 0.98) pairs the 1,000W custom-thermal MLPerf submission's throughput with the 700W power figure. NVIDIA's own writeup: 700W H200 gave "up to 28%" over H100; the custom 1,000W design "unlocked 11% and 14% more performance," for totals of 43%/45%. Corrected iso-power elasticity to bandwidth = 0.63, not 0.98. Corrected energy/token = -21.4%, not -29.7%. Read at the power the quoted throughput actually required, energy per token improved by 0.0% (1000W/31,712 tok/s = 31.5 mJ vs H100 31.4 mJ). The single datapoint refutes the thesis it was recruited to support. Separately, "energy floor set by bandwidth-per-watt" holds bytes-per-token fixed, which is false (FP4 quantization, GQA/MLA, speculative decoding, distillation all cut the numerator), and Epoch AI's measured inference-price-at-fixed-capability series (9x-900x/yr, 40x/yr for GPT-4-level science QA) is irreconcilable with a 19.4%/yr serving-efficiency rate. The Pope et al. 3TB citation inverts a paper whose stated contribution is cutting that term up to 32x. What IS verified: the Del Sozzo paper (arXiv:2601.20115, v3 2026-05-29) is real and the 55.4%/19.4% quote is transcribed correctly — but it is an ~18-year log-linear regression spanning the GDDR->HBM transition, and the finding's own flagship checks span 2.5%/yr to 19%/yr depending on endpoints.

(2) MECHANISM — does not reach the named line, for two independent reasons.
  (a) WRONG HORIZON. The memo horizon is 3-12 months. GEV has 116 GW under contract (53 GW firm backlog + 63 GW slot reservations) and RPO of $176B. Shipments through 2028 are constrained by the Greenville ramp, not by marginal beliefs about 2030 AI load. The finding concedes this itself: "This is a terminal-value / probability-re-weighting finding... there is no line item that moves on Oct 28." A finding with no line item that moves inside the horizon is not a wedge.
  (b) WRONG BILLING UNIT — this is the subtler break and it is the one the brief warned about. The finding converts GW to services dollars via a $25M/GW-yr annuity. GEV's 10-K bills services "based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event," and GER-3620P sets HA intervals in FACTORED FIRED HOURS (25,000 CI/HGP, 50,000 MI). The finding's argument delivers robustness in AI MEGAWATT-HOURS; GEV's services line needs FIRED HOURS ON GEV UNITS. Those diverge hard right now: ~60% of planned US gas for 2026-27 delivery is simple-cycle peakers at ~10% capacity factor, which accrue factored hours roughly 6x slower than combined cycle at 62-66%, and US combined-cycle generation FELL 3.2% in 2025. So "AI load won't shrink" is compatible with flat or falling fired-hours yield — which is exactly what the -$218M H1'26 net unfavorable service-profitability revisions (vs -$42M H1'25) and the $15M/GW-yr realized yield against management's $25M/GW-yr are already telling you. The finding uses an installed-GW proxy the business model explicitly does not use.

(3) MATERIALITY — overstated, and one input is arithmetically impossible. Verified from gev_segments.csv: Power Product FY25 $6,420M, Power Service $13,072M, segment total $19,767M, Gas Power subsegment $16,006M, and segment operating profit FY25 $2,902M = 14.7% margin. Two problems:
  - The $310-360M/GW equipment figure divides ALL Power Product revenue by GAS GW shipped, but Power Product includes Hydro ($806M), Nuclear ($1,018M) and Steam ($1,937M) — $3,761M of non-gas, much of it equipment/project-weighted. Gas-only product revenue is plausibly $3.2-4.5B on ~15 GW = $215-300M/GW. The finding's "conservative end" is above my central estimate.
  - The 30% services margin is falsified by the segment P&L. $13,072M x 30% = $3,922M, which EXCEEDS total Power segment operating profit of $2,902M — it would require equipment margin of about -15%. Services margin cannot exceed roughly 22% even holding equipment at zero.
  Rebuilt full-branch number: 10 GW x $260M = $2.6B equipment + 50 GW x $25M = $1.25B services = $3.85B incremental revenue at 18% (top of the FY26 segment guide, generous for incremental) = $693M EBIT x 25 / 266,333,581 = $65.04/share (6.9%), vs the claimed $78.85. And the finding does not claim the branch — it claims a 25-40 point probability re-weight, giving $16.26-26.02/share (1.7%-2.8%), on a probability shift that is asserted with no anchor whatsoever. Strip the unanchored probability delta and there is no quantified claim left.

(4) SO-WHAT AT $250B — fails. The dated test is not dated (it fires only if some lab publishes a training-efficiency headline, which may not happen before Oct 28), and the retrace criterion both passed in 3 days and was invalidated by a lower low 2 months later in the one episode available. The Q3'26 print on Oct 28 2026 contains nothing that confirms or denies this.

SCORES I WOULD ASSIGN: novelty 2 (the idea is the consensus Jevons/memory-wall rebuttal; only the footnote is new), confidence 1 (central experiment is wrong), materiality 2 (after correcting margins and the $/GW derivation, and net of the unanchored probability step).

WHAT TO SALVAGE — one genuinely useful artifact, and it is NOT the physics. The cross-sectional price evidence for 2025-01-27, pulled from the corpus prices table: GEV -21.52% (437.71 on 01-23 -> 420.49 -> 330.00), VRT -29.88%, ETN -15.56%, SPY -1.41%, NEE +1.37%. A regulated utility with identical underlying power-demand exposure rose while the equipment names collapsed. That cleanly isolates the shock as AI-capex sentiment, not a power-demand revision, and it is a fact, not a model. Use it as a one-line risk-framing point. Do NOT build a thesis on the memory-bandwidth exponent.

RECOMMENDED REDIRECT for the team's remaining days: the fired-hours-vs-installed-GW gap I surfaced in (2b) is the live, in-horizon, underexploited question — the corpus has EIA-923 net_generation_mwh by plant and prime mover and EIA-860M nameplate MW across 43 vintages, which permits directly computing realized capacity factors and implied fired hours on GE-linked units from the projects table, and testing the $15M vs $25M vs $70M per GW-yr yield ladder against physical duty cycles. That is a mechanism the business model actually bills on, it moves the Power services line, and it has a dated test in the FY26 10-K service-profitability revisions. It has nothing to do with GPU memory bandwidth.

STEP 1 — Physical quantity: the aftermarket airfoil claim rate.
GER-3620 Rev P: HA HGPI at 25,000 factored fired hours (FFH) OR 900 starts, whichever first; stage-1 buckets/nozzles/shrouds replaced at 3 HGPI = 75,000 FFH or 2,700 starts.

Blended cadence at ~50/50 CC/peaker: ~10.8 yr, claim rate ~0.093 GW-equiv/yr per GW installed.

That is wrong as a measure of GEV's TOTAL airfoil claim, because GEV's legacy E/F-class serviced fleet already consumes SX/DS stage-1 hardware continuously. GE's globally installed heavy-duty base is commonly put near 400-500 GW, of which GEV services roughly half under CSAs; I assume 250 GW serviced (MY ASSUMPTION, unverified — the largest single input I introduced).
- 2026: new build 20 GW + HA aftermarket (50 GW / 10.8) 4.6 + legacy aftermarket (250/10.8) 23.1 = 47.7 GW-equiv
- 2030: new build 30 GW + HA aftermarket (143 GW / 10.8) 13.2 + legacy 23.1 (flat; declining as E-class retires) = 66.3 GW-equiv
Growth = 66.3/47.7 - 1 = +39%.
That is NOT 2.5x GE Aerospace's +30% guide. It is +39% vs GEAE +30% and vs Bernstein's +38% Howmet blade-capacity add by end-2026. THE HEADLINE GAP LARGELY DISAPPEARS. This is my single biggest disagreement with the original.

Gas Power total FY2025 = $16.006B; Power SERVICE = $13.072B. The "2.5x faster than aero" framing, which is the entire novelty claim, is an artifact of an incomplete denominator.

2. $/GW IS 25% TOO HIGH. The original's $500M/GW is not supported by the filings. gev_segments.csv gives FY2025 Power product revenue of $6.420B for the whole segment; backing out non-gas and dividing by ~12 GW shipped gives $375-400M/GW, confirmed by the H1'26 run-rate ($375M/GW). 3. THE CADENCE AND THE DOLLARS ARE NOT CONNECTED. The elegant GER-3620 physics does no work in the valuation. Any number could be substituted and the arithmetic would be equally "valid." That is the structural flaw.

4. THE KILL CONDITION MAY ALREADY BE TRIPPED. The finding's kill condition (a) is "GEV hits a 20 GW annualized gas output run-rate and reaffirms 24 GW for 2028 while naming secured casting capacity." The Q2'26 earnings transcript of 22 July 2026 (corpus src:3161, gevernova.com/sites/default/files/gev_webcast_transcript_07222026.pdf) already states, in management's own words, that GEV has "now reached our 20-gigawatt annualized run rate," is "on track for 24 gigawatts in '28," sees 30 GW in 2030 "in a capital-efficient manner," and has "already secured significant supply chain capacity, all funded by customer down payments." That is two of the three limbs of the kill condition, stated two months BEFORE this finding was written. The third limb (naming casting specifically) is not met, so this is not a clean kill — but it is close enough that the team should treat the finding as substantially pre-falsified rather than as a live short thesis.

WHAT I AGREE WITH: the GER-3620 replacement-cadence physics is correctly read; the EPRI "rotor forgings and hot-section blades... primary bottleneck" sourcing is real; the observation that no published note has done a GEV-SIDE read-through of the CPP deal is, as far as I can also tell, correct; and the author's own caveats are unusually honest, including the admission that CPP has never been publicly named as a GEV supplier. - 4 GW (base): $320M -> $30.04/share = 3.19%
- 8 GW: $640M -> $60.08/share = 6.39%
Strictly linear, which is itself the tell — the valuation is a one-input model wearing a physics costume.

Sensitivity on the input I introduced (legacy serviced fleet, which drives whether the shortfall happens):
- 125 GW legacy: 2030/2026 demand growth = +49%
- 250 GW (base): +39%
- 400 GW: +33%
Across that entire plausible range the growth rate lands between +33% and +49%, i.e. within shouting distance of GEAE's +30% and Bernstein's +38%. No setting of this input reproduces the original's +74%. The headline is not robust.

Sensitivity on fired hours (the physics input the original leaned on):
- 3,250 h/yr: 23 yr cadence, HA aftermarket claim halves
- 6,000 h/yr (base): 12.5 yr
- 8,000 h/yr: 9.4 yr
Doubling or halving fired hours swings the HA aftermarket component by roughly +/-50%, but that component is only ~10-20% of total airfoil demand once the legacy base is included, so total demand growth moves only ~+/-6pp. The physics assumption the original agonized over barely matters; the arithmetic is dominated by inputs it did not examine.

Framing sensitivity, which dwarfs all of the above: permanent cap $30.04/share vs one-year deferral $0.11/share. A 273x spread on an interpretive choice with no physical content.

## [Verify] skeptic:smr_nuclear_timeline:Four independent sources put rea

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: THE CENTRAL ERROR IS CIRCULARITY, and it is visible in the paper's own input table.

1) The benchmark and the benchmarked quantity are the same datum. The finding presents Darlington as an independent realized capex point tested "against" the Li/She/Zhang threshold. But the paper's own FOAK anchor IS Darlington. From sources.id=3899, Table 2 / Section 2 verbatim: "The three reactor capital anchors are $14,700 kW-1 e for FOAK, from the Ontario Power Generation (OPG) Darlington unit budget on an SMR-unit-only basis (shared four-unit site infrastructure excluded); $7,615 kW-1 e for the mid-range (Moderate) NLR ATB reactor-capital case... and $2,250 kW-1 e for NOAK, a GE-Hitachi long-run vendor target." The paper already ran Darlington and already reported the answer: scenario group G4, grid-cost margin -232% (Case 1) / -244% (Case 2) at FOAK $14,700/kWe. There is no new "assembly" here. The finding rediscovers a row of Figure 5b and presents it as an original benchmarking exercise. Its novelty_check claim that the pairing "appears not to be" published is wrong: it is published, in the very paper it cites, as a named scenario.

2) Two of the "four independent sources" are one project. "OPG's four-unit Darlington envelope C$20.9B/1,200MW = US$12,530/kW" and "OPG unit 1 ~US$15,000/kW" are the same build. Independence is 4 claimed, ~2 actual.

3) The $40B/3GW = $13,333/kW arithmetic is not a capex derivation. The US-Japan announcement is a financing/investment package envelope (equity, supply chain, fuel, multiple sites), not a construction cost estimate. Dividing a sovereign financing headline by nameplate GW to produce an overnight cost is a category error. The finding treats "nobody has stated this arithmetic" as evidence of novelty; the better explanation is that it is not a valid computation. This is the single weakest evidence item and it is doing a quarter of the work.

4) Non-comparable cost bases stacked into one band. C$20.9B is all-in including interest during construction and shared site infrastructure; TVA's $17,949/kW is overnight excluding financing and escalation; the paper's $14,700/kWe is deliberately SMR-unit-only with shared four-unit infrastructure EXCLUDED. These three are on three different boundaries. The finding says "both land in the same band, which is the point" — but the band is manufactured by mixing conventions, and by coincidence the two adjustments run in opposite directions.

5) Nameplate vs net electrical output. Every $/kW figure divides by 300 MW nameplate; the paper models the BWRX-300 as 870 MWth / 270 MWe net. On a net-MWe basis the figures are ~11% higher. This does not hurt the finding's direction, but it confirms the numbers were not re-derived on a consistent basis.

6) The threshold is not a constant — the paper says so explicitly, and the finding suppresses it. Verbatim from sources.id=3899: "the $5,000 kW-1 e parity threshold identified below is specific to the 2023 price year." Re-solved under 2024 ERCOT prices (scenario group G9), NOAK capital of $2,250/kWe yields margins of -0.5% and -34%. That is decisive: under 2024 prices even GE Hitachi's own advertised $2,250/kW FAILS the test. If the vendor's best-case number and the realized number both fail, capex is not the discriminating variable — the market-price regime is. The entire "5.6-8.0x advertised, 2.5-3.6x threshold" framing implies that closing the capex gap would open the market. The paper's own G9 sweep says it would not, in the more recent price year.

WHAT DOES CHECK OUT: the 19%/doubling learning-rate arithmetic is correct (4.0 = 6.1 x 4^-b, b = 0.3045, 2^-0.3045 = 0.810, LR 19.0%). But the comparison to Tolley & Jones' 3-10% is a category mismatch: unit 1's C$6.1B carries FOAK engineering, licensing and first-unit tooling that standard learning-curve fitting removes before regression, and Tolley & Jones measured national industry learning across heterogeneous designs, not a single four-unit site with a common turbine island. The number is right; the indictment it is used to support is not clean.
- **mechanism_sound**: False

Crucially, a sentiment de-rating of an optionality bucket does NOT require the accounting chain to work — the market can mark down the SMR option on a headline without any RPO, revenue or impairment event ever occurring, which is precisely the objection I raise in the mechanism. This is the most important novelty failure and it required no web search to establish — only reading past the abstract of the paper already in the corpus.

(b) The $2,250/kW advertised-vs-realized gap is independently tabulated in Rao, Kaffine & Hodge, "The consequences of high SMR operating costs in electricity markets," arXiv:2609.08929v1 (corpus sources.id=3901), Table 1.

(c) The cost critique itself is a crowded published genre, which the finding concedes: IEEFA, the World Nuclear Industry Status Report, SACE/Schlissel, Decouple, and Ramana's IEEE Access "Reality Check" (corpus sources.id=1433). I could not run additional WebSearch to check sell-side coverage — this session's web search budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could query for broker notes on BWRX-300 capex. The team should treat the sell-side novelty question as UNVERIFIED by me. It does not change the verdict, because (a) alone is sufficient.
- **refuted**: True
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED on all four tests. Do not use.

PHYSICS — circular. The paper's FOAK anchor is the Darlington budget. The finding "tests" Darlington against a threshold derived from a model whose own worst-case input is Darlington, and presents the result as a new assembly. The paper printed that result as scenario G4. Additionally: two of the four "independent" points are the same project; the $40B/3GW = $13,333/kW figure divides a sovereign financing envelope by nameplate GW, which is not a capex derivation; the three cost bases (all-in with IDC / overnight excl. financing / unit-only excl. shared infra) are mixed into one band; and all $/kW use 300 MW nameplate against the paper's 270 MWe net. Most damaging, the finding suppresses the paper's own qualifier that the $5,000/kWe threshold "is specific to the 2023 price year" — under 2024 ERCOT prices the paper's G9 sweep shows GE Hitachi's advertised $2,250/kW ALSO fails (-0.5% / -34%). If the vendor's best case and the realized case both fail, capex is not the discriminating variable and the 2.5-3.6x ratio carries no decision content.

MECHANISM — breaks in four places.
1. Wrong customer test. The $5,000/kWe frontier governs a MERCHANT 200 MWe ERCOT colocation against wholesale grid supply. GEV's announced BWRX-300 pipeline is overwhelmingly regulated or sovereign — OPG (Ontario ratebase), TVA (federal), Synthos Green Energy (Poland), SaskPower, UK. A ratebased utility recovers capex through rates at an allowed ROE and never faces a merchant LCOE hurdle. The finding's own materiality math concedes this by carving out "government-backstopped" units — but that carve-out is most of the pipeline, not the exception. The threshold does not govern the population being modeled.
2. Wrong slice of the dollar. The $12,530-17,949/kW is TOTAL INSTALLED PROJECT cost — civil works, EPC, turbine island, owner's costs, IDC. GEV/GEH supplies the NSSS, fuel and services. Most of that per-kW figure is revenue for Aecon, Kiewit and AtkinsRéalis, not GEV. High project capex does not compress GEV's revenue or margin per converted unit; it can only reduce unit count. So the entire chain rests on the conversion argument alone, with no support from the capex number itself.
3. No accounting event exists. Per the task's own framing, GEV recognizes equipment revenue over time on costs incurred. Announced pipeline that never converts never enters RPO and was never in revenue or backlog. There is nothing on the balance sheet to impair. The finding's "$3.56B impairment" is a multiple de-rating of an unobservable, not an impairment — and GEV has never disclosed a BWRX-300-specific RPO line, so no filing will ever confirm or deny it. Calling it an impairment in a memo would be a factual error a judge can catch.
4. Wrong value model. GEV's own 10-K frames BWRX-300 as creating "a new installed based for future fuel and services." The value is a multi-decade fuel-and-outage annuity, which a 3-12 month horizon barely discounts.

MATERIALITY — fails "so what." $13.38/share = 1.42% of a $250B cap, less than a normal day's move, and it is not an estimate — it is an assumption about what the market capitalized ($550M/GW x 60% x 15 GW), a quantity that is nowhere observable and nowhere disclosed. Remove that assumption and the finding has no dollar figure at all. The finding self-scores materiality 2; that is the correct score and it is below the bar.

DATED TEST — non-falsifiable in the direction that matters. "No new BWRX-300 order will carry a disclosed all-in cost below US$8,000/kW" will be true almost regardless of the thesis, because vendors and utilities essentially never disclose all-in $/kW at announcement — absence of disclosure confirms the prediction without confirming the claim. "GEV's FY26 10-K will not disclose a BWRX-300-specific RPO figure" predicts the continuation of a practice GEV has never departed from. Neither can fail if the thesis is wrong. The one genuinely informative test — Darlington units 2-4 approval — is in 2028, outside the horizon, as the finding admits.

WHAT TO SALVAGE: nothing as a wedge. Two items are worth keeping as background only, both requiring primary-source work first: (i) pull the underlying TVA Clinch River filing directly — the $17,949/kW is currently third-hand (SACE reporting Schlissel testimony reporting TVA), and Schlissel is an intervenor witness, so the figure is advocacy-framed until verified; (ii) the paper's G9 result that $2,250/kW fails under 2024 prices is the genuinely interesting number in this whole file, and it points the opposite way from the finding's headline — toward power-price regime, not capex, as the binding constraint on SMR colocation. If anyone on the team wants to revisit SMR, that is the thread, and it should be attacked as its own question rather than as a rescue of this one.

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: REBUILD FROM SCRATCH — every step and assumption stated.

Root cause — decode is HBM-bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound — is sound physics and will generalize.

STEP 1 — exposed GEV line, measured not assumed.
From data/financials/gev_segments.csv (OperatingSegmentsExcludingIntersegmentElimination;ElectrificationSegment):
  Q1'26 revenue $2,959M + Q2'26 $3,637M = H1'26 $6,596M -> annualized $13.19B. I round to $14.0B FY26 (H2 is seasonally heavier). 
  MVA-priced subsegments H1'26: PowerTransmission $3,257M + GridSystemsIntegration $1,497M + PowerConversionAndStorage $1,016M = $5,770M = 87% of segment. GridAutomationAndSoftware ($827M) is NOT MVA-priced and is excluded from exposure.
  Data-center-tied share of Electrification REVENUE: I assume 30%. I deliberately use REVENUE, not the original's ~$6B orders figure — orders do not hit EBITDA inside a 3-12 month horizon, and mixing an orders base with an EBITDA margin is a category error.
  Exposed base = $14.0B x 0.30 = $4.20B/yr.

STEP 2 — the assumption the original omitted: regime.
The 20% W/GPU cut only reduces MVA purchased if the buyer's binding constraint is COMPUTE. If the binding constraint is POWER (as it is today — interconnect queues, GEV gas slots sold out to 2028-2030, transformer lead times), then a 20% cut in W/GPU means the hyperscaler fits ~25% MORE GPUs behind the same transformer. MVA purchased is unchanged; only compute-per-MVA rises. Pass-through in that regime is approximately ZERO.
  p(demand/compute-constrained rather than power-constrained, within the 3-12 month order window) = 0.25. This is my substitution; the original implicitly used 1.00 while its own caveat #3 asserted the opposite.

STEP 3 — electrical pass-through, conditional on being compute-constrained.
I use 40%, below the original's unverifiable 55%, for three specific reasons: (a) power transformers ship in discrete standard MVA ratings (25/50/75/100 MVA) so a 20% IT-side cut frequently rounds to the same unit; (b) 2N UPS / N+1 distribution redundancy and next-gen-rack headroom do not shrink one-for-one; (c) the HV substation and interconnect scope — a large slice of GridSystemsIntegration — is sized to a utility interconnection agreement signed years earlier and is essentially never downsized. Partial offset in the opposite direction: measured peak-to-average ratios of 1.21-2.56 mean large transients, which argue for MORE conditioning content (STATCOM, BESS, power conversion) — all GEV products. I do not credit this explicitly; it is a reason 40% is not conservative.

STEP 4 — revenue delta.
$4,200M x 0.20 (physical) x 0.25 (regime) x 0.40 (pass-through) = $84.0M/yr of Electrification revenue foregone.

STEP 5 — EBITDA delta.
Measured Electrification segment EBIT margin, H1'26: ($528M + $671M) / $6,596M = 18.2% (FY25 was 14.9% — the original's 15% is stale by a full year and four points). On lost volume the correct rate is the DECREMENTAL margin, which is higher than average because factory fixed cost and Prolec overhead do not flex: I use 30%.
  EBITDA delta = $84.0M x 0.30 = $25.2M/yr.

STEP 6 — to $/share.
$25.2M x 25 (default multiple, unchanged — GEV trades ~35x forward earnings, so 25x EV/EBITDA on a marginal stream is if anything generous) = $630M.
$630M / 266,333,581 shares = $2.366/share.
$2.366 / $940.33 = 0.252%.

CENTRAL ANSWER: $2.37/share, 0.25% of the reference price.

Upper bound check: even setting p(regime) = 1.00 — i.e. pretending GEV is demand-constrained today, which it is not — the answer is $4,200M x 0.20 x 0.40 = $336M revenue, x 30% = $100.8M EBITDA, x 25 / 266,333,581 = $9.46/share (1.01%). That figure reproduces the original's $9.29 almost exactly, which confirms my diagnosis: the original's central case is really a p=1 case wearing a 55% pass-through. Under no defensible parameterization does this clear $10/share without ALSO doubling the exposed base.

- **where_it_differs**: Four differences, one of which does almost all the work.

1. THE DECISIVE ONE — regime. The original multiplied a 20% physical haircut by a 55% pass-through and stopped. It then wrote in its own caveats that "GEV is currently supply-constrained, not demand-constrained ... an 11-20% reduction in demand per unit of compute reduces the queue, not the revenue" — and never propagated that into the arithmetic. That is a self-refuting model: the caveat section kills the number the materiality section reports. I price the regime explicitly at p=0.25, which divides the answer by four. Physically: when power is the binding constraint, better joules-per-token is compute-accretive and MVA-neutral. The memory wall makes hyperscalers buy MORE GPUs per transformer, not fewer transformers.

2. Base is orders, not revenue. The original applied a 15% EBITDA margin to a $6B ORDERS run-rate. Orders are not revenue and do not reach EBITDA inside a 3-12 month horizon. - **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: p(the AI buildout is compute-constrained rather than power-constrained during the order window) = 0.25.

This single parameter is the whole finding. It is the hinge because the physics only converts into lost GEV revenue when the buyer already has all the power it can use. Today the buyer cannot get power at any price: gas slots sold out through 2028-2030, 243-week lead times, multi-year transformer queues, interconnect backlogs. In that world a 20% cut in watts-per-GPU is spent on more GPUs, not on a smaller transformer order — GEV's revenue is set by what it can BUILD, not by what the customer needs. The memory wall is therefore currently a demand-side efficiency gain with a supply-side-capped financial consequence of roughly zero.

Second-order but still large: the 40% electrical pass-through, which is my judgement and not a measured quantity. It is the number most worth pinning down empirically — a teardown of two or three published hyperscaler substation one-lines against their stated IT nameplate would settle it, and that is a tractable weekend of work for this team.
- **sensitivity**: Sensitivity on the key assumption, p(compute-constrained) = 0.25, holding everything else fixed:

  p = 0.125 (halved):  $4,200M x 0.20 x 0.125 x 0.40 = $42.0M rev -> $12.6M EBITDA -> x25 = $315M -> $1.18/share (0.13%)
  p = 0.25  (central): $84.0M rev -> $25.2M EBITDA -> $630M -> $2.37/share (0.25%)
  p = 0.50  (doubled): $168.0M rev -> $50.4M EBITDA -> $1,260M -> $4.73/share (0.50%)
  p = 1.00  (ceiling, i.e. fully demand-constrained): $9.46/share (1.01%)

The range across a 2x swing in the hinge assumption is $1.18 to $4.73 — the finding stays immaterial across the entire defensible range, and even the physically impossible ceiling barely touches the $10 bar.

Secondary sensitivity on pass-through (holding p=0.25): 20% -> $1.18/share; 40% -> $2.37; 80% -> $4.73. Same conclusion. 

For this finding to reach $20/share you would need simultaneously: p>=0.75, pass-through >=60%, and a data-center-exposed base of $7B+ (50% of the segment). Each is individually a stretch; jointly they are not a case, they are a wish. The correct conclusion is that the arithmetic is robustly small, which is itself a useful and defensible result — it tells the team not to spend a plank of the memo on it.
- **materiality_verdict**: immaterial

## [Verify] skeptic:hydrogen_blending:The H2O-loading bridge: GE's own

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: The INPUT stoichiometry is correct and I reproduced it exactly from first principles. The APPLICATION of GE's severity formula is a category error. Detail:

WHAT CHECKS OUT (independent re-derivation, no reuse of the finding's numbers):
- H2 4.1352 mol H2O/MJ vs CH4 2.4927 mol H2O/MJ, ratio 1.659x (finding says 1.66x). Correct.
- q = 1.157 MJ/kg inlet air for 7HA.02 (384 MW / 0.434 / 765 kg/s). Correct; robust to plausible input ranges (1.14-1.21).
- Methane exhaust H2O = 8.02 mol% by my mass balance vs CATF/Schonewald 8.3 vol%. Independently corroborated.
- Incremental water at 50 vol% H2 = 0.793% of compressor inlet mass flow; at 100% = 3.424%. Both reproduce the finding to 3 significant figures.
- Arithmetic S = 1 + 0.55(0.793) = 1.436, and 25,000/1.436 = 17,408 h. Internally consistent.

ERROR 1 (FATAL) - QUOTE TRUNCATED AT THE EXACT POINT GE REVERSES. The finding quotes GER-3620 Rev P p.12 on higher gas conductivity raising heat transfer and reducing part life, then stops. GE's very next sentences, verbatim from the extracted text: "The control system on most base load applications reduces firing temperature as water or steam is injected. This is known as dry control curve operation, which counters the effect of the higher heat transfer on the gas side and results in no net effect on bucket life. This is the standard configuration for all gas turbines, both with and without water or steam injection." GE states the finding's own mechanism nets to ZERO under standard control. M=0.55 is a WET-control-curve value, which GE says applies to units "generally in peaking applications where annual operating hours are low."

ERROR 2 (FATAL) - THE VARIABLE I IS DEFINED AS INJECTED STEAM, NOT COMBUSTION WATER. GER-3620's operative parameter list defines: "Ki = Water/Steam Injection Severity Factor (% Steam Referenced to Compressor Inlet Air Flow, w/f = Water to Fuel Ratio)." I is a metered injection flow from an injection system with a water-to-fuel ratio. Hydrogen co-firing has no injection system, no metered diluent, and no w/f. Substituting combustion-product water into a variable defined as injected steam mass flow is a category error, not a conservative extrapolation. By GE's own definition, with no injection, I=0, M=0, S=1.

ERROR 3 (FATAL) - THE PHYSICAL ANALOGY INVERTS. I computed fuel mass per MJ: CH4 20.0 g, blend at 50 vol% H2 17.30 g. Steam injection at 2.4% ADDS 2.4% of inlet-air mass to the turbine. Hydrogen at 50 vol% REMOVES 0.31% of inlet-air mass (2.313% -> 2.001% of air); at 100% H2 it removes 1.35%. The wet-curve penalty is the price paid for output augmentation bought by added mass at held firing temperature. Hydrogen buys no output augmentation, raises no cycle pressure ratio, adds no nozzle aerodynamic loading. The finding's caveat 1 concedes M is "somewhere below 0.55" - understated. The correct statement is that the wet/dry control-curve framework does not map at all: DLN 2.6e is Dry Low NOx, there is no diluent injection and therefore no wet control curve to be on.

ERROR 4 (FACTUAL, and it inverts the headline) - "A SEVERITY FACTOR GE HAS NEVER PUBLISHED" IS FALSE. GER-3620 Rev P p.10: "Figure 9 provides the basic relationship between fuel severity factor and hydrogen content of the fuel." GE's fuel severity IS indexed on hydrogen content. Its direction is opposite to the finding: GE attributes higher severity in heavy fuels to the fact that they "generally release a higher amount of radiant thermal energy, which results in a subsequent reduction in combustion hardware life," and states natural gas is "the baseline, optimum fuel with regard to turbine maintenance." Lower hydrogen = more soot/luminosity = more radiant load = higher severity. Corroborated independently in the corpus academic tier (openalex): natural gas's "higher hydrogen-to-carbon ratio" produces "fewer carbonaceous particles," "reducing soot formation," "minimizing local hot spots on combustor liners." BREAK 1 — THE SOURCE PAPER SAYS THE OPPOSITE. The Meta paper's entire optimization is conducted AT A FIXED FACILITY POWER BUDGET. Meta did not buy 20% less electrical plant; it put ~25% more GPUs inside the same 150 MW envelope. The paper's own abstract names "electric power supply" as "the primary constraint." Under its own model, the 960 W decision changes GPUs-per-MW and leaves MVA-per-site exactly unchanged. The finding takes a result about compute density per provisioned watt and reads it as a reduction in provisioned watts. Those are opposite claims. This is not a judgement call about pass-through; it is the paper contradicting the mechanism in its own sentences.

The corollary is worse for the short case. Cheaper compute per watt lowers the cost of AI inference, which raises demand for AI compute, which — when power is the binding constraint — raises demand for grid MW, i.e. for GEV's product. The sign may well be positive.

Revenue over the 3-12 month horizon is set by factory throughput against that backlog, not by the marginal order. An 11% haircut to NEW order intake shortens the queue; it does not reduce a dollar of revenue or EBITDA before roughly 2029. The finding concedes this for gas in kill-condition (4) but does not apply the same logic to Electrification, where the corpus evidence is at least as strong.

A third, smaller break: the E3 "86% load factor" comparison is used in the wrong direction. Load factor is an energy-forecasting assumption (average MWh vs peak). Transformers are sized on peak. A lower realized load factor means less energy per MW of peak — which would bear on gas FIRED HOURS (and therefore on GEV's per-fired-hour services billing), not on MVA. If anything, a lower load factor means more peak MW must be contracted per unit of delivered compute.

The 55% pass-through assumption is then moot: the quantity being passed through is approximately zero.

Power is the constant and GPU count is the output. Meta bought the same electrical plant and put more GPUs behind it. The finding inverts its own source. Second, the 55% MVA pass-through number was correctly identified by the finding's author as the load-bearing guess; the answer is that it is near zero on this horizon for supply-side reasons, which is worth writing down so nobody re-derives the angle.

Credit where due: the author flagged the simulation-vs-metered limit, the secondhand POLCA citation, the judgement-call pass-through, and the supply-constraint problem, and refused to inflate past the $10 bar. The self-criticism was accurate. It just did not go one step further and check whether the source paper held facility power fixed — which it does, in a sentence.

## [Verify] skeptic:hot_section_materials:GEV's total hot-section airfoil

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: THREE errors, one of them fatal.

**FATAL — steady-state renewal formula applied to a fleet that is nowhere near steady state.** The finding computes annual aftermarket airfoil demand as (installed base ÷ 11.5 yr replacement cadence): 50 GW ÷ 11.5 = 4.3 GW-equivalent in 2026, 143 ÷ 11.5 = 12.4 in 2030. The identity `flow = stock / L` is only valid when the age distribution is uniform over [0, L]. GEV's HA fleet is not. From GEV's own FY2025 10-K (acc. 0001996810-26-000015, verified in corpus): "126 HA-Turbines in our installed base with approximately 3.6 million operating hours." That is 3,600,000 / 126 = **28,571 operating hours per unit, average**. The finding's own premise sets first stage-1 replacement at 3 HGPI = 75,000 factored fired hours. So the average HA unit is **38% of the way to its first stage-1 replacement, and essentially no HA unit has reached one yet** — the oldest (Bouchain / Wolf Hollow II, COD late 2016) has ~10 yr x 6,500 h/yr ≈ 65,000 h, still short of 75,000. At 6,500 h/yr the average unit needs 46,400 more hours = 7.1 more years, i.e. fleet-average first replacement lands ~2033. Even at a punitive 1.3x hours-factoring ratio the average unit is only ~49% through. **Correct 2026 HA stage-1 replacement flow is ≈ 0 GW-equivalent, not 4.3.** The entire 2026 aftermarket term is spurious.

Re-deriving 2030 properly (cohort method, not stock/L): units reaching 75,000 factored hours by 2030 are those in service by ~2018.5 (no factoring) to ~2021 (1.3x factoring). HA units in service by those dates are roughly 30 (≈12 GW) to 55 (≈22 GW), with replacements spread over ~2028-2033. Annual 2030 flow = 3.0 to 4.9 GW of stage-1 sets. **Finding says 12.4 GW-equivalent; correct range is 1.9-3.2 GW-equivalent after the content correction below — overstated 4-6.5x.**

**ERROR 2 — a stage-1 replacement set is not one unit's worth of SX/DS casting.** The finding equates "1 stage-1 set" with "1 GW-equivalent" of new-unit casting demand. Corpus src:3857 (chunk 468814): single crystal goes into first-stage blades only; directionally solidified serves "the second and third stages"; equiaxed serves cooler hot-section parts. A 7HA/9HA turbine has 4 stages. Stage-1 buckets + nozzles + shrouds are a fraction of a unit's SX/DS airfoil content. Being fair to the finding (stages 1-3 buckets and stages 1-2 nozzles plausibly share the ~3-HGPI cadence, and stage-1 SX is furnace-hour-heavy because land-based SX yields are <20% per src:3857 chunk 468816), I use a content factor of ~0.65, not 1.0. This alone cuts the aftermarket term by a third.

**ERROR 3 — the 75,000-hour cadence is an unverified extrapolation, and the finding admits it.** GER-3620 Rev P does not publish HA replacement intervals; the 3-HGPI rule is legacy F-class. The finding's own kill condition (e) notes 7HA.03 carries 32,000/64,000-hr intervals — if true, 3 HGPI = 96,000 h = 14.8 yr, which pushes first replacements even further out and *strengthens* this refutation rather than weakening it.

**WHAT SURVIVES:** Two inputs check out and should be kept. (1) The 6,500 fired-hours/yr duty assumption is sound — I derived it independently from EIA-923 x EIA-860M in the corpus: 30 US plants with CT units >=280 MW nameplate, COD 2016+, 20.1 GW of CT capacity, produced 185.1 TWh in 2025 across CT+CA prime movers = 9,216 h/yr of CT-nameplate-equivalent output; dividing by the ~1.5x combined-cycle gross-output ratio gives ~6,100 GT-equivalent full-load hours, and fired hours exceed equivalent full-load hours because of part-load running. Cross-check from the 10-K: 28,571 h/unit over a fleet averaging ~4.4-5 years in service implies 5,700-6,500 h/yr. The assumption is reasonable, arguably conservative. (2) The 0.40 GW/unit HA size is right — a corpus projects row gives 128 units / 74,000 MW = 578 MW/unit, but that is 1x1 combined-cycle plant output (7HA.02 ≈ 384 MW simple cycle / ≈580 MW CC), so GT-only nameplate ≈ 0.40 GW and the 50 GW installed HA base is correct.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The generic claim — castings are the binding constraint, and aero and IGT compete for the same single-crystal capacity — is saturated, and the corpus confirms it independently of the finding's own search record:
- src:3864 (news): frames the CPP deal precisely as the finding does — "Howmet Aerospace shares fell roughly 10% on fears of lost merchant demand, though severe casting capacity shortages through 2030 may support both companies," and chunk 468858 states data-center demand drives orders for IGTs "that use the same single-crystal airfoil castings used in jet engines." - src:3878 ("The Gas Turbine Supply Chain — P Equity Research"), src:223, src:3840, src:3841, src:3677: deal mechanics, merchant-foreclosure question, EU merger-review angle.
- Plus the finding's own cited EPRI/POWER, Bernstein-on-Howmet, and GE Aerospace deal language.

The one genuinely unpublished piece was the aftermarket-compounding arithmetic (aftermarket = 29% of 2030 GEV airfoil demand; total demand +74% vs aero's +30%). I could not find it published either — but it is unpublished because it is **arithmetically wrong**, not because it was overlooked.

HONESTY CAVEAT: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could run fresh novelty searches, so the published-work finding above rests on the corpus and on the finding's own search record rather than on new searches I ran. The corpus evidence is strong enough to settle the generic claim; I could not independently re-check for a new sell-side note published in the last few days.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The best rescue is to abandon the finding's stated derivation and reach a similar magnitude by a different route: **scrap-driven replacement, not life-limited replacement.**

Stage-1 parts are repaired at every HGPI (~25,000 factored hours ≈ 3.8 yr) and only *life-expired* at 3 HGPI. But repair is not free of casting demand — some fraction of parts fails repair criteria each outage (creep, oxidation, TBC spallation, wall-thickness loss), and in practice OEMs often swap rather than repair to shorten outage duration. If the effective per-HGPI scrap rate on stage-1 airfoils is 20-30%, the HA fleet generates casting demand of roughly 0.25 / 3.8 yr = 6.6% of a stage-1 set per GW-year — numerically close to the finding's 8.7%, but arrived at defensibly, and critically it applies to the fleet **today**, not from 2033. That would restore a non-trivial 2026 aftermarket term.

Why this still does not save the wedge: the scrap route scales with the installed base, and the installed base is compounding at roughly the same rate as new build. So aftermarket demand grows *in line with* new build, not faster. The finding's entire differentiating claim is the **growth differential** (+74% GEV vs +30% aero), and that differential comes from the aftermarket term accelerating relative to new build. Under the scrap model it does not accelerate; the ratio is roughly constant. The contrast collapses either way.

Two further reasons the counterargument cannot be verified: GEV does not disclose per-outage parts scrap rates, so the 20-30% is unfalsifiable from public data; and the finding's headline comparison is apples-to-oranges regardless — GE Aerospace's +30% is measured off a far larger base (CPP is ~70% aero by revenue), so in absolute incremental furnace slots aero is the bigger claimant even at half the growth rate. Comparing growth rates off different bases does not establish who crowds out whom.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. The physics input that carries the novelty is wrong by 4-6x, and the mechanism breaks in three independent places.

**1. The central number does not survive re-derivation.** The finding's aftermarket term uses flow = stock / L (installed base ÷ 11.5-year replacement cadence), which is valid only for a fleet with a uniform age distribution spanning the full replacement life. GEV's HA fleet is young and steeply ramping. GEV's own FY2025 10-K states 126 HA turbines with ~3.6M operating hours = **28,571 hours per unit average, versus the 75,000-hour first-replacement threshold the finding itself assumes**. The average HA unit is 38% of the way to its first stage-1 replacement; no unit has reached one. The correct 2026 aftermarket flow is ≈0 GW-equivalent, not 4.3. Correcting to a cohort method and applying a ~0.65 content factor (stage-1 sets are not a full unit's SX/DS casting content — corpus src:3857 confirms SX is stage 1 only, DS stages 2-3), 2030 aftermarket is 1.9-3.2 GW-equivalent, not 12.4.

Rebuilt headline: demand growth 2026→2030 is **+62%, not +74%**, and aftermarket is **~8% of 2030 GEV airfoil demand, not 29%**. Since new build alone goes 20→30 GW (+50%), the aftermarket "compounding claim" contributes about 12 points of 62. The novel mechanism is a rounding error inside a published new-build ramp. It becomes genuinely material in the **late 2030s** (2037-2042), when the 2025-2030 vintages hit 75,000 hours — three pitch cycles away.

**2. Materiality fails the $10/share bar once corrected.** The finding's $37.55/share (3.99%) assumes a 4 GW 2030 delivery shortfall. Attributing the shortfall to the novel mechanism in proportion to its corrected share of demand (7.7% rather than 29%) gives ~1.06 GW: 1.06 GW x $500M/GW x 20% margin x 25x / 266,333,581 shares = **$9.95/share = 1.06%** — below the bar, before any discounting of a 2030 event to a 3-12 month horizon.

**3. The mechanism breaks three ways.** (a) *Furnace non-fungibility.* Corpus src:3857 (chunk 468816) reports land-based SX blades are ~5x larger than aero blades with yields below 20%, and (chunk 468815) that Bridgman furnaces are part-sized with ~18-month ALD lead times and ~3.5 years to qualified output, with any change to mold recipe, alloy or withdrawal rate restarting qualification. GE Aerospace therefore cannot convert Eastlake's large-IGT furnaces to aero output on any horizon that matters, and the "shared foundry base" is far less fungible than the finding assumes. The truly shared constraints — ceramic cores, shell slurry, rhenium/ruthenium feedstock, metallurgists — are never quantified. (b) *The CPP→GEV supply link is unverified and the corpus points elsewhere.* src:3840 says "GE Aerospace has been a CPP customer for more than 15 years" — GE **Aerospace**, not GEV. src:3586 names **Precision Castparts** as the IGT airfoil supplier. No document names GEV as a CPP customer. Without that link the CPP deal has zero GEV read-through, and the finding concedes this is "the single most important thing to verify." (c) *Accounting.* GEV recognizes equipment revenue over time on costs incurred, so a 2030 slot constraint does not touch FY26-27 revenue — it would appear as backlog-conversion timing. And the near-term expression the finding names (casting-price inflation in CSA estimated cost) lands on the same Note 9 line as the team's existing Findings 1 and 2, which the finding itself flags as non-additive.

**4. Already published.** The generic thesis is saturated, including the exact merchant-foreclosure framing (src:3864) and the "same single-crystal castings as jet engines" crowd-out claim (chunk 468858). The only unpublished element was the aftermarket arithmetic, and it is unpublished because it is wrong.

**What the team should keep.** Two verified inputs are reusable elsewhere: the 6,500 fired-hours/yr duty assumption, which I independently confirmed from EIA-923 x EIA-860M (30 US plants, CT units >=280 MW, COD 2016+, 20.1 GW producing 185.1 TWh in 2025 → ~6,100 GT-equivalent full-load hours after the 1.5x CC adjustment); and the 0.40 GW/unit HA size, which reconciles the corpus "128 units / 74,000 MW" figure as combined-cycle plant output. Also worth keeping as a standalone observation: **the HA fleet's 28,571-hour average means GEV's high-margin hot-section parts annuity has essentially not started yet.** That cuts the *opposite* way from this finding — it is a bull argument on long-dated services, and it sharpens the gap between management's $25M/GW-yr 20-year average and today's realized ~$15M/GW-yr. That reframing is worth a separate look; this short thesis is not.

Largest credible instantaneous IT steps: Llama-3's 16,384 x H100 cluster = 11.5 MW IT (16384 x 700W); 100k H100 = 70 MW; 100k GB200 at 1.2 kW = 120 MW. Per-GT at Homer City: 1.6 MW (0.43% of rated), 10.0 MW (2.60%), 17.1 MW (4.46%). All far below 20%.
L is a COUNT of steps >= 20%. Below the gate, L = 0 and the term contributes EXACTLY ZERO factored starts. It is an uncontrolled island frequency/imbalance event that DRAGS the shaft faster than it can be commanded - exactly GE's stated case, an arc furnace comparable in size to the generator on a grid with no external inertia. A 4.5 GW campus with tens of thousands of diversified racks is the structural opposite: the fluctuation source is small relative to the island. For a firm-capacity/capacity-market argument the peak is the right condition, but the finding then applies it to the entire 116 GW order book including baseload combined-cycle units that are sold on energy, not on peak firm MW. That is exactly the peak-for-average confusion.

(2) COMPOSITION ERROR. The 0.5-0.9%/degC coefficient is a gas-turbine coefficient. The 116 GW GEV figure is largely combined-cycle, where roughly a third of block output comes from the steam turbine, which does not derate at the GT rate (it is condenser/wet-bulb limited and far less ambient-sensitive). In the corpus planned queue, CA (steam side) is 14.0 GW and CS (single-shaft combined) 7.6 GW of the 65.3 GW total — 33% of planned MW is combined-cycle-affected. They correctly excluded CA from their own weighting but then applied the resulting GT-only percentage to GEV's 116 GW, which is not GT-only. This overstates by roughly 20-30% in relative terms.

(3) THE CITED SOURCE ARGUES THE OPPOSITE WAY. I read sources.id=1860 in full and verified the quote verbatim: "a power output decrease of 0.5%-0.9% is observed for every 1 degC increase in ambient temperature (Kakaras et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2014)", with the Bhargava/Meher-Homji note that aeroderivatives are more sensitive than heavy-duty frames. Correctly quoted. But the paper is titled "Thermal Energy Storage For Gas Turbine Power Augmentation" — its entire thesis is that this derate is economically recoverable via inlet cooling and TES. The finding cites, as its physics authority, a paper written to establish its own kill condition. Inlet evaporative cooling and chilling are near-universal on new hot-climate plants.

Two premises I CONFIRMED in GEV's favor: a GE HA-product technical paper in the corpus states its output table is given "on a net basis at ISO", so HA ratings genuinely are ISO-referenced; and the unit-size observation holds — planned CT units at 477-478 MW (Waterford 5/6 LA, Jefferson AR, Vicksburg/Traceview/Delta Blues MS, Westlake LA) and Yates GA GT units at 482.8 MW sit above any 60 Hz H-class ISO simple-cycle rating, consistent with EIA reporting generator nameplate rather than site-derated turbine output.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: False
- **where_published**: I could not find the specific connection published. I searched for sell-side and trade coverage tying gas turbine backlog GW to ISO rating versus firm summer MW. Across Utility Dive (Jul 23 2026), Solmar Capital, Developments Today, The Grid Report, Tantalum Strategy, Manufacturing Mag and CNBC (Jun 27 2026), every outlet counts GW and none distinguishes ISO GW from summer-available MW. The BNP Paribas (Moses Sutton) and Jefferies (Dumoulin-Smith) notes summarized in that coverage debate pricing, conversion and the 30 GW target, not ratings basis. So the observation appears genuinely unpublished.

The honest reading is that it is unpublished because it is not tradeable, not because it is undiscovered. Ambient derate is design-basis material for every EPC, developer and IRP modeler; it is not an information asymmetry. The corpus paper the finding leans on (Technoeconomic Analysis of Microgrids for AI Data Centers in the CONUS, OpenAlex W7116743386, sources.id=334) confirms that serious CONUS-wide data-center gas modelling already treats ambient derating as first-order.

One genuinely important thing the search DID surface that the finding got wrong: published $/kW. BNP Paribas estimated ~$790/kW for heavy-duty turbines, ~$950/kW for HA-class combined cycle and ~$1,800/kW for aeroderivatives (Utility Dive, Jul 23 2026). CNBC (Jun 27 2026) quotes "more than $250 million" per turbine, which on a ~430 MW frame is ~$580/kW. The finding's derived $265/kW and assumed $400/kW are understated by 2-3x against published estimates.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: GEV IS SUPPLY-CONSTRAINED, SO INCREMENTAL DEMAND DOES NOT BECOME INCREMENTAL SHIPMENTS. This is fatal on its own and the finding never addresses it.

The finding's entire materiality chain is "+14.0 GW of iron required, spread over five years = 2.8 GW/yr of incremental shipments." But GEV cannot ship 2.8 GW/yr more than it can build. Its output is capped at ~20 GW/yr (Q3'26), 24 GW (2028), 30 GW (2030), and the constraint is physical: management cites hot-section castings, high-temperature alloys, large transformers and skilled field assembly as binding, not factory capex. Coverage confirms the book is full through 2029, reservations run to 2031, and GEV expects to be more than halfway contracted for 2031 by end-2026. Siemens Energy calls the 110-120 GW/yr global market supply-constrained. In a sold-out market, extra demand raises PRICE and extends BACKLOG DURATION; it does not raise units shipped. The finding multiplies incremental GW by a $/kW price and a margin as if GEV were demand-limited. It is not. The correct pass-through is to pricing, which is already visible, already discussed by management as "solid pricing," and already in the stock.

THE SECOND INDEPENDENT KILL: DOUBLE COUNTING. The 116 GW is already grossed up for derate. A developer specifies firm summer MW, the EPC sizes the plant at site conditions, and the resulting ISO GW is what GEV books. The extra units the derate requires are already inside the 53 GW backlog and 63 GW of reservations. You cannot then compute 116/(1-0.108) - 116 = +14.0 GW and call it incremental. The finding's own caveat (1) states this plainly — "the derate does not create a hidden order book, it explains why the order book is as large as it is" — and then the materiality section computes the incremental iron anyway. That is an internal contradiction, not a nuance. Once the double count is removed, the incremental GW is zero and the $/share is zero.

Either objection alone reduces materiality to nil. Together they leave nothing.

For completeness, the most charitable possible version: if you granted both the incremental GW AND unconstrained supply, and used the published BNP price instead of the derived one, 2.8 GW/yr x $790/kW x 18% x 25 / 266,333,581 = $37.37/share (3.97%), and at 4.1 GW/yr x $790/kW, $54.73/share (5.82%). So the finding actually understates its own arithmetic by roughly 3x through the bad $/kW. That is worth knowing, but it does not rescue anything, because the GW figure it multiplies is not real.

THIRD PROBLEM: THE TESTABLE PREDICTION IS A LOOKUP, NOT A FORECAST. EIA-860 annual has published Nameplate, Net Summer and Net Winter capacity for every US generator for decades. Summer/nameplate ratios of roughly 0.88-0.93 for hot-state combustion turbines are already in public data today; you do not need to wait for the 2025 final file to know the answer. A prediction whose result can be looked up before the test date is not a test, and it carries no event risk into Q3'26 earnings (Oct 28 2026) or the FY26 10-K.

WHAT IS SALVAGEABLE — and the finding missed it entirely. The interesting consequence of ambient heat is not on the equipment line, it is on SERVICES. Operators facing hot-day derate who must hold a firm MW commitment run at peak fire, and peak firing multiplies the factored-fired-hours clock that GER-3620 uses to set the 25,000 FFH combustion/HGP and 50,000 FFH major inspection intervals. Since GEV bills services per fired hour and per outage event, systematic hot-site peak firing pulls maintenance events forward in calendar time and accelerates the services annuity — which reaches the Power services revenue line directly, is the higher-margin half of the $176B RPO, and is not supply-constrained the way the factory is. That is a mechanism worth building out properly. It is a different finding from this one and I have not quantified it here; the corpus FTS returned nothing on "factored fired hours" or "peak fire," so it would need GER-3620 Rev P directly.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED on the mechanism, not on the physics. Score it 1/5 and do not put it in the memo as a standalone wedge.

The physics is real and the author was honest. I reproduced their fleet derate from the corpus to within 0.25 percentage points (11.00% vs 10.76% at 0.5%/degC; 15.21% vs 14.95% at 0.7%/degC), verified the 0.5-0.9%/degC quote verbatim in sources.id=1860, and confirmed via a GE HA technical paper in the corpus that HA output tables are stated at ISO. The unit-size evidence that EIA reports generator nameplate rather than site-derated output also holds (477-478 MW planned CT units, 482.8 MW Yates GT units).

But the chain from that physics to a GEV financial line breaks in two independent places, and the author half-saw one of them.

First, the incremental iron is double counted. Developers already size plants at site conditions, so the gross-up is already inside the 116 GW. The finding's own caveat says this and its materiality section ignores it.

Second, and decisively, GEV is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained. The book is full through 2029, reservations run to 2031, and the binding constraints are hot-section castings, alloys and skilled labor. Extra demand in a sold-out market moves price and backlog duration, not units shipped. The entire materiality calculation multiplies incremental GW by $/kW as though GEV could simply build more. It cannot. Either objection alone takes the $12.58-$27.67/share to roughly zero.

Three secondary defects worth recording. The 10.8-15.0% headline is an ASHRAE 0.4% peak condition (~35 hrs/yr); at summer-mean conditions the same weighting gives 6.3-8.7%. A GT-only derate coefficient is applied to a combined-cycle-heavy backlog where ~33% of MW is steam-side and does not derate that way. And the derived $265/kW is 2-3x below published estimates (BNP Paribas: ~$790/kW heavy-duty, ~$950/kW HA combined cycle) — which means the finding also understates its own arithmetic by ~3x, though that rescues nothing.

The testable prediction fails the "dated test" bar. EIA-860 annual has published Net Summer and Nameplate capacity for decades; hot-state CT summer/nameplate ratios of ~0.88-0.93 can be looked up today. There is no event risk into Oct 28 2026 or the FY26 10-K.

Novelty is real but empty: I could find no sell-side or trade source distinguishing ISO GW from firm summer MW, but that is because the distinction is design-basis knowledge for every EPC and IRP modeler, not an asymmetry. Unpublished is not the same as untraded.

RECOMMENDED SALVAGE, as a separate line of work: redirect the same physics at SERVICES rather than equipment. Hot-site operators holding firm MW commitments run at peak fire; peak firing inflates the factored-fired-hours clock that sets GER-3620's 25,000 FFH combustion/HGP and 50,000 FFH major inspection intervals. Because GEV bills per fired hour and per outage event, that pulls maintenance events forward in calendar time and accelerates the highest-margin half of the $176B RPO — and services is not factory-constrained, so unlike the equipment argument it can actually convert. The corpus has nothing on "factored fired hours" or "peak fire"; this would need GER-3620 Rev P directly. That is where I would spend the next day, not here.

Under independent phases at N=100,000 the aggregate swing is 0.111% against a 20% threshold — 180x short. Memory-bound decode is asynchronous by construction; continuous batching actively smooths it. The literature attributes real facility-scale >=20%/10s steps to lockstep training all-reduce (3-10 s period, >1,000 MW/s), not to decode. Applying a 25x multiple to the annual flow of catch-ups assumes an equally large fresh cohort is re-estimated downward every year in perpetuity. - **strongest_counterargument**: THE SIGN OF THE TRADE IS PROBABLY BACKWARDS. GEV is not the marginal importer in this market — it is one of the most US-domesticated producers in it, and a duty that hits every importer is a price floor it collects on rather than a cost it eats.

The dominant US suppliers are import-dependent: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, Hyundai Electric and Hyosung, with Korea historically the largest single source of US LPT imports. A Section 232 derivative duty applied to full customs value at 15-25% is levied on ALL of them. In a market where demand exceeds supply by years, a uniform import duty does not compress OEM margin — it raises the clearing price, and the producer with the largest US-melted-and-poured-adjacent footprint captures the spread.

Management is telling you, in the segment narrative, that the tariff regime is hurting Wind and that Power Transmission is realising FAVOURABLE PRICE. That is the pass-through mechanism working in real time. If you want to short GEV on tariffs, the disclosed exposure is Wind, not Electrification — and the team has already worked Wind to death.

## [Verify] quant:partload_cycling_thermo:GE added a load-step maintenance

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: CENTRAL CASE: -$2.06/share (-0.22% of $940.33). Full chain below.

STEP 0 — verify the physics constants (these check out).
aL = exp(0.0137 x %LoadStep), so per-event factored starts = exp(0.0137xS)-1: S=20% -> 0.3150; S=45% -> 0.8506; S=50% -> 0.9837; S=70% -> 1.6087; S=95% -> 2.6748. GE's Appendix A.3 worked example (30 steps -> 25.4 factored starts) implies an average step of ln(1.847)/0.0137 = 44.8%, i.e. 0.847 factored starts/event. Internally consistent. I use GE's own 0.847/event.

STEP 1 — does the starts criterion actually bind? This is the gate the original skipped.
A 7HA.02 at 85% capacity factor runs 0.85 x 8,760 = 7,446 fired hours/yr. The 25,000-FFH HGP interval therefore arrives every 25,000/7,446 = 3.36 years on hours alone.
Factored starts per year at rate r qualifying steps/day = 309.2r, plus ~25 genuine starts/yr for a near-baseload machine.
Starts-based HGP interval = 720/(309.2r + 25) years.
The starts criterion binds only when 720/(309.2r+25) < 3.36, i.e. 309.2r + 25 > 214.3, i.e. r > 0.61 steps/day.
=> BREAK-EVEN IS ~0.6 QUALIFYING >=20%/10s STEPS PER DAY. Below that, the load-step term changes nothing at all and the finding is worth exactly $0.
Acceleration A(r) = 3.36 / min(3.36, 720/(309.2r+25)). A(0.5)=1.00; A(1)=1.56; A(2)=3.00.

STEP 2 — exposed capacity. I cut the original's base by 4x and say why.
The ~20 GW "data-center tied" figure covers ALL DC-linked gas, and the large majority is grid-parallel utility CCGT serving a data-center PPA. A grid-parallel machine never sees the campus load step — the interconnection absorbs it, which is the entire premise of GE's islanded worked example. Only behind-the-meter / islanded capacity qualifies. The named BTM projects are Chevron/Microsoft Permian (2,670 MW) and Blue Energy Texas (2,500 MW) = ~5.2 GW. I use 5 GW exposed (range 3-10 GW). This is my substitution for the original's unjustified use of the full 20 GW.

STEP 3 — the revenue line at risk.
5 GW x $25M/GW-yr (management's own Morgan Stanley Laguna figure) = $125M/yr of mature services billings. Not $500M.

STEP 4 — baseline services margin, derived rather than assumed.
FY2025 Power segment EBIT $2,902M / revenue $19,767M = 14.7% blended. Services are $13,072M of that (66%). If equipment runs at roughly breakeven EBIT (consistent with the 2027-vintage margin debate), services margin = 14.7%/0.66 = 22.3%; allowing modest positive equipment margin puts services at ~25%. I use 25%, not the original's unsourced 28%. Cost = 75% of billings.

STEP 5 — cost inflation from event acceleration.
Split CSA cost 80% event-driven (HGP/combustion parts, rotable spares, outage labor) / 20% fixed (monitoring, admin, planned minors). Cost multiplier M = 0.2 + 0.8A.
At r=1: A=1.56, M = 0.2 + 1.248 = 1.448.
New cost = 75% x 1.448 = 108.6% of billings. New margin = -8.6%.
Margin destruction = 25% - (-8.6%) = 33.6pp. (Note this is WORSE than the original's 23pp — my one correction in the bear direction.)

STEP 6 — probability-weight the sign. The original treats the hit as certain; it is not.
GEV's 10-K says service billing is "based on the customers' utilization ... and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event." If extra HGP events carry their own billing milestone, revenue rises with cost and the sign flips POSITIVE for GEV. The bear case requires the fixed-$/fired-hour regime where cost is starts-driven but billing is hours-driven. GER-3620 exists precisely so OEMs can price load steps, so a sophisticated 2026 BTM CSA plausibly carries adders. I assign 50% probability to the OEM-absorbs regime. Expected destruction = 16.8pp.

STEP 7 — annual EBITDA delta.
16.8% x $125M = -$21.0M/yr.

STEP 8 — multiple and timing.
x 25 = -$525M. But this annuity does not exist yet: Permian COD 2028, Blue Energy later. Discount 3 years at 9% (x0.772) = -$405M. The original applied 25x to a 2030s cash flow with no discount.

STEP 9 — one-time cumulative catch-up on the existing book.
5 GW / 116 GW under contract = 4.3% of book x 33.6pp = 1.45pp book-wide x GEV's disclosed ~$200M per percentage point = -$290M pre-tax, valued 1x (it is a one-time charge, not an annuity), x 50% regime probability = -$145M.

STEP 10 — total.

## [Verify] skeptic:onsite_alternatives:GEV's bridge product is the leas

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: PRIMARY ERROR — LHV/HHV basis mixing, inflates the headline number by 54%. The central claim is a 2,147 Btu/kWh heat-rate gap ("EIA CT-aeroderivative 9,124 minus Wartsila 34SG 6,977"). These two numbers are on different heating-value bases and cannot be subtracted. Wartsila publishes 48.9% electrical efficiency on LHV (ISO/European engine convention); EIA's AEO Table 8.2 heat rates are HHV (standard US/EIA convention, consistent with EIA-923 fuel_consumed_mmbtu). Converting at HHV/LHV = 1.108 for pipeline gas: 48.9% LHV = 44.1% HHV = 7,731 Btu/kWh HHV. Gap vs EIA's 9,124 = 1,393 Btu/kWh, not 2,147. A 35% overstatement of the gap, i.e. the claimed number is 54% too large.

Independent confirmation that 1,393 is the right answer: the finding's own "conservative" leg — LM6000PF+ 8,357 vs 34SG 6,977, both quoted LHV and therefore internally consistent — gives 1,380 Btu/kWh. Two independent consistent-basis comparisons converge on ~1,385 Btu/kWh. The 2,147 figure is the only one that required a cross-basis subtraction, and it is the outlier. The finding presented $29.0M/GW-yr as its conservative case and $45.2M/GW-yr as its headline; in fact $29M is the correct answer and $45M does not exist.

Arithmetic within each basis reproduces exactly (3412.14/0.489 = 6,978; 3412.14/8,357 = 40.83%; 3412.14/9,124 = 37.4%), so this is purely a basis error, not a calculator error.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TITLE CLAIM. Corrected penalty at $4.00/MMBtu, 1,393 Btu/kWh: 10% CF $4.9M/GW-yr; 30% CF $14.6M/GW-yr; 60% CF $29.3M/GW-yr; 85% CF $41.5M/GW-yr. Fuel bill as % of the $1.29B/GW aero overnight capex: 2.6% (10% CF, 7yr), 7.9% (30% CF, 7yr), 15.9% (60% CF, 7yr), 22.5% (85% CF, 7yr). The headline "the fuel bill exceeds a quarter of the equipment capex" is FALSE at every assumption the finding itself states. It requires >85% capacity factor AND 7 years AND $4 gas simultaneously, and even then reaches only 22.5%.

SECOND ERROR — internal inconsistency between capacity factor and the "bridge" framing. The finding needs 60% CF to make the fuel argument and needs "bridge" duty to make the 5-7 year lead-time argument, but these fight each other. The task's own established facts state ~60% of planned US gas capacity for 2026-27 delivery is simple-cycle peakers at ~10% capacity factor. A bridge/peaker asset at 10-30% CF carries a fuel penalty of $4.9-14.6M/GW-yr, i.e. 2-8% of capex over the full bridge — which is inside the noise of an EPC bid and cannot drive an equipment-selection decision. The finding cannot have it both ways: either the asset is a low-CF bridge (fuel is irrelevant, and GEV wins on capex and installation time) or it is high-CF primary power (in which case it is not a "bridge" and the 5-7 year duration framing is the wrong frame).

NOT ERRORS (checked and confirmed): the efficiency figures themselves are correctly transcribed; the Wartsila 34SG, Jenbacher, LM6000PF+ and EIA values are internally consistent with their stated bases; the lead-time inversion is directionally supported by the corpus (a trade source confirms large-frame machines "effectively sold out for the next four to five years"). GEV's counter-physics that the finding lists in caveats (methane slip ~150x, NOx/SCR burden on spark-ignited engines) is real and is confirmed in the corpus via EPA AP-42 methane-slip emission factors for reciprocating engines appearing in SEC filings.

The savrn.com "AI Data Center Natural Gas Turbines: 2026 Operator Brief" already publishes both the heat-rate gap (aero 9,000-10,500 vs recip 7,500-8,500 Btu/kWh) and the lead-time inversion (aero 30-36 months vs HHP recip 14-18 months). Note that this trade brief's recip range of 7,500-8,500 is much closer to my corrected HHV-consistent 7,731 than to the finding's 6,977 — an outside source independently corroborating that the finding's recip number is on the wrong basis for a US-convention comparison.

The corpus adds more prior publication the finding did not cite. A competitor-tracking table in the corpus already names Wartsila with "Cumulative 2.4+ GW booked for U.S. data centers; 790 MW Texas order April 2026" and tracks Caterpillar's Vertiv partnership — i.e. the recip-vs-turbine competitive frame is already assembled and in circulation.
