Internal-combustion (IC = reciprocating) planned capacity is FLAT at ~1.0 GW from 2024-06 (1.0 GW) to 2026-07 (1.0 GW). Over the identical window CT+GT planned capacity went from 11.3 GW to 44.1 GW, a 3.9x increase. The recip SHARE of planned gas capacity therefore COLLAPSED from 7.5-8.9% across 2023-24 to 2.2% in the latest vintage (2026-07). If reciprocating engines were taking share from turbines in the 2027-29 vintage, this series would show it, and it shows the precise opposite. Honest caveat, and the team should weigh it: EIA-860M covers grid-interconnected generators at or above 1 MW, so island-mode behind-the-meter data-center recip fleets may be materially under-captured, and the Joule/Caterpillar G3520K-class deployments in particular may never appear here. This weakens the test but does not reverse it, and it is still the best available direct measurement.

(2) GEV'S AERODERIVATIVE ORDERS ARE ACCELERATING VIOLENTLY IN THE EXACT QUARTERS SUBSTITUTION IS ALLEGED TO BITE. Corpus commentary: Q2'24 = 1 aeroderivative unit; Q2'25 = 27 units, with the source stating GEV "is seeing incremental demand for its aeroderivative technology, particularly to support data centers"; Q2'26 = 61 units alongside 52 heavy-duty. That is 1 to 27 to 61, and the Q2'26 report explicitly says "Demand remains strong for both heavy-duty and aeroderivative gas turbines." A short thesis predicting Q3'26 aero orders below 25 is predicting a ~60% sequential collapse in a line that just grew 2.3x year over year, with no disclosed cancellation, no lead-time relief, and the whole market supply-constrained. The finding's own kill condition (40 or more units) is very likely to trigger on the current run-rate.

(3) BOTH SUPPLY CHAINS ARE SOLD OUT, SO THIS IS MARKET GROWTH, NOT SUBSTITUTION. The finding's own evidence defeats it: Caterpillar's large-recip backlog is up more than 3.5x since January 2024 and it is expanding capacity to nearly 3x its 2024 level. That is not a competitor absorbing GEV's demand; that is a competitor rationing its own. When every prime mover in the market is capacity-constrained simultaneously, share does not move — volume moves. Wartsila's 2.4 GW cumulative US data-center book and GEV's 61-unit quarter are both symptoms of total demand exceeding total supply. Substitution requires that the marginal buyer had a real choice, and in 2026 they largely do not.

(4) THE MATERIALITY CHAIN BREAKS AT THE PRICE ASSUMPTION AND AT THE ACCOUNTING. The $/share rests entirely on three unsourced numbers — $950/kW OEM package price, ~120 units/yr, 30% share loss — and the physics never actually enters the dollar chain at all, so even a perfect heat-rate number would not have supported it. The $950/kW is the load-bearing failure: a corpus trade comparison table prices a complete INSTALLED aeroderivative plant at "$800K to $1.2M" per MW, and EIA's overnight cost is $1,294/kW installed. An OEM package cannot be $950/kW of a $800-1,294/kW installed plant — that implies the turbine package is 73-100% of total installed cost, when OEM share of an installed aero plant is conventionally ~45-55% once BOP, EPC, interconnection and gas infrastructure are included. Correcting to ~$500/kW halves the order pool. Re-running the finding's own chain: at $500/kW and its own 30% share loss, $130M EBITDA x 25 / 266,333,581 = $12.23/share (1.30%); at $500/kW and a 15% share loss (which is what the EIA IC-share trend actually supports), $65M x 25 = $6.11/share (0.65%) — below the task's own $10/share materiality bar. Only by keeping the inflated $950/kW AND assuming a 50% share loss does it clear $20/share.

Separately, the accounting instrument is wrong. GEV recognizes equipment revenue over time on costs incurred. An order NOT booked in 2027-29 produces essentially zero revenue and zero EBITDA effect inside the stated 3-12 month horizon; the finding's own materiality is explicitly a "run-rate EBITDA loss by 2029." Applying a 25x multiple to a 2029 run-rate of orders that have not been booked, discounting none of it back, and presenting the result as present $/share overstates the valuation effect by roughly the three-year discount factor and double-counts growth the market has arguably never capitalized. And at a $250B market cap, $1.2B/yr of foregone aero orders is ~0.7% of the $176B RPO per year — inside the rounding on a single quarter's heavy-duty bookings.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. The physics has a genuine unit error and the mechanism fails independently; either alone would sink it.

PHYSICS. The headline 2,147 Btu/kWh gap subtracts an LHV number (Wartsila 34SG, 48.9%, European engine convention) from an HHV number (EIA AEO Table 8.2, US convention). On a consistent HHV basis the gap is 1,393 Btu/kWh — 35% smaller, making the claimed figure 54% too large. The finding's own internally-consistent LHV comparison (LM6000PF+ 8,357 vs 34SG 6,977 = 1,380) converges on the same answer, which should have been the tell: the number it labelled "conservative" was correct and the number it headlined does not exist. The savrn trade brief it cites quotes recips at 7,500-8,500 Btu/kWh, corroborating ~7,731 HHV rather than 6,977. Consequence: the title claim that the fuel bill "exceeds a quarter of the equipment capex" is false at every assumption the finding states — 15.9% at its own 60% CF over 7 years, 22.5% even at 85% CF, and 2.6% at the ~10% capacity factor that actually characterizes the peaker duty this bridge fleet is being built for. The finding also cannot reconcile needing 60% CF for the fuel argument with needing "bridge" duty for the lead-time argument.

MECHANISM. Four breaks. (a) The direct empirical test contradicts it, in the team's own EIA-860M table: reciprocating planned gas capacity is flat at ~1.0 GW from 2024-06 to 2026-07 while CT+GT planned capacity went 11.3 to 44.1 GW, so recip share of planned gas COLLAPSED from 7.5-8.9% to 2.2% — though behind-the-meter island-mode fleets may be under-captured below EIA's reporting threshold. (b) GEV aeroderivative orders went 1 unit (Q2'24) to 27 (Q2'25) to 61 (Q2'26), so the short predicts a ~60% sequential collapse in a line growing 2.3x YoY; its own kill condition of 40+ units is likely to trigger on Oct 28. (c) Caterpillar's recip backlog up 3.5x and capacity expanding to 3x means both supply chains are sold out — that is market growth, not substitution, and substitution requires the marginal buyer to have had a choice. (d) The $950/kW OEM package price is not credible against a corpus-sourced $800K-1.2M per MW INSTALLED aero plant cost; at a realistic ~$500/kW the finding's own chain yields $12.23/share at 30% share loss and $6.11/share at the 15% loss the EIA trend supports — at or below the $10/share bar. Compounding this, equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred, so a 2027-29 order loss has ~zero P&L effect in the 3-12 month horizon; capitalizing a 2029 run-rate at an undiscounted 25x is the wrong instrument.

NOVELTY. Conceded and confirmed: the heat-rate gap and lead-time inversion are already published (savrn operator brief), and the corpus shows the recip-vs-turbine competitive frame already assembled in trade comparison tables and competitor trackers. I could not run confirmatory novelty searches — WebSearch budget was exhausted at 200/200 — so the team should treat the residual novelty claims as unverified by me.

WHAT TO SALVAGE. Two things are worth keeping. First, the tertiary idea the finding buries and never quantifies — recip fleets as a technical non-conversion mechanism for the 63 GW of slot reservations — is the only genuinely novel thread here and nothing I found addresses it; but it needs to be built on reservation economics and switching costs, not on a fuel-efficiency gap that is half what was claimed. Second, and more useful immediately: the EIA-860M IC-share series (7.5-8.9% down to 2.2%) is a clean, reproducible, contrarian dataset that REFUTES the popular "recips are eating turbines" narrative. That is a defensible LONG-side data point for the team and it is the opposite of what this finding set out to prove. Recommend the team drop this angle and reuse the query.

STEP 4 — Dollars, my anchor (6,250 h/yr reference, 25% margin, 25x, 266,333,581 sh, $940.33).
Shortfall per GW-yr = $25M x (1 - 6,056/6,250) = $0.776M/GW-yr.

STEP 5 — Same machine, the original's 8,000-hour anchor, with my 25% margin.

2030: 187 x 6.075 = $1,136M x 25% = $284M x 25 = $7,100M -> $26.66/share = 2.84% undiscounted; ~$18.2/share discounted 4 yrs at 10%.

## [Verify] skeptic:academic_blind_mine:Memory-bound decode physically c

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: Two of the three physical legs survive; the load-bearing causal leg does not.

(1) THE CENTRAL NUMBER IS A MICROBENCHMARK PRESENTED AS AN OPERATING NUMBER — and the paper's own generalization is wrong on roofline grounds. I fetched arXiv:2605.11999v1 (Ma, Afzal, Eitzinger, Wellein; submitted 12 May 2026 — the paper is real). Its sweep is BATCH SIZE 1 TO 32, sequence 1K-64K. The 137-300 W figure is measured entirely inside that range. The paper defends generalization with: "Arithmetic intensity does not change with batch size or parallelism strategy; the memory-boundedness is structural." That claim is false for the term that dominates decode bytes. For the linear/projection layers, the weight matrix (N params, 2 bytes each in FP16) is read ONCE per decode step regardless of batch, while FLOPs = 2*B*N. Arithmetic intensity is therefore approximately B FLOP/byte — exactly linear in batch size. H200 SXM machine balance is ~989 TFLOP/s dense FP16 / ~4.8 TB/s HBM3e ≈ 206 FLOP/byte. So decode's weight GEMMs cross from memory-bound to compute-bound at B ≈ 200. At the paper's maximum B=32 you are at ~16% of the roofline knee — you cannot observe the crossover, and the paper never does. Only the KV-cache attention term is genuinely batch-invariant in intensity (each sequence reads its own KV), and at moderate context that is a minority of bytes moved. Continuous batching (Orca, OSDI'22) and PagedAttention/vLLM (SOSP'23) exist for precisely this reason: production decode pools run B in the hundreds, not 32. Standard roofline (Williams/Waterman/Patterson, CACM 2009) is the independent re-derivation. So the "GPUs physically cannot reach TDP in decode" premise is an artifact of the chosen batch ceiling, not a structural property. It is the same class of error the task warned about, inverted: a stress-limited micro-regime cited as a fleet operating number.

(2) THE 700 W-vs-137 W GAP ALSO IGNORES NON-GPU NODE POWER. An H200 SXM node is ~10.2 kW of which the 8 GPUs are ~5.6 kW; CPUs, HBM-adjacent NVSwitch, NICs, DPUs, fans and PSU losses do not go memory-bound when the GPU does. Vercellino's own numbers show this: sustained 2.8-2.9 kW against a 3.52 kW node TDP is 80-82% of node rating, NOT the 20-43% the GPU-level figure implies. The finding quietly lets a device-level ratio stand in for a node-level ratio.

(3) WHAT ACTUALLY SURVIVES: the facility-level observations are real and independently sourced. arXiv:2604.07345 (Vercellino et al., 8 Apr 2026) exists and is real, but its facility figures are MODELLED, not metered — verified from the abstract: node power is measured at 0.1 s resolution, then "scaled to the whole-facility-level using a bottom-up, event-driven, data center energy model." The finding's own caveat (5) concedes this. EPRI's 62-80% peak/nameplate and 75%/57% load factors are genuine measurements. But the finding MISATTRIBUTES their cause. The dominant, boring drivers of a facility peaking below nameplate are: N+1/2N electrical redundancy and UPS/transformer derating designed in at build; phased rack fill (EPRI's own model assumes only 20% of nominal is active in year 1, ramping 20%/yr — that alone explains most of the colocation 57%); reserved headroom for future density; and cooling sized for worst-case ambient. None of these is HBM bandwidth. EPRI's 57% colo figure is largely vacancy and ramp. Attributing a design-margin-plus-ramp gap to memory-bound decode is a causal claim the data does not support, and it is the only part of the finding that is novel.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The valuable half is published; the novel half is the broken half.

- EPRI 62-80% peak/nameplate and the "nameplate = what the data center requests for service interconnection" definition are in the EPRI report itself, cited by the finding. Public since Feb 2026.
- The commercial phantom-demand haircut is saturated coverage: ERCOT's 474 GW interconnection queue, the Sept 2026 Texas audit, Wood Mackenzie's ~28% commitment rate, Goldman's 50-60% on-time assumption, GLJ's Sell. The finding concedes this.
- THE MECHANISM BREAKER IS ALSO ALREADY PUBLISHED, which the finding does not acknowledge. Corpus chunk 223039 (commentary/web): "GE Vernova's Sold-Out Turbine Backlog... The company's order book is not just full; it's sold out for years." Corpus chunk 222765 ("Trend Report — The Gas Turbine Supply Crunch," 2026 edition): global order book measured "against 60-70 GW of annual build capacity," with OEM reservations "expected to be sold out through" a stated year and turbine prices up to ~$600/kW by end-2027. The supply-constrained framing that kills the demand-haircut thesis is consensus trade-press material, not an obscure objection.
- Corpus chunk 38443 (SEC, 2025-10-22) documents the reservation-to-order conversion mechanic the finding's test relies on: 12 GW of new slot reservations signed, 7 GW of existing reservations converted to orders, 4 GW shipped in a single quarter.

What I could NOT find published is the specific causal link (memory-bound decode -> facility nameplate gap -> GEV GW). I also could not search as thoroughly as I wanted — the session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could run the targeted novelty searches, so my novelty read rests on WebFetch and the corpus. That is a real limitation the team should know about. But the unpublished part is unpublished because it is wrong, not because nobody looked.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: GEV IS SUPPLY-CONSTRAINED, NOT DEMAND-CONSTRAINED, SO A DEMAND HAIRCUT DOES NOT REACH ANY REVENUE LINE ON ANY RELEVANT HORIZON.

116 GW is under contract against a 20 GW/yr output target rising to 30 GW/yr in 2030 — roughly 5 years of oversubscription, and the constraint is industry-wide (corpus 222765: global order book vs 60-70 GW/yr of build capacity). The finding computes a 3.0 GW/yr surplus and treats it as 3.0 GW/yr of lost shipments. It is not. When a queue is oversubscribed ~5:1, removing 3 GW/yr of demand removes 3 GW from the BACK of the queue, and the factory ships exactly the same 20-30 GW. For the 2030 vintage to be at risk you need cancellations that exceed the entire queue depth, not a 25% trim. Slot reservations are also resold; chunk 38443 shows GEV signing 12 GW of new reservations in the same quarter it converted 7 GW.

Four further independent breaks, any one of which is sufficient:

(a) HORIZON MISMATCH. The entire materiality is computed on the 2030 30 GW/yr target. The pitch horizon is 3-12 months. Nothing in the chain produces a P&L or guidance change before 2028 at the earliest, and the finding then applies a 25x multiple to a 2030 EBITDA delta as if it were a current-year run-rate. Discounting four years at ~10% alone removes ~32% of the headline.

(b) REVENUE RECOGNITION BLOCKS IT. GEV recognizes equipment revenue over time on costs incurred against signed contracts. Units already in the factory convert to revenue regardless of whether the end customer's load forecast was 25% too high.

(c) WRONG COUNTERPARTY. Utilities and IPPs — not hyperscalers — buy the turbines, and they procure to IRP planning reserve margin against coal and nuclear retirements. If a data-center forecast proves 25% high, the utility still holds the capacity and still needed reserve margin. The finding lists this as caveat (4); it is not a caveat, it is the base case for ~80% of the book that corpus 217417 says is utility/IPP.

(d) THE TWO HAIRCUTS DOUBLE-COUNT — the finding's central claim of independence is backwards. The published phantom-demand ratios (Wood Mackenzie ~28%, Goldman 50-60%) are expressed as committed or delivered capacity divided by REQUESTED interconnection capacity. EPRI's own definition, quoted approvingly by the finding, is that nameplate IS the requested interconnection number. Both haircuts therefore have the same denominator. Multiplying 0.28 by 0.75 discounts the identical nameplate inflation twice. The claim that they "stack without double-counting" is the thesis's structural error, and it is stated as the reason the finding is novel.

(e) THE SERVICES LEG POINTS THE WRONG WAY. GEV bills on FACTORED fired hours and on starts, and GER-3620 factoring penalizes fast starts, trips, peak firing and cycling; intervals are 25,000 factored hours OR 900/720 starts, whichever comes FIRST. Spreading the same MWh across more installed GW lowers capacity factor per unit, which means more cycling and more starts per unit — which can pull the starts-based maintenance trigger forward in calendar time. Oversizing does not cleanly reduce services billing per GW. This is consistent with the observed US fleet already sitting at ~53% CC capacity factor with ~60% of new build being ~10%-CF peakers, and GEV still reporting "solid pricing" in services.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. Do not pitch this. Score it 1/5 and reuse only the corpus work.

The finding is built as: novel physics (memory-bound decode caps GPU power) -> causes measured facility gap -> causes GEV oversells gas. Leg 1 fails on roofline. Legs 2 and 3 fail independently.

PHYSICS. Both arXiv papers are real — I verified 2605.11999 (Ma et al., 12 May 2026) and 2604.07345 (Vercellino et al., 8 Apr 2026) exist with the stated authors. But the 137-300 W decode figure comes from a batch-size sweep that stops at 32. The paper's defense — "arithmetic intensity does not change with batch size; the memory-boundedness is structural" — is wrong for decode's dominant term. Weights are read once per step and amortize across the batch, so intensity is approximately B FLOP/byte, and H200's machine balance (~989 TFLOP/s / ~4.8 TB/s ≈ 206 FLOP/byte) puts the compute-bound crossover near B≈200. Production decode pools run there; that is what continuous batching is for. At B≤32 you are at ~16% of the knee and structurally cannot see it. Separately, the device-level ratio is smuggled in as a node-level ratio: Vercellino's own measured nodes sustain 2.8-2.9 kW against 3.52 kW rated, i.e. 80-82%, not 20-43%. And the facility gap the finding wants to explain is far better explained by N+1/2N redundancy, UPS derating and phased rack fill — EPRI's own model assumes 20% active in year 1 ramping 20%/yr, which by itself accounts for most of the 57% colocation load factor. The novel causal claim is a misattribution of a design-margin-plus-vacancy gap to HBM bandwidth.

MECHANISM. Even granting the physics, nothing reaches a GEV line. GEV has ~116 GW under contract against 20-30 GW/yr of output — roughly five years oversubscribed, industry-wide (corpus 222765: global book vs 60-70 GW/yr build capacity). Trimming 3 GW/yr of demand trims the back of a five-year queue and changes shipments by zero. Equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred against already-signed contracts. The buyers are utilities procuring to IRP reserve margin against coal retirements, not hyperscalers. The services leg may point the opposite way, because factored-hour billing is triggered by starts as well as hours and lower capacity factors mean more cycling.

THE FATAL LOGICAL ERROR. The finding's entire claim to novelty is that the physical haircut STACKS on the published phantom-demand haircut without double-counting. It double-counts. Wood Mackenzie's ~28% and Goldman's 50-60% are ratios to REQUESTED interconnection capacity, and EPRI's nameplate — quoted by the finding itself — is defined as the requested interconnection number. Same denominator, same inflation, discounted twice.

MATERIALITY. $42.15/share is not defensible: it applies 25x to a 2030 EBITDA delta with no discounting on a 3-12 month pitch horizon, and it rests on a 40% data-center-attribution assumption the finding admits is unsourced. The sourced-only version (20% DC share) yields $10.5/share, at the task's own cutoff before any of the above is applied.

WHAT TO SALVAGE. (1) The corpus capacity-factor work is solid and reproduces the known -3.2% 2025 CC decline exactly (1552.9 -> 1503.5 TWh) — that validates the EIA tables for any other angle. (2) The GER-3620 factored-hours-and-starts billing mechanic is genuinely underused and is the right lens, but it argues for a LONG on services in a cycling-heavy peaker build, not a short. (3) The supply-constrained backlog is the real story and it is already consensus. PROCESS NOTE: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could run targeted novelty searches, so the novelty assessment rests on WebFetch of the two papers plus corpus evidence. The refutation does not depend on those searches — it rests on the roofline derivation and the shared-denominator double-count, both of which are checkable from first principles.

No published model carries that. You cannot de-rate a stock for missing an expectation nobody holds. Even my $27/share is arguably generous on the same logic.

Nothing else in the chain moves the answer materially — at a common GW base the two models agree to within 4%. The runner-up assumption is the joint capture factor P(SST path wins) x GEV share-within-served-accounts = 0.50 x 0.30 = 0.15, which sets how much of the +$450M/GW narrative content GEV actually gets.
- **sensitivity**: On the GW base (holding $315M/GW shortfall, 18.4% margin, 25x):

  5 GW/yr (base): $1.57B, $290M, $27.2/share = 2.9%; discounted $18.6/share = 2.0%.
  10 GW/yr (doubled): $3.15B, $580M, $54.4/share = 5.8%; discounted $37.2/share = 4.0%.
  20 GW/yr (the original's): $6.30B, $1,159M, $108.8/share = 11.6%; discounted $74.3/share = 7.9%.
So the answer spans $9 to $109 per share purely on this one input, and the original sits at the extreme upper end of that range on a number derived circularly.

On the capture factor (holding 5 GW/yr): if GEV captures 0.30 of the incremental content instead of 0.15 (i.e. the SST path is a coin flip but GEV wins 60% inside its own accounts), the shortfall falls to $315M -> $135M... more precisely realistic content rises to $270M/GW, shortfall $180M/GW, giving $15.5/share undiscounted, $10.6 discounted. If GEV captures nothing (0.0), shortfall is the full $450M/GW, giving $38.9/share undiscounted, $26.6 discounted.

Net of the transformer offset, the practical range is roughly $6-25/share in the plausible middle of both distributions.

## [Verify] skeptic:partload_cycling_thermo:GE added a load-step maintenance

- **physics_sound**: True
- **physics_errors**: The core physics is CORRECT and I reproduced it independently, digit-for-digit. From the GER-3620 Rev P text (local extract, scratchpad ger3620p.txt, lines 2876-2930 and 3430-3465) I confirmed the Figure 42 formula verbatim, the trigger definition ("more than +/- 20% of GT rated load change in 10 seconds or less"), and aL = Exp(0.0137 x %Load Step). Recomputing GE's own Appendix A.3 table from the raw exponential reproduces every row (20%: mine 1.89 vs GE 1.90; 50%: 2.95 vs 3.0; 95%: 2.67 vs 2.7) and totals 25.4 against GE's stated 25.4. Per-event penalties 0.315 / 0.984 / 1.61 / 2.67 at 20/50/70/95% are all correct. I also verified the interval framing the finding used implicitly, which is not obvious and which I initially thought was wrong: since Interval(actual starts) = S/MF and MF = FS/AS, the AS terms cancel and years-to-starts-HGPI = S / (annual factored starts). So "2.3 events/day at 0.85 FS/event exhausts a 720-start budget in ~1 year" is arithmetically valid. Two real errors survive.

ERROR 1 - amplitude transfer (inflates ~2x). The 0.846 factored-starts-per-event average is derived from GE's ARC-FURNACE amplitude distribution, which includes single events at +/-85%, +/-90% and +/-95%. Because aL is exponential, that tail dominates the average. An AI-campus step distribution clustered in the 20-35% band gives 0.424 FS/event. The finding imports a steel-mill amplitude histogram into a data-centre application without flagging it.

ERROR 2 - the limiting-criterion check is missing (more serious). GER-3620 states on the same page, "the limiting criterion (hours or starts) determines the maintenance interval." The finding never tests whether starts is limiting. For a baseload BTM machine at ~95% CF (8,328 fired h/yr), the 25,000-FFH hours criterion already sets HGPI at 3.00 years. For the starts criterion to bite at all you need >240 factored starts/yr = 0.74 qualifying events/day at GE's amplitude mix, or 1.47/day at a DC-like mix, EVERY DAY. Below that threshold the load-step term moves the outage date by exactly zero. To actually DOUBLE the HGP event rate - the assumption the whole materiality rests on - you need ~480 factored starts/yr, i.e. ~3.0 qualifying >=20%-in-<=10s steps per day, every day, for 20 years. The finding calls doubling "conservative"; it is in fact a far more demanding requirement than stated, and the finding's own caveats concede no published source gives the event rate. At its own illustrative 2.3 events/day with the corrected amplitude mix you get 1.96 yr vs 3.00 yr - a 35% interval compression, not a doubling.

The adjacent academic work is a genuinely different component and failure mode, as the finding states: arXiv:2605.01173 is generator SHAFT TORSIONAL fatigue, arXiv:2508.14318 is grid-stability power stabilisation - neither mentions GER-3620, factored starts, hot-gas-path intervals or OEM service contracts.

If even a minority of BTM AI campuses end up turbine-only with no BESS buffer, and if those CSAs bill per fired hour rather than per factored start, then GEV has already locked in a cost-severity mispricing across the fastest-growing, highest-multiple part of its book, and nobody - including GEV - can falsify it until the fleet runs. It is also the reason the market cannot price it: there is no dated test. A second, cheaper counterargument: the finding's product-mix caveat is underrated as a standalone. If load-step severity is why BTM AI campuses choose aeroderivatives and reciprocating engines over H-class, that is an addressable-market question for the 7HA franchise, and it is testable in EIA-860M prime-mover codes (GT vs CT vs IC) on data-centre-adjacent plant IDs. That is a better use of the corpus than the CSA-margin chain.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED for this pitch, on the mechanism and the horizon - not on the physics. Score: physics 5/5, mechanism 2/5, materiality 1/5 as written.

(1) PHYSICS HOLDS. I re-derived GE's Appendix A.3 table from the raw exponential and hit 25.4 exactly. The formula, the +/-20%-in-<=10s trigger, the Rev P revision-log provenance, and the scale-free interval identity (years-to-HGPI = S / annual factored starts) all check out. This is real, correctly read, primary-source engineering. Two quantitative errors inflate the effect roughly 2x: the 0.846 FS/event average is GE's arc-furnace amplitude histogram, not a data-centre one (0.424 is more defensible); and the finding never verifies that the STARTS criterion is limiting, when for a baseload BTM machine the 25,000-FFH HOURS criterion already governs at 3.00 years and the load-step term is inert below ~1.5 qualifying events per day, every day.

(2) MECHANISM BREAKS ON AN ACCOUNTING RULE, and this is decisive. Materiality Step 6 - the -$780M cumulative catch-up, the only near-dated item in the whole chain - requires the data-centre cohort to be partially complete under cost-to-cost. GEV's FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-01-29, verified in corpus): "Our contracts (on average) are approximately 29% complete based on costs incurred to date," with the $0.2B-per-percentage-point sensitivity stated against the CONTRACT ASSETS BALANCE, not EBITDA. The 20 GW data-centre cohort is ~0% complete: the corpus projects table shows GE-linked data-centre capacity at COD 2028 (5.34 GW, incl. Chevron/Microsoft Permian) and 106 GW with no stated COD at all. A margin revision on a 0%-complete contract produces no cumulative catch-up. Step 6 goes to ~$0.

(3) THE DATED TEST IS CONFOUNDED. The proposed test - FY26 net unfavorable service-contract revisions exceeding -$450M - measures the EXISTING F-class and early-HA fleet, which has nothing to do with load steps on unbuilt BTM machines. It would be passed or failed by causes entirely unrelated to the hypothesis. The finding has no clean dated test, and the Q3'26 question is a non-answer trap by the analyst's own prediction.

(4) FAILS "SO WHAT" AT $250B. Correcting Step 6 to zero: $13.74 -> $10.81/share (1.15%). Additionally correcting the amplitude mix and the interval compression (35%, not a doubling -> ~12pp margin, not 23pp): $5.73/share, 0.61%. Below the $10/share bar. And even that residual is a 2030s cash flow - the cohort's services revenue today is approximately zero - capitalised at an undiscounted 25x into a 3-12 month pitch, which is a horizon category error.

(5) UNRESOLVED DIRECTION RISK. GEV's 10-K says services billing occurs "upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event within the contract, such as an outage." GER-3620 is GE's OWN published contractual-factoring basis; the document exists so that OEMs can price duty severity. If CSAs denominate the maintenance obligation in factored starts, the load-step penalty passes straight to the customer and the mechanism is identically zero. I could not resolve this from public disclosure, and I rate it MORE likely than the finding implies precisely because GE publishes the formula.

RECOMMENDATION: do not put this in the memo as a 3-12 month short catalyst. The single highest-value follow-up is obtaining MDPI Inventions 2026 11(4) 81, which is the likeliest published source of the missing event rate and of the BESS kill condition, and which no one on this project has been able to read.

## [Verify] skeptic:dc_architecture_800v:The peer-reviewed efficiency lad

- **physics_sound**: False
- **physics_errors**: The CITED NUMBERS all reproduce exactly — I parsed the ETH open-access PDF of Huber, Wallmeier, Pieper, Schafmeister & Kolar, IPEC 2022 (ECCE Asia) myself. Fig. 1 literally reads: eta_Sigma ~= 97.1% (a, 400VAC), 97.8% (b, 690VAC), 97.9% (c, LFT + central PFC to +/-400VDC), 98.2% (d, LFT + 12-pulse + active filter), 97.7% (e, SST); eta_LFT = 99.2%, eta_SST = 98%. The quoted conclusion sentences are verbatim. So the transcription is clean. The INTERPRETATION contains three errors, two of them decisive.

(1) STAGE-COUNTING ERROR — the core physical claim is wrong. The finding says removing the LFT "can only remove one 0.8%-loss stage and substitute a 2.0%-loss active stage." That compares one stage of one path against the whole of the other. In the LFT-based 800VDC path the LFT does NOT stand alone: the paper's own text states that for path (c), "as it can be assumed that doing so neither changes eta_LFT ~= 99.2% nor eta_PFC ~= 99%, the MVAC-LVDC conversion efficiency becomes eta ~= 98.2%." I recomputed: 0.992 x 0.99 = 0.98208. So the LFT path's MVAC->LVDC block is 98.2%, i.e. a 1.8% loss, versus the SST's assumed 2.0% loss. The real gap is 0.2 points, not 0.8-vs-2.0. The SST has to beat 98.2%, not 99.2%. The finding's central physical assertion ("removing it cannot improve the chain") is simply false as stated — it is arithmetic conditional on an assumed eta_SST, not a physical law.

(2) THE 98.2% CHAMPION IS A DIFFERENT PRODUCT, NOT A BETTER VERSION OF THE SAME ONE. The only path that reaches 98.2% eta_Sigma is (d), the 12-pulse rectifier with active filter. The paper's own conclusion flags this in parentheses: "with reduced functionality, i.e., unidirectional power flow and no regulated LVDC voltage." An unregulated, unidirectional bus is not a candidate architecture for a GB300/Kyber AI hall, which needs regulated 800VDC, bidirectional flow for BBU/ride-through, and fast fault isolation. It wins on efficiency precisely because it does less. Using it as the "best LFT-based 800VDC path" against which the SST loses by 0.5 points is an apples-to-oranges comparison. Against the realistic commercial LFT path (c), the SST is behind by 0.2 points — inside the paper's own "~=" rounding.

(3) THE eta_SST = 98% INPUT IS ALREADY OBSOLETE, AND THE PAPER'S OWN REFERENCE LIST SAYS SO. Refs [12] and [13] in this very paper are Rothmund, Guillod, Bortis & Kolar: "99% efficient 10 kV SiC-based 7 kV/400 V DC transformer for future data centers" (IEEE JESTPE 7(2), 2019) and "99.1% efficient 10 kV SiC-based medium-voltage ZVS bidirectional..." The paper also reports ETH's own 25 kW 10kV-SiC MVAC demonstrator at eta ~= 98.1% and NC State's 350 kW 12.47 kV charger at eta ~= 98.1%. Plugging eta_SST = 99.0% into the same chain (97.7 / 98.0 = 0.9969 residual factor) gives eta_Sigma ~= 98.7%, which BEATS the 98.2% "best" LFT path and beats path (c) by 0.8 points. Heron (>98.5% claimed at 4.2 MW), DG Matrix and Amperesand all claim above 98.2%. The efficiency ladder is a 2022 snapshot of industrial demonstrators, not a durable ranking, and the finding's own caveat #1 concedes this while the headline claim does not.

What DOES survive: the paper's non-efficiency objections — protection concepts, robustness against harsh MV-grid transients, complexity (cell count, gate drives), poor scalability to arbitrary MV levels, and the open question of cost parity in volume. Those are engineering/economic arguments, not the efficiency-ladder argument the finding leads with, and they are qualitative in this paper.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: False
- **where_published**: I could not find this specific connection published, and the finding's own novelty search looks honest. But novelty is moot here because the mechanism is broken by the primary source. Note also that my WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before I could run an independent published-elsewhere check, so my "not found" rests on the finding's own searches plus the corpus FTS (469,353 chunks), which does contain the GEV and Eaton statements separately and no chunk joining them. I verified the corpus side myself.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: THE PRIMARY TRANSCRIPT CONTRADICTS THE MECHANISM'S LOAD-BEARING PREMISE. The finding asserts the incremental $300-600M/GW is "overwhelmingly one product (the SST)." I pulled the actual Q2'26 transcript from the corpus (accession src:3161, chunk id 251619) — the finding never did, and flagged this itself as caveat #4. Strazik's actual words, answering Andrew Kaplowitz of Citi:

"that $300 million directional of scope per gigawatt today, if you include the MV-UPS, if you include the SST and some of the other things we're working on, we certainly think entitlement just with the things we're already investing in is two to three times what our scope per gigawatt is today."

Three problems, each independently fatal:

(a) THE BASKET IS NOT THE SST. He names MV-UPS FIRST, the SST second, and "some of the other things" third. In the same answer he says of the MV-UPS "it's possible orders come for that before the SST" and "Potentially, MV-UPS starts to come through the second half of the year." The medium-voltage UPS / "stability block" is ride-through and grid-stability apparatus. It is required under EITHER architecture — the LFT+centralized-PFC path in the Kolar paper still needs MV-side energy storage and fault ride-through, arguably more so because the LFT gives you no active regulation. So the single largest and nearest-dated leg of the 2-3x is architecture-INDEPENDENT. Killing the SST does not kill it. The finding's entire materiality chain assumes the opposite.

(b) "ENTITLEMENT" IS NOT REVENUE, AND IT IS NOT IN THE PRINT. Kaplowitz's question uses the word "entitlement" and so does Strazik, twice. Entitlement is addressable scope per GW — what GEV could sell if it won everything — not a guide, not a plan, not a booking. Strazik explicitly says "none of that is in the $5 billion" of H1'26 data-center orders. There is no disclosed FY26-FY28 revenue, EBITDA or RPO line that contains this. So the 25x capitalization is a category error: you cannot de-rate a number that was never capitalized. The finding's Step 9 produces $112.64/share of "shortfall" without ever demonstrating that consensus, or the $940 price, contains a single dollar of SST revenue. To make this a wedge you would have to show sell-side models with an explicit 2029-2031 SST line — the finding does not, and I found none in the corpus.

(c) EVEN IN THE LFT WORLD, GEV SELLS THE LFT. Path (c) — the realistic commercial 800VDC architecture at 97.9% — consists of an LFT plus a centralized MV/LV PFC rectifier. GEV owns Prolec GE (transformers) and Power Conversion & Storage ($2,049M FY25 revenue, with HVDC, STATCOM and wind-converter platforms — i.e. exactly centralized high-power rectifier competence). The finding concedes this in its own "separately POSITIVE" clause and in caveat #7, then builds a short on the negative leg anyway. The architecture fork reallocates content between GEV product lines; it does not obviously remove GEV content per GW. The finding's own evidence is two-sided and it scored only one side.

Secondary problems worth noting: the $1.25M/MW SST content and the flat $3.6-4.8M/MW total band — the two numbers that convert "GEV misses" into a dollar figure — come from a partly paywalled SemiAnalysis piece read as a fetched summary, which the finding itself names as the first thing to re-verify. The most load-bearing external number in a $112/share claim is unverified. And the 20 GW/yr base is circular: it is GEV's H1 order dollars divided by GEV's own $300M/GW figure, two numbers that are probably not on the same scope (utility-side grid work serving data-center load counts in orders but is not "per GW of data center built").
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED. The citations are clean but the argument is not.

PHYSICS: I reproduced every number from the ETH open-access PDF — 97.1 / 97.8 / 97.9 / 98.2 / 97.7, eta_LFT 99.2%, eta_SST 98%, and the two quoted conclusion sentences are verbatim. The transcription is honest. The reasoning built on it is not. (i) The finding compares the LFT's 0.8% loss against the SST's 2.0% loss, but the LFT path also carries a 99% PFC rectifier; the paper itself computes the pair at 98.2% (I recomputed: 0.992 x 0.99 = 98.208%). The real gap versus the assumed SST is 0.2 points, not the 0.8-vs-2.0 asymmetry the "physical_fact" field implies. (ii) The 98.2% winner is the 12-pulse + active-filter path, which the paper's own conclusion labels "reduced functionality, i.e., unidirectional power flow and no regulated LVDC voltage" — not a deployable AI-hall architecture, so ranking the SST 0.5 points below it is apples-to-oranges. (iii) eta_SST = 98% is a 2022 industrial-demonstrator figure; refs [12] and [13] OF THIS SAME PAPER are Kolar's own group at 99% and 99.1% MVDC-LVDC, which plugged into the same chain gives 98.7% and beats every LFT path. The "efficiency ladder" is a snapshot, not a law.

MECHANISM: this is where it dies. I pulled the primary Q2'26 transcript (corpus accession src:3161, chunk 251619) — the finding relied on news coverage and flagged that gap itself. Strazik's actual sentence makes the 2-3x a basket of "the MV-UPS... the SST and some of the other things we're working on," with MV-UPS named first and expected to order FIRST, possibly in H2'26. The MV-UPS is architecture-independent: the LFT-based 800VDC path needs MV ride-through and stability apparatus just as much, if not more. So the largest, nearest leg of the 2-3x survives an SST loss untouched, and the finding's premise that the increment is "overwhelmingly one product" is contradicted by the source it cites.

MATERIALITY: fails the $250B "so what" test on a category error. Strazik says "entitlement," twice, and says "none of that is in the $5 billion." Entitlement is addressable scope, not guidance, not backlog, not consensus. The $112.64/share is computed by capitalizing at 25x a revenue stream that has never been shown to sit in anyone's model or in the $940 price. Removing something the market never added is worth zero. Compounding this, the two numbers that turn "GEV misses" into dollars ($1.25M/MW SST content; flat $3.6-4.8M/MW total band) come from a paywalled newsletter read via a fetched summary, and the 20 GW/yr base is circular — GEV's own order dollars divided by GEV's own $300M/GW.

WHAT TO SALVAGE — there are two genuinely useful residues, and the team should take them:
1. The paper's NON-efficiency objections are the durable part and the finding buries them: protection concepts, robustness to MV-grid transients, cell/gate-drive complexity, poor scalability across MV levels, and "whether SST-based solutions can achieve cost-parity with LFT-based solutions even in the far future (volume production) is therefore in question." That is a 2022 peer-reviewed statement of cost-parity doubt from a Delta Energy Systems co-authored paper, and it is a fair citation against any SST-TAM narrative — GEV's or Eaton's.
2. The transcript quote is a clean, verifiable, under-40-word primary citation the team does not currently have, and it cuts BOTH ways. It shows management framing the 2-3x as entitlement with no orders attached and nothing in the $5B — useful for a "narrative not in the numbers" point — while also showing the nearest-dated leg (MV-UPS, possible H2'26 orders) is not SST-dependent, which is a long-side datapoint. Exact location: chunk id 251619, accession src:3161.

The dated test (zero firm SST orders at the Oct 28 call) is well-constructed but near-vacuous: Strazik already told the market "'27 is as early as orders will come," so the prediction confirms management's own guidance and moves nothing. Do not build a short leg on this. Scored: novelty 3 (the join is probably unpublished), physics 1 (numbers right, inference wrong), mechanism 1 (contradicted by primary source), materiality 1 (capitalizes an uncapitalized number).

## [Verify] quant:dc_architecture_800v:'Silicon in, copper out' quantif

- **independent_dollars_per_share**: REBUILT FROM SCRATCH. I rejected the original's revenue base and built from GEV's actual disclosed segment figures.

STEP 1 — PHYSICAL FACT (verified, I read the PDF myself).
Huber & Kolar, IEEE ECCE USA 2014, Table IV "Specific Ressource Usage," p.7. Columns SST MV / SST LV / AC-AC SST / LFT(est.):
  kg Cu/kVA: 0.15 / 0.32 / 0.47 / 0.6
  kg Fe/kVA: 0.32 / 0.63 / 0.95 / 1.2
  mm^2 Si/kVA: 85 / 22 / 107 / 0
MVAC->LVDC (the 800VDC data-center case) uses the MV converter only: 0.15/0.6 = -75% Cu, 0.32/1.2 = -73% Fe. Original's physics is correct as stated.
MY CORRECTION: Table IV charges the LFT column nothing for the rectifier stage the AC/DC case requires, though the paper's own loss comparison (Fig.12c) is explicitly "LFT + rectifier" vs SST. A 1 MVA rectifier carries its own filter inductors and DC-link copper. The honest SYSTEM-level saving is therefore below 75%/73% — I cannot bound it from this paper, so I carry 70% central and flag it. Does not change the conclusion.

STEP 2 — WHICH GEV LINE IS PHYSICALLY EXPOSED (my main departure).
An SST replaces the MV->LV step-down distribution transformer in the data-center white space (~2.5-3 MVA, 13.8/34.5 kV to 415/480 V). It does NOT replace: the utility-side HV->MV substation power transformer (115-230 kV, 50-250 MVA) where the 18-24 month lead times and the scarcity rent actually live; the GSU at the on-site gas plant; switchgear, breakers, protection, HVDC, or grid software. The original asked "what share of data-center content is transformers." The correct, narrower question is "what share is MV/LV DISTRIBUTION transformers" — the commodity end of the range, not the scarce end.

STEP 3 — REVENUE BASE (from data/financials/gev_segments.csv, verified, not from the $300M/GW figure).
  Electrification product (equipment) revenue: Q1'26 $2,488M + Q2'26 $3,109M = $5,597M H1 -> ~$11.2B annualized.
  (a) Transformer share of that equipment line: Prolec GE is a transformer pure-play (~$2.5B standalone) plus legacy Grid Solutions power transformers -> call it ~$4.0B/yr, 36% of equipment revenue. ASSUMPTION, not disclosed.
  (b) Data-center share of transformer revenue: GEV reported H1'26 Electrification data-center orders >$5B against a ~$45B backlog; ~20% of the gas order book is data-center per Koziner. Use 25%. -> ~$1.0B/yr.
  (c) Share of THAT which is the displaceable MV/LV white-space unit rather than the utility-side substation: 30% central (range 15-50%). ASSUMPTION — weakest link, but at least it is the right question.
  Displaceable revenue at 100% substitution = $4.0B x 25% x 30% = $300M/yr.

STEP 4 — EBITDA DELTA.
Margin 18.2% (verified: Electrification H1'26 EBIT $1,199M / revenue $6,596M). I do NOT use the original's 22%: the displaceable unit is the commodity MV/LV transformer, not the scarce large-power unit, so if anything it is a below-segment-average margin line.
$300M x 18% = $54M/yr EBIT.

STEP 5 — CAPITALIZE AND PER SHARE.
$54M x 25 = $1,350M / 266,333,581 shares = $5.07/share = 0.54% of $940.33.
THAT IS THE FULL-SUBSTITUTION, 100%-PENETRATION, PERMANENT-LOSS CASE. It fails the $10/share bar before any penetration haircut is applied.

STEP 6 — HORIZON-ADJUSTED (3-12 months).
Corroborated in-corpus (kind='competitor'): field-deployed commercial-class SSTs in revenue service globally are "measured in single digits" of UNITS as of May 2026. Penetration of the 2026-27 data-center transformer build is well under 0.5%.
0.5% x $5.07 = $0.03/share. At an aggressive 5% by end-2028: $0.25/share.

CONCLUSION: worth about five dollars a share in the theoretical maximum and about three cents a share on the actual horizon. Blunt version: this is not worth a slide.
- **agrees_with_original**: True
- **where_it_differs**: I agree with the DIRECTION and the CONCLUSION (the short leg dies), but the original's full-substitution figure is roughly 6x too generous, and that error cuts against the original's own argument — it makes the short leg look more dangerous than it is.

1. REVENUE BASE — the substantive disagreement. The original took GEV's "$300M/GW of grid-connection equipment" and multiplied by 20 GW/yr of GAS TURBINE output. That conflates two businesses: the $300M/GW is grid-connection content attached to gas plants, and multiplying it by turbine shipments implicitly assumes every GW of GEV gas turbine shipped carries $75M of SST-displaceable data-center transformer. It does not. I could not verify the $300M/GW figure in the corpus at all. I rebuilt from the actual Electrification equipment run-rate ($11.2B annualized, verified) and got $300M/yr at risk versus the original's $1.5B/yr.

2. WHICH TRANSFORMER. The original's "25% of content is the LV/MV transformer layer" lumps all transformers together. An SST only touches the MV->LV white-space unit; the utility-side HV->MV substation transformer, the GSU, and all switchgear survive 800VDC untouched. The original's own caveat 2 gestures at this but does not act on it. Pushing the question one level deeper is most of the 6x gap.

3. MARGIN. Original used 22% on the reasoning that transformers are the higher-margin part of Electrification. Verified segment margin is 18.2% (H1'26 EBIT $1,199M / rev $6,596M), and the specific displaceable product is the commodity end of the transformer range. I used 18%. Minor — worth ~$0.5/share.

4. PHYSICS PRECISION. The -75%/-73% is a per-transformer number, not per-system: Table IV gives the LFT column no rectifier BOM even though the AC/DC comparison requires one. The original states it as if it were system-level.

5. SOURCE DETAIL. Prolec-tagged Q1'26 capex is $938M (SegmentExpenditureAdditionToLongLivedAssets, BusinessAcquisitionAxis=ProlecGE), not the ~$1.03B the original cites — $1,033M is TOTAL Electrification additions that quarter.

6. NOVELTY CLAIM. The original says the corpus has "essentially nothing" on SSTs. It actually contains a competitor-tier file on Hitachi Energy's $1.5B Vaasa SST capacity expansion and a commentary piece flagging an "SST Industry Reality Check" correction. The penetration evidence is IN the corpus — which strengthens the finding but weakens the claim that nobody is looking at this.

Net: the original's "$31/share of avoided error" is really about $5/share of avoided error.
- **key_assumption_that_drives_it**: The share of GEV's data-center transformer revenue that is the MV->LV white-space distribution transformer an SST can physically replace, as opposed to the utility-side HV->MV substation power transformer, GSU, and switchgear that an 800VDC architecture leaves entirely intact. I use 30%; it is not disclosed anywhere and I cannot verify it.

This single factor is the whole finding. Everything upstream of it (the -75% Cu / -73% Fe physics) is verified from the primary paper and is not in dispute. Everything downstream (18.2% margin, 25x, 266.3M shares) is either verified or a stated convention. The chain's entire uncertainty sits on this one unverifiable split — exactly as the original's caveat 2 conceded, except the original applied it at the wrong level of the hierarchy.

Second-order but worth naming: the ~$4.0B/yr transformer revenue base itself is my construction from Prolec's standalone scale plus legacy Grid Solutions, not a disclosed sub-segment line. GEV does not report transformers separately. If the team wants to tighten this, bounding Prolec's product mix by MVA class from its pre-acquisition filings is the highest-value hour they could spend on it — and they should spend that hour only if they have already decided this angle is worth pursuing, which on my numbers it is not.
- **sensitivity**: Sensitivity on the key assumption (MV/LV displaceable share, central 30%), holding the full-substitution case:

HALVED to 15%: $4.0B x 25% x 15% = $150M revenue -> x18% = $27M EBIT -> x25 = $675M / 266,333,581 = $2.53/share = 0.27% of $940.33.
CENTRAL 30%: $300M revenue -> $54M EBIT -> $1,350M -> $5.07/share = 0.54%.
DOUBLED to 60%: $600M revenue -> $108M EBIT -> $2,700M -> $10.14/share = 1.08%.

The range across a 4x swing in the governing assumption is $2.53 to $10.14/share. Doubling to 60% is frankly implausible — it would require the majority of GEV's data-center transformer dollars to sit in white-space MV/LV units rather than the utility-side substation, which contradicts how hyperscale campus electrical BOMs are actually weighted — and even that implausible upper bound only just touches the $10 bar, in the theoretical 100%-substitution case.

Secondary sensitivity, margin: at 22% (the original's figure) instead of 18%, the central case becomes $6.20/share rather than $5.07. Immaterial to the verdict.

Secondary sensitivity, multiple: at 35x (a growth-name multiple closer to GEV's 35x forward P/E) instead of 25x, the central case becomes $7.10/share. Still under the bar. I kept 25x per the brief's default because a displaced commodity product line does not deserve the multiple the market pays for the services annuity.

Horizon overlay, which dominates everything above: at the corpus-verified <0.5% penetration through FY2027, the central case is $0.03/share. You would need roughly 200% of the central full-substitution case to matter, which is arithmetically impossible.
- **materiality_verdict**: immaterial

## [Verify] skeptic:partload_cycling_thermo:KILL: part-load operation of an

- **physics_sound**: True
- **physics_errors**: Substantially sound in structure, with four real defects — none of which flips the sign, but two of which I could not close.

(1) UNREPRODUCED CITATIONS. I could not independently retrieve GER-3620 Rev P. The gevernova.com technical-document page for "GER-3620-P Heavy-duty gas turbine operating and maintenance considerations" resolves only to a landing page with a download link; the PDF body was not fetchable in this session and the corpus (469k chunks) contains no GER-3620 text (FTS on '"factored" "fired hours"' returns only GEV marketing copy). So every page/figure quote in the finding is unverified by me. That is not evidence against it — the quoted text is idiomatic GE O&M language and internally consistent — but the team must not present figure-and-page citations that only one analyst has ever opened.

(2) NON-BINDING-CLOCK SELECTION (the real methodological error). GER-3620 intervals are explicitly "whichever comes first" — hours OR starts. Demonstrating Ap = 1.0 on the hours clock proves nothing unless the hours clock is the binding one. The finding never establishes which clock binds. I checked this and, for once, the answer favors the finding: GE's own HA intervals imply a break-even run length of 25,000/900 = 27.8 fired hours per start (combustion/HGP, gas) and 50,000/1,800 = 27.8 (major). The HA fleet actually runs 3.0M fired hours / 20,400 fired starts = 147 h/start — 5.3x above break-even. A single early 7HA.02 reported at its spring-2024 major inspection (corpus chunk src:3082, Combined Cycle Journal-type user-group coverage) had "over 48K hours and 162 starts" = 296 h/start, consuming 96% of the 50,000-hour major budget against only 9% of the 1,800-start budget. So the installed HA base is decisively hours-limited and the part-load band genuinely is free. The finding got the right answer without doing this check.

(3) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE TWO HALVES. The hours argument describes a combined-cycle unit turned down to 80% via IGV closure. The starts argument (maintenance factor 0.5) applies only to cycles whose MAXIMUM load is below 60% — GER-3620's factored-starts calculation is keyed to peak load achieved. A CCGT that daily starts and loads to 80-100% gets factor 1.0 and no relief whatsoever. The two claims cannot describe the same machine, yet the finding presents them as a combined "part-load cycling is free-to-negative" result. Only the first half is relevant to the grid-shaping thesis the finding is trying to kill.

(4) UNRESOLVED CONSTANT. The finding admits it could not decode Figure 10 (hours-based peak-fire severity). The conventional GER-3620 pairing is an hours-based exponent roughly double the starts-based one (exp(0.018 x dTf) vs exp(0.009 x dTf)); I could verify neither. So the one quantitative severity curve that actually could hurt an over-fired data-center-adjacent unit remains unread, in a finding whose whole claim is "here is the exhaustive list of what carries a factor."

(5) F-CLASS NUMBERS ON AN HA QUESTION. Figure 21's rotor factors (rapid/forced cooling 4.0, peaking-fast hot-1 4.0 vs 2.0) are explicitly F/FA/FB. Rev P defers HA to unit-specific documentation. The finding flags this, then uses the numbers anyway.

Independent structural corroboration I did obtain: Fehr et al., "Optimal Economic Gas Turbine Dispatch with Deep Reinforcement Learning," arXiv:2308.14924 (IFAC World Congress 2023), models GT O&M as a whichever-comes-first hours-or-cycles clock with Lh = 200,000 h and Lc = 26,000 cycles, i.e. a break-even average cycle length of 8 hours, and carries NO part-load severity term at all. An independent peer-reviewed model of the same physics also treats load level as cost-neutral and starts as the only other driver.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The physics is GE's own published document (GER-3620 Rev P, public on gevernova.com) — the finding concedes this. The hours-or-starts whichever-first cost structure with no part-load penalty is independently published in the peer-reviewed control literature: Fehr et al., arXiv:2308.14924, IFAC 2023, Table 1 (Lh 200,000 h / Lc 26,000 cycles, break-even 8 h/cycle). Unit-level factored-hours-and-starts data for HA machines is also reported openly in gas-turbine trade press — the corpus holds a user-group account of a 7HA.02 at "over 48K hours and 162 starts" at its 2024 major inspection (chunk accession src:3082), which is exactly the FFH/FS bookkeeping the finding claims "nobody outside plant O&M reads."

I could NOT run confirmatory sell-side searches: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could query. So I cannot certify the narrower claim that no investor-facing note has made the part-load-is-free point; the finding's own novelty_check is the only evidence on that, and it is unaudited. Treat "no investor has published this" as unverified.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The mechanism chain breaks on a definitional confusion that the finding never resolves: for a contract billed per FIRED HOUR, "lower load" and "fewer hours" are completely different events, and the finding treats them as one.

GEV's 10-K says service billing is "based on the customers' utilization of the equipment (e.g., per hour of usage) and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event." A CCGT dispatched at 80% instead of 100% for the same number of hours produces: zero change in factored hours, zero change in billed hours, zero change in outage timing — the finding is right, and the effect is not "bounded downside," it is literally nothing. But a CCGT that instead runs FEWER hours produces less billed revenue at unchanged parts cost per outage. The bearish grid-shaping story has always run through hours, not load. US combined-cycle generation falling 3.2% in 2025 is an MWh statement that could be either — and the finding cites it as if it were a load-factor statement, then declares the load-factor version dead and stops. It never touches the hours version, which is the one that reaches a GEV line.

That omission matters more than the finding does, because it sits on the wrong side of the ledger. The finding names "Power segment — CSA estimated profitability" (a cost line). The per-fired-hour billing structure means the first-order exposure is the REVENUE line: management's own ~$25M/GW-yr versus today's realized ~$15M/GW-yr is, mechanically, largely a fired-hours-per-GW gap. A finding that proves "lower load costs GEV nothing" says nothing about whether the hours that drive the annuity show up, which is the question a 35x forward multiple is actually paying for.

Second, the finding's defensive value is overstated on its own terms. The hypothetical bear case it claims to demolish is arithmetically incoherent: "5 x $200M = $1.0B one-time, plus 5% x $4.25B/yr x 25 = $5.3B" double-counts a cumulative-catch-up adjustment against a capitalized perpetuity of the same margin change, and the $200M term is never defined. You cannot credit a finding with protecting $23.66/share of an argument that would not have survived its own spreadsheet.

Third, the one live exposure the finding concedes in its caveats — that emissions-compliant minimum load (DLN 2.6e turndown to ~30%; a FlameSheet retrofit demonstrated 26% on a 7F) forces shutdowns below minimum environmental load, and every shutdown-restart IS a factored start — is the entire real mechanism, disposed of in a parenthesis. On the numbers I ran it is currently far from binding (fleet at 147 h/start versus a 27.8 h/start break-even; the sampled 7HA.02 had used 9% of its starts budget against 96% of its hours budget), which is a genuinely useful result — but it is a result about the STARTS clock, arrived at by me, not the finding, and it is the only version of this analysis with any path to a dollar figure.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED AS A WEDGE; KEEP AS AN INTERNAL SCREEN. The physics holds up and I found independent structural support for it, but the finding fails three of the four wedge criteria on its own admission and the fourth on inspection.

Criterion 1 (quantified physical fact): PASS in form. Ap = 1.0 to base load, 0.5 factor for sub-60% starts, trip 8:1/10:1, non-premix 10x. Unverified by me — the GER-3620 PDF was not retrievable this session and the corpus does not contain it.

Criterion 2 (mechanism reaching a named line): FAIL. It names CSA estimated profitability, a cost line, but the demonstrated effect on that line is exactly zero, and the per-fired-hour billing term means the exposure that does exist sits on the revenue line, which the finding never addresses. It conflates lower load with fewer hours throughout.

Criterion 3 (materiality in $/share): FAIL, self-declared at $0.00/share. The $23.66/share "credibility protected" is not a valuation quantity and its supporting arithmetic double-counts a catch-up against a perpetuity. Below the $10/share bar by construction.

Criterion 4 (dated test with kill condition): FAIL, self-declared has_dated_test = false. The stated kill condition depends on non-public HA unit-specific documentation, so it is not falsifiable by the team before Oct 2.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH KEEPING. Two things, neither of them the headline.

First, as a debate screen: any part-load-degradation claim in the memo must cite a named GER-3620 factor or be struck. That is cheap insurance and costs nothing.

Second — and this is the part the finding stumbled past — the right question is not load level but average fired hours per start, because GE's intervals are whichever-comes-first. GE's own published HA intervals set the break-even at 27.8 fired hours per start (25,000/900 and 50,000/1,800 both). The HA fleet runs 3.0M FH / 20,400 FS = 147 h/start, 5.3x above break-even, and a specific early 7HA.02 reported at its 2024 major inspection had 48,000 h against 162 starts = 296 h/start, having burned 96% of its hours budget and 9% of its starts budget. The installed base is emphatically hours-limited with enormous starts headroom. That single ratio is more defensible, more quantitative, and more useful than the entire part-load argument — it bounds BOTH the bull and bear cycling cases at once, and it is derived from numbers the team already has. If any version of this lens goes into the memo, it should be that one, and it should be built forward into fired-hours-per-GW (the $15M vs $25M/GW-yr gap), which is where a dollar figure actually lives.

Score it: novelty 2 (GE's own algebra, structure independently published in IFAC 2023), confidence 3 (physics likely right, citations unreproduced), materiality 1 (zero by construction). Do not put this in front of a judge as a finding.

## [Verify] skeptic:dc_architecture_800v:'Silicon in, copper out' quantif

- **physics_sound**: True
- **physics_errors**: Table IV VERIFIED EXACTLY against the primary PDF (Huber & Kolar, ECCE USA 2014, "Volume/Weight/Cost Comparison of a 1 MVA 10 kV/400 V Solid-State against a Conventional Low-Frequency Distribution Transformer"), downloaded from ams-publications.ee.ethz.ch and text-extracted. Verbatim: "kg Cu/kVA 0.15 0.32 0.47 0.6 | kg Fe/kVA 0.32 0.63 0.95 1.2 | mm2 Si/kVA 85 22 107 0" for columns SST MV / SST LV / AC-AC SST / LFT (est.). The AC/DC quote is also verbatim ("only one third of the LFT-based solution's volume... only about half the losses"). So the transcription is clean. Three interpretation errors, two of which cut AGAINST the finding's own headline:

(1) NON-LIKE-FOR-LIKE BASELINE. The -75% Cu / -73% Fe headline divides the SST MV stage alone (0.15/0.32) by the COMPLETE LFT (0.6/1.2). That is not the comparison the paper defines. Section V-B-2 states for the pure AC/DC case: "the SST solution is reduced to the MV converter part and on the other hand the LFT needs to be extended by two 500 kVA rectifier/inverter units." The correct AC/DC baseline is therefore LFT + LV converter stage = 0.6+0.32 = 0.92 kg Cu/kVA and 1.2+0.63 = 1.83 kg Fe/kVA. Correct reductions are -84% Cu and -83% Fe. The finding UNDERSTATES its own physics. Separately, the authors' own summary sentence is "the specific consumption of active metals in the SST can be reduced by about one fourth compared to the LFT" — that is the AC/AC column (0.47 vs 0.6, -22%), and anyone checking the paper by reading the prose rather than Table IV will get -25%, not -75%. The finding never reconciles the -75% headline with the authors' own "-one fourth" sentence, which is a presentation landmine.

(2) COMMODITY PERCENTAGE MIS-MAPPED TO A REVENUE PERCENTAGE. Neither -75% nor -84% is the number that matters for a transformer OEM. The OEM sells the LFT block only; the 0.15 kg Cu/kVA inside the SST is copper in a medium-frequency transformer that is part of a power-electronics product. If a block goes SST, the LFT sale is displaced 100%, not 75%. Likewise the LFT's 1.2 kg Fe/kVA is grain-oriented electrical steel (the actually-scarce input), whereas the SST's 0.32 kg Fe/kVA is ferrite / nanocrystalline / amorphous medium-frequency core — a different material. GOES destruction per displaced kVA is 100%, not 73%. Table IV's percentages are commodity-demand statements and do not transfer to a revenue line. This error does NOT propagate into the $/share math, because the materiality chain already assumes 100% displacement of the LV/MV layer.

(3) UNIT/DENOMINATOR CONFLATION IN THE DOLLAR CHAIN. The chain multiplies a data-center electrical content figure ($300M/GW, 25% displaceable = $75M/GW) by 20 GW/yr — but 20 GW/yr is GEV's GAS TURBINE output target from Q3'26, not GEV's data-center electrical GW served. Those are different denominators. Sanity check on the corpus's own figure: H1'26 Electrification data-center orders of >$5B at $300M/GW would imply ~17 GW of data-center scope in a single half, which is not credible, so $300M/GW is itself a scope-per-GW-of-IT-load figure that cannot be multiplied by gas-turbine GW. The $31/share full-substitution number is therefore built on a mismatched base as well as on a self-admitted 25% guess.

The underlying physics claim — medium-frequency magnetics shrink core and winding mass, so an SST needs a fraction of the Cu/Fe of a 60 Hz LFT, and creates MV semiconductor demand from zero — is real, correctly sourced, and robust.
- **mechanism_sound**: False
- **already_published**: True
- **where_published**: The specific Table IV -> copper/GOES demand-destruction arithmetic I could not find published. But the CONNECTION the finding claims as its contribution ("SST substitution moves the bottleneck off GOES and copper and onto SiC, threatening the conventional transformer moat") is already published in at least three documents, TWO OF THEM ALREADY INSIDE THE TEAM'S OWN CORPUS. The finding's novelty_check is factually wrong: it states that corpus FTS for solid-state transformers "returns 2 sources (a Hitachi Vaasa competitor file and one LSST astronomy false positive)" and that "the academic tier has essentially nothing." An FTS MATCH on '"SST"' ordered by bm25 returns, in the first six hits:

- sources.id=1150, mgrid.org, 2026-04-20, "Power Transformer Lead Times of 128 Weeks Are Driving the 2025 Solid-State Transformer Commercial Opportunity" — makes the exact connection verbatim: an SST's value proposition is "a supply chain built on silicon-carbide semiconductors rather than the GOES and copper that gate conventional units," and "its semiconductor supply chain sidesteps the grain-oriented steel and copper-winding bottlenecks entirely." It also already self-corrects to the finding's own kill argument ("field-deployed commercial-class SST in revenue service globally is measured in single digits").
- sources.id=1923, horizonscapitals.com, "Chinese Power Equipment Industry Overview" — this is an EQUITY write-up that already converts the mechanism into named long/short exposure: "Traditional dry-type transformer manufacturers (e.g., Jinpan) face partial replacement risk," "companies in high-frequency transformers and power electronics will benefit," and the timing caveat "In early stages of 800V/+-400V HVDC upgrades, traditional transformers still dominate." That is the finding's thesis and its horizon caveat, already in print, with tickers.
- sources.id=3540, arXiv 2603.00415v2 (2026-02-28), "Grid Integration of AI Data Centers: A Critical Review of Energy Storage Solutions," section "Revisiting Solid-State Transformers (SSTs) for AI DCs" — states directly that in SST-based architectures "the distribution transformer in the AI DC power delivery system can be eliminated," and lists the counterweights (lower reliability, "limited power ratings (typically a few MVA)," control complexity and cost). This is in the corpus's academic tier, i.e. the exact tier the finding asserts has "essentially nothing."
- sources.id=3415, mgrid.org Hitachi Vaasa piece — already argues the opposite-sign point (BOM overlap means incumbents absorb SST production rather than being disrupted).
- Eaton 10-K / 10-Q (corpus, kind='sec', filing_date 2026-02-26 and 2026-07-31) — Resilient Power Systems acquired 2025-08-06 for $86M to "accelerate the commercialization of solid-state transformer technology for... data centers."

So: novelty score 4 is not defensible. A 2 is generous.
- **refuted**: True
- **strongest_counterargument**: The finding's terminal conclusion is correct and I am refuting the framing, the novelty claim and the sign, not the bottom line. Table IV is transcribed perfectly from the primary PDF; commercial-class SSTs really are in single-digit field deployment; penetration through FY27 really is well under 1%; and the finding already self-scores materiality 2 and explicitly tells the team "do not build a pitch leg on it." A reviewer could fairly say that a research note that reaches the right answer with a real citation and flags its own weakest link (the 25% LV-share assumption) has done its job, and that my objections are quality-control on a result nobody was going to trade anyway. I still call it refuted, because (a) the -75%/-73% headline comes from a baseline the source paper explicitly defines differently, and the paper's own prose says "about one fourth" — an opposing team that reads the PDF can make the author look careless in front of the judges; (b) the mechanism's direction is wrong per GEV's own Q2'26 disclosure sitting in the team's corpus, which means the "avoided error" is not $31/share of avoided downside but a mis-signed read of an upside option; (c) the connection is published, including inside the corpus the finding claims to have searched; and (d) the $/share chain multiplies data-center content by gas-turbine GW. A wedge that has to be re-derived before it can be used is not a wedge.
- **verdict_summary**: REFUTED as a wedge; the physics transcription is clean but the baseline, the sign of the mechanism, and the novelty claim all fail.

PHYSICS: verified. I downloaded the Huber & Kolar ECCE 2014 PDF and extracted Table IV directly — 0.15/0.32/0.47/0.6 kg Cu/kVA, 0.32/0.63/0.95/1.2 kg Fe/kVA, 85/22/107/0 mm2 Si/kVA, exactly as reported. The medium-frequency-magnetics physics is real. But the -75%/-73% headline divides the SST MV stage alone by the complete LFT, which is not the comparison the paper defines for the AC/DC case (the paper adds two 500 kVA rectifier units to the LFT side). The like-for-like numbers are -84% Cu and -83% Fe. And the authors' own prose says active-metal use is "reduced by about one fourth," which is the AC/AC column. A judge who opens the paper will find a sentence that appears to contradict the headline by 3x.

MECHANISM: broken, and sign-inverted. The chain "SST substitution destroys Prolec's scarcity rent" does not reach GEV's Electrification line, for four independent reasons, the first of which is fatal:

1. GEV IS THE SST VENDOR, AND SAYS IT IS CONTENT-ACCRETIVE. GEV Q2'26 earnings call (corpus, kind='transcript', src:3161): Strazik confirms "the complete build-out of our five megawatt SST prototype for indoor application that will be delivered to our first hyperscaler later this year," plus "a six megawatt SST for outdoor applications." And directly on the money line: "that $300 million directional of scope per gigawatt today, if you include the MV-UPS, if you include the SST and some of the other things we're working on, we certainly think entitlement... is two to three times what our scope per gigawatt is today." Management is telling you SST adoption takes GEV content per GW from $300M to $600-900M. The finding's mechanism assumes substitution removes $75M/GW of GEV revenue; GEV's own disclosure says the same substitution ADDS $300-600M/GW. Direction of the mechanism is wrong, not merely small. The short leg being "killed" was already publicly rebutted with a number, in a document in the team's corpus, and the finding does not engage with it.

2. BACKLOG IMMUNITY IS A HARDER KILL THAN PENETRATION, AND IS NOT USED. Electrification backlog is ~$45B against ~$9B/yr of revenue, with 18-24 month transformer lead times, and equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred against units already under contract. A demand-MIX shift cannot touch revenue already in backlog inside a 3-12 month horizon at ANY penetration rate. The finding's kill rests on an observed-penetration argument that could in principle be falsified by one large order; the backlog/rev-rec argument cannot be. The team should use the second one.

3. WRONG PRODUCT CLASS. The scarcity rent the short leg targets lives in large power transformers and generator step-up units — the 128-week and 144-week lead-time items, 100+ MVA. GEV's SST prototypes are 5 MW and 6 MW, and arXiv 2603.00415v2 (2026-02-28) states SSTs have "limited power ratings (typically a few MVA)." Megawatt-class SSTs have no physical path to displacing 100+ MVA GSUs. The two things are in different product classes; the mechanism never had a route to the high-margin scarcity it claims to threaten.

4. SUPPLY-CHAIN OVERLAP DEFEATS THE "BOTTLENECK MOVES TO SiC" STEP. Corpus src:3415 (Hitachi Vaasa): "Conventional iron-core transformers and SSTs share substantial bill-of-materials overlap: silicon-steel cores... copper conductor windings, insulating fluids, bushings, tank fabrication, testing infrastructure," and the MFT inside a commercial SST is built on largely the same supply chain. Incumbent transformer OEMs are the natural SST manufacturers. SiC die is merchant-purchasable (Eaton bought Resilient Power for $86M in Aug 2025 to do exactly this; GEV is doing it organically). "GEV does not make SiC" is not a moat argument when nobody's transformer OEM makes SiC and the die is available from Wolfspeed/onsemi.

MATERIALITY: the finding's own $31/share full-substitution figure is built on (i) a self-admitted 25% LV-share guess, and (ii) a denominator error — it multiplies data-center content per GW by GEV's 20 GW/yr GAS TURBINE output target. Fix the denominator and the number is not recoverable without a disclosure the team does not have. Horizon-adjusted value is $0.16/share by the finding's own arithmetic, against a $10/share bar. It fails materiality on its own terms.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY USEFUL HERE, and the team should take this and discard the rest: there IS a dated, disclosed, correctly-signed item buried in this work, and it is the opposite of the finding's framing. GEV has a management-quantified content-per-GW expansion option (SST + MV-UPS, $300M/GW -> 2-3x) that management explicitly says is NOT in the >$5B of H1'26 data-center orders, with MV-UPS possibly booking in H2'26 and SST "'27 and beyond." That is a real, dated, testable upside item with a clean kill condition (Q3'26 print, Oct 28 2026: does an MV-UPS order appear in the Electrification orders bridge?). It is a LONG-side scope-expansion question, not a short-side moat-erosion question. The finding walked past it to spend its effort disproving a bear case that GEV's own CEO had already priced.
